lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find Someone Who...' with food/drinks cards. Students mingle, ask 'Do you like...?' and collect signatures. Teacher models: 'Do you like tea? Yes, I do / No, I don't.'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Flashcard Race' - two teams race to match food/drink pictures to words on the board.
Alternative 2: 'I Spy' - teacher says 'I spy something sweet' and students guess 'Is it cake?'
lp.pres: Presentation: Show a cafe menu flashcard. Model dialogue: 'Would you like coffee?' 'No, thanks. I'd like tea, please.' 'Can I have a sandwich?' 'Certainly.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down: 'Would you like cake?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a story about a boy at a cafe, acting out the key phrases.
Alternative 2: Realia - hold up a cup, ask 'Would you like a cup of tea?'
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Menu Match' - pairs match food/drink pictures to words. Then 'Dialogue Drill' - students repeat after teacher, then practice in pairs. Support: sentence frames on the board.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Order Relay' - teams take turns saying 'I'd like...' for items on the board.
Alternative 2: 'Gap-fill' - complete simple dialogues with 'Would you like...?' or 'I'd like...'
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a KET-style cafe dialogue audio. Students listen and circle the correct order (e.g., 'tea or coffee?'). Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand Up, Sit Down' - teacher says 'Would you like coffee?' students stand, 'I'd like tea' students sit. Fast-paced to refocus after break.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Cafe Roleplay' - students use menus they made earlier. One is waiter, one is customer. Waiter asks 'Would you like...?', customer orders 'I'd like... / Can I have...'. Rotate roles.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read a simple cafe menu and match dishes to sections (Drinks, Food, Desserts). Then write 3 sentences: 'I'd like...', 'Would you like...?', 'Can I have...?'
lp.st: Story / song + goodbye: Sing 'The Food Song' (Super Simple Songs). Close with: 'Today we learned to order politely. Thank you, class! Goodbye!'
g: Students mark off food/drinks called out; first to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Students pass a toy; when music stops, holder says 'I'd like...' and class repeats.
Teams race to write 'I'd like coffee' on the board correctly.
Teacher removes 2 items from the menu; students guess 'Is it cake?'
Pairs perform their dialogue; best pair gets 'Waiter of the Day' badge.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a 'Dream Cafe' poster with 5 items and prices.
Support: Use picture-based menus with words written in Arabic script below.
hw: Homework 1: Write your ideal cafe menu with 5 items and prices.
Homework 2: Write a 6-line dialogue ordering food at a cafe.
Homework 3: Interview a family member about their favorite drink and write 2 sentences.
lp.tip: Tip: Use local cafe names (e.g., 'Café de France') to make it culturally relevant. Praise polite language use heavily to reinforce the objective.

weeks.obj: give simple directions and describe their neighborhood with there is/are
weeks.lang: there is/there are; prepositions of place; imperatives (turn, go)
weeks.act: Map of Oujda pair task; treasure hunt directions; describe-and-draw neighborhoods
weeks.hw: Participation checklist

skills.L: Listen to directions audio and follow the map
skills.S: Give directions from school to 3 places
skills.R: Read direction phrases and sequence them on a map
skills.W: Write directions from home to school

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find Someone Who' with neighborhood questions. Students mingle with a handout asking 'Find someone who lives near a mosque/school/market'. They ask 'Do you live near...?' and write names. Teacher reviews answers on the board.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Neighborhood Bingo' - Students have bingo cards with places like 'bakery', 'park', 'library'. They ask classmates 'Is there a... near your home?' and mark off answers.
Alternative 2: 'Quick Draw' - Teacher calls out places (e.g., 'mosque'), students draw it on mini-whiteboards and hold up.
lp.pres: Presentation: Show a large map of Oujda with landmarks marked. Model sentences: 'There is a mosque near my school.' 'There are shops on the main street.' Use gestures for 'near', 'on', 'next to'. Check understanding by asking 'Where is the hospital?' and having students point.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a story about 'Ali's neighborhood' with flashcards of places. Ask 'Is there a park in Ali's neighborhood?' to model 'there is/are'.
Alternative 2: Bring realia (toy buildings, toy cars) to create a 3D neighborhood on the table. Students describe it using 'there is/are'.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Map Directions' pair task. Students have a simple Oujda map with missing places. They ask and answer: 'Is there a cinema near the station?' 'Yes, there is. It's next to the post office.' Teacher monitors and corrects prepositions.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Place the Flashcards' - Students work in pairs to place flashcards of places on a blank map, then describe using 'there is/are'.
Alternative 2: 'Preposition Race' - Teacher calls out 'Put the book on the chair', students race to follow the imperative.
lp.ls: Listening slot: Students listen to an audio of someone giving directions from school to the American Space. They follow along on a map and circle the route. Then they listen again and write down 3 landmarks mentioned (e.g., 'turn left at the mosque').
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Simon Says' with direction imperatives. Teacher says 'Simon says turn left', 'Simon says go straight'. Students who make a mistake sit down. Last student standing wins.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Treasure Hunt' groups. Groups create a simple treasure map of the classroom with 3 clues (e.g., 'Go to the door. Turn right. There is a book under the chair'). They trade maps with another group and follow the clues to find the 'treasure' (a small prize).
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read 4 simple direction phrases (e.g., 'Turn left at the park', 'Go straight to the market'). They cut and paste them in the correct order on a map from home to school. Then they write 2 directions for their own route.
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Sing 'The Wheels on the Bus' with modified lyrics: 'The wheels on the bus go round and round, all through the town!' Close with 'Today we learned to give directions and describe neighborhoods. Thank you, class!'
g: Students match picture cards of places to their names on a worksheet.
Students act out directions (e.g., 'turn left') for others to guess.
Students draw a place (e.g., 'bakery') and others guess using 'Is there a...?'
Students hop to different spots in the room as teacher calls 'on the chair', 'next to the door'.
Students trace a route on a map with a crayon as teacher gives oral directions.
diff: Fast finishers: Draw a dream neighborhood and label 5 places using 'there is/are'.
Support: Use a partially completed map with word banks for directions.
hw: Homework 1: Draw a map of your route from home to school. Write 3 sentences using 'there is/are' and 'turn/go'.
Homework 2: Interview a family member about places near their home and write 2 sentences.
Homework 3: Write 5 direction phrases (e.g., 'Turn left at the mosque') for a classmate.
lp.tip: Use local landmarks (e.g., King Mohammed VI Avenue, Sidi Yahia) to make directions relevant and boost engagement. Teens respond better when learning connects to their daily lives.

weeks.obj: handle a simple shop exchange: sizes, colors, prices
weeks.lang: clothes vocabulary; How much is/are...? this/that/these/those
weeks.act: Shop roleplay rotation with price lists; this/that auction game; dialogue reconstruction
weeks.hw: dialogue writing (shop exchange, 6 lines)

skills.L: Listening folder: shopping dialogues (sizes, prices)
skills.S: Shop roleplay: sizes, colours and prices
skills.R: Read a shop ad and answer price questions
skills.W: Write a shop conversation (6 lines)

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Clothes Line' — Students form a line, teacher calls out a clothing item, students race to grab a flashcard and line up holding it. Teacher asks 'What is this?' and students reply 'It's a T-shirt'.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'I Spy' — Teacher says 'I spy something blue', students guess clothing items.
Alternative 2: 'Mime the Item' — Student mimes a clothing item, classmates guess 'Are you a jacket?'
lp.pres: Presentation: Use real clothes (T-shirt, jeans, dress) and flashcards. Teacher holds up items and says 'This is a red T-shirt. That is a blue dress'. Drill 'this/that/these/those' with students pointing. Ask 'What color is this?' to check understanding.
presAlt: Alternative 1: 'Fashion Show' — Teacher models clothes with exaggerated poses, students repeat vocabulary.
Alternative 2: 'Price Tag Game' — Stick price tags on items, teach 'How much is this?' with fake coins.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'This/That Auction' — Students in pairs bid on flashcards using 'This/That is... dollars'. Teacher gives fake money, highest bidder wins. Support with price lists and sentence frames.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Color Match' — Students match clothing flashcards to color cards, saying 'This is a green shirt'.
Alternative 2: 'Size Drill' — Hold up size flashcards (S/M/L), students repeat 'This is small'.
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a dialogue from the 'Listening folder' (shop assistant asking 'What size?' and customer replying 'Medium'). Students listen and circle the correct size on a worksheet.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Clothes Relay' — Two lines of students race to dress a mannequin with paper clothes, shouting 'This is a hat!' as they run.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Shop Roleplay Rotation' — Students rotate as shopkeeper/ customer using price lists. Shopkeeper asks 'Can I help you?' Customer replies 'How much are these jeans?' and 'I'll take this'.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Read a simple shop ad with prices (e.g., 'T-shirts: $10'). Students answer 'How much is the T-shirt?' in notebooks. Then write a 6-line dialogue for homework.
lp.st: Story + goodbye: Read 'The New Dress' story, then close with 'Today we learned to shop for clothes. Thank you, class!'
g: Students bid on flashcards using 'This/That is... dollars'
Race to dress a mannequin with paper clothes
Rotate as shopkeeper/customer with price lists
Match clothes flashcards to color cards
Hold up size flashcards and repeat 'This is small'
diff: Fast finishers: Design a dream outfit and write prices.
Support: Use sentence frames for dialogue (e.g., 'How much is ___?')
hw: Homework 1: Write a 6-line shop dialogue (customer/shopkeeper)
Homework 2: Draw 5 clothes items and label them in English
Homework 3: Ask family about clothes prices and write 3 sentences
lp.tip: Use realia (clothes) to make shopping vocabulary tangible for Moroccan teens, linking to local markets like souks.

weeks.obj: report weather and invite/react to simple suggestions
weeks.lang: What is the weather like?; Shall we...? Let's...; responses
weeks.act:
Weather report mini-presentations; invitation roleplay cards; pair plan-making task
Christmas around the world jigsaw reading; party planning task with a budget in English.
weeks.hw:
Participation checklist
Write the class party invitation (10 lines).

skills.L: Listen to a weather report and choose the picture
skills.S: Report weather; invite and react: Shall we...?
skills.R: Read a weekend-plan text and find the suggestions
skills.W: Write 3 invitations with replies

lp.wu: Weather Charades: Students act out weather words (sunny, rainy, windy) while others guess using 'Is it...?' The winner acts next. Props: Weather flashcards.
wuAlt: Weather Bingo: Students draw 6 weather symbols; teacher calls words, students cross off. Winner shouts 'Bingo!'
Weather Chain: One student says 'It's sunny', next adds 'It's sunny and rainy', etc., building a chain.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of weather and activities (e.g., sunny/beach, snowy/skiing). Model: 'What's the weather like? It's sunny. Shall we go to the beach?' Elicit responses. Check understanding with 'What do we ask about weather?'
presAlt: Weather Report Video: Play a 1-minute kids' weather video; pause to ask 'What's the weather like in London?'
Weather Song: Sing 'What's the weather like today?' with gestures; drill key phrases.
lp.prac: Weather Report Cards: Students pick a city card and weather card; practice reporting to partners. Teacher monitors and corrects 'Shall we...?' sentences.
pracAlt: Weather Dice Game: Roll a die for weather (1=sunny, 2=rainy); roll again for activity. Say: 'It's... Shall we...?'
Matching Pairs: Match weather to activities (e.g., rainy/watch a movie); then practice invitations.
lp.ls: Listen to a 1-minute weather forecast for 3 cities. Students tick the correct picture on their worksheet. Checks listening for specific details.
lp.re: Weather Action: Teacher calls out weather (e.g., 'It's windy!'), students fan themselves; 'It's rainy!', students pretend to hold umbrellas. Fast-paced review.
lp.prod: Christmas Party Invitations: In pairs, students plan a party using a budget ($50). They write 3 invitations using 'Shall we...?' and reactions (e.g., 'Great idea!').
lp.rw: Christmas Around the World: Jigsaw reading. Group A reads about Morocco's Aid, Group B about USA's Christmas. Then share 1 fact each. Write 2 sentences about their own holiday.
lp.st: Sing 'We Wish You a Merry Christmas' with actions. Close with: 'Today we learned to talk about weather and make plans. Thank you, class!'
g: Students draw 6 weather symbols; teacher calls words, students cross off. Winner shouts 'Bingo!'
One student says 'Shall we play football?', next adds 'Yes! Let's go!', then starts a new chain.
Groups plan a $50 party; must include food, activity, and decoration. Present their plan.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a dream Christmas party poster with 5 activities.
Support: Use sentence frames for invitations: 'Shall we...?' 'Yes, let's...' or 'Sorry, I can't.'
hw: Write 3 party invitations using 'Shall we...?' (10 lines total).
Draw the weather in Oujda today and write 2 sentences.
Ask a family member about their favorite holiday and write 1 sentence.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan holidays (like Aid) to compare with Christmas, making the theme relevant. Teens connect better when local culture is included.

weeks.obj: talk about yesterday and childhood with was/were
weeks.lang: was/were; time expressions (yesterday, last year)
weeks.act:
Childhood memories board; was/were human sentence; when-was-it quiz
Resolutions with will / going to: vote on the class top-5 resolutions.
weeks.hw:
6 sentences about your last weekend (part 1)
Write 5 resolutions with will and going to.

skills.L: Listen to yesterday stories with was / were
skills.S: Talk about yesterday and childhood with was/were
skills.R: Read a diary text and underline was / were
skills.W: Write Yesterday I was... (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Stand in a circle. Throw a soft ball to a student. They say 'Yesterday I was [happy/tired]'. Throw to the next student. Repeat until everyone has spoken.
wuAlt: Play 'Two Truths and a Lie'. Students write three sentences about yesterday, one false. Class guesses the lie.
Show flashcards of emotions (happy, sad, tired). Students mime and say 'Yesterday I was [emotion]'.
lp.pres: Display a photo of a child's birthday party. Ask 'Who was happy?'. Elicit 'The boy was happy'. Point to the cake. 'The cake was big'. Model 'was/were' with positive sentences. Ask 'Was the girl sad?'. Elicit 'No, she wasn't'. Check understanding with thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Tell a short story about your own childhood: 'When I was five, I was small. My house was old'. Use gestures for 'was/were'.
Draw a simple timeline on the board: 'Now', 'Last year', 'When I was 10'. Write sentences for each time.
lp.prac: Give each pair a set of 'was/were' sentence cards. They race to match them to picture cards (e.g., 'The cat was black' with a black cat picture). Monitor and correct pronunciation.
pracAlt: Play 'Find Someone Who'. Students walk around asking 'Were you at school yesterday?'. Find someone who answers 'Yes, I was'.
Complete the gap-fill worksheet: 'Yesterday I ___ at the park. My friends ___ with me.'
lp.ls: Play a short audio clip of two teens talking about their weekend. Students listen and tick the activities they hear on a worksheet (e.g., 'watched TV', 'played football').
lp.re: Play 'Freeze'. Play music. Students dance. When music stops, a student must say a sentence with 'was/were' (e.g., 'I was dancing').
lp.prod: In groups, create a 'Childhood Memories' poster. Draw pictures of when they were younger. Write sentences: 'When I was five, I was [small/fast]. My toy was [red].'. Present to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short diary entry about a boy's New Year's Eve. Students underline all examples of 'was/were'. Then, write 3 sentences about their own last weekend using 'was/were'.
lp.st: Read the story 'The New Year's Resolution' from the coursebook. Discuss the resolutions. Close with: 'Today we talked about yesterday using was/were. Thank you, class!'
g: Students match picture cards to 'was/were' sentences.
Each student adds one sentence to a story using 'was/were'.
Teacher describes a picture with 'was/were'. Students guess what it is.
Students have bingo cards with past tense sentences. Teacher calls out clues.
Students line up to form a sentence with 'was/were' word cards.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 5 more sentences about their childhood.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'When I was ___, I was ___.'
hw: Write 6 sentences about your last weekend using 'was/were'.
Write 5 New Year resolutions using 'will' and 'going to'.
Draw a picture of your last weekend and label it with 'was/were' sentences.
lp.tip: Use personal examples from your own life to make 'was/were' more relatable for teens. Connect it to local events like the Green March to build cultural relevance.

weeks.obj: tell a simple story in the past with regular verbs; enjoy a Christmas text
weeks.lang: past simple regular (-ed); Christmas vocabulary
weeks.act: Story chain: last Saturday; verb auction; Christmas text with comprehension teams
weeks.hw: finish your weekend story

skills.L: Listen to a Christmas text and complete the gaps
skills.S: Tell a simple past story with regular verbs
skills.R: Read a Christmas text and find the -ed verbs (Seasonal pack)
skills.W: Write my last-Christmas story (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Play 'Find Someone Who...' with past regular verbs: Students walk around asking 'Did you... [watch TV] last weekend?' and write names on a bingo sheet.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: Play 'Verb Charades' with past regular verbs; students guess 'Did you... [play football]?'
Alternative 2: Quick review of last week's 'was/were' with 'Where was I?' game using classroom objects.
lp.pres: Show a picture sequence of 'My Last Christmas' (opening presents, eating dinner, visiting family); model 'I opened a present', 'We ate turkey', 'They visited my grandma'; check understanding with 'What did I do?' questions.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a Christmas storybook with regular verbs, stopping to ask 'What happened?'
Alternative 2: Realia with a wrapped box; students unwrap and say 'I opened the box'.
lp.prac: Verb Auction: Teams bid on sentences with correct past regular verbs (-ed) from a list; teacher reads sentences aloud, teams write 'buy' or 'pass' on mini-whiteboards.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Past Tense Dominoes' matching infinitive to past form
Alternative 2: 'Chain Drill' where each student adds one sentence to a story about last Saturday.
lp.ls: Listen to a short audio about 'Christmas in Morocco' (adapted for local context); students fill gaps in a worksheet with -ed verbs (e.g., 'They visited the souk', 'They bought gifts').
lp.re: Christmas Verb Relay: Teams race to write past regular verbs on the board from teacher prompts (e.g., 'What did you do?' 'I played music').
lp.prod: Pair work: Students interview each other about 'My Last Christmas' using 'What did you do?' and write 3 sentences on a Christmas card template.
lp.rw: Read a short text 'Christmas Traditions' and underline all -ed verbs; then write 5 sentences about their own last Christmas using past regular verbs.
lp.st: Read a simple Christmas story 'The Lost Present' with regular verbs; close with 'Today we learned to tell stories about the past with -ed verbs. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams bid on correct past sentences with play money
Match infinitive to past form dominoes
Teams race to write -ed verbs on the board
Ask classmates about past weekend activities
Add sentences to a story about last Saturday
diff: Fast finishers: Draw a comic strip of 'My Last Christmas' with speech bubbles using past verbs
Support learners: Use sentence starters 'I...', 'We...', 'They...' with verb list
hw: Option 1: Write 5 sentences about your last weekend with -ed verbs
Option 2: Interview a family member about their last Christmas and write 3 sentences
Option 3: Complete the 'Christmas in Morocco' worksheet with missing -ed verbs
lp.tip: Use local Christmas references (e.g., 'Christmas in Morocco') to make the theme relatable and build cultural awareness while teaching grammar.

weeks.obj: complete the written paper and the paired speaking task
weeks.lang: all S1 outcomes
weeks.act: Written paper (35 min); paired speaking tasks while others work on review pack
weeks.hw: Semester marks recorded; report cards issued

skills.L: Listening paper across S1 topics (Tests)
skills.S: Paired speaking task (assessment kit)
skills.R: Reading paper across S1 topics
skills.W: Guided writing task (5-6 sentences)

lp.wu: Students play 'Stand Up If...' with teacher calling out S1 review prompts: 'Stand up if you like pizza', 'Stand up if you can swim', 'Stand up if you have a brother'. Students stand and say 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'.
wuAlt: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid of S1 verbs (like, play, have, can) and mingle to find classmates who match.
Students play 'Quick Quiz' with flashcards showing S1 vocabulary (food, school items, free time activities) and race to name them.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a sample KET-style writing task prompt on the board: 'Write about your best friend. Name, age, what you like to do together'. Models 2-3 sentences: 'My best friend is Ali. He is 13. We like football'. Checks understanding by asking 'What do you write about?'
presAlt: Teacher distributes a guided writing worksheet with sentence starters: 'My name is... I am... I like... I can...' and students complete it.
Teacher shows a model speaking task video and highlights key phrases: 'This is my friend. He/She is... We like...'
lp.prac: Students complete a 35-minute written paper with 4 parts: matching, sentence completion, short email, and guided writing. Teacher circulates to clarify instructions but not help with answers.
pracAlt: Students work in pairs to practice a speaking task from the assessment kit: 'Describe your family' using prompts (mother, father, brother, sister).
Students do a peer review of each other's guided writing tasks using a simple checklist (name, age, activity).
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio about a boy's daily routine (S1 topic) and number the pictures in order (wake up, eat breakfast, go to school, play football, do homework). Teacher pauses to check comprehension.
lp.re: Students play 'Simon Says' with S1 action verbs: 'Simon says stand up', 'Simon says jump', 'Simon says touch your nose'. The game is fast-paced to re-energize after the break.
lp.prod: Students take turns in pairs doing the KET-style speaking task: 'Describe your best friend' using the prompt card. They ask and answer 3-4 questions each (What's his/her name? How old is he/she? What do you like to do?). Teacher uses a checklist to assess.
lp.rw: Students read a short text about a girl's free time (S1 topic) and answer 3 multiple-choice questions. Then, they write 5 sentences about their own free time using the text as a model.
lp.st: Teacher tells a simple story about a boy's first day at school using S1 vocabulary (new friend, classroom, lunch). Ends with the goodbye routine: 'Today we did our assessment. Well done, everyone! Thank you, class.'
g: Students write 6 S1 words on a grid and listen as teacher calls them out; first to cross all 3 in a row wins.
Students get a flashcard with a S1 question, quiz a partner, trade cards, and repeat.
Students sit in a circle and say 'I like...' adding one new word each turn (e.g., 'I like football', 'I like football and pizza').
Teacher calls out S1 verbs; students race to write them on the board.
Students use word cards to make correct sentences about S1 topics.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write 3 more sentences about their best friend including 'He/She can...' and 'He/She has got...'.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'My best friend is ___. He/She is ___. We like ___.'
hw: Review S1 vocabulary flashcards (15 mins).
Write 5 sentences about your family using 'have got' and 'can'.
Practice the speaking task prompt with a family member.
lp.tip: For Moroccan teens, connect assessment to their goals (e.g., 'This helps you pass KET for university abroad'). Use local examples like 'Write about your friend who likes couscous' to make it relevant.
checklist: I can write 5-6 sentences about myself or a friend.
I can understand a short audio about daily routines.
I can read a short text and answer simple questions.
I can ask and answer questions about family and friends.
I can use 'have got', 'can', and 'like' correctly.
I can follow instructions for a KET-style task.
I can work with a partner to complete a speaking task.

weeks.obj: talk about learning goals and review semester 1 language
weeks.lang: review structures; goal language (I want to... I will try...)
weeks.act: Goal-setting one-pager; semester 1 team quiz; error correction auction (gentle)
weeks.hw: goals paragraph

skills.L: Listen to goal statements and match them to people
skills.S: Talk about my goals: I want to... I will try...
skills.R: Read S1 review texts and self-check can-dos
skills.W: Write 3 learning goals for the year

lp.wu: Goal Bingo: Students get a bingo grid with 9 simple semester 1 words (e.g., 'school', 'friend', 'pizza'). Teacher calls out definitions or shows pictures, students mark the word and say it aloud when they get a line.
wuAlt: Word Chain: Students say a word from S1, next student says a word starting with the last letter, e.g., 'book' → 'kite' → 'elephant'.
Flashcard Race: Two lines of students race to slap the flashcard the teacher names (e.g., 'Show me red!')
lp.pres: Teacher shows a New Year's resolution poster with 'I want to...' and 'I will try...' (e.g., 'I want to learn English', 'I will try to read more'). Models 3 examples, asks students to repeat. Checks understanding with thumbs up/down: 'Do you want to learn English?'
presAlt: Goal Charades: Teacher acts out a goal (e.g., 'running'), students guess and complete the sentence: 'You want to...'.
Story Time: Show a short comic strip of a teen making a resolution, students identify the goal language.
lp.prac: Goal-Setting One-Pager: Students fold a paper into 4 sections. In each, they draw/write one S1 topic (e.g., food, school) and a goal using 'I want to... I will try...'. Teacher monitors, helps with spelling.
pracAlt: Goal Match-Up: Cards with 'I want to...' on one side and activities (e.g., 'do homework') on the other. Students match pairs and make sentences.
Pair Drill: Student A says a goal, Student B asks 'Why?', Student A answers 'Because I want to...'
lp.ls: Listen and Match: Audio of 4 teens saying goals (e.g., 'I want to play football'). Students match each voice to a picture of the activity on their worksheet.
lp.re: Stand Up If...: Teacher calls out goals (e.g., 'Stand up if you want to learn English!'), students stand and repeat the sentence.
lp.prod: Goal Survey: Students walk around asking 3 peers 'What do you want to learn this year?' and write down their answers. Report back: 'Fatima wants to...'
lp.rw: S1 Review Paragraph: Students read a short text about a teen's semester (e.g., 'I go to school. I have friends. I can play football'). Circle 3 things they can do. Then write 3 sentences about their own semester.
lp.st: Song: Play 'Auld Lang Syne' instrumental, teach students to hum along. End with: 'Today we talked about goals. Thank you, class! Goodbye!'
g: Students mark S1 words on a grid as teacher calls them.
Two lines race to slap the correct S1 flashcard.
Match 'I want to...' cards to activity pictures.
Stand and repeat goal sentences when called.
Ask peers about goals and report back.
diff: Fast finishers: Draw a comic strip of someone achieving their goal.
Support: Trace or copy goal sentences from the board.
hw: Write 3 learning goals for the year: 'I want to... I will try...'
Draw a picture of one goal and write a sentence under it.
Ask a family member their goal and write it down.
lp.tip: Use local context: link goals to Moroccan events like Green March or Independence Day to increase relevance, e.g., 'I want to learn about Moroccan history.'

weeks.obj: describe jobs and talk about work with have to
weeks.lang: job vocabulary; have to / don't have to
weeks.act: Dream job presentation pairs; have-to guessing game (job charades); job ad reading
weeks.hw: Participation checklist

skills.L: Listen to job descriptions and guess the job
skills.S: Describe jobs with have to / don't have to
skills.R: Read a job profile and complete the fact file (Reading tasks)
skills.W: Write my dream-job paragraph

lp.wu: Job charades: Teacher acts out 3 jobs (doctor, teacher, chef), students guess and shout 'You're a [job]!'
wuAlt: Job Pictionary: Students draw jobs on the board for others to guess
Job Bingo: Teacher calls out jobs, students cross them off their bingo sheet
lp.pres: Show flashcards of 5 jobs, model sentences: 'A doctor has to help people.' 'A teacher has to work in a school.' Ask students to repeat, then ask 'What does a chef have to do?' to check understanding.
presAlt: Job stories: Tell a short story about a day in the life of a firefighter using 'have to'
Job charades with prompts: Teacher mimes jobs and students say the sentence
lp.prac: Job charades pairs: Student A mimes a job, Student B says 'You have to...' or 'You don't have to...' Teacher circulates to correct sentences.
pracAlt: Job dominoes: Match job cards to 'have to' sentences
Job matching worksheet: Draw lines from jobs to their duties using 'have to'
lp.ls: Listen to 3 job descriptions (teacher, chef, doctor) and write the job next to each description. Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Job relay: Teams race to write 'have to' sentences on the board for different jobs. First team to write 3 correct sentences wins.
lp.prod: Dream job pairs: Student A asks 'What's your dream job?', Student B answers 'My dream job is a [job]. I have to...' Then they swap roles.
lp.rw: Read a short job profile for 'video game tester' and complete a fact file with 'have to' sentences. Then write 2 sentences about their own dream job.
lp.st: Sing 'What Do You Want to Be?' with gestures. End with: 'Today we learned to talk about jobs using have to. Great job, everyone! Thank you, class.'
g: Students take turns miming jobs while others guess using 'You have to...'
Match job cards to their 'have to' duties
Listen to 'have to' sentences and cross off the matching job
Ask 3 classmates about their dream jobs and write down their answers
Draw jobs on the board for others to guess the sentence
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write 3 more 'have to' sentences for their dream job
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'My dream job is a ___. I have to ___.'
hw: Complete the 'My Dream Job' worksheet with 5 sentences using 'have to'
Draw a picture of your dream job and label 3 things you have to do
Interview a family member about their job and write 2 sentences using 'have to'
lp.tip: Use Moroccan job examples (like 'tour guide' in Oujda) to make the lesson culturally relevant. Teens respond better when they can connect the language to their local context.

weeks.obj: compare two cities, foods, or teams with comparative adjectives
weeks.lang: comparatives (-er, more... than)
weeks.act: City debate teams; compare-and-write pairs; adjective duel game
weeks.hw: 5 comparisons about Oujda vs another city

skills.L: Listen to city comparisons and note the -er forms
skills.S: Compare two cities, foods or teams with comparatives
skills.R: Read a comparison text and find the comparatives
skills.W: Write 4 comparison sentences

lp.wu: City Bingo: Students get bingo cards with city names (Oujda, Casablanca, Paris, London, New York). Teacher says clues like 'This city is bigger than Oujda' or 'This city is more modern than Rabat'. Students mark the city and shout 'Bingo!' when they have a line.
wuAlt: Adjective Race: Students line up. Teacher shows flashcards of adjectives (big, small, old, new, tall, short). Students race to say the comparative form (bigger, smaller, older, newer, taller, shorter).
Find Someone Who: Students walk around asking 'Is your city bigger than your friend's city?' and write names of people who say yes.
lp.pres: Teacher shows two city flashcards (Oujda and Paris). Models sentences: 'Oujda is smaller than Paris. Paris is bigger than Oujda.' Uses gestures for 'small' and 'big'. Asks students to repeat chorally. Checks understanding by pointing to flashcards and asking 'Which city is bigger?'
presAlt: Realia Comparison: Teacher holds two objects (a small Moroccan tagine and a big American coffee mug). Models: 'The tagine is smaller than the mug. The mug is bigger than the tagine.' Students repeat.
Picture Story: Shows a simple comic strip with two characters comparing their cities. Reads aloud: 'My city is older than yours. Your city is newer than mine.'
lp.prac: Adjective Duel Game: Students in pairs get a set of adjective cards (big, small, old, new, tall, short). Teacher says two cities (e.g., 'Oujda and Rabat'). Students race to flip the card for the correct comparative ('Oujda is smaller than Rabat'). First pair to get 3 points wins.
pracAlt: Comparative Pairs: Students work in pairs. Each pair gets two city cards. They take turns making one comparative sentence about the cities (e.g., 'Casablanca is more modern than Fes'). Teacher monitors and corrects.
Flashcard Line-Up: Students get flashcards of cities. They line up in order from smallest to biggest, saying sentences as they move: 'Oujda is smaller than Tangier.'
lp.ls: City Comparison Audio: Students listen to a short audio where two teens compare their cities (Oujda and Agadir). They have a worksheet with two columns: 'Agadir' and 'Oujda'. They write down the comparatives they hear (e.g., 'Agadir is more modern. Oujda is older.')
lp.re: Comparative Charades: One student comes to the front. Teacher whispers a comparative sentence (e.g., 'Tall'). The student acts being 'tall' and then 'taller' by stretching up. Class guesses the comparative word.
lp.prod: City Debate Teams: Divide class into two teams (Team Oujda vs Team Rabat). Each team has 5 minutes to prepare 3 comparative sentences to argue why their city is better (e.g., 'Oujda is more beautiful than Rabat. Rabat is noisier than Oujda.'). Teams take turns presenting their sentences. Class votes for the most convincing team.
lp.rw: Read and Compare: Students read a short text comparing two Moroccan cities (Marrakech and Chefchaouen). The text has gaps with comparatives (e.g., 'Marrakech is _____ (big) than Chefchaouen. Chefchaouen is _____ (old) than Marrakech.'). Students fill in the gaps with -er or more. Then they write 2 sentences comparing their own city to another.
lp.st: Sing 'The Comparative Song': A simple chant to the tune of 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star': 'Bigger, smaller, taller, shorter. More than, less than, it's easy. Compare two things and you will see. How they are different, you and me.' End with 'Today we learned to compare cities with -er and more. Great job, everyone! Thank you, class!'
g: Students race to flip the correct comparative card for two cities.
Students mark cities on bingo cards based on comparative clues.
Students act out comparatives for the class to guess.
Students line up city cards and say comparative sentences.
Teams argue why their city is better using comparatives.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write 5 comparisons between Oujda and a city of their choice (e.g., 'Oujda is sunnier than London.')
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'Oujda is _____ (adjective) than _____ (city).' with a word bank of adjectives (big, small, old, new).
hw: Write 5 comparisons about Oujda vs another city (e.g., 'Oujda is smaller than Casablanca.')
Draw two pictures of your city and another city. Label 3 things in each picture and write 1 comparative sentence (e.g., 'The mosque in Oujda is older than the one in Tangier.')
Interview a family member: 'Is Oujda bigger than your hometown? Write down their answer and 1 more comparison.'
lp.tip: Use local cities (Oujda, Rabat, Casablanca, Tangier) to make the comparisons relevant and engaging. Teens are more motivated to talk about places they know.

weeks.obj: use superlatives to nominate classmates for fun awards
weeks.lang: superlatives (the -est, the most...)
weeks.act:
Class awards ceremony planning; superlative survey; the-best-of presentations
Project: a guide to Ramadan in Oujda, written for foreign visitors.
weeks.hw:
Participation checklist
Write 6 tips for visitors during Ramadan.

skills.L: Listen to award nominations and identify the winner
skills.S: Nominate classmates with superlatives
skills.R: Read class-award texts and find the superlatives
skills.W: Write 3 superlative award sentences

lp.wu: Awards Nomination Relay: Students stand in two lines. The first student in each line runs to the board, writes a superlative about a classmate (e.g., 'Fatima is the kindest'), and runs back. The next student does the same with a different classmate and superlative.
wuAlt: Superlative Bingo: Each student writes 5 superlatives (e.g., 'the tallest', 'the funniest') on a grid. The teacher calls out classmates' names with superlatives; students mark if they match.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Who is the most...?' (e.g., 'Who is the most helpful?') and write names.
lp.pres: Show 3 flashcards: a student helping (kind), a student running (fast), a student laughing (funny). Model sentences: 'Amina is the kindest. Youssef is the fastest. Omar is the funniest.' Ask 'Who is the kindest?' to check understanding.
presAlt: Realia Awards: Bring in a trophy or medal. Hold it up and say 'This is for the best student in class. Who is the best?' Elicit responses with superlatives.
Class Photo Awards: Show a class photo. Point to students and say 'He is the tallest. She is the prettiest.'
lp.prac: Superlative Survey: In pairs, students ask 3 classmates 'Who is the most...?' (e.g., 'Who is the most creative?') and write names. Teacher monitors and corrects errors. Then, groups share their findings.
pracAlt: Superlative Memory Game: Students sit in a circle. Each student adds a superlative about the previous student (e.g., 'You are the tallest. He is the funniest.').
Superlative Chain Drill: Teacher starts with 'I am the oldest.' Each student says a superlative about themselves or the previous student.
lp.ls: Listen to Award Nominations: Teacher reads 5 award nominations (e.g., 'Karim is the most helpful because he always helps with homework.'). Students write down the winner for each award (e.g., 'Karim').
lp.re: Superlative Charades: One student acts out a superlative (e.g., 'the tallest' by standing on tiptoes), others guess and say the full sentence.
lp.prod: Class Awards Ceremony: In groups, students plan 3 awards (e.g., 'The Best Artist', 'The Funniest Joke') with superlatives. Each group presents their awards and winners to the class.
lp.rw: Ramadan Visitor Guide: Students write 6 tips for visitors during Ramadan using superlatives (e.g., 'The most important tip is to respect fasting hours.'). They use a word bank with 'the most', 'the best', 'the most important'.
lp.st: Song: 'The Best Day Ever' (Super Simple Songs). Students sing along and do actions. Close with 'Today we learned superlatives for class awards. Thank you, class!'
g: Students rotate in pairs, asking 'Who is the most...?' and writing answers.
Students draw a superlative (e.g., 'the fastest') and others guess.
Two teams race to write superlatives about the teacher on the board.
Groups add one sentence with a superlative to a story about Ramadan.
Students throw a ball and say a superlative about the person who catches it.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a trophy for their award winner with a superlative caption.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame '______ is the most ______ because ______.'
hw: Write 3 superlative sentences about your family.
Interview a family member about Ramadan and write 2 tips with superlatives.
Draw a picture of your 'Best Ramadan Day' and write a superlative sentence.
lp.tip: Use peer nominations to build rapport—teens respond well to positive recognition from classmates. Connect superlatives to Ramadan to make language relevant to local culture.

weeks.obj: describe weekend and holiday plans with going to
weeks.lang: going to (plans); time expressions
weeks.act: Plan grid mingle; going-to fortune teller (paper craft); plan swap listening
weeks.hw: 6 sentences about next weekend

skills.L: Listen to weekend plans with going to
skills.S: Describe my weekend and holiday plans
skills.R: Read plan texts and underline going to
skills.W: Write my weekend plan (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Weekend Plans Bingo: Students write 5 weekend activities on a bingo grid. Teacher calls out activities (e.g., 'play football', 'visit family'). Students mark off and shout 'Bingo!' when complete, then share one plan.
wuAlt: Two Stars and a Wish: Students share one good thing and one wish for the weekend, then guess a partner's plans.
Quick Poll: Teacher asks 'What are you going to do this weekend?' Students raise hands for options like 'study', 'play games', 'go out'.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of weekend activities (e.g., 'visit grandma', 'study English', 'play football'). Model sentences: 'I'm going to visit grandma on Saturday.' Elicit time expressions ('on Saturday', 'in the evening'). Check understanding by asking 'What are YOU going to do?'
presAlt: Plan Grid Poster: Draw a 3x3 grid on the board with 'Saturday morning', 'Saturday afternoon', etc. Fill in plans with 'going to' and elicit from students.
Dialogue Roleplay: Teacher and a student act out a conversation about weekend plans using 'going to' and time expressions.
lp.prac: Plan Grid Mingle: Students receive a half-filled grid with time slots (e.g., 'Saturday morning'). They mingle, ask 'What are you going to do [time]?', and write partners' answers. Swap grids and repeat.
pracAlt: Going-To Fortune Teller: Students fold paper into a fortune teller, write activities inside. They ask partners 'What are you going to do?' and lift flaps to reveal 'predictions'.
Sentence Relay: Teams race to write correct 'going to' sentences on the board for prompts like 'Sunday / clean room'.
lp.ls: Plan Swap Listening: Students listen to 3 audio clips of teens talking about weekend plans. They match each speaker to a time slot on a handout (e.g., 'Speaker 1: Saturday afternoon / Speaker 2: Sunday morning').
lp.re: Action Charades: Teacher mimes an activity (e.g., 'swimming'). Students shout 'You're going to swim!' and mime the action. Fast-paced to re-energize.
lp.prod: Holiday Plans Survey: Students interview 3 partners using 'What are you going to do during the next holiday?'. They tally responses (e.g., '2 students: visit family') and share findings with the class.
lp.rw: Read and Underline: Students read a short text about a teen's holiday plans (e.g., 'I'm going to travel to Agadir with my family. We're going to swim and eat seafood.'). They underline all 'going to' phrases and write 1 new sentence about their own holiday.
lp.st: Sing 'What Are You Going to Do?' (to the tune of 'Frère Jacques') with actions. End with: 'Today we learned to talk about future plans with going to. Thank you, class! Goodbye!'
g: Students swap written weekend plans and correct errors using 'going to'.
Match activity cards to time expression cards (e.g., 'watch a movie' + 'Saturday evening').
Students sit in a circle and build a sentence: 'I'm going to play football on Saturday. What are YOU going to do?'
Cut up a 'going to' sentence and students reassemble it correctly.
Students draw emojis for activities and write sentences: 'I'm going to 😊 on Sunday.'
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 'going to' sentences about a dream holiday.
Support: Use sentence frames: 'I'm going to ___ on ___.' with word bank.
hw: Write 6 sentences about your next weekend using 'going to' and time expressions.
Draw a picture of your weekend plans and label 3 activities with 'going to' sentences.
Interview a family member about their weekend plans and write 2 sentences about them.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan holidays (e.g., Eid, Green March) as examples to make plans culturally relevant and boost engagement.

weeks.obj: make simple predictions about the future
weeks.lang: will/won't (predictions); maybe, probably
weeks.act: Prediction panel about 2040; agree/disagree corners; prediction bingo
weeks.hw: Participation checklist

skills.L: Listen to predictions about the future; agree or disagree
skills.S: Make predictions with will / won't + maybe
skills.R: Read prediction lists and rank them likely / unlikely
skills.W: Write 3 predictions about 2030

lp.wu: Future Timeline: Draw a timeline on the board from 2024 to 2040. Students write one thing they did last year and predict one thing they will do next year using 'I will/won't'.
wuAlt: Prediction Ball: Toss a ball and ask 'Will you...?' questions (e.g., 'Will you eat pizza this week?'). Students respond with 'Yes, I will' or 'No, I won't'.
Flashcard Future: Show flashcards of activities (e.g., 'travel', 'study'). Students make sentences like 'I will travel to Casablanca'.
lp.pres: Show a video clip of Moroccan teens predicting 2040 (e.g., 'We will have flying cars'). Highlight 'will/won't + maybe/probably' on the board. Drill sentences like 'Maybe we will have robots at school'. Check understanding with 'thumbs up/down' for true/false predictions.
presAlt: Future Forecast: Display weather symbols (sun, rain) and use them to model 'It will probably be sunny tomorrow'. Students repeat and swap symbols to practice.
Prediction Cards: Give students cards with prompts (e.g., 'school in 2030'). They write predictions and share, focusing on 'will/won't'.
lp.prac: Agree/Disagree Corners: Label two corners 'Agree' and 'Disagree'. Read a prediction (e.g., 'People won't use phones in 2040'). Students go to the corner and explain why using 'I agree because...' or 'I disagree because...'.
pracAlt: Prediction Chain: Students sit in a circle. Each adds to a prediction chain (e.g., 'I will study English. You will travel. He will...').
Fill-in-the-Blanks: Worksheet with sentences like 'In 2030, I ___ (learn) to drive'. Students complete with 'will/won't'.
lp.ls: Listen to 3 short audio clips of teens predicting their future (e.g., 'I will become a doctor'). Students write 'Likely' or 'Unlikely' next to each prediction on their worksheet.
lp.re: Future Charades: Students act out a future action (e.g., 'flying a drone'). Others guess using 'Will you...?'
lp.prod: Prediction Panel: Groups create a poster with 5 predictions about 2040 (e.g., 'Morocco will host the World Cup'). They present to the class using 'We think... will probably...'.
lp.rw: Read a list of 10 predictions about 2030 (e.g., 'Everyone will have a robot'). Students rank them 1-5 (most likely to least likely) and write 3 sentences about their own predictions.
lp.st: Sing 'What Will the Weather Be?' song with actions. Close with 'Today we learned to make predictions with will/won't. Thank you, class!'
g: Students write 9 predictions in a grid. T reads sentences; they cross off matches and shout 'Bingo!'
T holds up cards with verbs; students race to say 'will' or 'won't' + the verb.
Roll a dice; students make predictions about the number (e.g., 'It will rain 7 times this week').
Pick a card with 'maybe/probably'; use it to complete a sentence like 'Maybe I will visit...'.
Teams line up; each student adds to a prediction and the next team member agrees/disagrees.
diff: Fast finishers: Draw a comic strip of their 3 predictions for 2030.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'I will ___ because ___' to scaffold writing.
hw: Write 3 predictions about your family in 2030 (e.g., 'My brother will get married').
Interview a family member: Ask them to predict 1 thing about you in 5 years and write it down.
Watch a short video about the future; write 1 prediction you agree with and 1 you disagree with.
lp.tip: Use local examples (e.g., 'Oujda will have a new library') to make predictions relevant. Teens engage more when connected to their community.

weeks.obj: give simple health advice with should
weeks.lang: should/shouldn't; body and illness vocabulary
weeks.act: Doctor-patient roleplay; advice column pairs; problem page writing
weeks.hw: write advice for 3 problems

skills.L: Listen to doctor-patient dialogues
skills.S: Give health advice with should / shouldn't
skills.R: Read a health leaflet and find the advice (Lesson Plans/Emergency)
skills.W: Write advice for 3 health problems

lp.wu: Play 'Simon Says' with body parts and health actions (e.g., 'Simon says touch your head', 'Simon says pretend to cough'). Students stand up and follow commands. Teacher models and corrects pronunciation.
wuAlt: Play 'Charades' with body parts and illness actions (e.g., 'sneeze', 'stomach ache') for students to guess.
Use flashcards of body parts/illnesses for a quick 'What's missing?' game.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of common illnesses (headache, cold, stomach ache) and model advice: 'You should drink water' or 'You shouldn't eat ice cream'. Use a doctor-patient dialogue with a puppet to demonstrate. Check understanding with 'What should I do if I have a headache?'
presAlt: Read a simple health leaflet from 'res' and highlight 'should/shouldn't' sentences.
Use a story about a character with a cold and elicit advice from students.
lp.prac: Play 'Doctor Says' in pairs: one student pretends to have an illness, the other gives advice using 'should/shouldn't'. Teacher circulates to correct and model. Use sentence frames on the board for support.
pracAlt: Complete a gap-fill worksheet with 'should/shouldn't' and health vocabulary.
Play 'Advice Race': teams write correct advice for illnesses on the board.
lp.ls: Listen to a doctor-patient dialogue from 'res' and circle the correct advice (e.g., 'should rest' or 'should play football'). Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Play 'Pass the Action': students pass a ball and say a health advice sentence (e.g., 'You should sleep') while doing an action (yawn, stretch).
lp.prod: Roleplay 'Advice Column' in pairs: one student writes a problem (e.g., 'I have a stomach ache'), the other gives advice. Swap roles. Teacher monitors for correct language use.
lp.rw: Read a 'Problem Page' from 'res' and write advice for 3 problems using 'should/shouldn't'. Share answers with a partner.
lp.st: Sing the 'Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes' song with actions. Close with: 'Today you gave health advice with should/shouldn't. Thank you, class!'
g: Students follow commands with 'should/shouldn't' (e.g., 'You shouldn't run').
Act out illnesses for others to guess and give advice.
Teams write advice for illnesses on the board.
Pass a ball and say advice with an action.
Read and write advice for health problems.
diff: Fast finishers: write a dialogue for a doctor-patient scenario.
Support: use sentence frames with 'should/shouldn't' and vocabulary lists.
hw: Write advice for 3 health problems (e.g., 'My friend has a cold').
Draw a comic strip showing someone giving advice.
Record a voice message giving advice for an illness.
lp.tip: Use real-life examples from students' experiences (e.g., 'What should you do if you eat too much couscous?') to make the language relevant.

weeks.obj: tell a simple travel story and ask travel questions
weeks.lang: past simple review; travel vocabulary
weeks.act:
Holiday brochure corner design; travel buddy interview; reading jigsaw
How we celebrate: compare Eid here and holidays abroad (paragraph + venn).
weeks.hw:
Participation checklist
Write 8 sentences comparing Eid with another holiday.

skills.L: Listening folder: travel dialogues - book and confirm
skills.S: Tell a travel story and ask travel questions
skills.R: Read a travel text and complete the itinerary
skills.W: Write a postcard from a trip (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Travel Bingo: Students get bingo cards with travel pictures (plane, hotel, beach, etc.). Teacher calls out words, students mark them and shout 'Bingo!' when they have a line. They say 'I went to [place]' for each marked item.
wuAlt: Travel Pictionary: One student draws a travel word, others guess. They say 'Is it a hotel?'
Travel Charades: Students act out travel actions (flying, swimming), others guess 'Are you swimming?'
lp.pres: Show a picture of Eid al-Fitr celebration and a holiday abroad (e.g., beach holiday). Point and say 'On Eid, we visit family. On holiday, we swim.' Elicit sentences from students using 'I went to...' and 'I saw...'. Check with thumbs up/down if they understand 'past simple for finished actions'.
presAlt: Use a simple story: 'Last Eid, I visited grandma. Last summer, I went to Agadir.' Ask 'When did you go?'
Bring realia: a prayer mat (Eid) and sunglasses (holiday). Students handle them and make sentences.
lp.prac: Travel Buddy Interview: Students work in pairs. Interview each other with 'Where did you go last holiday?' and 'What did you see?'. Write answers in a table. Support with sentence starters on the board.
pracAlt: Holiday Brochure Match: Match picture cards (beach, mountain) to word cards. Say 'This is a beach holiday.'
Past Simple Drill: Teacher says 'go', students say 'went'. Repeat with 'see/saw', 'visit/visited'.
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue between two friends talking about their Eid and holiday trips. Students fill in a simple grid with 'Name', 'Place', 'Activity'. Check answers with 'Who went to the mountains?'
lp.re: Simon Says Travel: Teacher says 'Simon says swim like you're at the beach!' or 'Simon says pray like it's Eid!'. Students move and repeat the actions. Fast-paced to re-energize.
lp.prod: Holiday Brochure Corner: Groups design a simple travel brochure for 'Eid in Morocco' or 'A Holiday Abroad'. Include 3 pictures and 3 sentences using 'I went to...' and 'I saw...'. Present to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short text about a boy's Eid and a girl's holiday trip. Complete a Venn diagram with similarities and differences. Then write 4 sentences comparing them using 'Both... and...', 'But...'.
lp.st: Read a simple story about a child's Eid holiday. Sing 'If You're Happy and You Know It' with travel actions (clap if you went swimming, stomp if you visited family). End with 'Today we learned to talk about past holidays. Thank you, class!'
g: Students flip over picture cards (travel words), find pairs, and say a sentence with each word.
Teams race to write past tense forms on the board (go->went, see->saw).
One student describes a holiday, others guess 'Was it Eid or a beach holiday?'
Students mark off travel words called by the teacher, shout 'Bingo!' when done.
Students use word cards to make past simple sentences about holidays.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 more sentences about their own Eid or holiday.
Support: Use sentence frames 'I went to ______. I saw ______.' to write.
hw: Write 8 sentences comparing Eid al-Fitr with another holiday (e.g., Christmas, summer holiday). Use 'Both... and...' and 'But...'.
Draw a picture of your favorite holiday and write 3 sentences about it using past simple.
Interview a family member about their past holiday and write 2 sentences they said.
lp.tip: Use the local context of Eid al-Fitr to make past simple practice relevant. Compare it with holidays abroad to build cultural awareness and keep teens engaged with familiar themes.

weeks.obj: express and justify opinions about music
weeks.lang: I think... because; opinion adjectives
weeks.act: Lyric listening gap-fill (clean song); top-5 band discussions; opinion line-up
weeks.hw: 5-line opinion paragraph

skills.L: Listen to song excerpts and catch the opinion words
skills.S: Express and justify opinions about music
skills.R: Read a short music review and find the opinions
skills.W: Write a 3-sentence song review

lp.wu: Music Opinions Relay: Write 'I think... because' on the board. Students line up in two teams. Each student runs to the board, writes one word (e.g., 'think', 'because', an adjective like 'good'), and runs back. The team with the correct sentence first wins.
wuAlt: Quick Poll: Ask 'Do you like pop music?' Students stand if yes, sit if no. Ask follow-ups: 'Why?'
Word Association: Say 'music'. Students say one word (e.g., 'fun', 'loud', 'singing')
lp.pres: Show flashcards of music genres (pop, rock, rap). Model sentences: 'I think pop is good because it's fun.' Ask students to repeat. Check understanding by asking: 'Is pop good or bad? Why?'
presAlt: Realia: Bring a phone with music. Play a song and say: 'I think this song is great because it's happy.'
Story: Draw a simple comic of a boy saying 'I think rock is cool because the drums are strong.'
lp.prac: Lyric Gap-Fill: Distribute lyrics to 'Count on Me' by Bruno Mars (clean version). Remove opinion adjectives (e.g., 'good', 'nice'). Students work in pairs to fill gaps. Check answers as a class.
pracAlt: Matching Game: Cards with opinion adjectives (good, bad, fun, boring) and reasons (because it's fast, because it's slow). Students match them.
Sentence Builders: Give students word cards to build 'I think... because...' sentences.
lp.ls: Opinion Listening: Play a 1-minute clip of a teen saying: 'I think rap is exciting because the words are strong.' Students write down the opinion and the reason. Check answers together.
lp.re: Opinion Line-Up: Call out an opinion (e.g., 'I think music is boring'). Students line up on one side if they agree, the other if they disagree. Quick discussion: 'Why?'
lp.prod: Top-5 Band Discussion: Groups of 3. Each group writes their top 3 music genres. They use 'I think... because...' to justify. Groups present their choices to the class.
lp.rw: Music Review Reading: Give a short review of a song (e.g., 'This song is great because it's happy and easy to sing.'). Students underline the opinion and the reason. Then write 3 sentences about their favorite song using 'I think... because...'.
lp.st: Play the song 'Count on Me' again. Students sing along. Close with: 'Today we learned to say our opinions about music using I think... because. Thank you, class!'
g: Students write 5 opinion adjectives (good, bad, fun, boring, loud). Teacher calls out reasons (e.g., 'because it's fast'). Students cross off if they have a matching adjective.
Play music. When it stops, students say an opinion about the last song (e.g., 'I think it's loud!').
Student 1: 'I think pop is good.' Student 2: 'Because it's fun.' Student 3: 'I think rock is cool.' Continue the chain.
Teacher describes a genre (e.g., 'This music is fast and has strong drums'). Students guess: 'Rock!'
Two teams. Each student runs to the board, writes one word to complete 'I think... because...'. First correct team wins.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 more sentences about music they don't like.
Support: Use sentence frames: 'I think ____ is ____ because ____.'
hw: Write a 5-line paragraph about your favorite song: 'My favorite song is ___. I think it is ___. because ___. It is ___. I like it.'
Draw a picture of your favorite song and write 2 sentences about it using 'I think... because...'.
Interview a family member: 'Do you like music? Why?' Write their answers.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan music examples (e.g., Gnawa) to connect the theme to students' culture, making the language more relevant and memorable.

weeks.obj: talk about devices and habits; use like/love/hate + -ing with verbs
weeks.lang: tech vocabulary; verb patterns (like doing / want to do)
weeks.act: Tech survey creation and analysis; device charades; usage debate mini
weeks.hw: Participation checklist

skills.L: Listen to tech-habit interviews
skills.S: Talk about devices; like doing / want to do
skills.R: Read a tech survey and report the results
skills.W: Write my tech habits (4 sentences)

lp.wu: Tech Charades: Students draw a tech word (phone, laptop, game) from a hat and act it out without speaking. Others guess 'Is it a phone?' or 'Is it a game?'
wuAlt: Tech Pictionary: Students draw a tech device on the board for others to name
Tech Word Race: Two teams race to write 5 tech words on the board
lp.pres: Show flashcards of tech devices (phone, laptop, tablet, TV). Model sentences: 'I like using my phone.' 'I love playing games.' 'I hate watching TV.' Students repeat chorally. Check understanding with thumbs up/down: 'Do you like using a laptop?'
presAlt: Realia Demo: Show a phone and say 'I like taking photos' then ask students to say what they like doing with it
Story: Draw a simple comic of a teen using devices and model sentences from the speech bubbles
lp.prac: Match-Up Game: Students match device cards to verb phrases (using, watching, playing). Then in pairs, they ask 'Do you like using a phone?' and respond with 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'
pracAlt: Sentence Relay: Teams race to write correct sentences like 'I love watching TV' on the board
Tech Survey Prep: Students fill in a simple grid with 'like/love/hate' for 3 devices
lp.ls: Listen to a short audio of two teens talking about their tech habits. Students tick boxes on a worksheet for 'likes' and 'dislikes' (e.g., 'Ahmed likes playing games').
lp.re: Device Freeze: Teacher calls out a device (e.g., 'laptop'), students mime using it. When teacher says 'freeze!', they stop. Last one moving sits down.
lp.prod: Tech Survey Creation: In groups, students design a 3-question survey about tech habits (e.g., 'Do you like using a phone?'). They ask 3 classmates and report back to the class: 'Fatima likes using a phone'
lp.rw: Read a simple bar graph showing 'tech habits' (e.g., 5 students like phones, 2 hate tablets). Students write 2 sentences: '5 students like phones.' '2 students hate tablets.'
lp.st: Sing 'Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes' but replace body parts with tech words: 'Phone, laptop, tablet, mouse!' End with 'Good job today! You can talk about tech habits. Thank you, class!'
g: Act out a tech device without speaking for others to guess
Match device cards to verb phrases like 'using' or 'playing'
Mime using a device when called, freeze on command
Groups race to ask classmates 3 tech habit questions
Teams race to write correct 'like/love/hate' sentences
diff: Fast finishers: Write 2 more sentences about their family's tech habits
Support learners: Use sentence frames 'I like ___. I love ___. I hate ___.' with word bank
hw: Draw 3 tech devices and write 'I like/love/hate ___' for each
Ask 5 family members 'Do you like using ___?' and write their answers
Write 4 sentences about your daily tech habits (e.g., 'I use my phone every day')
lp.tip: Use local tech examples like mobile apps popular in Morocco (e.g., TikTok, WhatsApp) to make the theme relevant and increase engagement.

weeks.obj: tell what was happening with past continuous support
weeks.lang: past continuous (was/were + -ing)
weeks.act: Story from pictures; while-clause chains; fable reading with roles
weeks.hw: picture story (6 sentences)

skills.L: Listen to a story and note what was happening
skills.S: Tell what was happening with past continuous
skills.R: Read a fable and find the past continuous verbs (Reading tasks/Fables)
skills.W: Write a 6-line story with was/were + -ing

lp.wu: Mime the action: Students take turns miming an action (e.g., eating, studying, playing football) while others guess using 'He/She was ...-ing'. Teacher writes guesses on the board.
wuAlt: Chain reaction: Student 1 mimes an action, Student 2 adds another, forming a story chain using 'and then he was ...-ing'
Find someone who: Students walk around asking 'Were you ...-ing last night?' and find classmates who say yes.
lp.pres: Show a 4-picture comic strip of a boy at the park. Point to each picture and model: 'He was playing football. He was eating ice cream. He was sitting on a bench. He was watching birds.' Elicit more examples from students using the pictures.
presAlt: Use realia: Hold up a toy car and a toy person; move them to show actions while saying 'He was driving the car'
Draw a simple scene on the board with 3-4 characters doing different things and label with past continuous sentences.
lp.prac: While-clause chains: In pairs, Student 1 starts with 'While I was walking to school, I saw ...', Student 2 continues with 'While he was seeing ..., he heard ...', and so on. Teacher provides sentence starters on the board.
pracAlt: Picture match: Give students 6 action cards and 6 location cards; they make sentences like 'She was swimming at the beach'
Fill-in-the-blank worksheet with 10 past continuous sentences to complete.
lp.ls: Listen to a short story about a rainy day. Students listen and draw 3 things the family was doing (e.g., 'Dad was cooking', 'Mum was reading', 'Sister was painting'). Check drawings as a class.
lp.re: Action relay: Two lines of students race to the board to write a past continuous sentence about a teacher's mimes (e.g., 'Teacher was clapping'). First team to write 3 correct sentences wins.
lp.prod: Group story: Each group gets 6 picture cards showing a sequence of actions (e.g., getting ready for school). They write 6 sentences using past continuous to tell the story, then present it to the class.
lp.rw: Read 'The Hare and the Tortoise' fable. Students underline all past continuous verbs (e.g., 'was running', 'was sleeping'). Then, in pairs, they write 2 new sentences about what another animal was doing during the race.
lp.st: Read a simplified version of 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf' with student volunteers acting out the past continuous actions (e.g., one student pretends to be the boy 'was shouting', another pretends to be a villager 'was running'). End with: 'Today we learned to talk about actions in the past using was/were + -ing. Great job, everyone! Thank you for your hard work.'
g: Students act out past continuous actions (e.g., 'was sleeping') for teammates to guess
Teams race to write past continuous sentences about pictures shown on the projector
Teacher writes sentences with errors (e.g., 'He was play football'); students correct them
Each student adds one past continuous sentence to continue a class story
Teacher shows a picture, students say 3 things people were doing in it
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 4-sentence story about what their family was doing last night
Support: Use sentence frames like 'He/She was ________ing at ________' to write their story
hw: Option 1: Draw 6 pictures of what you were doing at different times yesterday and write a sentence under each
Option 2: Write 6 sentences about what a character from your favorite cartoon was doing last weekend
Option 3: Interview a family member about what they were doing at 3 specific times yesterday and write down their answers
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references like 'While I was eating couscous, my friend was playing football' to make the grammar more relatable and memorable for local learners.

weeks.obj: complete sample A2 Key reading tasks and understand the format
weeks.lang: KET reading part formats; skimming and scanning
weeks.act: Guided KET reading part 1-2 practice; strategy notes; team question hunt
weeks.hw: KET reading homework set

skills.L: KET listening part 1 samples - format tour
skills.S: KET-style personal questions in pairs
skills.R: Complete KET reading parts 1-2 (skimming) (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style sentence writing (part 6 style)

lp.wu: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with KET reading task prompts. Teacher hands out a grid with 'Find someone who can read a short text quickly' and 'Find someone who knows what skimming means'. Students mingle, ask questions, and mark names. They report back to the class: 'Youssef can read a short text quickly!'
wuAlt: Students play 'Quiz Quiz Trade' with KET reading terms. Each student gets a card with a term like 'skimming' or 'scanning', they quiz a partner, trade cards, and find a new partner.
Students do a 'Picture Prompt' game. Teacher shows a KET reading part 1 image, students shout out what they see in English to build vocabulary.
lp.pres: Teacher uses a PowerPoint slide to show the KET reading part 1 format (multiple-choice matching). Teacher models skimming by reading a short text aloud quickly, then asks 'What is this text about?'. Students repeat the process with a new text. Teacher checks understanding by asking 'Do we read every word for skimming?' and students answer 'No!'.
presAlt: Teacher uses flashcards with KET reading task numbers (1, 2, 3) and describes each part: 'Part 1 is matching pictures to words'. Students repeat the task numbers and descriptions.
Teacher draws a simple KET reading part 2 (multiple-choice) on the board and explains 'We choose A, B, or C'. Students practice saying the options.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs on a guided KET reading part 1 worksheet. Teacher circulates and helps with skimming strategies. They then play 'Reading Race' where they time each other to complete the task. Teacher gives support by highlighting key words in the text.
pracAlt: Students play 'Team Question Hunt' in groups of three. Teacher hides KET reading questions around the room. Groups race to find and answer them, writing answers on a whiteboard.
Students do 'Sentence Match-Up' with KET reading part 2. Teacher cuts up sentences and options, students work in pairs to match them correctly.
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio description of a KET reading part 3 (text completion). They listen and fill in the missing words on their worksheet. Teacher plays the audio twice to check real comprehension.
lp.re: Students play 'Simon Says' with KET reading actions. Teacher says 'Simon says skim the text!' or 'Simon says scan for names!'. Students move around the room to stay active.
lp.prod: Students work in groups of four to create their own KET reading part 1 quiz. They draw four simple pictures and write matching descriptions. Each group quizzes another group, and the class votes on the best quiz.
lp.rw: Students complete a short KET reading part 2 (multiple-choice) text about a school trip. They read the text and choose the correct answers (A, B, or C). Then, they write two simple sentences about their own school trip using 'I went to...' or 'I saw...'.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short, simple story about a student who prepares for a KET exam. Students listen and answer comprehension questions. Close with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned about KET reading parts. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams race to match KET reading questions to the correct answers on the board.
Students toss a ball and name a KET reading word when they catch it.
Teacher calls out a word from the text, students find it in their books and point.
One student is the quiz master, others answer KET reading questions.
Students search a text for specific words and raise their hands when found.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a short paragraph about their favorite book using KET reading vocabulary.
Support / weaker learners: Use a word bank with key vocabulary from the texts to complete the reading tasks.
hw: Complete a KET reading part 1 worksheet from the KET folder.
Write three sentences about what you read today in English.
Find a short English text online (like a menu or sign) and practice skimming it.
lp.tip: Use local Moroccan examples in the reading tasks, like a text about the Green March or a local café, to make the exam format more relatable and engaging for students.

weeks.obj: complete a KET-style paired speaking task confidently
weeks.lang: KET speaking part 1-2 frames
weeks.act: Mock KET speaking in pairs with observer rubric; feedback circles; retry
weeks.hw: Participation + speaking rubric notes

skills.L: KET listening part 2 samples
skills.S: KET speaking parts 1-2 with frames
skills.R: KET reading part 3 practice (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style short message writing

lp.wu: Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three sentences about their free time (e.g., 'I play football', 'I watch TV', 'I speak Spanish'), then share with a partner who guesses the lie. Teacher models first with own sentences.
wuAlt: Find Someone Who: Students walk around asking 'Do you...?' questions (e.g., 'Do you play video games?') and tally responses on a bingo sheet.
Free Time Charades: Students act out free time activities (e.g., 'swimming', 'reading') while classmates guess the verb phrase.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of free time activities (e.g., football, cinema, music). Model KET Part 1 frames: 'What do you like doing in your free time?' and 'I like...' with answers. Elicit responses from students and check understanding with thumbs up/down for correct/incorrect answers.
presAlt: Realia Display: Bring in props (e.g., football, book, headphones) and ask 'What do you do with this?' to elicit activity vocabulary.
Dialogue Modeling: Teacher and student role-play a short conversation using KET frames, then students repeat in pairs.
lp.prac: KET Part 1 Drill: Students practice asking and answering 'What do you like doing?' with a partner using flashcards. Teacher circulates to correct pronunciation and provide sentence starters like 'I like...' or 'I don't like...'.
pracAlt: Matching Game: Students match activity pictures to verb phrases (e.g., 'play football') and then use them in sentences.
Chain Reaction: One student says 'I like...', the next repeats it and adds their own, building a chain.
lp.ls: KET Listening Part 2: Play a recording of two friends discussing free time activities. Students listen and tick the activities they hear (e.g., 'swimming', 'cinema') on a worksheet. Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Free Time Relay: Divide class into two teams. One student runs to the board, writes an activity verb (e.g., 'play'), and returns to tag the next, who adds the noun (e.g., 'football'). Fastest team wins.
lp.prod: Mock KET Speaking Part 2: Students work in pairs. Student A describes their free time preferences using 'I like...' and 'I don't like...'. Student B asks follow-up questions like 'Why?' or 'When do you...?'. Teacher uses a rubric to observe and note strengths/areas for improvement.
lp.rw: KET Reading Part 3 Practice: Students read a short text about a teenager's free time (e.g., 'My name is Sam. I like football and music.') and answer multiple-choice questions (e.g., 'What does Sam like?') by circling A, B, or C.
lp.st: Sing 'What Do You Like to Do?' song with actions (e.g., 'clap hands' for 'clap hands'). Close with: 'Today we practiced KET speaking questions about free time. Thank you, class!'
g: One student mimes an activity (e.g., 'swimming') while others guess using 'Do you...?'
Students listen to teacher call out activities and mark them on their bingo cards
Students match activity pictures to verb phrases on cards
Students ask 'What do you like doing?' to three classmates in 2 minutes each
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 sentences about a friend's free time using 'He/She likes...'.
Support: Use sentence frames ('I like...') and picture prompts during the mock speaking task.
hw: Record yourself answering 'What do you like doing in your free time?' and send to teacher.
Write 5 questions to ask a friend about their free time.
Draw 3 free time activities and label them in English.
lp.tip: Encourage students to use 'I like...' and 'I don't like...' naturally, not just memorized answers. Pair stronger students with weaker ones to build confidence during mock exams.

weeks.obj: review the year across stations with accuracy and speed
weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.act:
5 stations with passport; team challenge quiz; error auction
Project: eco-poster campaign for the Space; must/should for green rules.
weeks.hw:
Complete pre-assessment checklist
Design a 5-rule green poster with must/should.

skills.L: Listening station - mixed S1/S2 audio
skills.S: Speaking station carousel with speed rounds
skills.R: Reading station - mixed texts and tasks
skills.W: Writing station - sentence transformations

lp.wu: Earth Day Quiz: Teacher shows 5 flashcards (recycle bin, tree, plastic bottle, light bulb, water tap) and asks 'What is this?' Students shout answers in pairs, then teacher adds 'Why is it important?' for quick discussion.
wuAlt: Green Pictionary: Students draw Earth Day words (e.g., 'plant a tree') for teammates to guess.
Quick Poll: 'How many times did you recycle this week?' Students raise hands, count together.
lp.pres: Teacher introduces 'must/should' using flashcards of bad habits (littering, wasting water) and good ones (recycling, turning off lights). Models 'You must not litter' and 'You should recycle'. Checks understanding with thumbs up/down for sentences.
presAlt: Rule Posters: Show examples of eco-rules with must/should, students repeat chorally.
Charades: Teacher acts out eco-actions (e.g., 'turn off lights'), students guess and form sentences.
lp.prac: Error Auction: Teams bid on sentences with mistakes (e.g., 'You must litter'). Winners correct them. Teacher monitors and praises accurate corrections.
pracAlt: Green Dominoes: Match halves of must/should sentences (e.g., 'You should...' + 'save water').
Sentence Relay: Teams race to write correct must/should rules on the board.
lp.ls: Listening Station: Students listen to 3 short dialogues about Earth Day (e.g., 'Should I use a plastic bag? No, you must bring a reusable one'). They tick the rules heard on their passport.
lp.re: Eco-Action Relay: Students line up and race to mime eco-actions (e.g., 'turn off lights', 'put paper in bin') while teammates shout the must/should rule.
lp.prod: Eco-Poster Campaign: Groups design a poster for the American Space with 5 must/should rules (e.g., 'We should use recycled paper'). They present it to the class.
lp.rw: Reading & Writing: Students read a short text about Earth Day at the American Space, then write 3 sentences about what they must/should do there using the text as support.
lp.st: Song: Play 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' with actions. Close with 'Today we reviewed must/should for Earth Day. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams answer KET-style questions about must/should rules (e.g., 'What must you do in the library?' 'Be quiet').
Students complete station tasks to collect stamps in their passport, first team to finish wins.
Students act out eco-actions, teammates guess and say the must/should rule.
Teams bid on correct/incorrect must/should sentences, highest bidder wins points for accuracy.
Teams race to write must/should rules on the board, fastest and most accurate wins.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a second eco-poster for their school.
Support learners: Use sentence starters (e.g., 'We should...') for their poster rules.
hw: Complete the pre-assessment checklist for the year.
Design a 5-rule green poster for your home with must/should.
Write 3 sentences about what you must/should do to help the planet.
lp.tip: Use local examples (e.g., 'We should save water in Oujda') to make the rules culturally relevant and increase engagement.

weeks.obj: complete final written and speaking assessments; celebrate
