weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.act:
Final papers; speaking slots; awards and thank-you circle
Dream job interviews: question forms + reporting answers.
weeks.hw:
Final reports; certificates at ceremony
Write your dream-job interview Q&A (6 exchanges).

skills.L: Final listening paper
skills.S: Paired final speaking, then celebrate
skills.R: Final reading paper
skills.W: Final guided writing task

lp.wu: Play 'Job Charades': Students act out jobs (teacher, doctor, chef) while others guess, saying 'You are a [job]!'
wuAlt: Play 'Job Bingo' with flashcards
Play 'What's my job?' with clues like 'You work with numbers'
lp.pres: Show job flashcards (teacher, doctor, chef, engineer) and model Q&A: 'What is your dream job? I want to be a chef.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Read a short story about different jobs
Use realia (toy doctor kit, chef hat) to introduce jobs
lp.prac: Do 'Job Interview Pairs': Student A asks 'What is your dream job?', Student B answers, then swap. Monitor and model pronunciation.
pracAlt: Play 'Job Match' with picture cards
Do 'Dream Job Survey' in groups
lp.ls: Listen to a KET-style audio of two friends talking about dream jobs. Students tick the correct job mentioned on their worksheet.
lp.re: Play 'Job Relay': Teams race to write dream jobs on the board after hearing clues like 'You help sick people.'
lp.prod: Conduct 'Dream Job Interviews': Students pair up, ask 3 questions (What job? Why? Where?), and report answers to the class.
lp.rw: Complete a KET-style reading task matching job descriptions to pictures, then write 3 sentences about their own dream job using 'I want to be...'
lp.st: Read 'The Dream Job' story about a child choosing a job, then sing 'What Do You Want to Be?' with actions. Close with 'Today we assessed our English and celebrated our learning. Thank you, class!'
g: Students act out jobs while others guess
Match job flashcards to bingo cards
Teams race to write jobs after clues
Ask classmates about their dream jobs
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph about their dream job
Support: Use sentence starters like 'I want to be a...'
hw: Complete the final report worksheet
Practice speaking about your dream job with family
Draw a picture of your dream job and label it
lp.tip: Use peer assessment during interviews to build confidence and mimic real exam conditions, while keeping the tone celebratory.
checklist: I can ask and answer about dream jobs
I can understand short audio about jobs
I can read job descriptions
I can write 3 sentences about my dream job
I can participate in a job interview
I can report what my partner said
I can celebrate my learning progress

levels.desc: A first English class for teens aged 12–16. Thirty weeks build a strong A1 base — present simple, be, have got, can, daily routines, food, directions — through teen-relevant themes (identity, friends, school, free time), with pair and group work every week and the first KET-style tasks appearing from mid-S1.

levels.label: Teens · Intermediate

weeks.theme: Welcome and getting to know you
weeks.obj: Ask and answer 6 getting-to-know-you questions with detail; introduce themselves, ask 5 get-to-know-you questions, and complete a partner profile
weeks.lang: be (am/is/are); Wh- questions (what, where, how old); possessive adjectives + question forms review; Wh- + how often
weeks.act: Group project: a poster about getting to know you with 5 facts
weeks.hw: record yourself speaking for 1 minute about getting to know you

skills.L: Listen for detail in getting-to-know-you interviews
skills.S: Ask and answer 6 questions with follow-ups
skills.R: Read detailed profiles in KET part 1 style (KET folder)
skills.W: Write a detailed self-profile paragraph

lp.wu: Human Bingo: Students walk around with bingo cards containing facts like 'has a pet' or 'likes football'. They ask classmates 'Do you have a pet?' and mark squares if the answer is yes. First to get a line wins.
wuAlt: Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three statements about themselves, two true and one false. Partners guess which is the lie.
Name Chain: Students stand in a circle and say their name plus an adjective starting with the same letter (e.g., 'I'm Amazing Ali').
lp.pres: Use flashcards showing people with different hobbies and nationalities. Model sentences: 'What's your name? I'm Ali. Where are you from? I'm from Morocco. How old are you? I'm 14.' Check understanding by asking students to repeat and translate the questions.
presAlt: Realia: Show objects representing hobbies (football, book, guitar) and ask 'What's your hobby?' Model answers with 'I like football.'
Dialogue: Read a short conversation between two teens meeting for the first time, highlighting the target questions and answers.
lp.prac: Find Someone Who... worksheet with prompts like 'Find someone who speaks French.' Students walk around asking 'Do you speak French?' and writing names. Monitor and correct errors in question forms.
pracAlt: Question Cards: Students draw cards with Wh- questions (e.g., 'Where do you live?') and ask partners. Partners answer in full sentences.
Interview Relay: In pairs, Student A asks 3 questions, Student B answers, then they swap roles.
lp.ls: Listen to a KET-style audio of two teens introducing themselves. Students complete a profile worksheet with details like name, age, and hobbies. Play twice for comprehension.
lp.re: Stand Up Sit Down: Call out facts like 'Stand up if you have a sister.' Students stand or sit, practicing 'Do you have a sister?' responses.
lp.prod: Group Poster Project: Groups of 3 create a poster titled 'Getting to Know Us' with 5 facts per member (e.g., 'Ali is 14 and likes football'). They present their poster to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short KET-style profile about a teen named Sara. Answer 3 multiple-choice questions about her details (name, age, hobby). Then write a 40-word paragraph introducing yourself using the same structure.
lp.st: Sing 'Hello, Hello' with actions. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to ask and answer getting-to-know-you questions. Thank you, class! Goodbye!'
g: Students mark squares on bingo cards when their classmates say facts matching the prompts.
Students sit in a circle and ask the next student a Wh- question, who answers and asks the next.
Students describe a classmate using 'He/She is...' and others guess who it is.
Students interview 3 different partners in 2 minutes each, writing down answers.
Students sit in a circle and say 'My name is [name] and I like [hobby]' each person repeats all previous names and hobbies.
diff: Fast finishers: Add a 6th question to their poster, e.g., 'What do you want to be in the future?'
Support weaker learners: Use sentence starters like 'My name is ___. I am ___ years old. I like ___.' on their worksheet.
hw: Record a 1-minute video introducing yourself with 5 facts (name, age, family, hobbies, future dream).
Write a 50-word paragraph about a new friend you met in class today.
Interview a family member in English and write down 3 things you learned about them.
lp.tip: Encourage students to use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'I like couscous' or 'I celebrate Eid') to make personal connections and build confidence.

weeks.obj: Describe my family's personalities with examples; describe 4 family members or friends with simple details
weeks.lang: possessive 's; have got; adjectives (tall, kind, funny) + present simple vs present continuous; character adjectives
weeks.act: Roleplay cafe/shop/street situation about family and friends
weeks.hw: do the family and friends worksheet from the library folder

skills.L: Listen to personality descriptions with examples
skills.S: Describe my family's personalities with examples
skills.R: Read a family text (present simple vs continuous)
skills.W: Write a family description using both tenses

lp.wu: Students stand in a circle. Teacher tosses a soft ball to a student and asks 'Who is this person?', pointing to a family photo. Student catches ball, says 'This is my brother. He is funny.' and tosses ball back.
wuAlt: Students draw 3 family members in 30 seconds, then hold up drawings and say 'This is my mother. She is kind.'
Teacher shows flashcards of family members (mother, father, sister, friend). Students race to shout the correct possessive phrase: 'That's my sister!'
lp.pres: Teacher shows a large family tree poster with photos. Models sentences: 'My father is tall. He has got brown eyes. He is working in the garden now.' Elicits and drills key adjectives and present simple vs continuous with student volunteers.
presAlt: Teacher reads a short paragraph about a fictional family, underlining present simple and continuous verbs. Students repeat sentences with gestures (tap head for simple, wave arms for continuous).
Students sort adjective cards into 'always' (kind) and 'now' (eating) columns with teacher guidance.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs. Each pair gets a set of family member cards with adjectives. They take turns: 'This is my uncle. He is funny. He is watching TV now.' Teacher monitors and corrects possessive 's and tense usage.
pracAlt: Students play 'Guess Who?' with family photos. One student describes a person ('She is tall. She is cooking.') and the other guesses who it is.
Teacher writes sentences on board with errors. Students race to correct them in teams, focusing on 's and tenses.
lp.ls: Students listen to an audio recording of a boy describing his family. They fill in a simple chart with names and one adjective for each person, plus one continuous action (e.g., 'My sister is playing football now').
lp.re: After break, students play 'Charades Family'. Teacher mimes a family action (e.g., cooking, sleeping, studying). Students shout 'He/She is ____ing!' to guess the continuous action.
lp.prod: Students roleplay a cafe conversation. One is a waiter asking 'Tell me about your family?' The other describes 4 family members using both tenses. They must ask follow-up questions like 'Is he funny?'
lp.rw: Students read a short text about a Moroccan family celebrating a holiday (e.g., Eid). They answer 3 true/false questions about the text, then write 2 sentences about their own family using present simple and continuous.
lp.st: Teacher tells a simple story about a family's Green March celebration, using visuals. Students repeat key sentences. Close with: 'Today we described family personalities and actions. Thank you, class! Goodbye.'
g: Students mark adjectives on bingo cards as teacher calls them out, shouting 'Bingo!' when they get a line.
Teams race to write an adjective on the board for a family photo first.
Students sort sentence strips into simple/continuous piles in teams.
Students walk around asking 'Find someone who has got a sister.' and write names.
Students draw a family scene and label it with simple/continuous sentences.
diff: Fast finishers write a paragraph about their best friend using 5 adjectives and 2 continuous actions.
Support learners use a sentence frame: 'This is ___. He/She is _____. He/She is _____ing now.'
hw: Complete the family and friends worksheet from the library folder, filling in blanks with adjectives and correct tenses.
Write 4 sentences about your family: 2 simple, 2 continuous. Draw a picture.
Interview a family member about their day and write 3 sentences in present continuous.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan family structures and holidays (like Eid or Green March) to make the theme culturally relevant and boost student engagement with familiar contexts.

weeks.obj: Compare my weekday and weekend routines; describe their school day using present simple I/you/we/they
weeks.lang: present simple; time expressions (at 7 o'clock, in the morning) + adverbs of frequency; on weekdays / at weekends
weeks.act: KET-style task carousel on daily routines in teams
weeks.hw: interview a family member about daily routines in English

skills.L: Listen to weekday / weekend routine contrasts
skills.S: Compare my weekday and weekend routines
skills.R: Read a survey text and report the numbers
skills.W: Write my routines with adverbs of frequency

lp.wu: Students play 'Routine Race' in pairs. One student mimes a daily routine action (e.g., brushing teeth), the other guesses 'You brush your teeth in the morning'. Swap roles.
wuAlt: Students do a quick 'Find Someone Who' survey with prompts like 'Find someone who wakes up early' and write names.
Teacher shows flashcards of routine actions, students race to shout the time expression (e.g., 'at 7 o'clock' for 'wake up').
lp.pres: Teacher projects a weekly schedule with color-coded weekdays (blue) and weekends (green). Models sentences: 'On weekdays, I wake up at 6 o'clock. At weekends, I wake up at 9 o'clock'. Checks understanding with thumbs up/down for true/false statements.
presAlt: Teacher tells a short story about 'Fatima's Week' using a picture timeline, highlighting weekday/weekend differences.
Students sort picture cards into 'weekday' or 'weekend' piles, then make sentences with 'On weekdays/At weekends I...'.
lp.prac: Students play 'Routine Bingo' in teams. Each team gets a bingo grid with times/actions (e.g., '8:00 - breakfast', 'Saturday - football'). Teacher calls out sentences like 'At weekends, I play football', teams mark the grid.
pracAlt: Students do 'Sentence Scrambles' in pairs, unjumbling present simple sentences with adverbs (e.g., 'I always / eat / breakfast / at 7am').
Teacher models a 'My Day' chant with claps (e.g., 'I wake up! At 7 o'clock!'), students repeat and add their own routines.
lp.ls: Students listen to a recording of two teens talking about their routines. They fill in a table with times/actions for weekdays vs weekends. Teacher plays twice, then checks answers in pairs.
lp.re: After break, students play 'Action Charades'. One student mimes a routine action (e.g., 'go to school'), others shout 'He/She goes to school!'. Fast-paced and physical.
lp.prod: In teams, students conduct a 'Routine Survey'. They interview 3 classmates using prompts like 'What time do you wake up on weekdays?'. They tally results and present findings to the class (e.g., 'Two students wake up at 7 o'clock').
lp.rw: Students read a short text about 'Ahmed's Weekend' and circle all the time expressions. Then, they write 3 sentences about their own weekend using 'at' and 'on' (e.g., 'On Saturday, I go to the market at 10am').
lp.st: Teacher sings a modified 'This is the Way We Brush Our Teeth' song with weekday/weekend verses. Close with: 'Today we compared weekday and weekend routines. Thank you, class!'
g: Students race to write 5 weekday routines on the board in 1 minute.
Students walk around asking 'Find someone who eats lunch at 1pm' and write names.
Teams mark routines called by teacher; first to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Students mime routines; others guess using present simple sentences.
Teams interview classmates; fastest to tally results wins points.
diff: Fast finishers write a paragraph comparing their weekday and weekend routines (40-50 words).
Support learners use a sentence frame: 'On weekdays, I ___ at ___. At weekends, I ___ at ___.'
hw: Interview a family member about their daily routines in English and write 3 sentences.
Draw a picture of your weekday routine and label 5 activities with times.
Write a short paragraph (30 words) about what you do on Saturdays.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'Friday prayers' for weekend routines) to make the theme relatable. Encourage code-switching to Darija for clarification if needed, but insist on English output.

weeks.obj: Talk about school rules with have to; compare school subjects and say what they like and why
weeks.lang: school subjects; like/don't like + noun; because + must / have to / don't have to
weeks.res: Lesson Plans (topics set); Worksheets/Print outs; KET
weeks.act:
Two-corner debate on school life
Spooky story chain: each pair writes one paragraph, read aloud with lights off; Halloween taboo.
weeks.hw:
write 5 quiz questions about school life for next class
Write the ending of the class spooky story (6-8 lines).

skills.L: Listen to school-rules dialogues (must / have to)
skills.S: Talk about school rules with have to
skills.R: Read a school-rules text and complete the rules
skills.W: Write our class rules with must / have to

lp.wu: Quick Quiz: Teacher shows flashcards of school subjects (Math, Science, Art, PE). Students stand up and say 'I like [subject]' or 'I don't like [subject]' when the card is shown. Teacher asks follow-up questions: 'Why?'
wuAlt: Two Corners: Label two walls 'Like' and 'Don't Like'. Teacher calls out a subject; students run to the corner matching their opinion.
Survey: Students interview 3 classmates about their favorite subject and why, using 'I like... because...'
lp.pres: Show a picture of a haunted classroom. Model: 'In this school, students have to wear a ghost costume.' Point to a 'No Phones' sign: 'Students must not use phones.' Elicit rules from students using 'have to'/'must'. Check with thumbs up/down: 'Do students have to eat lunch here?'
presAlt: Rule Cards: Give students cards with school rules (e.g., 'You have to be on time'). They match them to pictures.
Spooky Dialogue: Listen to a dialogue between two students complaining about Halloween school rules: 'We have to clean the classroom!'
lp.prac: Halloween Taboo: In pairs, one student describes a school subject (e.g., 'Math') using only 'like/don't like + because + must/have to' (e.g., 'I like it because we have to solve puzzles'). The other guesses the subject. Teacher monitors for correct modal use.
pracAlt: Picture Prompt: Students look at spooky classroom pictures and write 2 sentences each using 'have to' and 'must not'.
Chain Drill: Teacher starts 'In my school, we have to wear uniforms'. Each student adds one new rule using 'must' or 'have to'.
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue between two students discussing their Halloween-themed school day. Complete a gap-fill: 'We _____ (have to) wear costumes.' 'We _____ (must) bring candy.' Check comprehension with true/false questions.
lp.re: Spooky Statues: Teacher says commands like 'You have to stand like a zombie!' Students freeze in poses. Fastest/most creative gets a point.
lp.prod: Spooky Story Chain: In pairs, students write one paragraph of a Halloween school story using 'must/have to' (e.g., 'We have to explore the haunted library'). Teams swap stories and add a paragraph. Volunteers read aloud with lights off and spooky sound effects.
lp.rw: Read a short text about a spooky school rule (e.g., 'On Halloween, students must not enter the basement'). Write 3 new rules for the American Space Oujda using 'must' or 'have to'.
lp.st: Read the ending of the spooky story aloud with dramatic pauses: 'Suddenly, the ghost appeared! We had to run. But we must not forget the key. Now, we have to go back. Will we survive? Goodbye, brave students! Thank you for your spooky stories today!'
g: Students draw a 3x3 grid and write subjects. Teacher calls out 'I like Science!', students cross it off.
Teams race to write 'must/have to' sentences on the board for a spooky picture.
Students sit in a circle. Each says 'I like Math because...' and the next must add a reason using 'must/have to'.
Students survey the class about Halloween school rules and report back using 'We have to...'
Teams compete to describe a subject without saying the name, using target language.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a spooky school poster with 5 rules using 'must/have to'.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'In my school, we have to...' for the writing task.
hw: Write 5 quiz questions about school rules using 'must/have to' for next class.
Draw your dream Halloween classroom and label 3 rules.
Write a short paragraph (40 words) about what students must do at the American Space Oujda.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'In our school, we have to respect Ramadan rules') to connect grammar to students' lives. Teens respond better when lessons reflect their identity.

weeks.obj: Talk about hobbies with love / like / hate + -ing; talk about hobbies using like + -ing and adverbs of frequency
weeks.lang: like/love/hate + -ing; always, sometimes, never + verb patterns: like/love/hate + -ing
weeks.res: Lesson Plans (topics set); Games/Game ideas; KET
weeks.act:
Write and swap 5 quiz questions about hobbies and free time
Project: Green March timeline posters, presented in the past simple.
weeks.hw:
read the short hobbies and free time text and note 5 new words
Write 5 past-simple sentences about the Green March.

skills.L: Listen to verb-pattern sentences (love / stop / try)
skills.S: Talk about hobbies with love / like / hate + -ing
skills.R: Read hobby texts and find the verb patterns
skills.W: Write about my hobbies with 3 verb patterns

lp.wu: Students stand in a circle. Teacher tosses a ball to a student and says 'I like playing football.' The student catches it and says their own sentence, e.g., 'I love reading books,' then tosses the ball to another student.
wuAlt: Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about hobbies: 'I like swimming, I love painting, I hate cooking.' Others guess the lie.
Teacher shows flashcards of hobbies; students race to say 'I like/love/hate + -ing' for each.
lp.pres: Teacher writes 'I like swimming' on the board. Elicits the pattern 'like + -ing'. Teaches 'love/hate + -ing' with gestures. Models: 'I love hiking, I hate cleaning.' Checks understanding by asking 'Do you like or hate studying English?'
presAlt: Teacher tells a short story: 'Last weekend, I loved eating pizza, but I hated doing homework.' Students identify the verb patterns.
Students match hobby pictures to sentences: 'I love playing video games' vs 'I hate tidying my room'.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs. They receive a 'Hobbies Bingo' card with phrases like 'likes dancing' or 'hates studying'. Teacher calls out sentences; students mark the card and say 'Yes, I do!' or 'No, I don't!' when they get a line.
pracAlt: Students play 'Find Someone Who': walk around asking 'Do you like + -ing?' and writing names. Teacher monitors for correct verb forms.
Teacher gives a 'Verb Pattern Maze' worksheet; students trace the path from 'like' to correct -ing forms.
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio of a boy talking about his weekend: 'I always play football on Saturdays. Sometimes I visit my friends. I never watch TV.' They tick the activities he does and circle the adverbs.
lp.re: Students play 'Simon Says' with verb patterns: 'Simon says: pretend you like swimming!' Students mime the action. 'Simon says: pretend you hate cleaning!' Incorrect movers sit down.
lp.prod: In groups, students create a 'Green March Timeline Poster' with 3-4 events in the past simple (e.g., 'People walked to the capital,' 'They carried Moroccan flags'). They present their timeline to the class, using 'Our group liked working together.'
lp.rw: Students read a short text about a teen's hobbies: 'Sara loves painting. She sometimes draws in the park. She never plays video games.' They underline all 'like/love/hate + -ing' and circle the adverbs.
lp.st: Teacher sings a simple song about hobbies: 'I like, like, like swimming! Love, love, love reading! Hate, hate, hate cleaning!' End with: 'Today we talked about hobbies using like/love/hate + -ing. Thank you, class!'
g: Students act out a hobby (e.g., 'playing football') while others guess using 'Do you like + -ing?'
Teams race to write 'like/love/hate + -ing' on the board for teacher-called hobbies.
Students jump on squares marked 'always/sometimes/never' and say a sentence with that adverb.
Students ask 5 classmates 'Do you like + -ing?' and tally results.
Match 'walked' to 'They walked to the capital' for Green March events.
diff: Fast finishers write 5 more sentences about their hobbies using 'always/sometimes/never'.
Support weaker learners use sentence frames: 'I like/love/hate _______ing. I always/sometimes/never _______.'
hw: Read the short hobbies text and write 5 new words in your notebook.
Write 5 past-simple sentences about the Green March (e.g., 'People walked to the city.', 'They carried flags.')
Ask your family about their hobbies and write 3 sentences using 'like/love/hate + -ing'.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references like the Green March to make past simple practice meaningful; teens connect better when local history is part of the lesson.

weeks.obj: Describe abilities past and present; say what they can and can't do; hold a short can-can't interview
weeks.lang: can/can't for ability; adverbs (well, fast) + can / could for ability
weeks.act: Picture description relay with sports and abilities photos
weeks.hw: write a 6-8 sentence paragraph about sports and abilities

skills.L: Listen to could / was-able-to ability stories
skills.S: Describe my abilities past and present
skills.R: Read an ability profile and complete the grid
skills.W: Write past-and-present ability sentences

lp.wu: Students play 'Ability Charades' in teams. One student mimes a sport or action (e.g., running fast, swimming well), others guess 'Can you [verb]?' The miming student replies 'Yes, I can' or 'No, I can't'.
wuAlt: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid of sports/actions, asking peers 'Can you [verb]?' and signing names.
Students quickly share one sport they can do well using 'I can [verb] well.'
lp.pres: Teacher shows flashcards of sports (football, swimming, basketball) and actions (run, jump, write). Models sentences: 'I can play football well' and 'I couldn't swim last year'. Elicits similar sentences from students about their own abilities. Checks understanding by asking 'Can you jump?' and 'Could you read when you were five?'
presAlt: Teacher tells a short story about a child who couldn't ride a bike last year but can now, using past/present 'can'.
Teacher demonstrates a simple task (e.g., juggling) and says 'I can do this now, but I couldn't last week'.
lp.prac: Students complete a 'Can/Could' worksheet with gaps (e.g., 'I ___ swim now, but I ___ last year'). Then they drill in pairs, asking 'Can you [verb]?' and 'Could you [verb] when you were young?' with teacher monitoring.
pracAlt: Students play 'Ability Bingo' with sentences like 'I can play tennis' on cards, listening for teacher's prompts.
Students match sports to ability adverbs (well, fast) in a cut-and-paste activity.
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio clip of a teen talking about their sports abilities now and in the past. They tick a grid with sports like 'swimming', 'football' and mark 'now' or 'before'.
lp.re: After break, students play 'Stand Up If You Can...'. Teacher calls out abilities (e.g., 'Stand up if you can run fast!'), students who can stand up.
lp.prod: Students work in pairs for a 'Can-Can't Interview'. They ask each other 3 questions about sports/abilities now and 3 about the past (e.g., 'Can you play basketball?' 'Could you swim when you were 10?'). They take notes and share one interesting fact about their partner with the class.
lp.rw: Students read a short text about a Moroccan athlete (e.g., Hicham El Guerrouj) and complete a grid with 'now' and 'past' abilities from the text. Then they write 3 sentences about their own abilities using 'can' and 'could'.
lp.st: Teacher tells a simple story about a boy who learns to skateboard, using 'can' and 'could'. Ends with the goodbye routine: 'Today we talked about what we can and can't do. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams race to write sentences about abilities on the board, e.g., 'I can run fast.'
Students mime actions for peers to guess using 'Can you...?' or 'Could you...?'
Students survey classmates to find someone who can do a specific sport.
Students match sports to adverbs like 'well' or 'fast'.
Teacher asks 'Could you...?' questions, students answer 'Yes, I can now' or 'No, I still can't'.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a paragraph about a famous athlete's abilities now and in the past.
Support learners: Use sentence starters like 'I can ___ well' and 'I couldn't ___ when I was young'.
hw: Write 6-8 sentences about your sports abilities now and when you were younger.
Interview a family member about their abilities and write 5 sentences.
Draw a picture of yourself doing a sport and write 3 sentences about it using 'can' and 'could'.
lp.tip: Use local sports like football or athletics to connect with students' interests, and praise effort over accuracy to build confidence.

weeks.obj: Use Halloween words in a spooky story plan; understand a short Halloween text and exchange themed vocabulary
weeks.lang: Halloween vocabulary; there is/there are (spooky room descriptions) + past simple introduction; regular -ed endings
weeks.act:
Speed-chat: 3 rotations of Halloween questions
Project: 18 November 1955 - timeline cards and a mini museum walk with captions.
weeks.hw:
record yourself speaking for 1 minute about Halloween
Write a short paragraph: what independence means to me.

skills.L: Listen to a spooky story in the past simple
skills.S: Plan and pitch a spooky story opening
skills.R: Read a Halloween text and find the past forms
skills.W: Write a spooky story plan (characters + events)

lp.wu: Spooky Charades: Students draw Halloween words (ghost, witch, pumpkin) from a hat and act them out while others guess. Props: flashcards with pictures, a hat.
wuAlt: Halloween Pictionary: Students draw vocabulary words on the board for others to guess.
Halloween Word Association: Teacher says a word (e.g., 'Halloween'), students take turns saying a related word.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a spooky room picture on the board and models sentences: 'There is a ghost. There are bats.' Checks understanding by asking 'What is in the room?' Students respond in full sentences.
presAlt: Realia Mystery Box: Teacher places spooky objects (plastic spider, fake cobwebs) in a box; students guess using 'There is/There are'.
Spooky Story Starter: Teacher writes a sentence on the board (e.g., 'Last night, I saw a ghost.') and explains past simple.
lp.prac: Spooky Room Description: Students work in pairs to describe a picture using 'There is/There are'. Teacher provides sentence frames for support.
pracAlt: Find Someone Who: Students walk around asking 'Is there a ghost in your house?' and write names.
Spooky Sentence Race: Teams race to write correct sentences with 'There is/There are' about a spooky scene.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short spooky story in past simple (e.g., 'The ghost walked. The witch laughed.'). Students listen and write down 3 past tense verbs they hear.
lp.re: Zombie Tag: One student is 'it' (zombie) and chases others; when tagged, students freeze and say a Halloween word to unfreeze.
lp.prod: Spooky Story Pitch: Students plan a story opening with characters and events (e.g., 'A ghost lived in a house. He saw a witch.') and pitch it to the class.
lp.rw: Students read a short Halloween text and underline all past simple verbs. Then, they write 3 sentences about their own spooky experience using past simple.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short Halloween story with actions, then closes with: 'Today we learned Halloween words and past simple. Thank you, class!'
g: Students mark Halloween words on bingo cards as teacher calls them out.
Teams race to write past tense verbs from the story on the board.
Students add one sentence to a story in turns, using past simple.
Teacher hides a ghost flashcard; students ask 'Is it near the door?' to find it.
Students match Halloween words to pictures.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a longer spooky story (5 sentences).
Support: Use word banks for story planning.
hw: Record yourself speaking for 1 minute about Halloween using past simple.
Write a short paragraph: What independence means to me (40-50 words).
Draw a spooky scene and label 5 things using 'There is/There are'.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural connections (e.g., compare Halloween to local festivals like Eid or Independence Day) to make the theme relatable and engaging.

weeks.obj: Talk about food quantities; categorize food vocabulary and ask about quantities
weeks.lang: countable/uncountable; some/any; How much/How many + countable / uncountable; some, any, much, many
weeks.act:
Pair interview, then report your partner to the class
Compare Thanksgiving with harvest customs here; gratitude survey with graphs.
weeks.hw:
do the food and drinks worksheet from the library folder
Interview 3 people: one thing they are thankful for; report back.

skills.L: Listen to quantity dialogues (much / many / a lot)
skills.S: Talk about food quantities accurately
skills.R: Read a food text and classify countable / uncountable
skills.W: Write a recipe-style paragraph with quantities

lp.wu: Students play 'Food Charades' in teams. One student mimes a food or drink (e.g., eating an apple, drinking juice), teammates guess in English: 'Is it an apple?' 'Are you drinking milk?'
wuAlt: Students play 'I Spy with My Little Eye' with food flashcards: 'I spy something red and sweet.' 'Is it a strawberry?'
Students do a quick 'Find Someone Who...' survey: 'Find someone who likes pizza.' 'Do you like pizza?'
lp.pres: Teacher shows flashcards of Thanksgiving foods (turkey, potatoes, gravy, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie). Elicit: 'Is it countable or uncountable?' Model: 'How much gravy?' 'How many potatoes?' Check with thumbs up/down: 'Turkey is countable? Yes/No.'
presAlt: Teacher uses a real basket with countable (apples) and uncountable (rice) items. Students touch and say: 'Apples are countable.' 'Rice is uncountable.'
Teacher draws a simple dinner plate on the board and adds food icons, asking: 'How many carrots? How much soup?'
lp.prac: Students work in pairs with a 'Thanksgiving Shopping List' worksheet. They ask: 'Do we need any potatoes?' 'How much gravy?' and write quantities. Teacher circulates to correct 'some/any/much/many' errors.
pracAlt: Students play 'Bingo' with food quantities called out: 'Find a card with many apples.' 'Find a card with some milk.'
Teacher does a 'Drill and Repeat' with food flashcards: 'How much butter?' 'Much butter!' 'How many eggs?' 'Many eggs!
lp.ls: Students listen to a dialogue between two friends planning a Thanksgiving meal. They tick the foods they hear (turkey, potatoes, cranberry sauce) and write quantities (e.g., 'two turkeys', 'a little gravy').
lp.re: After break, students play 'Food Relay'. Two lines race to the board to write 'How much...?' or 'How many...?' for a teacher's prompt (e.g., 'cheese' → 'How much cheese?', 'apples' → 'How many apples?').
lp.prod: Students interview a partner: 'What food do you eat for Thanksgiving here? How much rice? How many vegetables?' Then, they report to the class: 'Fatima eats couscous for Thanksgiving. She has a little rice and many vegetables.'
lp.rw: Students read a short text 'A Moroccan Thanksgiving' about a family combining Thanksgiving with local harvest customs. They underline countable nouns (apples, bread) and circle uncountable nouns (honey, oil). Then, they write 3 sentences: 'We eat many apples.' 'We use a little honey.'
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story 'The Gratitude Pumpkin' about a boy who writes things he's thankful for on a pumpkin. Students repeat key phrases: 'I am thankful for...' Close with: 'Today we talked about food quantities. Thank you, class!'
g: Students mark off foods called out by the teacher: 'Find something sweet! Pumpkin pie!'
Teams race to write 'How much/many?' on the board for teacher's prompts: 'butter!', 'oranges!'
Students ask peers: 'Find someone who likes pumpkin pie.' 'Do you like it?' and tally answers.
Students turn over food cards and say: 'There are some apples.' 'There is much rice.'
Students draw a meal and ask: 'How many carrots? How much soup?' for partners to guess.
diff: Fast finishers write a short paragraph: 'For Thanksgiving, I eat many... and much...'
Support learners use a word bank with 'some/any/much/many' and food pictures.
hw: Complete the 'Food and Drinks' worksheet from the library folder (match words to pictures, write sentences).
Interview 3 people: 'What is one thing you are thankful for?' Write their answers: 'Amina is thankful for her family.'
Draw your ideal Thanksgiving meal and label 5 foods with 'some/any/much/many'.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan harvest festivals like 'Achoura' to connect Thanksgiving to local culture, making the lesson more relatable and meaningful for students in Oujda.

weeks.obj: Order a meal and change an order politely; order food and drink politely in a roleplay
weeks.lang: Would you like...? I'd like...; Can I have...? + would like / could I have; cafe roleplay
weeks.res: Listening (graded cafe dialogues mp3); Lesson Plans/Food; Reading tasks
weeks.act: Group project: a poster about at the cafe with 5 facts
weeks.hw: interview a family member about at the cafe in English

skills.L: Listening folder: cafe dialogues - requests and changes
skills.S: Order a meal and change an order politely
skills.R: Read cafe reviews and find the polite requests
skills.W: Write a cafe dialogue with a problem (8 lines)

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find Someone Who...' with cafe-related questions (e.g., 'Find someone who likes coffee'). Students mingle, ask questions, and write names. They report back: 'Ali likes coffee.'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Cafe Bingo' with food/drink pictures; students call out items in English.
Alternative 2: 'Quick Quiz' on last week's vocabulary (e.g., 'What is a menu?').
lp.pres: Presentation: Show flashcards of cafe items (coffee, cake, tea). Model polite requests: 'Can I have a coffee?' and 'I'd like tea.' Elicit responses. Check understanding with 'thumbs up/down' for correct/incorrect sentences.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Roleplay a short dialogue using puppets (waiter/customer).
Alternative 2: Use a real cafe menu to point and say 'I'd like...'.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Order Relay' in teams. Teams take turns ordering from a picture menu using 'Can I have...?' or 'I'd like...'. Correct orders earn points. Teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Match the Request' worksheet (match 'I'd like cake' to a picture).
Alternative 2: 'Chain Drill' where each student adds one item to the order (e.g., 'I'd like coffee, cake, and tea').
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a KET-style dialogue of a customer changing an order. Students listen and write what the customer changes (e.g., 'from coffee to tea'). Replay for clarification.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Cafe Charades'. Students act out cafe actions (e.g., ordering, drinking) while others guess the phrase: 'He's ordering coffee!'.
lp.prod: Production task: Group poster project. Groups create a poster with 5 facts about cafes (e.g., 'You can order tea here'). They present to the class using 'We like...' and 'We recommend...'.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Read a short cafe review. Underline polite requests. Then write an 8-line dialogue with a problem (e.g., 'The order is wrong'). Use 'Could I have...?' and 'I'd like...'.
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Sing 'The Coffee Song' (chant). Close with: 'Today we learned to order politely at a cafe. Thank you, class!'.
g: Teams race to order from a picture menu using 'Can I have...?'.
Students act out cafe actions for others to guess.
Match sentences to cafe item pictures.
Students build a group order one item at a time.
Mingle to find classmates who like cafe items.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second dialogue with a different problem (e.g., 'The bill is wrong').
Support: Use sentence starters ('I'd like...', 'Can I have...?') for the dialogue.
hw: Option 1: Interview a family member about their favorite cafe item in English.
Option 2: Draw a cafe menu and label 5 items.
Option 3: Write 3 polite requests for a cafe.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cafe culture (e.g., mint tea) to make the theme relatable. Encourage students to compare local and international cafe customs.

weeks.obj: Give directions with landmarks; give simple directions and describe their neighborhood with there is/are
weeks.lang: there is/there are; prepositions of place; imperatives (turn, go) + imperatives + prepositions of place; go past, opposite
weeks.act: Roleplay cafe/shop/street situation about my city and directions
weeks.hw: write 5 quiz questions about my city and directions for next class

skills.L: Listen to directions with landmarks
skills.S: Give directions with landmarks from memory
skills.R: Read a town guide and map the places
skills.W: Write directions using 2 landmarks

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find the Landmark' — show flashcards of local Oujda landmarks (e.g., Hassan II Mosque, Prince Square) and students race to point to them on a printed map while saying 'It's near the post office.'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Describe Your Spot' — students draw their favorite local spot and say 'There is a cafe near my school.'
Alternative 2: 'Simon Says with Directions' — teacher commands like 'Simon says turn left' and students mime the action.
lp.pres: Presentation: Use a large Oujda map on the board; model sentences like 'Go past the mosque, turn right at the fountain.' Check understanding by asking 'Where do I turn?' and having students point.
presAlt: Alternative 1: 'Realia Walk' — place toy buildings on desks; students give directions to move a toy car.
Alternative 2: 'Photo Tour' — show Google Street View images of Oujda streets; students describe what they see with 'There is a...'.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Direction Drill' — pairs get a mini-map with landmarks; one student gives directions like 'Go past the bank, turn opposite the school' and the other traces the path with a finger.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Command Chain' — students sit in a circle; each adds one direction to build a route, e.g., 'Go left... then go past...'
Alternative 2: 'Flashcard Sort' — students match preposition phrases (e.g., 'next to the mosque') to picture cards.
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a KET-style audio of someone giving directions to a cafe; students listen and circle the correct starting point on their worksheet.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Human Maze' — students stand in a grid; teacher calls out directions like 'Turn left past Ali!' and students move accordingly.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Roleplay: Lost Tourist' — in groups, one student is a lost tourist asking for directions to a landmark (e.g., the American Space), others give landmarks-based replies like 'It's opposite the library.'
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read a short text about Oujda's old medina; then write 3 sentences describing their neighborhood using 'There is/are' and a landmark.
lp.st: Story/Song + goodbye: Sing 'The Directions Song' (to the tune of 'Head, Shoulders, Knees, and Toes') with gestures; close with 'Today we learned to give directions with landmarks. Thank you, class!'
g: Students mark off landmarks on a bingo card as teacher calls out directions like 'Go past the market.'
Students draw a landmark and others guess its location using 'It's near...'.
Students mime 'opposite' or 'next to' for others to guess the preposition.
Teacher draws a path on the board; students write directions using 2 landmarks.
Students race to give directions from memory to a classmate who draws the path.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a riddle about a local landmark using 'It's opposite...'
Support learners: Use a word bank with landmarks and prepositions for the writing task.
hw: Homework 1: Write 5 quiz questions about Oujda directions (e.g., 'What is opposite the train station?')
Homework 2: Draw a map of your route to school with 2 landmarks and directions.
Homework 3: Record a voice note giving directions to a friend's house.
lp.tip: Use local landmarks to boost engagement—students will remember directions better when tied to places they know, like the American Space or Prince Square.

weeks.obj: Compare two shops and two products; handle a simple shop exchange: sizes, colors, prices
weeks.lang: clothes vocabulary; How much is/are...? this/that/these/those + comparatives: cheaper, more stylish than
weeks.act: KET-style task carousel on shopping and clothes in teams
weeks.hw: read the short shopping and clothes text and note 5 new words

skills.L: Listening folder: shopping dialogues - comparisons
skills.S: Compare two shops and two products
skills.R: Read shop ads and compare the offers
skills.W: Write a product comparison (4 sentences)

lp.wu: Students play 'Shopkeeper Says' with clothes flashcards: teacher commands like 'Show me a red shirt' or 'Point to the cheapest shoes'; students grab the correct card and say 'This is a red shirt' or 'Those shoes are cheaper'.
wuAlt: Students do a 'Clothes Quiz' in teams: teacher shows flashcards, teams race to shout the English word first.
Students play 'Guess What I'm Wearing': teacher describes an outfit (e.g., 'I'm wearing a blue jacket and jeans'), students guess the item.
lp.pres: Teacher holds up two shop ads (e.g., 'Zara' vs 'H&M') and models comparisons: 'Zara is more stylish than H&M, but H&M is cheaper than Zara'; students repeat chorally; teacher checks understanding by asking 'Which shop is cheaper?'.
presAlt: Teacher uses realia (two T-shirts, one plain, one printed) to demonstrate comparatives: 'This T-shirt is more stylish than that one'.
Teacher draws two shops on the board and adds prices/stylishness ratings; students compare them using sentence frames.
lp.prac: Students do a 'Shop Comparison Race' in pairs: each pair gets two shop ads, they race to write 3 comparisons (e.g., 'Zara has more styles than H&M'); teacher monitors and corrects errors.
pracAlt: Students play 'Find the Difference' with two clothing catalogues: they spot 3 differences and write sentences (e.g., 'These jeans are more expensive than those jeans').
Students do a 'Comparative Chain Game' in teams: one student says a comparison (e.g., 'This bag is bigger'), next student adds another (e.g., 'This bag is bigger and cheaper').
lp.ls: Students listen to a dialogue between two friends comparing two shops (Zara vs. H&M); they tick which shop is cheaper and more stylish on a worksheet; teacher plays the audio twice.
lp.re: Students play 'Price Tag Swap': teacher calls out a price (e.g., '100 dirhams'), students quickly swap places with a partner and say 'This is cheaper than that' with a point.
lp.prod: Students roleplay a shop exchange in pairs: one is a customer, one is a shopkeeper; customers ask about sizes/colors/prices (e.g., 'How much are these jeans?'), shopkeepers respond and handle exchanges (e.g., 'These are too big, do you have smaller ones?'); teacher circulates and notes errors.
lp.rw: Students read a short text comparing two shops (e.g., 'Zara vs. H&M: Which is better?') and underline 5 new words (e.g., 'stylish', 'discount', 'fabric'); then write 4 sentences comparing the shops using comparatives.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a teen shopping for clothes, using comparatives (e.g., 'She liked the blue shirt more than the red one because it was cheaper'); class closes with the goodbye routine: 'Today we compared shops and clothes—great work! Thank you, class.'
g: Students mark off items on a bingo card as the teacher calls out clothes vocabulary.
Teacher writes a price on the board, students guess the item (e.g., 'Is it 50 dirhams for a T-shirt?').
Teams race to write comparative sentences on the board (e.g., 'This is cheaper than that').
Pairs swap roles after 2 minutes to practice both customer and shopkeeper.
Students find clothes/comparative words in a worksheet.
diff: Fast finishers write 5 extra sentences comparing their favorite shop to another.
Support weaker learners use a sentence frame: 'This shop is _______ than that shop because _______.'
hw: Read a shop ad from a Moroccan store (e.g., Marjane) and note 5 new words.
Write 4 sentences comparing two local shops (e.g., 'Souk El Had is cheaper than Carrefour').
Ask a family member about their favorite clothes shop and write 2 comparisons.
lp.tip: Use local examples (e.g., comparing Marjane vs. Carrefour) to make the theme relevant; teens engage more when they see real-world connections.

weeks.obj: Make weekend plans with going to; report weather and invite/react to simple suggestions
weeks.lang: What is the weather like?; Shall we...? Let's...; responses + be going to (plans); What are you doing...?
weeks.act:
Two-corner debate on weather
Christmas around the world jigsaw reading; party planning task with a budget in English.
weeks.hw:
write a 6-8 sentence paragraph about weather
Write the class party invitation (10 lines).

skills.L: Listen to arrangement dialogues (going to)
skills.S: Make weekend plans with going to
skills.R: Read a plan text and complete the diary
skills.W: Write my weekend plan with times

lp.wu: Weather Charades: Teacher mimes actions like shivering, sweating, or using an umbrella; students guess 'It's cold/hot/rainy' in full sentences. Teacher writes correct sentences on the board.
wuAlt: Weather Bingo: Students draw 9 weather symbols, teacher calls out 'It's sunny/rainy...' and students mark the matching symbol.
Weather Chain: One student says 'I like sunny weather', next says 'I like sunny weather and I like snowy weather', etc.
lp.pres: Teacher shows flashcards of different weather and asks 'What is the weather like?'; models answers 'It's sunny/rainy/snowy'. Then shows a calendar with 'Saturday' and asks 'What are you going to do on Saturday?'; models answers 'I'm going to play football/watch TV'.
presAlt: Weather Report Video: Play a short cartoon weather forecast, pause and ask students to report the weather using the target language.
Plan Your Day: Teacher draws a simple timeline of their Saturday and says 'I'm going to wake up at 8, I'm going to have breakfast...', students repeat.
lp.prac: Weather and Plans Matching: Students have cards with weather on one side and activities on the other; they match them and make sentences like 'It's sunny, I'm going to the park'. Teacher monitors and corrects.
pracAlt: Find Someone Who...: Students walk around and ask 'What are you going to do this weekend?'; find someone who matches each activity and write their name.
Picture Prompt: Students get a picture of a weather scene and must tell their partner what they are going to do in that weather.
lp.ls: Listen to two friends making weekend plans; students complete a table with 'Name' and 'Plan' (e.g., 'Lina: going to the cinema'). Teacher plays the audio twice, then checks answers as a class.
lp.re: Weather TPR: Teacher calls out weather commands like 'If it's sunny, jump! If it's rainy, cover your head!', students act them out quickly to reactivate vocabulary.
lp.prod: Christmas Party Planning: In groups, students plan a Christmas party with a 500-dirham budget. They must decide on food, games, and decorations using 'We're going to buy... We're going to play...'. Each group presents their plan.
lp.rw: Christmas Around the World Jigsaw: Students read short texts about Christmas in different countries (e.g., USA, UK, Morocco). They then share one fact from their text with a partner and write a sentence about it.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a character's Christmas plans, using target language. End with 'Today we learned to talk about weather and make plans. Thank you, class!'
g: Students mime weather actions for others to guess in sentences.
Students write their weekend plans on paper and swap with a partner to ask questions.
Students mark off party items as the teacher calls them out.
Students ask classmates about weekend plans and find matches.
Teacher says 'Sunny weather is better than rainy weather'; students go to corners and defend their choice.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a dream Christmas party with no budget limit and present it to the class.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'I'm going to...' and 'It's...' for the party planning task.
hw: Write a 6-8 sentence paragraph about the weather in Oujda this weekend and what you are going to do.
Write a 10-line invitation to a class Christmas party, including the date, time, and activities.
Draw a picture of your weekend plans and write 5 sentences about it using 'going to'.
lp.tip: Use local context: Discuss how Moroccans celebrate Christmas (family gatherings, special foods) to make the theme relevant and build cultural awareness.

weeks.obj: Tell a story about last weekend; talk about yesterday and childhood with was/were
weeks.lang: was/were; time expressions (yesterday, last year) + past simple irregular verbs; time markers
weeks.act:
Write and swap 5 quiz questions about the past
Resolutions with will / going to: vote on the class top-5 resolutions.
weeks.hw:
record yourself speaking for 1 minute about the past
Write 5 resolutions with will and going to.

skills.L: Listen to last-weekend stories with irregular verbs
skills.S: Tell a story about last weekend
skills.R: Read a story and collect the irregular past forms
skills.W: Write my last-weekend story (6 sentences)

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find Someone Who...' game. Students walk around asking peers 'Did you [eat couscous yesterday]?' and mark names on their bingo sheet. Teacher models first question with flashcard of couscous.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Past Tense Ball Toss'. Teacher says a verb (e.g., 'go'), students toss a ball and say past form ('went') in pairs.
Alternative 2: 'Memory Chain'. Teacher starts 'Yesterday I ate...', each student adds one food item in past tense.
lp.pres: Presentation: Show New Year's Eve flashcards (fireworks, family, food). Model sentences: 'Last year, I was at home with my family. We were happy.' Elicit time expressions (yesterday, last year). Check understanding with thumbs-up/down for true/false sentences about the teacher.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a short video clip of New Year celebrations. Pause and ask 'Where were they? What were they doing?'
Alternative 2: Draw a timeline on the board with 'now' and 'last year'. Students write sentences about themselves using 'was/were'.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Past Tense Tic-Tac-Toe'. In pairs, students choose a square with a subject (e.g., 'I') and make a 'was/were' sentence. Correct sentences get an X/O. Teacher monitors for errors and provides sentence frames.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Verb Be Bingo'. Students fill grids with 'was/were' sentences. Teacher calls out prompts (e.g., 'at school yesterday') for students to mark.
Alternative 2: 'Find the Mistake'. Teacher writes 5 sentences with 'was/were' errors. Students correct them in pairs.
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a 1-minute audio of a teen describing last New Year's Eve. Students listen and circle correct 'was/were' sentences on their worksheet. Then, listen again and write one detail they heard about the person's celebration.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Past Taction'. Teacher calls out a past verb (e.g., 'ate'), students mime the action and say the past form. Speed increases to keep energy high after the break.
lp.prod: Production task: 'New Year's Quiz Swap'. Students write 5 quiz questions about the past (e.g., 'Were you born in Oujda?'). Swap with a partner and answer. Then, share one interesting fact about their partner with the class.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Read a short story (40 words) about a child's New Year's Eve. Underline all 'was/were' and past verbs. Then, write 6 sentences about their own last weekend using 'was/were' and time markers.
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Play 'Auld Lang Syne' instrumental while showing New Year images. Close with: 'Today we learned to talk about the past with was/were. Thank you, class!'
g: Students mime past actions (e.g., 'ate') for others to guess the verb.
Teams race to write correct 'was/were' sentences on the board.
Students sit in a circle and take turns adding to a story using past tense.
Teacher says a past verb, students find a partner and say the past form together.
Teams race to write 5 sentences using 'was/were' about a given topic.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 10-sentence story about their best New's Eve.
Support: Use sentence frames like 'I was ___.' 'We were ___.' with word banks.
hw: Option 1: Record a 1-minute voice note about your childhood using 'was/were'.
Option 2: Write 5 resolutions with 'will' (e.g., 'I will learn English') and 5 with 'going to' (e.g., 'I am going to study more').
Option 3: Draw a picture of last weekend and write 5 sentences about it using past tense.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'Aid al-Adha', 'Green March') to make past tense practice relatable and boost engagement.

weeks.obj: Narrate a Christmas memory; tell a simple story in the past with regular verbs; enjoy a Christmas text
weeks.lang: past simple regular (-ed); Christmas vocabulary + past simple review; first, then, after that
weeks.act: Picture description relay with Christmas photos
weeks.hw: do the Christmas worksheet from the library folder

skills.L: Listen to a Christmas memory narrative
skills.S: Narrate a Christmas memory with sequencers
skills.R: Read a narrative and order the events (first, then)
skills.W: Write my Christmas memory paragraph

lp.wu: Christmas Memory Chain: Students sit in a circle. Teacher starts with 'Last Christmas, I ate a cookie.' Student 1 repeats and adds: 'Last Christmas, I ate a cookie and drank hot chocolate.' Each student repeats the full chain and adds one new past verb phrase.
wuAlt: Christmas Verb Bingo: Teacher calls out Christmas verbs (opened, wrapped, decorated) and students cross them off their bingo cards.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Did you...?' questions about Christmas activities.
lp.pres: Teacher shows 4 flashcards: 1) a wrapped present, 2) a Christmas tree, 3) a plate of cookies, 4) a family dinner. Models sentences: 'I wrapped a present. Then I decorated the tree. After that, I ate cookies.' Checks understanding by asking 'What did I do first?' and having students point to the flashcards.
presAlt: Past Tense Timeline: Teacher draws a timeline on the board and writes 3 past verbs from the flashcards, asking students to order them.
Christmas Story Circle: Teacher starts a short story and each student adds one sentence using a past verb.
lp.prac: Picture Description Relay: In pairs, students get a Christmas photo. They take turns describing one action in the photo using 'first, then, after that' (e.g., 'First, they decorated the tree. Then, they put presents under it.'). Teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation of -ed endings.
pracAlt: Verb Match-Up: Students match Christmas verbs to pictures and then write sentences.
Sentence Race: Teams race to write correct past simple sentences from prompts on the board.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 1-minute audio of a teen describing their Christmas memory. They fill in the blanks in a worksheet with past verbs (e.g., 'I ___ (wrap) presents for my family'). Teacher plays the audio twice.
lp.re: Christmas Verb Charades: Students act out Christmas verbs (e.g., 'wrapped', 'decorated') while others guess the verb in the past simple.
lp.prod: Christmas Memory Writing: Students write a 40-word paragraph about their own Christmas memory using 'first, then, after that' and at least 3 regular past verbs. They then share their paragraph with a partner who asks one follow-up question.
lp.rw: Reading and Sequencing: Students read a short text (50 words) about a Christmas day and cut out 4 sentences to order them using 'first, then, after that'. They glue them in the correct order.
lp.st: Teacher reads a short Christmas story (e.g., 'The Gingerbread Man's Christmas') and students repeat key sentences. Goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to talk about Christmas memories using past simple verbs. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams race to write past verbs on the board from prompts.
Students mark past verbs called out by the teacher.
Pairs describe Christmas photos using sequencers.
Students order sentence strips using 'first, then, after that'.
Students build a story chain with past verbs.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second paragraph about a different holiday memory using past verbs.
Support: Use a sentence frame with verbs already filled in (e.g., 'First, I _____. Then, I _____.')
hw: Complete the Christmas worksheet from the library folder (ordering events and writing sentences).
Write 5 sentences about your favorite Moroccan holiday using past verbs.
Draw a picture of a Christmas memory and label 3 actions in the past simple.
lp.tip: Emphasize the pronunciation of -ed endings (/t/, /d/, /ɪd/) by having students 'feel' the sounds with their hands on their throats. Connect to local culture by asking how Christmas memories might differ from Moroccan celebrations like Eid.

weeks.obj: Show my progress in the semester quiz; complete the written paper and the paired speaking task
weeks.lang: all S1 outcomes + semester 1 review
weeks.res: Tests (teacher-selected level items); assessment kit; Reading tasks
weeks.act: Mixed-skills revision circuit in teams
weeks.hw: revise your notes for the assessment week

skills.L: Listening paper across S1 (Tests)
skills.S: Paired speaking task plus the quiz
skills.R: Reading paper across S1 topics
skills.W: Guided writing (7-8 sentences)

lp.wu: Students play 'Quiz Quiz Trade' with KET-style flashcards. Each student gets a card with a question (e.g., 'What time do you get up?'). They walk around, ask their question, trade cards, and repeat with a new partner.
wuAlt: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a semester review grid (e.g., 'Find someone who likes football').
Students play 'Memory Race' with vocabulary cards from S1 topics.
lp.pres: Teacher presents a KET speaking task rubric. Model a paired dialogue using flashcards of hobbies and locations. Ask students to identify the key phrases (e.g., 'I like...', 'Can you...?'). Check understanding with thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Teacher uses a short video of a KET speaking task to model.
Teacher presents a 'good vs bad' speaking example with exaggerated errors.
lp.prac: Students practice the paired speaking task in groups of three. One student acts as the examiner, one as Candidate A, one as Candidate B. Teacher circulates and provides feedback on fluency and task completion.
pracAlt: Students play 'Role Card Relay'—draw a role card and act out the scenario with a partner.
Students complete a 'dialogue gap-fill' worksheet for the speaking task.
lp.ls: Students listen to a KET-style listening track about daily routines. They complete a multiple-choice worksheet with 5 questions. Play the track twice, then review answers as a class.
lp.re: Students play 'Simon Says' with action verbs from S1 (e.g., 'Simon says stand up', 'Simon says eat'). After the break, this reactivates energy and reviews vocabulary.
lp.prod: Students work in pairs to create a short dialogue (5-6 turns) about their weekend plans using 'going to' and 'will'. They perform for the class and receive peer feedback.
lp.rw: Students read a short text (50 words) about a Moroccan festival (e.g., Green March). They answer 3 multiple-choice questions and write 2 sentences about their own favorite festival.
lp.st: Teacher tells a story about a student preparing for the KET exam. Close with: 'Today we reviewed for the semester quiz—thank you, class!'
g: Students mark off KET vocabulary words on a bingo card as the teacher calls them.
Students draw S1 vocabulary words for their team to guess.
Teams answer KET-style questions for points.
Students add one sentence to a story about their semester.
Students interview partners about their hobbies using KET prompts.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 40-word paragraph about their best friend using comparatives.
Support learners: Use a sentence starter worksheet for the writing task.
hw: Review your S1 notes and write 5 sentences about your learning progress.
Create a flashcard set of 10 KET words you find difficult.
Do a 10-minute listening practice from the KET sample papers.
lp.tip: Use peer assessment during the speaking task to build confidence and mimic the exam format—teens respond well to structured feedback from classmates.
checklist: I can answer personal information questions in the speaking task.
I can understand short conversations about daily routines.
I can read a short text and answer multiple-choice questions.
I can write 7-8 sentences about my weekend plans.
I can use present simple and past simple correctly.
I can use comparatives (e.g., 'bigger than').
I can follow a KET-style speaking task with a partner.

weeks.obj: Talk about my goals for this year; talk about learning goals and review semester 1 language
weeks.lang: review structures; goal language (I want to... I will try...) + want to / would like to + infinitive
weeks.act: Pair interview, then report your partner to the class
weeks.hw: write 5 quiz questions about new year goals for next class

skills.L: Listen to goal interviews and note the targets
skills.S: Talk about my goals for this year
skills.R: Read strategy tips and self-assess can-dos
skills.W: Write goals with want to / would like to

lp.wu: Goal Ball Toss: Students stand in a circle. Teacher tosses a soft ball to a student and asks, 'What's one goal you have for this year?' The student answers and tosses the ball to another student. Repeat for 3-4 rounds.
wuAlt: New Year Bingo: Students write 5 goals (e.g., 'study more English') in a grid. Teacher calls out goals; students cross off matches and shout 'Bingo!' when they have 3 in a row.

Goal Chain: Students stand in a line. The first student says, 'My goal is to learn English.' The next says, 'My goal is to learn English, and play football.' Each student adds one new goal to the chain.
lp.pres: Teacher shows flashcards of goals (e.g., 'read more books', 'exercise', 'learn guitar'). Models sentences: 'I want to read more books.' 'I would like to exercise.' Elicits more examples from students. Checks understanding by asking, 'What do you want to do this year?'
presAlt: Goal Story: Teacher tells a short story about a character who sets goals (e.g., 'Fatima wants to learn English because she wants to travel'). Asks comprehension questions like, 'What does Fatima want to do?'
Goal Charades: Teacher acts out a goal (e.g., miming reading a book). Students guess and say, 'You want to read more books!'
lp.prac: Goal Match-Up: Students receive cards with goals (e.g., 'study harder') and sentence starters (e.g., 'I want to...'). They match the cards to form correct sentences. In pairs, they practice saying the sentences aloud. Teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation.
pracAlt: Goal Relay: Two teams race to write sentences on the board. Teacher shouts a goal (e.g., 'learn guitar'), and the first student from each team runs to write 'I want to learn guitar.' The team with the most correct sentences wins.
Goal Chain Drill: Students sit in a circle. The first student says, 'I want to study English.' The next says, 'He wants to study English, and I want to play sports.' Continue building the chain.
lp.ls: Goal Interviews Audio: Students listen to 2-3 short interviews where teens talk about their goals. They listen and write down 2 goals from each interview (e.g., 'Lina wants to learn French'). Teacher plays audio twice. Students compare answers in pairs.
lp.re: Goal Jump: After the break, students stand. Teacher says a goal (e.g., 'I want to travel'). If the student agrees, they jump once. If not, they stay still. Teacher checks for understanding by asking, 'Why did you jump?'
lp.prod: Pair Goal Interview: Students interview their partner using questions like, 'What do you want to do this year?' 'Why do you want to do that?' They take notes. Then, each student reports their partner's goals to the class (e.g., 'Sara wants to learn English because she wants to study abroad').
lp.rw: Goal Self-Assessment: Students read a short text with strategy tips (e.g., 'Write your goals on paper'). They circle 3 can-do statements (e.g., 'I can talk about my goals'). Then, they write 2-3 sentences about their own goals using 'want to' or 'would like to'.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a teen who achieves their New Year goal. Then, leads a goodbye routine: 'Today we talked about our goals. Thank you for sharing! See you next week!'
g: Students write 5 goals in a grid. Teacher calls out goals; students cross off matches and shout 'Bingo!' when they have 3 in a row.
Two teams race to write sentences on the board. Teacher shouts a goal, and the first student from each team runs to write 'I want to...'. The team with the most correct sentences wins.
Students take turns acting out a goal (e.g., miming cooking). The class guesses and says, 'You want to cook more!'
Students stand in a line. The first student says, 'My goal is to learn English.' The next says, 'My goal is to learn English, and play football.' Each student adds one new goal.
Students receive cards with goals and sentence starters. They match the cards to form correct sentences and practice saying them aloud.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a short paragraph (40-50 words) about 3 goals and why they are important.
Support / weaker learners: Use sentence frames like 'I want to ___ because ___' to write their goals.
hw: Write 5 quiz questions about New Year goals for next class (e.g., 'What does Omar want to do this year?').
Draw a picture of your top goal and write 1 sentence about it.
Interview a family member about their goals and write 2 sentences in English.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'learn Arabic calligraphy') to make goals relatable. Encourage students to connect goals to local events like the Green March or Independence Day.

weeks.obj: Describe jobs and what they involve; describe jobs and talk about work with have to
weeks.lang: job vocabulary; have to / don't have to + have to / has to for duties
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Jobs-Careers; Reading tasks/Famous people; Listening
weeks.act: Group project: a poster about jobs and dream jobs with 5 facts
weeks.hw: read the short jobs and dream jobs text and note 5 new words

skills.L: Listen to job-duties dialogues (have to / has to)
skills.S: Describe jobs and what they involve
skills.R: Read a famous-person profile and make notes
skills.W: Write a job profile with have to

lp.wu: Job Charades: Students take turns miming a job while others guess, saying 'You are a...' or 'Is he a...?' The teacher whispers the job to the mimer (e.g., 'doctor', 'chef') and writes new words on the board.
wuAlt: Job Bingo: Each student draws a 3x3 grid with jobs, the teacher calls out duties (e.g., 'You help sick people'), students mark the matching job.
Job Pictionary: Students draw a job, others guess using 'Is it a...?'
lp.pres: Show flashcards of 5 jobs (teacher, chef, doctor, engineer, artist). For each, model sentences: 'A teacher has to work in a school.' 'A chef has to cook food.' Ask 'What does a doctor have to do?' and check understanding with thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Job Story: Tell a short story about a day in the life of a chef, using 'has to' (e.g., 'He has to wake up early').
Realia: Bring a chef's hat, doctor's stethoscope, etc., and ask 'What does a chef have to wear?'
lp.prac: Job Duty Drill: In pairs, students take turns picking a job card and saying one duty (e.g., 'A pilot has to fly planes'). The teacher monitors and corrects 'have to' vs 'has to'.
pracAlt: Job Dominoes: Match job cards to duty cards (e.g., 'teacher' -> 'teach students') using 'has to'.
Job Memory Game: Flip cards, match jobs with duties, saying 'A doctor has to help sick people'.
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue between two teens talking about their parents' jobs. Students tick the duties they hear (e.g., 'My dad has to work late'). Play twice, check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Job Simon Says: 'Simon says a doctor has to wear a coat!' Students mime the action. If Simon doesn't say 'Simon says', they stay still. Fast-paced to refocus after break.
lp.prod: Group Poster Project: In groups of 3, create a poster about a dream job with 5 facts using 'have to' (e.g., 'A YouTuber has to make videos'). Include a drawing. Present to the class with follow-up questions like 'Why do you want that job?'
lp.rw: Read a short text about a famous Moroccan engineer (e.g., Latifa Laabiss). Students highlight 3 duties using 'has to' and write 2 sentences about her job on a sticky note.
lp.st: Sing 'What Do You Want to Be?' (to the tune of 'Twinkle Twinkle') with actions. Close with: 'Today we described jobs using have to. Thank you, class!'
g: Mime a job, others guess 'You are a...'
Match duties to jobs on your grid
Say 'A ___ has to ___' with job cards
Match jobs to duties with 'has to'
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 more dream jobs with duties on the back of their poster.
Support learners: Use sentence starters like 'A ___ has to ___' on the poster.
hw: Read the 'Jobs in Morocco' text and circle 5 new words.
Interview a family member about their job and write 2 duties using 'has to'.
Draw your dream job and write 3 sentences about it.
lp.tip: Pair strong/weak learners during the poster project to encourage peer teaching; use local jobs like 'artisan' or 'agricultural worker' to connect to their context.

weeks.obj: Compare two cities, two phones, two bands; compare two cities, foods, or teams with comparative adjectives
weeks.lang: comparatives (-er, more... than) + comparatives + much/a lot/far + comparative
weeks.act: Roleplay cafe/shop/street situation about comparatives
weeks.hw: write a 6-8 sentence paragraph about comparatives

skills.L: Listen to comparisons with much / a lot / far
skills.S: Compare two cities, phones or bands
skills.R: Read a comparison article and find the modifiers
skills.W: Write modified comparatives (much better than)

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find Someone Who...' Students mingle, ask 'Is [city] more modern than [city]?', and write names. Teacher models 'Is Rabat more historic than Casablanca?', students reply 'Yes, it is' or 'No, it isn't'.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'City Comparison Pairs' - Teacher writes two cities on board, students shout out differences (bigger, older, noisier)
Alternative 2: 'Guess the City' - Teacher gives clues 'It's smaller than Casablanca but more famous for tourism', students guess
lp.pres: Presentation: Show two phone flashcards (iPhone vs Samsung). Model 'The iPhone is more expensive than the Samsung'. Elicit 'more... than' for longer adjectives. Drill with 'Rabat is older than Agadir' and 'Casablanca is bigger than Fes'. Check with 'Which is bigger?' questions.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use local band posters (L'mencha vs Hoba') to compare 'more popular' and 'better'
Alternative 2: Bring two food items (orange juice vs mint tea) to compare 'sweeter' and 'more refreshing'
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Comparative Race' - In pairs, students get a list of adjective pairs (big/small, old/new). They race to write 5 correct sentences. Teacher monitors for 'more' vs '-er' errors. Support with sentence frames '[A] is [comparative] than [B]'.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Find the Difference' - Students compare two pictures of Moroccan cities (old medina vs new city) using comparatives
Alternative 2: 'Adjective Swap' - Students write 3 adjectives, swap with partner, and make comparative sentences
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play an audio of two tourists comparing Oujda and Tangier. Students tick 'True' or 'False' on a handout with statements like 'Oujda is more beautiful than Tangier'. Replay to check answers.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand Up If...' Teacher says 'Stand up if your city is more modern than your partner's'. Students stand, say '[My city] is more modern', and sit down.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Cafe Comparison Roleplay' - In groups of 3, students roleplay a conversation comparing two cafes (one local, one American). They use 'more expensive', 'better coffee', 'noisier', and 'friendlier'. Teacher circulates, noting good use of 'much/a lot/far'.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read a short text comparing Marrakech and Chefchaouen. Underline all comparatives with 'much' or 'a lot'. Then write 4 sentences about their own city using 'much bigger than' or 'a lot older than'.
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Play 'The City Song' (comparative lyrics). Close with 'Today we learned to compare cities with comparatives. Thank you, class!'
g: Students write 9 comparatives on a grid. Teacher calls out sentences, students mark if true
Students get city cards, race to shout 3 comparatives when teacher shows two
Students race to write -er or more before adjectives on the board
Students find someone whose city is 'far older' than theirs and write it down
Students form a chain: 'Rabat is older than...' next student adds '...but smaller than...'
diff: Fast finishers: Write 5 sentences comparing Oujda and another Moroccan city using 'much/a lot/far'
Support: Use a word bank with comparatives (bigger, older, more expensive) to complete sentences
hw: Option 1: Write a paragraph comparing two Moroccan cities (6-8 sentences)
Option 2: Record a voice note comparing two phones or bands
Option 3: Draw two pictures and label 5 comparatives (e.g., 'taller', 'cheaper')
lp.tip: Use local examples (Rabat vs Casablanca, mint tea vs coffee) to make comparisons meaningful and connect to learners' lives.

weeks.obj: Give class awards using superlatives; use superlatives to nominate classmates for fun awards
weeks.lang: superlatives (the -est, the most...) + superlatives: the most talented, the best
weeks.act:
KET-style task carousel on superlatives and class awards in teams
Project: a guide to Ramadan in Oujda, written for foreign visitors.
weeks.hw:
record yourself speaking for 1 minute about superlatives and class awards
Write 6 tips for visitors during Ramadan.

skills.L: Listen to award speeches with superlatives
skills.S: Give class awards using superlatives
skills.R: Read award texts and find the superlatives
skills.W: Write superlative award nominations

lp.wu: Awards Relay: Students race to write superlatives on the board (e.g., 'the tallest', 'the funniest') in teams, shouting the sentences as they run.
wuAlt: Superlatives Pictionary: Students draw prompts like 'the best singer' for teammates to guess using superlatives.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Who is the most ___?' to find classmates matching superlatives.
lp.pres: Show award certificates with superlatives (e.g., 'Most Talented') and model sentences like 'You are the most creative!' Elicit more examples from students and check understanding with thumbs-up/down for correct/incorrect sentences.
presAlt: Video clip: Play short award speeches with superlatives, then discuss the language used.
Realia: Bring in a trophy and have students write superlatives to describe the winner.
lp.prac: Superlatives Task Carousel: Teams rotate between KET-style tasks (matching superlatives to pictures, completing sentences, and writing nominations) with a worksheet. Monitor and provide sentence frames.
pracAlt: Superlatives Bingo: Call out prompts like 'the best at football' for students to mark on their bingo cards.
Nomination Cards: Students write superlative nominations for classmates on cards and share with the class.
lp.ls: Listen to a short award speech and circle the superlatives heard. Then, write one nomination using the language from the audio.
lp.re: Superlative Charades: Students act out superlatives (e.g., 'the fastest runner') for teammates to guess before the break.
lp.prod: Class Awards Ceremony: In teams, students prepare and present superlative awards to classmates, giving reasons like 'You are the most helpful because...'
lp.rw: Read a short text about Ramadan in Oujda, highlighting superlatives. Then, write 6 tips for visitors using superlatives (e.g., 'The most important tip is...').
lp.st: Watch a 2-minute video about Ramadan traditions in Morocco, then close with the goodbye routine: 'Today we gave awards using superlatives and learned about Ramadan. Great work, everyone!'
