g: Teams race to write superlatives on the board based on prompts.
Students draw superlative awards for teammates to guess.
Students ask and answer questions using superlatives to find classmates.
Students mark superlatives on their bingo cards as they are called out.
Students act out superlatives for teammates to guess.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a trophy and write a superlative award speech for a classmate.
Support: Use sentence frames like 'You are the most ___ because ___' to write nominations.
hw: Record a 1-minute video giving a superlative award to a classmate.
Write 6 superlative tips for visitors during Ramadan in Oujda.
Draw 3 pictures of superlative awards and label them in English.
lp.tip: Encourage students to connect superlatives to Ramadan (e.g., 'the most generous') to reinforce cultural context and make the language meaningful.

weeks.obj: Present detailed future plans; describe weekend and holiday plans with going to
weeks.lang: going to (plans); time expressions + going to + when/after clauses
weeks.act: Two-corner debate on future plans
weeks.hw: do the future plans worksheet from the library folder

skills.L: Listen to detailed plans with time clauses
skills.S: Present my detailed future plans
skills.R: Read a plan text and underline going to + when
skills.W: Write plans with going to + when / after

lp.wu: Plan Pictionary: Write weekend plans on slips (e.g., 'visit grandma', 'study English'). Students draw; classmates guess using 'Are you going to...?' and the drawer responds 'Yes, I am.' or 'No, I'm going to...'.
wuAlt: Plan Charades: Act out holiday plans; peers guess with 'Are you going to...?'
Plan Relay: Teams race to write 'going to' sentences about their weekend on the board.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of Moroccan holidays (Eid, Green March). Model: 'For Eid, I'm going to visit my family after I pray.' Elicit similar sentences. Check with thumbs-up/down: 'Are you going to...?'
presAlt: Use a calendar with events; ask 'What are you going to do on...?'
Show a video of a local festival; pause to ask 'What are they going to do next?'
lp.prac: Find Someone Who...: Students mingle, ask 'Are you going to... this weekend?', write names. Review with 'Yes, [name] is going to...' or 'No, but [name] is going to...'.
pracAlt: Plan Dominoes: Match 'going to' phrases with time clauses (e.g., 'after school' + 'do homework').
Plan Bingo: Call out plans; students cover if they match their own.
lp.ls: Listen to a teen's holiday plans (audio). Students tick activities heard and underline 'going to + when' phrases. Check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Plan Freeze: Teacher calls a plan (e.g., 'going to the beach'); students mime it. On 'Freeze!', they freeze and say a sentence (e.g., 'I'm going to swim after I eat lunch').
lp.prod: Two-Corner Debate: Divide class into 'City Holiday' vs. 'Beach Holiday'. Groups prepare 3 reasons using 'going to + when'. Present; peers ask follow-up questions ('When are you going to leave?').
lp.rw: Read a short text about a teen's Green March plans. Underline all 'going to' + time clauses. Write 3 similar sentences about their own Independence Day plans.
lp.st: Sing 'What Are You Going to Do?' (to the tune of 'Frère Jacques'). Close with: 'Today we talked about plans using going to. Thank you, class!'
g: Draw weekend plans; guess with 'Are you going to...?'
Teams race to write 'going to' sentences on the board
Mingle and ask about weekend plans
Mime plans and say sentences on 'Freeze'
Argue for city vs. beach holiday plans
diff: Fast finishers: Write a paragraph about a dream holiday using 3 'going to + when' clauses.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'I'm going to... after I...'.
hw: Complete the future plans worksheet from the library folder.
Write 5 sentences about your Labour Day plans using 'going to + when'.
Interview a family member about their weekend plans and report back.
lp.tip: Use local holidays (Eid, Green March) to make plans relatable; teens engage more when discussing familiar events.

weeks.obj: Make predictions about the future; make simple predictions about the future
weeks.lang: will/won't (predictions); maybe, probably + will / won't for predictions; probably
weeks.act: Write and swap 5 quiz questions about will for predictions
weeks.hw: interview a family member about will for predictions in English

skills.L: Listen to prediction debates and note the reasons
skills.S: Make and justify predictions
skills.R: Read a futures article and rank the predictions
skills.W: Write predictions with probably / likely to

lp.wu: Play 'Future Predictions Charades': teacher writes 'will/won't' predictions on slips (e.g., 'It will rain tomorrow'), students act them out while others guess using 'Will it...?'.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Prediction Relay' - teams race to write 'will/won't' sentences on the board about the teacher's prompts.
Alternative 2: 'Maybe, Probably' TPR - teacher gestures 'maybe' (shrug) or 'probably' (nod) for students to repeat.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of Moroccan holidays (Eid, Green March) and ask 'What will happen next Eid?'. Model 'It will probably be sunny' and 'Maybe people will visit family'. Check understanding with 'Thumbs up/down' for true/false sentences.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a short story about a boy planning Labour Day with 'will/won't' predictions.
Alternative 2: Display a weather forecast and elicit 'It will probably be hot'.
lp.prac: Play 'Prediction Bingo': students draw 4 grid squares and write predictions (e.g., 'I will pass my test'). Teacher reads statements; students mark off matches and shout 'Bingo!' when complete.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Scramble' - pairs reorder word cards to make correct 'will/won't' sentences.
Alternative 2: 'Chain Predictions' - students add to a class prediction circle (e.g., 'Aicha will... and then...').
lp.ls: Listen to a 1-minute dialogue about Independence Day predictions (e.g., 'There will be fireworks'). Students tick predictions they hear from a list.
lp.re: Play 'Stand Up If...': teacher calls out predictions (e.g., 'Stand up if you will eat couscous tonight'), students stand/sit to respond.
lp.prod: Write and swap 5 quiz questions about will for predictions (e.g., 'Will Morocco win the World Cup?'). Partners answer with 'Yes, probably' or 'No, maybe not'.
lp.rw: Read a short text about future tech in Morocco and rank predictions from 'most likely' to 'least likely'. Write 2 sentences about one prediction using 'will' or 'probably'.
lp.st: Read a story 'Aisha's Eid Predictions' with will/won't, then close with 'Today we learned to make predictions with will. Great work, class! Thank you!'
g: Draw 'will/won't' scenarios for others to guess
Add 'will' sentences to a shared story
Ask peers 'Will you...?' and tally responses
diff: Fast finishers: write 3 'unlikely' predictions using 'won't probably'.
Support: use sentence frames 'It will probably...' and 'Maybe it will...'.
hw: Interview a family member: 'What will you do next weekend?' and note answers.
Write 5 predictions about your city in 10 years using 'will' and 'probably'.
Watch a 1-minute weather forecast and write 3 predictions.
lp.tip: Use local events (like Green March) to make predictions relevant, and encourage students to justify guesses with 'because' to build longer turns.

weeks.obj: Give health and lifestyle advice; give simple health advice with should
weeks.lang: should/shouldn't; body and illness vocabulary + should / shouldn't; advice expressions
weeks.act: Picture description relay with health and advice photos
weeks.hw: write 5 quiz questions about health and advice for next class

skills.L: Listen to advice dialogues (should + expressions)
skills.S: Give health and lifestyle advice
skills.R: Read a lifestyle leaflet and extract the advice
skills.W: Write an advice paragraph with reasons

lp.wu: Play 'Simon Says' with health commands: 'Simon says touch your head', 'Simon says pretend to cough', 'Simon says drink water'. Students stand and follow, sitting if they miss a command.
wuAlt: Play 'Charades' with illness actions: student mimes 'headache', 'stomachache', 'fever', others guess in English.
Do a quick 'Body Parts Quiz': teacher points to body parts, students shout the English word.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of people with health problems (e.g., headache, cold). Elicit problems in Arabic/English, then model advice: 'You should rest', 'You shouldn't eat ice cream'. Check understanding with thumbs up/down for correct advice.
presAlt: Read a short dialogue between two friends: one says 'I have a sore throat', the other replies 'You should drink tea'. Highlight 'should/shouldn't'.
Use a role-play: teacher pretends to be sick, student gives advice using target language.
lp.prac: Play 'Advice Relay': teams take turns drawing a health problem flashcard and saying 'You should...' or 'You shouldn't...'. Award points for correct sentences. Monitor and correct pronunciation.
pracAlt: Do 'Match the Problem to the Advice': worksheet with problems on one side, advice on the other; students draw lines.
Play 'Find Someone Who...': walk around asking 'Should I...?' about health habits, e.g., 'Should I eat vegetables?'
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue between a doctor and a patient. Students fill in gaps in a worksheet: 'You should ________' (rest), 'You shouldn't ________' (play sports). Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Play 'Health Charades Relay': two lines of students race to mime a health problem (e.g., 'fever') and their partner guesses the word in English. First team to guess correctly wins a point.
lp.prod: Pair role-play: Student A is a friend with a health problem (e.g., 'I can't sleep'), Student B gives 2-3 pieces of advice using 'should/shouldn't'. Swap roles. Encourage follow-up questions like 'Why?'
lp.rw: Read a short 'Healthy Habits' leaflet. Underline all advice with 'should/shouldn't'. Then write 3 sentences about your own habits, e.g., 'I should drink more water'. Share with a partner.
lp.st: Sing 'Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes' with actions, then end with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to give health advice. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams race to say correct 'should/shouldn't' sentences for health problems.
Students mime illnesses for others to guess in English.
Match health problems to advice flashcards.
Ask classmates about health habits using 'should' questions.
Practice giving advice in pairs using problem cards.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 5-sentence paragraph about 'My best health advice'.
Support learners: use sentence starters like 'You should ________' on the board.
hw: Write 5 quiz questions about health advice, e.g., 'What should you do if you have a headache?'
Draw 3 pictures of health problems and write advice for each.
Interview a family member about their health habits and write 2 pieces of advice for them.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references, e.g., 'You should drink mint tea for a sore throat', to make advice relatable. Avoid sensitive topics like alcohol or pork.

weeks.obj: Plan a trip and book things; tell a simple travel story and ask travel questions
weeks.lang: past simple review; travel vocabulary + travel words; I'd like to book...
weeks.act:
Speed-chat: 3 rotations of travel and holidays questions
How we celebrate: compare Eid here and holidays abroad (paragraph + venn).
weeks.hw:
read the short travel and holidays text and note 5 new words
Write 8 sentences comparing Eid with another holiday.

skills.L: Listening folder: travel dialogues - booking
skills.S: Plan a trip and book things by phone
skills.R: Read travel texts and complete the booking form
skills.W: Write a booking email (4 sentences)

lp.wu: Travel Charades: Students take turns acting out travel words (e.g., 'flight', 'hotel', 'beach') while classmates guess. They shout 'Travel word!' when they know the answer.
wuAlt: Travel Pictionary: Draw travel words on the board for others to guess.
Travel Bingo: Call out travel words; students mark them on their bingo cards.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of travel scenes and model sentences like 'I went to the beach.' Elicit past simple forms from students. Ask 'Where did you go?' to check understanding before practice.
presAlt: Use a short story about a holiday to model travel vocabulary and past simple.
Bring in realia (plane ticket, hotel brochure) to introduce booking phrases.
lp.prac: Booking Dialogue Drill: Students practice 'I'd like to book a room' in pairs with a dialogue worksheet. Support with sentence starters on the board.
pracAlt: Travel Board Game: Roll dice and answer travel questions to move forward.
Travel Word Sort: Group travel vocabulary into categories (transport, accommodation, activities).
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue between a tourist and hotel receptionist. Students complete a booking form with details like dates and room type.
lp.re: Travel Relay: Teams race to write past simple sentences on the board about travel. The first team to write 5 correct sentences wins.
lp.prod: Plan an Eid Holiday: In groups, students plan a 3-day Eid trip using a worksheet. They present their plan using 'We'd like to book...' and 'We went to...'.
lp.rw: Read a short text about Eid celebrations in Morocco and abroad. Write 4 sentences comparing Eid with another holiday using 'more' or 'less'.
lp.st: Read a story about a child's Eid holiday. End with 'Today we learned to talk about travel and Eid. Thank you, class!'
g: Call out travel words; students mark them on their cards.
Act out travel words for others to guess.
Teams write past sentences about travel on the board.
Practice booking phrases in pairs with a worksheet.
Groups plan a holiday and present it to the class.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 5-sentence paragraph about their best holiday.
Support weaker learners: Use a word bank to complete the comparison sentences.
hw: Read the travel text and note 5 new words.
Write 8 sentences comparing Eid with another holiday.
Draw a picture of your dream holiday and label 5 things.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan travel examples (e.g., Chefchaouen, Agadir) to make the lesson relatable and boost engagement.

weeks.obj: Give and support opinions about music; express and justify opinions about music
weeks.lang: I think... because; opinion adjectives + opinion language: I think / In my opinion; because
weeks.act: Pair interview, then report your partner to the class
weeks.hw: write a 6-8 sentence paragraph about music and opinions

skills.L: Listen to song reviews and note the opinion language
skills.S: Give and support opinions about music
skills.R: Read music reviews and find the support phrases
skills.W: Write a song review with reasons

lp.wu: Music Opinions Charades: Students draw cards with music genres (e.g., rap, rock, pop) and act them out while others guess. The actor says 'I think this music is...' after guessing.
wuAlt: Quick poll: 'Stand if you like rap, pop, or traditional music.' Students say 'I like...' or 'I don't like...'
Music Bingo: Call out genres, students cross them off and say 'I think [genre] is...' when they get a line.
lp.pres: Show 3 flashcards with opinion adjectives (exciting, boring, relaxing). Model sentences: 'I think rap is exciting because it has strong beats.' Check understanding by asking 'Why do you think pop is boring?'
presAlt: Play 10-second song clips, students hold up flashcards (exciting/boring/relaxing) and say 'I think this is...'
Read a short review together, underline the 'I think... because' phrases.
lp.prac: Find the Match: Pair students, give them 5 genre cards and 5 reason cards (e.g., 'because it's fast', 'because it's calm'). They match them and say 'I think [genre] is... because...'.
pracAlt: Opinion Relay: Teams race to write 'I think [genre] is...' on the board with a correct reason.
Sentence Builder: Use word cards to make sentences like 'I think jazz is... because...'.
lp.ls: Listen to 2 short song reviews (KET-style). Students note the opinion words and reasons in a table. Check answers by replaying and pausing at key phrases.
lp.re: Genre Jump: Teacher calls out genres, students jump to the corner labeled 'exciting', 'boring', or 'relaxing' and say 'I think [genre] is... because...'.
lp.prod: Pair Interview: Students ask each other 'What music do you like? Why?' Then report to class: 'My partner, [name], thinks [genre] is... because...'.
lp.rw: Read a short KET-style review about a Moroccan singer. Underline all 'I think... because' phrases. Then write 3 sentences about a song they know using the same structure.
lp.st: Play the song 'Lamma Bada Yatathanna' (a traditional Arabic song). Discuss opinions using today's language. Close with 'Today we learned to give opinions about music. Great job, everyone!'
g: Students mark off 'I think... because' sentences called out by the teacher.
Students act out a genre while others guess using 'I think this is... because...'
Teams race to write 3 reasons why they like/dislike a genre.
Sort genre cards into 'exciting', 'boring', 'relaxing' with reasons.
Survey classmates about music tastes and report findings using 'I think... because...'
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 4-sentence review of a song from a Moroccan festival.
Support learners: Use sentence starters like 'I think... is... because...' on a worksheet.
hw: Write a 6-sentence paragraph about your favorite music genre using 'I think... because'.
Record a 30-second audio review of a song, explaining your opinion.
Draw a poster with 3 music genres and your opinions with reasons.
lp.tip: Encourage students to connect music to local festivals like the Gnaoua World Music Festival to build cultural relevance.

weeks.obj: Describe gadgets and compare them; talk about devices and habits; use like/love/hate + -ing with verbs
weeks.lang: tech vocabulary; verb patterns (like doing / want to do) + technology words; comparatives review
weeks.act: Group project: a poster about technology with 5 facts
weeks.hw: record yourself speaking for 1 minute about technology

skills.L: Listen to tech-debate arguments
skills.S: Describe gadgets and compare them
skills.R: Read a tech article and answer inference questions
skills.W: Write tech comparisons with comparatives

lp.wu: Gadget Charades: students pick a tech word flashcard (phone, laptop, headphones) and act it out without speaking; classmates guess 'Is it a...?'
wuAlt: Tech Vocabulary Race: write 5 tech words on the board, students race to circle the correct one when you say it
Tech Survey: ask 3 classmates 'Do you like using...?' and tally yes/no answers
lp.pres: Show real gadgets (phone, tablet, headphones) and model sentences: 'I like using my phone because it's fast'; 'I hate waiting for laptops to load'; check understanding with thumbs up/down for 'like/love/hate + -ing'
presAlt: Tech Poster Demo: display a poster with 5 tech facts, point and say 'This phone is cheaper than that one'; 'I love watching videos on tablets'
Dialogue Practice: read a short dialogue comparing phones, highlight 'like/hate + -ing' patterns
lp.prac: Match the Gadget: students match device pictures to sentences like 'I love listening to music on...' in pairs; monitor and correct verb patterns
pracAlt: Tech Sentence Race: in teams, race to write sentences with 'like/love/hate + -ing' about gadgets; first team to write 5 correct sentences wins
Gadgets Survey: ask 5 classmates 'Do you like using...?' and record answers with tally marks
lp.ls: Listen to a 1-minute debate: 'Phones vs Tablets for Students'; students circle 'phone' or 'tablet' based on who likes/dislikes each device; check answers in pairs
lp.re: Tech Freeze Dance: play music with tech sounds (typing, notifications); when music stops, students freeze and say 'I love/hate using...' about a gadget
lp.prod: Group Poster Project: in groups of 4, create a poster with 5 tech facts (e.g., 'Phones are cheaper than laptops', 'I love using tablets for games'); present to class with 'I like...' sentences
lp.rw: Read a short text 'My Tech Habits' (40 words); answer 3 inference questions: 'Does the writer like phones? Why?', 'What device does the writer use most?', 'Why does the writer hate laptops?'
lp.st: Watch a 2-minute animated story 'A Day Without Gadgets'; discuss 'What did you learn?'; end with 'Today we learned to describe gadgets—great work, goodbye!'
g: Teams race to write 3 comparative sentences about gadgets (e.g., 'Phones are smaller than laptops')
Students describe a gadget without saying its name (e.g., 'It's small, you call people')
Students write 'like/hate + -ing' sentences in bingo squares; cross off when classmates say them
Act out tech actions (typing, scrolling) for classmates to guess
Unscramble sentences like 'I love watching videos on tablets'
diff: Fast finishers: add 2 more comparisons to their poster (e.g., 'Tablets are heavier than phones')
Support: use sentence starters like 'I like... because...' on the poster
hw: Record a 1-minute video saying 3 tech facts (e.g., 'I love using phones for music')
Write 5 sentences comparing 2 gadgets (e.g., 'Laptops are bigger than phones')
Interview a family member about their tech habits and write 3 sentences
lp.tip: Use local tech examples (e.g., 'In Morocco, many people use phones for payments') to make the lesson relatable and culturally relevant.

weeks.obj: Tell a story with a past continuous background; tell what was happening with past continuous support
weeks.lang: past continuous (was/were + -ing) + past simple vs past continuous; when/while
weeks.act: Roleplay cafe/shop/street situation about stories
weeks.hw: do the stories worksheet from the library folder

skills.L: Listen to a story with when / while pauses
skills.S: Tell a story with a past-continuous background
skills.R: Read a fable and map past simple vs continuous
skills.W: Write a story with when / while (8 sentences)

lp.wu: Start with 'Yesterday's Timeline': Students draw 3 simple activities they did yesterday on a paper timeline. They share with a partner using 'I was...ing' (e.g., 'I was eating lunch at 1 PM').
wuAlt: 'Find Someone Who Was...' mingle: Students ask 'Were you...ing yesterday?' (e.g., 'Were you watching TV?') and find classmates who say yes.
'Picture Prompt': Show a busy street photo; students guess what people were doing using 'He/She was...ing'.
lp.pres: Present a short comic strip of a Moroccan souk scene with speech bubbles. Model sentences like 'While I was buying spices, the merchant was weighing dates.' Use flashcards of actions (buying, walking, talking) and elicit 'was/were + -ing'. Check comprehension with thumbs up/down for true/false sentences about the story.
presAlt: Use a realia box with Moroccan items (tea set, mint, babouches) to act out a story: 'While I was pouring tea, my friend was eating cookies.'
Show a 1-minute video clip of a busy market in Oujda; pause to ask 'What was he/she doing?'
lp.prac: Play 'Past Continuous Chain': Students sit in a circle. Student 1 starts with 'I was walking to school.' Student 2 says 'While he was walking to school, I was buying bread.' Continue the chain. Monitor for correct 'when/while' usage.
pracAlt: 'Sentence Race': Write two columns on the board (was/were). In teams, students race to write correct past continuous sentences about a picture (e.g., 'The boy was riding a bike').
'Matching Pairs': Match past continuous sentence halves (e.g., 'While the teacher was talking' + 'the students were taking notes').
lp.ls: Listen to a short audio diary of a teen's day at the American Space Oujda. Students fill in blanks with past continuous verbs (e.g., 'While I was ___ the computer, my friend was ___ a book'). Play twice; check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Play 'Freeze Frame': Call out an action (e.g., 'You were eating!'). Students freeze in a pose and say what they were doing. After the break, restart with a new action.
lp.prod: Roleplay 'Cafe Chaos': In pairs, one is a waiter, one is a customer. The waiter asks 'What were you doing when the order came wrong?' The customer responds with past continuous. Swap roles. Encourage follow-up questions like 'Why were you laughing?'
lp.rw: Read a short fable 'The Hare and the Tortoise' with past simple and continuous highlighted. Students underline all 'was/were + -ing' and write 3 sentences explaining what the hare was doing (e.g., 'While the tortoise was walking slowly, the hare was sleeping').
lp.st: Tell a simple story about a Moroccan wedding using past continuous: 'While the family was dancing, the bride was smiling.' End with a quick recap: 'Today we told stories about what was happening.'
g: Students sit in a circle and pass a ball, saying a past continuous sentence about the person next to them (e.g., 'You were smiling').
Show a busy photo; teams race to write 5 past continuous sentences about it.
Teacher mimes an action; students guess 'Were you...ing?' and the teacher responds.
Students act out an action; others guess using 'He/She was...ing'.
Roll a dice; land on a square and make a sentence with 'when' or 'while' using past continuous.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 4-sentence story about a Moroccan festival (e.g., Green March) using past continuous.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'While I was ___, my friend was ___' with word bank.
hw: Complete the 'Past Continuous Stories' worksheet from the library folder (fill in gaps with was/were + -ing).
Write 8 sentences about what you and your family were doing during last Friday's prayer time.
Draw a comic strip of 3 panels showing what was happening during a power cut at home; label with past continuous.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural contexts (souks, weddings, festivals) to make past continuous relatable. Teens engage more with stories they recognize.

weeks.obj: Do KET-style reading tasks and check strategies; complete sample A2 Key reading tasks and understand the format
weeks.lang: KET reading part formats; skimming and scanning + KET reading parts 1-3 strategies
weeks.act: KET-style task carousel on KET reading in teams
weeks.hw: interview a family member about KET reading in English

skills.L: KET listening - full part practice
skills.S: KET speaking with strategy checklists
skills.R: KET reading parts 1-3 with strategies (KET folder)
skills.W: KET writing - short message and story

lp.wu: KET Reading Relay: Students race in teams to match 5 KET reading part 1 sentences with 5 picture prompts, shouting 'Found it!' when correct.
wuAlt: KET Vocabulary Pictionary: Teams draw KET reading keywords (e.g., 'library', 'birthday') for others to guess.
KET Sentence Scramble: Teams unscramble 5 jumbled KET part 1 sentences.
lp.pres: Show a KET reading part 1 sample on the whiteboard, highlighting 'skimming' (reading for gist) and 'scanning' (finding keywords). Model with a think-aloud: 'I see the word 'library'—I'll scan for it.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down for 'skimming vs scanning'.
presAlt: KET Strategy Cards: Distribute cards with 'skim' or 'scan'—students hold up when you read a task instruction.
KET Video Clip: Play a 2-minute Cambridge video explaining KET parts 1-3, pausing to discuss.
lp.prac: KET Reading Task Carousel: Teams rotate 3 stations (parts 1-3), using strategy checklists. At part 1, they match sentences to pictures; part 2, match descriptions to people; part 3, read short texts for true/false. Support with sentence starters like 'This is part 1, so I need to...'.
pracAlt: KET Strategy Dice: Roll a dice (1=skim, 2=scan) to decide how to approach a task.
KET Peer Teaching: Stronger learners explain strategies to weaker ones in pairs.
lp.ls: KET Listening Part 1 Practice: Students listen to 5 short conversations and match speakers to pictures, using the same skimming/scanning strategies from reading. Check with a quick 'What did you hear?' round.
lp.re: KET Word Jump: Write KET reading keywords (e.g., 'cinema', 'museum') on the floor—students jump to the word when called, shouting the strategy ('Scan!').
lp.prod: KET Reading Quiz Show: Teams create 3 KET-style questions (parts 1-3) for others, using today's strategies. They present with 'This tests your skimming skills!'
lp.rw: KET Writing Part 1 Practice: Students write a 40-word short message to a friend about a book they read, using past simple and comparatives (e.g., 'It was interesting. The story was better than the movie.').
lp.st: Read a short story about a student preparing for KET, then close with: 'Today we learned KET reading strategies—thank you, class!'
g: Teams race to match 10 KET part 2 sentences with 5 people descriptions.
Students stand for true, sit for false after a KET part 3 text read aloud.
Find 5 hidden KET reading words in the classroom (e.g., 'library', 'cinema').
Pass a 'strategy' ball—when caught, name a skimming/scanning tip.
Mark off KET part 1 tasks as they complete them in teams.
diff: Fast finishers: Create a KET part 1 puzzle with their own drawings.
Support learners: Use a highlighted KET text with key words circled.
hw: Interview a family member about KET reading: 'What do you think is hardest about reading in English?' and write 2 sentences.
Write 3 KET part 2 questions for a classmate about their hobbies.
Watch a 5-minute KET reading video online and list 2 strategies.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'Green March') in KET texts to boost engagement—teens connect better with familiar contexts.

weeks.obj: Do a KET-style speaking task in pairs; complete a KET-style paired speaking task confidently
weeks.lang: KET speaking part 1-2 frames + KET speaking part 1: personal questions
weeks.res: KET folder; Speaking tests folder; Tests/Grammar
weeks.act: Two-corner debate on KET speaking
weeks.hw: write 5 quiz questions about KET speaking for next class

skills.L: KET listening - harder parts
skills.S: KET-style paired speaking under time
skills.R: KET reading parts 4-5: skimming and scanning
skills.W: KET-style form and message writing

lp.wu: KET Speaking Speed Dating: Students stand in two lines facing each other. The teacher calls a topic (e.g., 'hobbies'), and students in one line ask 'What do you like doing in your free time?' to the person opposite. After 30 seconds, the teacher claps, and one line shifts to the right to speak to a new partner. Repeat 3 times.
wuAlt: KET Speaking Bingo: Students write 9 personal questions (e.g., 'Where do you live?') on a grid. They mingle, asking questions, and getting signatures from classmates who answer 'Yes'. First to get 3 in a row wins.

KET Speaking Relay: Teams race to write KET Part 1 questions on the board. Each student writes one question (e.g., 'How old are you?'), then passes the marker. First team with 10 correct questions wins.
lp.pres: Show KET Speaking Part 1 flashcards (e.g., a house, a book, a football). Model answering 'Where do you live?' with 'I live in a house in Oujda.' Elicit similar answers for 'What do you read?' and 'What sports do you play?' Check understanding by asking students to repeat the model sentences chorally.
presAlt: Use a KET Speaking Part 1 dialogue script on the board. Read it aloud with a strong student, then have pairs read it in roles. Highlight the question-answer pattern.
Show a short video of two teens doing KET Speaking Part 1. Pause after each question, asking students to predict the answer. Discuss good responses.
lp.prac: KET Speaking Part 1 Drill: Students work in pairs with a worksheet of 10 personal questions (e.g., 'What time do you get up?'). They take turns asking and answering, using the model language. Monitor and correct pronunciation. Give stickers for good eye contact.
pracAlt: KET Speaking Question Chain: Students sit in a circle. Student 1 asks a question to Student 2 (e.g., 'What's your favourite food?'). Student 2 answers then asks a new question to Student 3. Continue around the circle, with the teacher helping if a question repeats.
KET Speaking Flashcard Match: Students match question flashcards (e.g., 'How many siblings do you have?') to answer flashcards (e.g., 'I have two brothers.'). Then practice the pairs in groups.
lp.ls: Play a KET Listening Part 1 audio where two teens introduce themselves. Students listen and tick the correct answers on a multiple-choice worksheet (e.g., 'What's Tom's favourite sport? A Football B Basketball'). Replay to check answers, focusing on names and details.
lp.re: KET Speaking Two Corners: Label corners 'Agree' and 'Disagree'. Read a statement (e.g., 'Teenagers should have a mobile phone'). Students run to a corner and explain why using 'I agree because...' or 'I disagree because...'. Switch statements quickly to keep energy high.
lp.prod: KET Speaking Part 2 Practice: Students work in pairs. Student A gets a card with a topic (e.g., 'My best friend') and must speak for 1 minute. Student B then asks 2 follow-up questions (e.g., 'How old is your friend?'). Swap roles. Time each turn and give feedback on fluency.
lp.rw: KET Reading Part 4: Students read a short text about a Moroccan festival (e.g., Green March). They answer 5 multiple-choice questions by scanning for keywords. Then, write 2 sentences about their own favourite festival using 'I like...' and 'Because...'.
lp.st: Play a KET Speaking-themed song (e.g., 'Hello, Hello, How Are You?'). End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we practiced KET Speaking Part 1-2. Great job, everyone! Thank you for your hard work. See you next week!'
g: Teams take turns answering KET Part 1 questions for points. If correct, they get 1 point; if they add a follow-up question, they get 2 points.
Students sit in a circle. Student 1 says 'My name is Ali and I like football'. Student 2 says 'My name is Sara and Ali likes football. I like reading'. Continue, adding names and hobbies.
Students draw cards with roles (e.g., 'new student', 'interviewer') and practice Part 1-2 conversations using prompts.
Students interview 3 different partners about their hobbies, family, and school. They write down 1 interesting fact from each interview.
Write 5 incorrect KET answers on the board (e.g., 'I like play football'). Students work in pairs to find and fix the errors.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a full KET Speaking Part 2 dialogue (questions and answers) about their dream holiday.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence starter worksheet (e.g., 'I live in...') to help with Part 1 answers.
hw: Write 5 quiz questions about KET Speaking Part 1 for next class (e.g., 'What's your favourite subject?').
Record yourself answering 3 KET Part 1 questions and bring it to class.
Draw a picture of your family and write 3 sentences about them using 'This is...' and 'He/She likes...'.
lp.tip: For KET Speaking practice, focus on fluency over accuracy. Praise confident answers first, then gently correct errors. In the Moroccan context, encourage students to share local festivals or hobbies to build cultural pride.

weeks.obj: Run a review carousel with teams; review the year across stations with accuracy and speed
weeks.lang: all year outcomes + semester 2 review
weeks.act:
Mixed-skills revision circuit in teams
Project: eco-poster campaign for the Space; must/should for green rules.
weeks.hw:
revise your notes for the assessment week
Design a 5-rule green poster with must/should.

skills.L: Listening carousel - mixed audio
skills.S: Team speaking carousel with time limits
skills.R: Reading carousel - mixed KET-style tasks
skills.W: Transformation and short-writing station

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Earth Day Quiz Relay' - Teams race to answer 5 quick questions about Earth Day (e.g., 'When is Earth Day?', 'What does recycle mean?') using flashcards. Winners get 1 point per correct answer.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Green Pictionary' - Students draw Earth Day words (e.g., 'tree', 'water') for teams to guess.
Alternative 2: 'Word Association Chain' - Start with 'Earth', each student adds one related word.
lp.pres: Present 'must/should' for rules using flashcards showing green actions (e.g., 'turn off lights'). Model: 'You must recycle bottles.' 'You should use a reusable bag.' Check understanding with thumbs-up/down.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a short story about a student who doesn't follow green rules, then correct with must/should.
Alternative 2: Show a video clip of littering, discuss what people must/should do.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Green Rules Sorting' - Teams sort 10 picture cards into 'must' (e.g., 'save water') and 'should' (e.g., 'plant trees') categories. Monitor and correct errors.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Builder' - Students match halves of sentences (e.g., 'You must...' + 'not waste food').
Alternative 2: 'Rule Relay' - Teams write one must/should rule per student on the board.
lp.ls: Listening slot: 'Earth Day Tips' - Students listen to a short audio (3 tips) and match them to pictures. Check with peer correction.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Green Charades' - Students act out green actions (e.g., 'compost') for teams to shout the verb form ('You must compost!').
lp.prod: Production task: 'Eco-Poster Campaign' - Teams design a 5-rule poster for the American Space using must/should (e.g., 'You must use both sides of paper'). Present with 1-2 sentences per rule.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: 'KET-style Gap Fill' - Students read a short text about Earth Day and fill in 5 gaps with must/should. Then write 2 sentences about their own green habits.
lp.st: Story: 'The Earth Day Hero' - Read a short story about a teen who makes green changes. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we reviewed must/should for green rules. Thanks for your hard work!'
g: Teams race to answer Earth Day questions for points.
Students draw Earth Day words for teams to guess.
Teams sort cards into 'must' and 'should' categories.
Students act out green actions for teams to shout.
diff: Fast finishers: Add a sixth rule with a 'must not' (e.g., 'You must not litter').
Support: Provide sentence starters (e.g., 'You must...') for the poster.
hw: Homework 1: Design a 5-rule green poster for your home using must/should.
Homework 2: Write 5 sentences about what you must/should do to help the planet.
Homework 3: Interview a family member about their green habits and report back.
lp.tip: Use local examples (e.g., 'You should save water in Oujda') to make the rules relevant and memorable.

weeks.obj: Show my progress in the final assessment; complete final written and speaking assessments; celebrate
weeks.lang: all year outcomes + full-year review; KET-style final tasks
weeks.act:
Mixed-skills revision circuit in teams
Dream job interviews: question forms + reporting answers.
weeks.hw:
revise your notes for the assessment week
Write your dream-job interview Q&A (6 exchanges).

skills.L: Final listening paper
skills.S: Final paired speaking, then celebrate
skills.R: Final reading paper
skills.W: Final writing - KET-style task

lp.wu: Students play 'Speed Review' in teams. Teacher shows flashcards of jobs (doctor, teacher, engineer). Teams race to say the job and one sentence about it (e.g., 'A doctor helps people').
wuAlt: Students do a 'Find Someone Who' survey about future jobs using 'Are you going to be...?' questions.
Teacher writes 5 job-related words on the board; students create sentences with them in 60 seconds.
lp.pres: Teacher introduces 'Dream Job Interviews' using a model dialogue. She pretends to be a job interviewer (e.g., 'Why do you want to be a teacher?'). Elicit question forms and model answers. Check understanding with 'What question did I ask?'
presAlt: Teacher uses a short video clip of a job interview (1 min) and discusses it with the class.
Students match interview questions to possible answers (e.g., 'What are your strengths?' → 'I am hard-working').
lp.prac: Students practice in pairs. One is the interviewer, the other is the job applicant. Teacher provides a question list (e.g., 'Why do you want this job?', 'What can you do?'). Monitor and correct errors.
pracAlt: Students play 'Interview Chain': one student asks a question, the next answers and asks a new question, etc.
Teacher distributes 'Job Role Cards' (e.g., 'You are a chef') and students prepare questions for that role.
lp.ls: Students listen to a KET-style listening recording of a job interview. They tick the correct answers on a worksheet (multiple choice).
lp.re: After break, students play 'Job Charades'. One student acts out a job; others guess using 'Are you a...?' questions.
lp.prod: Students conduct a 'Dream Job Interview' in pairs. They take turns asking and answering 6 questions about their dream job. Teacher observes for fluency and accuracy.
lp.rw: Students complete a KET-style writing task: 'Write 40-50 words about your dream job. Say what it is and why you want it.' Teacher provides a sentence starter: 'My dream job is...'
lp.st: Teacher reads a short story about a young person achieving their dream job. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we practiced job interviews and celebrated our progress. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams answer trivia questions about jobs (e.g., 'Where does a doctor work?')
Students describe a job without naming it (e.g., 'You wear a uniform and drive a bus')
Students write jobs on a bingo card; cross off when a classmate mentions it
Students switch partners every 2 minutes for quick interviews
Match job ads to the right person using picture cards
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph about a famous person's job.
Support: Use a word bank with job vocabulary and sentence starters.
hw: Write a dream-job interview Q&A (6 exchanges).
Review all your notes for the assessment week.
Watch a short video about a job and write 3 sentences about it.
lp.tip: Use peer feedback during the interview practice to build confidence—students learn from each other's mistakes in a low-stakes environment.
checklist: I can ask and answer questions about jobs
I can write 40-50 words about my dream job
I can understand a short interview recording
I can use 'going to' for future plans
I can compare jobs using 'better than'
I can use 'should' for advice
I can participate in a paired interview

levels.desc: For teens aged 13–17 who can handle A1 with confidence. The year consolidates A1 and pushes into A2 — present simple vs continuous, past simple, comparatives, going to + will, modals — through longer speaking turns, short text reading, and connected paragraph writing (40–50 words), with KET task types rehearsed weekly.

levels.label: Teens · Advanced

weeks.theme: Welcome and getting to know you
weeks.obj: Swap detailed profiles and ask follow-up questions; introduce themselves, ask 5 get-to-know-you questions, and complete a partner profile
weeks.lang: be (am/is/are); Wh- questions (what, where, how old); possessive adjectives + question tags; follow-up question drills
weeks.act: KET-style task carousel on getting to know you in pairs
weeks.hw: record a 90-second opinion clip about getting to know you

skills.L: Listen for follow-up cues in detailed interviews
skills.S: Swap detailed profiles and ask follow-up questions
skills.R: Read detailed profiles in PET part 1 style (PET folder)
skills.W: Write a full self-profile with details

lp.wu: Human Bingo: Students walk around with bingo cards containing prompts like 'speaks 3 languages' or 'has a pet'. They ask classmates 'Do you...?' and mark off squares. First to get a line shouts 'Bingo!'
wuAlt: Name Chain: Students stand in a circle, each says their name + one hobby, e.g., 'I'm Ali, I play football'. The next repeats the previous names and adds their own.
Two Truths and a Lie: Students write two true statements and one false about themselves, then read them aloud for others to guess the lie.
lp.pres: Show a flashcard of a teen with hobbies (football, music, reading). Model: 'My name's Sam. I'm 15. I live in Oujda. I like football. What about you?' Elicit questions using 'What?', 'Where?', 'How old?', then drill possessive adjectives + tags: 'You live here, don't you?'
presAlt: Profile Poster: Draw a simple profile on the board with blanks (Name: ___, Age: ___, Hobbies: ___). Fill it in with a student's info, then ask them questions about it.
Video Clip: Play a 30-second clip of a teen introducing themselves. Pause after each sentence to repeat and drill.
lp.prac: KET-Style Task Carousel: Set up 4 stations with profile cards (e.g., 'Lina, 16, likes cooking'). In pairs, students rotate stations, asking questions to complete a partner profile form. Monitor and correct 'be' + Wh- errors.
pracAlt: Find Someone Who...: Distribute a grid with prompts like 'Find someone who has a birthday in December'. Students mingle, asking 'Do you have...?' and writing names.
Profile Matchup: Give each student half a profile (e.g., 'I'm 15, I like music'). They must find the other half by asking questions.
lp.ls: PET-Style Audio Track: Play a 1-minute recording of two teens swapping profiles. Students listen and fill in a table with details (name, age, hobbies). Replay to check answers, then ask follow-up questions like 'Does he like football?'
lp.re: Stand Up, Sit Down: Call out profile facts (e.g., 'If you like music, stand up! If you live in Oujda, sit down!'). Students respond physically to reactivate the target vocabulary.
lp.prod: Partner Interview Swap: Students form new pairs. Each has 2 minutes to interview their partner using 5 questions (e.g., 'What's your name?', 'Where do you live?', 'How old are you?', 'What do you like?', 'Do you have a pet?'). Then swap roles and share 1 new fact about their partner.
lp.rw: Reading PET Part 1: Give students a short profile text (60 words) about a fictional teen. They answer 5 multiple-choice questions (e.g., 'Where does she live?'). Then write 3 sentences about themselves using the same structure.
lp.st: Read a short story about a teen making new friends at the American Space. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to swap detailed profiles. Thank you, class! See you next week!'
g: Students think of a classmate and describe them using 'He/She is... He/She likes...'. Others guess who it is.
One student says a fact about themselves, the next repeats it and adds one, e.g., 'Ali is 15. He likes football. I'm Fatima, I like music.'
Students draw a hobby or item (e.g., a football) and others guess 'Do you like football?'
Timer for 1-minute interviews with 3 different partners, rotating desks after each round.
Students write 3 statements about themselves, others ask 'Is this true?' to guess the fiction.
Students compare two similar profile cards and spot 3 differences by asking questions.
Students line up by age, then move to form groups based on hobbies, asking 'Do you like...?' to confirm.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 60-word profile of a celebrity, using the target language.
Support weaker learners: Use a sentence frame worksheet to complete their profile (e.g., 'My name's ______. I'm ______ years old. I live in ______. I like ______.')
hw: Record a 90-second video introducing yourself and answering 5 get-to-know-you questions.
Write a 70-word email to a new pen pal describing your hobbies and life in Oujda.
Create a poster with photos and captions about your family and friends, using 'be' + possessives.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'Do you like couscous?', 'Have you been to the Sahara?') to make the language relevant and build rapport with learners.

weeks.obj: Describe relationships and character with examples; describe 4 family members or friends with simple details
weeks.lang: possessive 's; have got; adjectives (tall, kind, funny) + character adjectives + -ed/-ing adjectives
weeks.act: Story circle: build a story about family and friends with target tenses
weeks.hw: do the family and friends reading task and answer in full sentences

skills.L: Listen to character descriptions with anecdotes
skills.S: Describe relationships and character with examples
skills.R: Read a character-based story extract
skills.W: Write a character description with examples

lp.wu: Family Charades: Students take turns acting out a family member (e.g., 'father cooking') while others guess using 'Is he/she your...?' and 'He/She's very...'.
wuAlt: Family Bingo: Students mark off adjectives on a bingo card as the teacher calls them out.
Find Someone Who: Students walk around asking 'Have you got a funny friend?' and tally responses.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of family members with adjectives (e.g., 'My uncle's kind') and elicit sentences. Model 'He's got blue eyes' and 'She's very funny'. Check understanding with 'What's his name? Is he tall?'
presAlt: Realia: Bring in photos of your family and describe them using possessive 's'.
Story: Read a short story about a family and highlight target language.
lp.prac: Adjective Relay: Teams race to write adjectives on the board for a family member. Then, 'Find the Pair' students match descriptions to photos using 'He's got...' and 'She's very...'.
pracAlt: Sentence Builder: Students arrange word cards to make correct sentences about family.
Describe and Draw: One student describes a family member; another draws it.
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue between two teens discussing their best friends. Students complete a table with names, adjectives, and examples (e.g., 'Layla: funny, tells jokes').
lp.re: Family Tree Tag: Students run to touch flashcards on the wall when the teacher says 'Touch the person who is kind!'
lp.prod: Story Circle: Groups build a story about a family problem (e.g., 'lost keys') using target language. Each student adds one sentence (e.g., 'My brother's tall. He's got the keys.').
lp.rw: Read a short story about a Moroccan family during Eid. Then, write 60 words describing your own family using 'have got' and 3 adjectives.
lp.st: Read 'The Funny Friend' picture book. Close with 'Today we described family and friends with examples. Thank you, class!'
g: Students ask 'Has he got brown hair?' to guess a mystery family member.
Teams list 5 adjectives for a family member in 1 minute.
Students draw family members for others to guess.
Each student adds one sentence to a story about friends.
Students match photos to descriptions using possessive 's'.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 50-word paragraph about a famous person's character.
Support: Use a word bank with adjectives and sentence starters.
hw: Read the text 'My Best Friend' and answer 3 questions in full sentences.
Draw your family tree and write 3 sentences about one person.
Write an email to a friend describing your family using 5 adjectives.
lp.tip: Use local examples (e.g., 'My uncle's kind, like during Ramadan') to make the theme relatable. Encourage students to share about Moroccan family traditions.

weeks.obj: Report on a class survey with numbers; describe their school day using present simple I/you/we/they
weeks.lang: present simple; time expressions (at 7 o'clock, in the morning) + adverbs of degree: quite, really, a bit
weeks.act: Group presentation: 3-minute talk about daily routines with visuals
weeks.hw: prepare a 1-minute presentation about daily routines for next class

skills.L: Listen to survey results with degrees (quite / really)
skills.S: Report on a class survey with numbers
skills.R: Read a survey article and check the figures
skills.W: Write a survey report paragraph

lp.wu: Students stand in a circle. Teacher throws a soft ball to a student and asks 'What time do you wake up?' The student answers and throws the ball to another student who asks a different routine question (e.g., 'What time do you eat lunch?').
wuAlt: Students play 'Routines Bingo' with a grid of activities (wake up, eat breakfast, go to school) and times (6:00, 7:00, 8:00). They ask classmates 'Do you wake up at 6:00?' and mark the grid.
Teacher shows flashcards of daily routines (brush teeth, go to school). Students race to say the English word when the flashcard is shown.
lp.pres: Teacher projects a survey bar chart showing 'How many students wake up at 6:00, 7:00, 8:00?' and models: 'Quite a few students wake up at 7:00. Really few students wake up at 8:00.' Students repeat the sentences. Teacher checks understanding by asking 'What time do quite a few students wake up?'
presAlt: Teacher uses realia: a clock and flashcards of routines. Sets the clock to 7:00 and holds up 'wake up' card, saying 'I wake up at 7:00. It's quite early.' Students mimic with different times and routines.
Teacher writes model sentences on the board: 'I wake up at 6:00. It's a bit early. I eat lunch at 1:00. It's quite late.' Students read and match times to routines.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs with a survey worksheet showing 5 routines and 3 time options. They ask their partner 'What time do you [routine]?' and mark the answers. Then they report: 'Mohammed wakes up at 6:00. It's really early.' Teacher circulates to correct pronunciation and model sentence structures.
pracAlt: Students play 'Survey Relay' in teams. Each team gets a paper with 5 routines. They run to ask classmates 'What time do you [routine]?' and write the answers. First team to complete and report wins.

Teacher gives students a 'Find Someone Who...' grid with routines like 'wakes up before 7:00'. Students mingle, ask questions, and write names. Then they report: 'Fatima wakes up at 6:00. It's really early.'
lp.ls: Students listen to a recording of a student talking about their school day: 'I start school at 8:30. It's quite early. I finish at 4:00. It's a bit late.' They fill in a gap-fill worksheet with the times and adverbs (quite, really, a bit).
lp.re: Students play 'Routine Charades'. Teacher whispers a routine (e.g., 'brush teeth') to a student, who acts it out. Classmates guess 'Do you brush your teeth at 7:00?' The actor nods or shakes their head.
lp.prod: Students prepare a 3-minute group presentation with visuals (drawn or printed). They survey their group about 3 routines (wake up, eat dinner, go to bed) and report: 'In our group, quite a few students eat dinner at 8:00. Really few students go to bed at 10:00.' Each group presents to the class.
lp.rw: Students read a short article about a Moroccan teen's school day (e.g., 'I wake up at 6:00 for Fajr prayer. I go to school at 8:30. I finish at 4:00. I help my family at 5:00.'). They underline all the times and adverbs (quite, really, a bit). Then they write 3 sentences about their own day using present simple.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about 'A Day in the Life of a Student in Oujda' using visual aids. Story includes: 'I wake up at 6:00 for Fajr. It's really early! I go to school at 8:30. It's quite busy. I finish at 4:00. I relax at home.' Class repeats key phrases. Close with: 'Today we reported on surveys and described our school day. Thank you, class!'
g: Students get a bingo grid with times (6:00, 7:00, 8:00). They ask classmates 'What time do you wake up?' and mark the grid if someone matches.
Teams race to write 5 routines on the board. First team to finish and say all routines correctly wins.
Students match time cards (e.g., '7:00') to routine cards (e.g., 'wake up') and make sentences.
Students act out adverbs (quite = slow, really = fast) while classmates guess.
Teams survey classmates about routines and write down the fastest answers. First team to finish wins.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a paragraph comparing their routine to a partner's using 'quite' and 'really'.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'I [routine] at [time]. It's [adjective].' with a word bank.
hw: Write 5 sentences about your daily routine using present simple and adverbs (quite, really, a bit).
Record a 1-minute video talking about your school day. Use: 'I start at... It's quite early.'
Draw a comic strip of your daily routine with captions in English.
lp.tip: Use local context (e.g., Fajr prayer, family time) to make routines relatable. Encourage students to use Moroccan holidays like Eid to compare routines.

weeks.obj: Discuss school topics with the right articles; compare school subjects and say what they like and why
weeks.lang: school subjects; like/don't like + noun; because + articles a/an/the; school collocations
weeks.res: Lesson Plans (topics set); Worksheets/Print outs; PET
weeks.act:
Roleplay with a complication around school life
Spooky story chain: each pair writes one paragraph, read aloud with lights off; Halloween taboo.
weeks.hw:
find a real article or video about school life and summarise it in 3 sentences
Write the ending of the class spooky story (6-8 lines).

skills.L: Listen for a / an / the use in school talk
skills.S: Discuss school topics with the right articles
skills.R: Read a school-life article and find the articles
skills.W: Write school paragraphs with accurate articles

lp.wu: Article Race: Write 'a/an/the' on the board. Students stand in teams. You say a school phrase like 'I like ___ science class.' Teams race to grab the correct article card and place it in the blank. First correct team gets a point.
wuAlt: Subject Charades: Students mime a school subject (e.g., 'math' by writing numbers, 'art' by painting). Others guess, 'Is it ___ art?'
Quick Quiz: Flashcards of school subjects. Students say 'I like ___ geography' or 'I don't like ___ history' with correct articles.
lp.pres: Use a spooky school poster. Point to subjects: 'Look, ___ science lab has a ghost! I like ___ science because it's interesting.' Drill 'I like/don't like + [article] + subject + because + [article] + reason.' Check with thumbs up/down: 'Do you like ___ math?'
presAlt: Mystery Box: Put school object props (book, ruler) in a box. Students pull one out and say, 'I like ___ ruler because it's useful.'
Video Clip: Show 1-min clip of a funny school scene. Pause and ask, 'What does he like? Does she like ___ PE?'
lp.prac: Halloween Taboo: In pairs, students get cards with a school subject and taboo words. They describe it for their partner to guess, e.g., 'It's ___ subject. You need a pen. I like it because it's creative.' Partner must say, 'Is it ___ art?'
pracAlt: Article Dice Game: Roll a die. 1=a, 2=an, 3=the, 4=like, 5=don't like, 6=because. Students make a sentence with the words rolled, e.g., 'I like ___ history because ___ teacher is nice.'
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking, 'Do you like ___ science? Why?' and write names.
lp.ls: Listen to a spooky school dialogue. Students fill in blanks with 'a/an/the': 'My friend hates ___ art class because ___ teacher is ___ ghost.' Check answers in pairs before class review.
lp.re: Zombie Tag: One student is 'Zombie Teacher'. They chase others. If tagged, the student must say, 'I don't like ___ P.E. because it's hard!' before unfreezing. Game continues for 2 mins.
lp.prod: Roleplay: 'The Haunted School'. In pairs, one student is a new kid, the other is a ghost guide. Guide says, 'Welcome to ___ school! I like ___ library because ___ books are magic.' New kid responds, 'Do you like ___ science? I don't like it because ___ lab is scary.'
lp.rw: Read a short article about a spooky school event. Circle all 'a/an/the'. Then write 3 sentences about your own school using the same structure: 'I like ___ subject because ___ teacher is ___ kind person.'
lp.st: Turn off lights. Read the spooky story chain paragraph by paragraph. End with, 'The ghost said, "I like ___ history because ___ past is full of secrets."' Close with: 'Today we talked about school subjects with articles. Thanks for your great ideas, goodbye!'
g: Teams grab 'a/an/the' cards for phrases like 'I like ___ math'
Describe school subjects without taboo words
Tagged students say 'I don't like ___ P.E.'
Ask 'Do you like ___ science?' and write names
Pull school objects and make sentences
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 4-line poem about a spooky school subject using articles
Support: Use a word bank with 'a/an/the' and subjects to build sentences
hw: Find a real article/video about school life and summarise it in 3 sentences
Write the ending of the class spooky story (6-8 lines)
Interview a family member about their school days and report back using 'I like/don't like... because...'
lp.tip: Use the Halloween theme to make article practice memorable—ghosts love grammar! For Moroccan teens, connect to local school traditions like the baccalaureate to increase engagement.

weeks.obj: Compare hobby habits with verb patterns; talk about hobbies using like + -ing and adverbs of frequency
weeks.lang: like/love/hate + -ing; always, sometimes, never + verb patterns: stop/try/enjoy + -ing vs to
weeks.res: Lesson Plans (topics set); Games/Game ideas; PET
weeks.act:
Write-swap: peer-edit a paragraph about hobbies and free time
Project: Green March timeline posters, presented in the past simple.
weeks.hw:
write a KET-style email (25+ words) about hobbies and free time
Write 5 past-simple sentences about the Green March.

skills.L: Listen to stop / try / enjoy + -ing in use
skills.S: Compare hobby habits with verb patterns
skills.R: Read hobby articles and find the patterns
skills.W: Write my hobby profile with 3 patterns

lp.wu: Hobby Charades: Students take turns miming a hobby while others guess using 'Do you like...?' or 'Are you...ing?'. The mimer responds with 'Yes, I love/like/hate + -ing' and an adverb of frequency.
wuAlt: Hobby Bingo: Students write 9 hobbies in a grid. The teacher calls out sentences like 'I sometimes swim', and students cross off matching hobbies.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Do you ever...?' to find peers who match the hobby on their sheet.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of hobbies (e.g., football, painting, coding). Model sentences: 'I always play football', 'I never paint', 'I enjoy coding'. Elicit adverbs of frequency from the board. Check understanding by asking 'What do you always do?'
presAlt: Hobby Survey Demo: Teacher surveys students with 'Do you like + -ing?', then models writing results on the board.
Story Time: Read a short paragraph about a teen's hobbies, highlighting verb patterns with colored chalk.
lp.prac: Verb Pattern Sort: Students sort sentence strips into 'like + -ing' and 'try + to' columns. In pairs, they write 3 sentences about themselves using each pattern. Monitor for accuracy.
pracAlt: Matching Game: Match hobby sentences (e.g., 'I love hiking') to adverbs of frequency (e.g., 'always') on the board.
Sentence Relay: Teams race to write correct sentences with target verb patterns on the whiteboard.
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue between two teens discussing hobbies. Students tick activities they hear and write down the verb patterns (e.g., 'I enjoy playing video games'). Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Hobby Hop: Stand in a circle. Teacher calls a hobby (e.g., 'swimming'), and students hop if they like it, jump if they love it, or squat if they hate it. Repeat with adverbs of frequency.
lp.prod: Green March Timeline Poster: In groups, create a poster with 5 key events of the Green March (past simple). Each student writes 1 sentence using 'I learned that...' + past simple verb. Present posters to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short article about Moroccan hobbies. Underline all examples of 'like + -ing' and 'stop + to'. Then write a paragraph about your own hobbies using 3 target patterns.
lp.st: Read a story about a teen's hobby journey. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we compared hobby habits using verb patterns. Great work, everyone! Have a great day!'
g: Teams race to write sentences with 'love/stop/enjoy + -ing' on the board.
Students toss a ball and make a sentence with the adverb they catch.
Survey classmates about hobbies using target language and tally results.
Teams write past simple sentences about the Green March on the board.
Answer questions about the Green March using past simple verbs.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second paragraph comparing their hobby habits with a partner's.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'I always/never/sometimes + verb + -ing'.
hw: Write a 25+ word KET-style email to a friend about your hobbies.
Write 5 past-simple sentences about the Green March.
Interview a family member about their hobbies and report back.
lp.tip: Use real-life Moroccan hobbies (e.g., mint tea preparation, henna art) to make the lesson culturally relevant and boost engagement.

weeks.obj: Talk about past and present abilities; say what they can and can't do; hold a short can-can't interview
weeks.lang: can/can't for ability; adverbs (well, fast) + could / was able to / be good at
weeks.act: Podcast-style panel discussion about sports and abilities
weeks.hw: write a 10-12 sentence text about sports and abilities with 2 paragraphs

skills.L: Listen to could / was-able-to achievement stories
skills.S: Talk about past and present abilities
skills.R: Read a sports profile and find the ability language
skills.W: Write my abilities timeline

lp.wu: Students stand in a circle. Teacher says 'I can play football' and throws a soft ball to a student, who must say a true sentence about their own ability and throw the ball to another student. The game continues until everyone has spoken twice.
wuAlt: Students write down 3 things they can do and 3 they can't, then mingle and share sentences with 3 partners using 'I can/can't...'
Teacher projects 5 sports images (football, swimming, running, tennis, basketball). Students guess 'He/She can play...' for each image.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a photo of a Moroccan athlete (e.g., Hicham El Guerrouj) and says 'He can run very fast. He could run 1500m in 3 minutes 26 seconds.' Teacher models 'can' for present ability and 'could' for past ability, highlighting the difference. Students repeat chorally and individually. Teacher asks 'What can you do now? What could you do when you were younger?' to check understanding.
presAlt: Teacher uses a timeline on the board: 'Now' and '5 years ago'. Students write sentences about their abilities in both tenses, then compare with a partner.
Teacher tells a personal story: 'When I was 10, I couldn't swim, but now I can swim well.' Students ask follow-up questions with 'Can you...?' and 'Could you...?'
lp.prac: Students work in pairs with a 'Find someone who...' grid with sports abilities (e.g., 'can swim 50m', 'can play basketball', 'could ride a bike at age 5'). They ask 'Can you...?' or 'Could you...?' and write names. Teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation of 'can/could'.
pracAlt: Teacher distributes flashcards with sports and abilities. Students pick one and create a sentence (e.g., 'I can play tennis' or 'He could run fast'). They then mingle and read their sentences to others, who guess the sport.
Students play 'Ability Charades': one student mimes a sport ability (e.g., swimming), others guess 'Can you swim?' or 'Could you swim?'.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 2-minute podcast clip where two teens talk about their sports achievements. They complete a gap-fill worksheet with sentences like 'Last year, I ___ (can/was able to) climb Mount Toubkal' and 'I ___ (can/could) swim before I ___ (can/could) ride a bike'. Teacher plays the clip twice, then reviews answers.
lp.re: Students stand in two lines. Teacher calls out an ability (e.g., 'can jump high'). The first student in each line mimes it, and the fastest team gets a point. The game continues with different abilities.
lp.prod: Students form groups of 3-4. Each group chooses a Moroccan sport (e.g., football, athletics, martial arts) and creates a 3-minute podcast panel discussion. They take turns saying 'I can/can't...' (present) and 'I could/couldn't...' (past), using adverbs like 'well' or 'fast'. Groups present to the class, and peers ask questions.
lp.rw: Students read a short profile of a Moroccan athlete (e.g., Noureddine Morceli) and underline all examples of 'can/could/was able to'. Then, they write 5 sentences about their own abilities, using at least one 'could' and one 'can'.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a young Moroccan footballer who practiced hard and 'could' eventually play professionally. Students reflect on 'What abilities do you need to achieve your goals?' Class ends with the teacher saying: 'Today we talked about what we can do now and what we could do before. Thank you for your hard work! Goodbye.'
g: Teams race to write sentences on the board with 'can/could' and sports words.
Students mime sports abilities for others to guess using 'Can you...?' or 'Could you...?'
Students create bingo cards with abilities; teacher calls them out and students mark if they can do them.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a paragraph about a famous Moroccan athlete's abilities using 'could' and 'can'.
Support learners: Use sentence starters like 'I can...' and 'I could...' to guide their writing.
hw: Write a 10-12 sentence text about your sports abilities: one paragraph about now (can/can't) and one about the past (could/couldn't).
Interview a family member about their sports abilities when they were young and write 5 sentences.
Draw a timeline of your sports abilities from age 5 to now, with a sentence for each age.
lp.tip: Use local sports heroes like Hicham El Guerrouj to make the theme culturally relevant and motivating for Moroccan learners.

weeks.obj: Write the opening of a Halloween ghost story; understand a short Halloween text and exchange themed vocabulary
weeks.lang: Halloween vocabulary; there is/there are (spooky room descriptions) + past continuous scene-setting; while/as
weeks.act:
Escape-room style grammar puzzle on Halloween
Project: 18 November 1955 - timeline cards and a mini museum walk with captions.
weeks.hw:
record a 90-second opinion clip about Halloween
Write a short paragraph: what independence means to me.

skills.L: Listen to a ghost-story opening
skills.S: Pitch a ghost-story opening dramatically
skills.R: Read a model ghost-story opening (Seasonal pack)
skills.W: Write the opening of a Halloween ghost story

lp.wu: Students play 'Mummy Wrap' in teams: one student is wrapped in toilet paper like a mummy by their team, who must shout Halloween-themed words (ghost, witch, pumpkin) as they wrap. The fastest team wins a small prize.
wuAlt: Alternative warm-up 1: Students draw a spooky room on the board, labeling items with 'There is/There are' sentences.
Alternative warm-up 2: Students play 'Halloween Pictionary' with vocabulary cards like 'bat', 'cobweb', 'tombstone'.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a spooky room picture on the projector, modeling sentences like 'There is a black cat in the corner' and 'There are cobwebs on the lamp'. Students repeat chorally, then write their own sentences about the picture. Teacher checks understanding with thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Alternative presentation 1: Teacher uses a 'Halloween Vocabulary' PowerPoint with images and definitions, drilling pronunciation.
Alternative presentation 2: Teacher distributes a 'Spooky Room' worksheet, and students label items using 'There is/There are'.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs to describe a haunted house picture using 'There is/There are'. Then, they play 'Escape Room Grammar': teams solve puzzles to unlock a box, matching Halloween vocabulary to sentences and correcting errors in 'There is/There are' structures.
pracAlt: Alternative practice 1: Students play 'Bingo' with Halloween vocabulary, calling out sentences like 'There is a witch'.
Alternative practice 2: Students complete a 'Fill-in-the-Blanks' worksheet with 'There is/There are' and spooky items.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 2-minute ghost story opening (audio from Seasonal pack), filling in a gap worksheet with past continuous phrases (e.g., 'While I was walking...'). They then compare answers in pairs before a class check.
lp.re: Students play 'Zombie Tag': one student is 'it' and must walk slowly like a zombie, tagging others who freeze. After the break, they re-energize by acting out Halloween words (e.g., 'boo', 'shriek').
lp.prod: In groups, students write the opening of a Halloween ghost story (60-80 words) using past continuous for scene-setting (e.g., 'The wind was howling as I opened the door'). They then pitch their story dramatically to the class, using gestures and tone.
lp.rw: Students read a model ghost story opening (Seasonal pack), highlighting past continuous and 'while/as' clauses. Then, they write their own spooky paragraph (50-70 words) using the target grammar, focusing on creating atmosphere.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short, interactive Halloween story with moral (e.g., 'Kindness defeats fear'), encouraging students to shout 'Boo!' at scary parts. Close with: 'Today we learned to write spooky story openings. Thanks for your creativity, class!'
g: Teams wrap a student in toilet paper while shouting Halloween words.
Teams solve puzzles to unlock a box, matching vocabulary to sentences.
Students walk like zombies and tag others who freeze.
Students draw words like 'bat' or 'tombstone' for others to guess.
Groups act out their story openings dramatically.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second paragraph using 'while/as' to describe another spooky scene.
Support: Use a sentence frame (e.g., 'While I was ___, I saw ___') to write their story.
hw: Homework option 1: Record a 90-second opinion clip about Halloween, using vocabulary from class.
Homework option 2: Write a short paragraph (50 words) on what independence means to you.
Homework option 3: Create a timeline of 18 November 1955 (Independence Day) with 3 key events.
lp.tip: Use the American Space Oujda context to connect Halloween to Moroccan traditions like 'Aicha Kandicha', emphasizing cultural exchange and respect for differences.

weeks.obj: Describe recipes with quantities; categorize food vocabulary and ask about quantities
weeks.lang: countable/uncountable; some/any; How much/How many + quantifiers: a little, a few, too much/many
weeks.act:
Two-corners debate, then switch sides on food and drinks
Compare Thanksgiving with harvest customs here; gratitude survey with graphs.
weeks.hw:
do the food and drinks reading task and answer in full sentences
Interview 3 people: one thing they are thankful for; report back.

skills.L: Listen to a recipe with quantifiers
skills.S: Describe a recipe with a little / a few
skills.R: Read recipe texts and classify the quantifiers
skills.W: Write my favourite recipe in steps

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Food Category Race' — Students stand in two teams. Teacher calls out a food group (e.g., 'fruits'), one student from each team runs to the board to write one correct word. First to write a valid word gets a point. Repeat with 'vegetables', 'dairy', etc.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'I went to the market' — Students sit in a circle. First student says 'I went to the market and bought an apple.' Next student repeats and adds another item (e.g., 'I went to the market and bought an apple and some milk.').
Alternative 2: 'Flashcard Quick Sort' — Teacher shows food flashcards; students shout 'countable!' or 'uncountable!' as quickly as possible.
lp.pres: Presentation: Show a simple Thanksgiving recipe (e.g., cranberry sauce) on the board. Highlight quantifiers: 'a cup of sugar', 'a few cranberries', 'too much water'. Elicit countable/uncountable nouns and model sentences like 'How much sugar?' 'How many cranberries?' Check understanding with quick thumbs-up/down for true/false statements about the recipe.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use realia (empty cups, spoons) to demonstrate quantities. Students say 'How much?' or 'How many?' as you pour/show items.
Alternative 2: Show a short video clip of a cooking show with clear quantifiers; students note down examples they hear.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Recipe Fill-in' — Students work in pairs to complete a worksheet with a recipe using 'a little', 'a few', 'some', 'any', 'too much/many'. Teacher monitors and corrects errors. Then, pairs swap worksheets and check answers together.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Quantifier Bingo' — Teacher calls out sentences like 'I have too many potatoes'; students cross off matching pictures on their bingo cards.
Alternative 2: 'Find Someone Who...' — Students walk around asking 'Do you have any apples at home?' and 'Do you eat too much sugar?' to find classmates who say yes.
lp.ls: Listening slot: Students listen to a recording of a Thanksgiving recipe (e.g., pumpkin pie) and fill in missing quantities on a worksheet. They then compare answers in pairs before a class check. This checks their ability to catch specific quantifiers in context.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand Up If...' — Teacher says prompts like 'Stand up if you like a little honey in your tea' or 'Stand up if you eat too many oranges'. Students stand up or sit down based on their preferences, moving their bodies to re-engage.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Two-Corners Debate' — Label corners 'Traditional Thanksgiving' and 'Moroccan Harvest Feast'. Students choose a corner and discuss in groups: 'Which foods are better? Why?' After 5 minutes, they switch corners and argue the opposite side. Encourage using 'a little', 'a few', 'too much/many' in their arguments.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read a short text comparing Thanksgiving and Moroccan harvest customs (e.g., Aid al-Fitr or Green March). They then write 3-4 sentences about one custom they find interesting, using quantifiers like 'many people' or 'a little food'.
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Play a short animated story about gratitude (e.g., 'The Thankful Turkey'). End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to describe recipes with quantities. Thank you, class! Have a great day!'
g: Students race to write food words on the board in teams.
Pairs complete a recipe worksheet with correct quantifiers.
Students cross off pictures matching teacher's sentences.
Students stand/sit based on food preference prompts.
Students debate food traditions, switching sides mid-activity.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 60-word email describing their favorite recipe using 5+ quantifiers.
Support: Use a word bank with quantifiers and countable/uncountable nouns during the debate.
hw: Homework 1: Read a short text about Thanksgiving foods; answer 3 questions in full sentences using 'how much/many'.
Homework 2: Interview 3 people: 'What are you thankful for?'; report back in 2-3 sentences each.
Homework 3: Write a simple recipe for a Moroccan dish using 'a little', 'a few', 'some', 'any'.
lp.tip: Tip: Use local harvest festivals (like Green March) to bridge cultural gaps and make quantifiers more relevant. Compare quantities in Moroccan dishes (e.g., 'a little cumin', 'many onions') to reinforce learning.

weeks.obj: Handle a cafe complaint politely; order food and drink politely in a roleplay
weeks.lang: Would you like...? I'd like...; Can I have...? + polite complaints: I'm afraid, Would you mind...?
weeks.res: Listening (graded cafe dialogues mp3); Lesson Plans/Food; KET
weeks.act: KET-style task carousel on at the cafe in pairs
weeks.hw: prepare a 1-minute presentation about at the cafe for next class

skills.L: Listening folder: cafe dialogues - polite complaints
skills.S: Handle a cafe complaint politely
skills.R: Read complaint emails and find the polite frames
skills.W: Write a short polite complaint message

lp.wu: Cafe Charades: Students mime actions (ordering, drinking, complaining) while others guess the phrase using 'Would you like...?' or 'I'd like...'.
wuAlt: Cafe Bingo: Students write 5 cafe items, teacher calls prompts (e.g., 'a cold drink'), students cross off if they have it.
Speed Dating Cafe: Students interview 3 peers about their favorite cafe drink using 'Can I have...?'
lp.pres: Show 2 flashcards (correct vs. wrong order) and model polite phrases: 'I'd like a coffee, please' vs. 'Give me coffee'. Elicit the polite version. Check understanding with 'thumbs up/down' for polite/rude examples.
presAlt: Role-play a rude customer vs. a polite one, highlighting phrases. Use a cafe menu realia.
Read a short dialogue gap-fill on the board, students fill in polite requests.
lp.prac: Polite Phrases Drill: Students stand in two lines, facing each other. Line A says 'Would you like...?' Line B replies 'I'd like...'. They rotate partners after 2 turns.
pracAlt: Cafe Menu Task: Pairs take turns ordering from a printed menu using target phrases.
