Chain Story: Each student adds one polite sentence to a cafe story (e.g., 'I went to a cafe. I'd like...').
lp.ls: Listen to a 2-minute dialogue of a customer politely complaining about cold coffee. Students circle the polite phrases ('I'm afraid', 'Would you mind...') on a worksheet.
lp.re: Cafe Relay: Teams race to write polite complaints on the board (e.g., 'Would you mind heating my pizza?'). One runner per team, first correct wins.
lp.prod: Cafe Complaint Roleplay: Pairs act as customer and waiter. Customer uses polite phrases to complain (e.g., 'I'm afraid my soup is cold'). Waiter apologizes and solves it. Switch roles.
lp.rw: Read a short email complaint about a cafe. Underline all polite phrases. Then write a 60-word reply from the manager, apologizing politely.
lp.st: Read a funny story 'The Polite Ghost at the Cafe'. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to order and complain politely in cafes. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams race to circle all polite phrases on a menu.
Students mime complaints for others to guess the phrase.
Teacher calls out rude phrases, students mark polite alternatives.
Students run to the board to write a polite order.
Pairs correct a rude cafe dialogue.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 2-minute dialogue between a very polite customer and a confused waiter.
Support: Use sentence starters ('I'd like...', 'Would you mind...') on flashcards for reference.
hw: Write a 1-minute presentation about your dream cafe, using polite phrases.
Record yourself ordering a drink and complaining politely, send audio.
Design a cafe menu with 5 items and write 3 polite orders for it.
lp.tip: Model Moroccan hospitality by emphasizing how polite phrases show respect—key in local culture. Pair strong/weak learners to boost confidence.

weeks.obj: Describe places with relative clauses; give simple directions and describe their neighborhood with there is/are
weeks.lang: there is/there are; prepositions of place; imperatives (turn, go) + relative clauses: the place where, the man who
weeks.act: Story circle: build a story about my city and directions with target tenses
weeks.hw: find a real article or video about my city and directions and summarise it in 3 sentences

skills.L: Listen to descriptions with relative clauses
skills.S: Describe places with who / which / where
skills.R: Read a city guide and find the relative clauses
skills.W: Write place descriptions with 2 relative clauses

lp.wu: City Map Race: Students get a simple map of Oujda with landmarks. In pairs, they race to find and say 3 places using 'There is/are', e.g., 'There is a mosque near the old market.'
wuAlt: Neighborhood Bingo: Each student gets a bingo grid with places (park, shop, school). Teacher calls out descriptions, e.g., 'a place where you play football', students mark the matching square.
Direction Charades: One student mimes an action (e.g., 'turn left'), others guess the imperative and say the full phrase.
lp.pres: Show a photo of Oujda's Medina with arrows. Introduce 'The place where...' and 'The man who...' with model sentences: 'The place where you buy spices is the souk.' 'The man who sells bread is at the corner.' Check understanding by asking 'What/Who...?' questions.
presAlt: Realia Tour: Bring in a Moroccan tea set or a mint bag. Describe it: 'This is the thing which we use for tea.' Students repeat and describe other objects.
Picture Story: Show a comic strip of someone getting lost. Use relative clauses to explain: 'He is the boy who is lost.'
lp.prac: Relative Clause Relay: In teams, students take turns adding a relative clause to a sentence about a city place, e.g., 'The café... where you meet friends.' Support with sentence frames on the board.
pracAlt: Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Find someone who lives in a place where there is a garden.' They write names and check answers.
Describe and Draw: One student describes a place using 2 relative clauses, partner draws it, then they swap roles.
lp.ls: Listen to a short audio tour of Oujda. Students tick places mentioned and circle the relative clauses used in the transcript. Check answers by having students read aloud the clauses they found.
lp.re: Simon Says Directions: After the break, play 'Simon says: Turn left towards the place where there is a fountain.' to reactivate imperatives and prepositions.
lp.prod: Neighborhood Guide Project: In groups, students create a 3-slide presentation (paper or digital) about their neighborhood using 'There is/are' and 2 relative clauses per slide, e.g., 'The park where we play football has a new bench.'
lp.rw: Read a short city guide paragraph. Underline all relative clauses. Then write 3 original sentences about Oujda using 'which' or 'where'.
lp.st: Read a folktale about a lost traveler in Morocco. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to describe places with relative clauses. Thank you, class!'
g: One student gives directions from point A to B using imperatives, partner traces the route on a map.
Students draw a place while others guess using 'Is it the place where...?'
Students build a story by adding one relative clause each turn, e.g., 'I went to a place where...'
Students hop to different spots in the room following 'Go to the place between... and...'
Teacher reads sentences, students stand up if they hear a relative clause.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 5-sentence paragraph about their dream neighborhood using 3 relative clauses.
Support: Use a word bank with 'which', 'where', 'who' to fill in blanks in sentences.
hw: Find a video about Oujda's landmarks and summarize it in 3 sentences with one relative clause.
Write an email to a friend describing your favorite place in Oujda using 'there is/are' and 'which/where'.
Draw a map of your route to school and write 5 directions using imperatives.
lp.tip: Use local landmarks (e.g., the King's Palace, the university) to make relative clauses meaningful and culturally relevant.

weeks.obj: Shop and negotiate with too and enough; handle a simple shop exchange: sizes, colors, prices
weeks.lang: clothes vocabulary; How much is/are...? this/that/these/those + too + adjective / not + adjective + enough
weeks.act: Group presentation: 3-minute talk about shopping and clothes with visuals
weeks.hw: write a KET-style email (25+ words) about shopping and clothes

skills.L: Listen to too / enough negotiations
skills.S: Shop and negotiate with too and enough
skills.R: Read product reviews and find too / enough
skills.W: Write a product review with too / enough

lp.wu: Flashcard Speed Review: Hold up clothing flashcards (jeans, t-shirt, dress, jacket, sneakers, scarf); students shout the English word and a price in Moroccan Dirhams. Teacher asks 'How much is/are...?' to prompt full sentences.
wuAlt: Price Guessing Game: Teacher mimes putting on an item; students guess 'Is it 100 DH?' until correct.
Clothes Charades: Students act out wearing an item; others guess 'Are you wearing a hat?'
lp.pres: Show a too-small t-shirt and too-big jeans; ask 'Why can't I wear this?' Elicit 'It's too small/big.' Drill model sentences: 'This shirt is too small for me.' 'These jeans aren't big enough.' Check with thumbs-up/down: 'Is this jacket too warm?'
presAlt: Realia Display: Bring in actual clothes; students compare sizes with 'too/ enough'.
Storytime: Show a comic strip of a shopping fail; students identify problems with 'too/ enough'.
lp.prac: Worksheet Gap-Fill: Complete sentences like 'This dress is _____ expensive.' with 'too' or 'enough'. Pair Drill: Student A describes an item ('This coat is not warm enough.'); Student B responds with a solution ('Try this one.')
pracAlt: Board Race: Two teams race to write 'too/ enough' sentences about clothing items.
Chain Drill: Students take turns adding to a story: 'I bought a shirt, but it was too small...'.
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue at a clothing store where a customer exchanges items; students tick problems (size/ color/ price) on a worksheet. Play twice: first for gist, second for details.
lp.re: Simon Says with 'too/ enough': 'Simon says touch something too expensive!' Students mime touching an item and saying 'This is too expensive!'
lp.prod: Roleplay Shop Exchange: In pairs, one is a customer returning a shirt (too small), one is a shop assistant. Use target language: 'This shirt is too small.' 'Do you have a bigger size?' 'These are not long enough.' Swap roles.
lp.rw: Read a short product review about sneakers; underline all sentences with 'too/ enough'. Then write 2-3 sentences reviewing a Moroccan market item using the same structure.
lp.st: Read a short story about a teen's shopping trip in Oujda; discuss with partners: 'What was too expensive?' End with 'Today we learned to negotiate with too/ enough. Thank you, class!'
g: Students bargain with fake Dirhams: '50 DH!' 'Too cheap! 100 DH!'
Call out 'too big/small'; students cross off matching clothing items.
Students walk and describe outfits: 'This hat is too colorful!'
Students remember prices of items and say 'The jeans are too expensive!'
Students swap items and explain why they can't use them.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a poster for a 'too/ enough' sale with slogans like 'Jeans too cheap? No! Enough cheap!'
Support: Use sentence starters: 'This is too _____.' 'These are not _____ enough.'
hw: Write a 25+ word email to a friend about shopping in Oujda; use 'too/ enough'.
Record a 1-minute video review of a local clothing store; mention prices and sizes.
Draw 3 clothing items and write sentences: 'This scarf is too warm.' 'These shoes are not comfortable enough.'
lp.tip: Use local currency (DH) and Moroccan shopping contexts (souks, bargaining culture) to make the language relevant and boost engagement.

weeks.obj: Discuss plans with possibility language; report weather and invite/react to simple suggestions
weeks.lang: What is the weather like?; Shall we...? Let's...; responses + might / may / could for possibility
weeks.act:
Roleplay with a complication around weather
Christmas around the world jigsaw reading; party planning task with a budget in English.
weeks.hw:
write a 10-12 sentence text about weather with 2 paragraphs
Write the class party invitation (10 lines).

skills.L: Listen to possibility dialogues (might / may)
skills.S: Discuss plans with possibility language
skills.R: Read an arrangements text and find the modals
skills.W: Write my weekend options with might

lp.wu: Weather Charades: Students take turns miming weather actions (e.g., shivering for cold, fanning for hot) while classmates guess using 'Is it...?' The teacher writes guesses on the board to review key vocabulary.
wuAlt: Weather Bingo: Students draw 6 weather symbols and mark them as the teacher calls them out in English.
Weather Pictionary: Students draw weather words for their team to guess using 'It's...'.
lp.pres: Teacher shows flashcards of Christmas traditions worldwide (e.g., fireworks in Brazil, Yule logs in Norway) and asks 'What might people do here?' to elicit 'They might...'. Model sentences: 'In Norway, they might light a Yule log.' Check understanding with 'What might people do in your country for Christmas?'
presAlt: Weather Forecast Video: Play a short clip of a weather forecast; pause to ask 'What might the weather be like tomorrow?'
Plan a Picnic Story: Read a story where characters decide on a picnic; highlight 'Shall we...?' and 'Let's...' with 'might' for rain.
lp.prac: Weather Plan Roleplay: Students work in pairs. One is a friend suggesting a plan (e.g., 'Shall we go to the beach?'), the other responds with possibility (e.g., 'It might rain, so we could go to the mall instead.'). Teacher circulates to correct errors.
pracAlt: Might/May/Could Sorting: Students sort sentence strips into three piles based on modality of possibility.
Plan a Party Cards: Students pick a card with a weather complication (e.g., 'It might snow') and suggest alternatives using 'could'.
lp.ls: Christmas Traditions Jigsaw: Students read short texts about Christmas in different countries (e.g., Japan, Mexico) in groups. They then listen to a partner's summary and fill in a table with 'might' verbs (e.g., 'In Mexico, they might have a posada party').
lp.re: Weather Relay: Two lines of students race to the board to write a sentence about a weather condition using 'might' (e.g., 'It might be sunny tomorrow'). The first team to write a correct sentence gets a point.
lp.prod: Christmas Party Planning: Groups plan a Christmas party with a $100 budget. They must use 'Shall we...?', 'Let's...', and 'might' for complications (e.g., 'It might be cold, so we could have hot chocolate'). Each group presents their plan to the class.
lp.rw: Write a Party Invitation: Students write a 10-line invitation to their planned party, including date, time, place, and a weather contingency (e.g., 'It might rain, so we'll be inside'). They use a model invitation on the board for support.
lp.st: Play 'Jingle Bells' with actions (clap, stomp) and end with a quick review: 'Today we talked about weather plans and Christmas traditions. Thank you, class!'
g: Students mime weather while classmates guess using 'Is it...?'
Pairs suggest plans with 'Shall we...?' and respond with 'It might rain, so we could...'
Students mark traditions as the teacher calls them out
Teams race to write sentences with 'might'
Groups present their party plan with budget and weather contingencies
diff: Fast finishers: Design a poster for their party with weather icons and modals.
Support learners: Use sentence starters like 'We might...' and 'It could be...' for the roleplay.
hw: Write a 10-12 sentence text about weather with 2 paragraphs: one for today, one for tomorrow using 'might'.
Write a 10-line invitation to a Christmas party, including a weather plan.
Draw 3 weather symbols and write a sentence for each using 'might' or 'could'.
lp.tip: Use local weather in Oujda (e.g., 'It might be sunny') to make the language relevant, and connect Christmas to Moroccan winter celebrations like New Year's Eve plans.

weeks.obj: Tell a dramatic story with two past tenses; talk about yesterday and childhood with was/were
weeks.lang: was/were; time expressions (yesterday, last year) + past simple vs continuous for drama
weeks.act:
Write-swap: peer-edit a paragraph about the past
Resolutions with will / going to: vote on the class top-5 resolutions.
weeks.hw:
record a 90-second opinion clip about the past
Write 5 resolutions with will and going to.

skills.L: Listen to dramatic stories with two past tenses
skills.S: Tell a dramatic story with past simple + continuous
skills.R: Read a story extract and analyse the tense choices
skills.W: Write a 2-paragraph dramatic story opening

lp.wu: New Year Timeline: Students draw a line on the board from December 31 to January 1. They add 3 personal events (e.g., 'I was at a party', 'I was tired') and 3 class events (e.g., 'We were in class').
wuAlt: Resolution Relay: Teams race to write 5 New Year resolutions on the board using 'will' and 'going to'.
Memory Chain: One student says 'Yesterday I was...', next student repeats and adds their own, chain continues.
lp.pres: Show a dramatic New Year's Eve story comic strip on the board. Highlight 'was/were' and past continuous (e.g., 'The fireworks were exploding'). Elicit and model 5 sentences. Check with thumbs-up/down if sentences are true.
presAlt: Use two photos: one of last year, one of this year. Ask 'Who was there? What were they doing?' to contrast.
Play a short audio of a chaotic New Year's story. Students draw what they hear, focusing on 'was/were' actions.
lp.prac: Past Tense Bingo: Cards have sentences like 'She was dancing'. Teacher calls out prompts ('At midnight...'). Students mark and say the full sentence. Support with sentence frames on the board.
pracAlt: Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Were you at a party?' and writing names. Winners share 3 findings.
Grammar Auction: Teams bid on correct/incorrect 'was/were' sentences. They must explain errors.
lp.ls: Listen to a 1-minute dramatic story about a disastrous New Year's Eve. Students complete a gap-fill with 'was/were' and past continuous verbs. Check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Freeze Drama: Teacher calls out a New Year scene (e.g., 'Countdown!'). Students freeze in a pose and say what they were doing ('I was screaming').
lp.prod: Write-Swap: Students write a dramatic 2-paragraph opening about a past New Year (e.g., 'Last year, I was at home...'). Swap with a partner, add one past continuous sentence, and return. Groups vote for the most dramatic story.
lp.rw: Read a short PET-style story extract about a childhood New Year. Underline all 'was/were' and past continuous verbs. In pairs, discuss why the author chose those tenses for drama.
lp.st: Read a funny New Year's folktale from Morocco. Close with the goodbye routine: 'Today we told dramatic past stories—great job! Thank you, class.'
g: Teams race to put 6 event cards in order, saying sentences like 'First, we were eating.'
Students write 3 resolutions, vote for class top 5, and present with 'I will...' or 'I am going to...'
Students act out 'was/were' actions (e.g., 'was sleeping') for others to guess.
Teams bid on correct/incorrect sentences, explaining errors.
Students ask 'Were you...?' and write 3 true findings.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a third paragraph for their story with a surprise ending.
Support: Use a word bank with 'was/were' and past continuous verbs for the writing task.
hw: Record a 90-second video saying 3 childhood memories using 'was/were'.
Write 5 resolutions: 3 with 'will', 2 with 'going to', and explain why.
Interview a family member about their New Year's Eve and write 3 sentences.
lp.tip: Use local context: Reference Moroccan New Year (Amazigh new year) to contrast with Western celebrations, making grammar more relatable.

weeks.obj: Retell a Christmas story in reported speech; tell a simple story in the past with regular verbs; enjoy a Christmas text
weeks.lang: past simple regular (-ed); Christmas vocabulary + reported statements: He said (that)...
weeks.act: Podcast-style panel discussion about Christmas
weeks.hw: do the Christmas reading task and answer in full sentences

skills.L: Listen to reported statements
skills.S: Retell a Christmas story in reported speech
skills.R: Read a news-style report and find the reported verbs
skills.W: Rewrite the quotes as reported statements

lp.wu: Christmas Memory Chain: Students stand in a circle. Student 1 says 'I decorated a Christmas tree.' Student 2 says 'Student 1 decorated a Christmas tree and I wrapped a present.' Continue, with each student repeating the previous chain and adding a new sentence using a past regular verb.
wuAlt: Christmas Vocabulary Race: Write past regular verbs on the board in a list. Students race to write a Christmas-related sentence for each verb.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Did you...?' questions about Christmas activities, e.g., 'Did you bake cookies?' and write names.
lp.pres: Show a 3-panel comic strip of a Christmas story. Model the story in direct speech: 'He said, "I wrapped the gift."' Then rewrite it as reported speech: 'He said (that) he had wrapped the gift.' Highlight the 'said (that)' structure and the verb change. Check understanding by asking students to point to the 'said' and the past verb in a new example.
presAlt: Use a short audio clip of two friends talking about Christmas. Transcribe the direct speech on the board, then transform it into reported speech.
Show a video clip of a Christmas scene. Pause and elicit direct speech sentences, then rewrite them as reported speech on the board.
lp.prac: Reported Speech Relay: In teams, students take turns rewriting a direct speech sentence (on a card) into reported speech on the board. Each student can only write one word. The first team to finish correctly wins. Support by providing a sentence frame: 'He/She said (that)...'
pracAlt: Matching Pairs: Prepare cards with direct speech sentences and their reported speech equivalents. Students match them in pairs.
Correct the Reporter: Give students a worksheet with incorrect reported speech sentences. They work in pairs to find and fix the mistakes.
lp.ls: Listen to a 2-minute podcast where three teens discuss their Christmas traditions. Students listen and fill in a table with the names of the speakers and their traditions in reported speech, e.g., 'Amina said (that) she visited her grandparents.'
lp.re: Verb Charades: After the break, act out a past regular verb related to Christmas (e.g., 'wrapping', 'singing'). Students shout the verb in the past form. The first to guess correctly becomes the next actor.
lp.prod: Christmas Panel Discussion: In groups of three, students roleplay a panel discussing 'What Christmas means to us.' Each student takes a turn to make a statement about their experience (direct speech), and the others must report it back to the group. Encourage 2-minute turns per student.
lp.rw: Read a short news article about how teens in different countries celebrate Christmas. Students underline all the reported verbs (e.g., 'explained', 'mentioned') and write three of their own reported sentences about the text, e.g., 'The article said (that) teens in Japan eat fried chicken.'
lp.st: Read 'The Gift of the Magi' by O. Henry (abridged version). Discuss the ending, then close with the goodbye routine: 'Today we practiced retelling stories in reported speech. Thank you for your hard work and have a great day!'
g: Create bingo cards with reported speech sentences. Call out direct speech sentences; students mark the matching reported speech.
Groups write a story one sentence at a time, using past regular verbs and reported speech.
Students crumble paper with past regular verbs and toss them. When a verb lands, they must use it in a reported speech sentence.
Read a mix of direct and reported speech sentences. Students stand up if it's reported speech.
Draw a Christmas activity; others guess and then report it: 'He/She drew (that) he was decorating a tree.'
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph (60 words) retelling their own Christmas memory using reported speech.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame with a word bank to complete reported sentences: 'He said (that) he _______ (verb) a _______ (noun).'
hw: Read the Christmas article again and write three more reported sentences about it.
Write a 60-word email to a friend describing your Christmas using at least five past regular verbs.
Record a 1-minute audio retelling a Christmas story using reported speech.
lp.tip: Emphasize the connection between reported speech and storytelling, as it's a key skill for the PET speaking exam. For Moroccan students, relate the theme to universal values of family and giving, avoiding religious specifics to respect cultural diversity.

weeks.obj: Show my progress in the semester quiz; complete the written paper and the paired speaking task
weeks.lang: all S1 outcomes + semester 1 review
weeks.res: Tests (teacher-selected level items); assessment kit; KET
weeks.act: Mixed-skills revision circuit in teams
weeks.hw: revise your notes for the assessment week

skills.L: Listening paper (PET-adjacent level)
skills.S: Paired speaking task
skills.R: Reading paper across S1 topics
skills.W: Guided writing (PET-style short task)

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Quiz Relay' in teams of 4. Students race to write 3 S1 review words (e.g., 'present perfect', 'past continuous') on the board. First team to write all 3 correctly wins a point.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Word Association Chain' - students say one S1 word related to the previous word.
Alternative 2: 'Quick Draw' - teacher draws a S1 grammar concept (e.g., 'used to'), students guess.
lp.pres: Presentation: Teacher shows a PET-style writing task example (email to a friend). Model sentences: 'I have been to...', 'I used to live...'. Check understanding by asking: 'What tense is used for experiences?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use flashcards for 'present perfect' vs 'past simple' with visuals (e.g., 'travel' icons).
Alternative 2: Realia - show old photos to elicit 'used to' sentences.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Grammar Match-Up' - students match sentence halves (e.g., 'I have never...' with '...been to the USA'). Teacher circulates to correct errors.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Auction' - students bet on correct S1 grammar sentences.
Alternative 2: 'Find Someone Who...' survey with S1 questions.
lp.ls: Listening slot: PET-style listening task (audio about a teen's holiday). Students answer 5 multiple-choice questions. Play audio twice, then review answers as a class.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand Up If...' - teacher says S1 review prompts (e.g., 'Stand up if you have ever eaten camel meat'), students stand up and say a full sentence.
lp.prod: Production task: Paired speaking task - 'My Dream Vacation'. Students take 2-minute turns describing their dream trip using S1 grammar. Teacher assesses using a checklist.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Read a short text about Moroccan festivals (e.g., Green March), then write 60-word email to a friend about a festival they enjoyed. Include 1 'present perfect' sentence.
lp.st: Story / song + goodbye: Teacher tells a short story about a teen's first time in Casablanca. Close with: 'Today we reviewed S1 for our assessment. Thank you for your hard work!'
g: Teams race to write 3 S1 words on the board.
Match sentence halves for S1 grammar.
Stand and speak when prompted with S1 grammar.
diff: Fast finishers: Write an extra paragraph about their dream vacation.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame for the email (e.g., 'I have... because...').
hw: Homework 1: Write 5 sentences about your family using 'used to'.
Homework 2: Record yourself describing your favorite festival (1-2 min).
Homework 3: Create a quiz with 5 S1 review questions for a friend.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural examples (e.g., 'Green March') to make grammar practice relatable and boost engagement.
checklist: I can use present perfect for experiences.
I can describe past habits with 'used to'.
I can write a 60-word email about a festival.
I can answer PET-style listening questions.
I can speak for 2 minutes about my dream vacation.
I can use 0/1 conditionals in sentences.
I can identify relative clauses in texts.

weeks.obj: Present my goals with reasons and steps; talk about learning goals and review semester 1 language
weeks.lang: review structures; goal language (I want to... I will try...) + would like to + plan clauses
weeks.act: Two-corners debate, then switch sides on new year goals
weeks.hw: find a real article or video about new year goals and summarise it in 3 sentences

skills.L: Listen to goal presentations with reasons
skills.S: Present my goals with reasons and steps
skills.R: Read a goal-setting guide (Critical thinking folder)
skills.W: Write my goal plan with steps

lp.wu: Goal Race: Write 3 goals on sticky notes, stick them on the board, and race to match them with reasons (e.g., 'I want to learn English because...').
wuAlt: Goal Charades: Act out goals (e.g., 'study', 'exercise') for others to guess and say the reason.
Goal Bingo: Call out goals and reasons; students mark off matching squares.
lp.pres: Show a New Year resolution video clip; model sentences like 'I want to improve my English because I need it for university' and 'I will try to study 30 minutes daily' with flashcards of goals and steps.
presAlt: Use a goal-setting infographic to highlight 'would like to + verb' (e.g., 'I would like to join a club') and 'plan to + verb' (e.g., 'I plan to read books').
Role-play a conversation between two friends discussing resolutions, drilling target language.
lp.prac: Goal Steps Relay: In pairs, write a goal and 3 steps on paper, then pass to another pair to add reasons; check for correct use of 'I will try...' and 'because'.
pracAlt: Goal Sort: Categorize goals into 'study', 'health', 'hobby' using flashcards, then make sentences.
Goal Chain: Each student adds one step to a class resolution chain, using 'plan to'.
lp.ls: Listen to a podcast clip about New Year goals; students complete a table with 'Goal', 'Reason', and 'Step' to check comprehension.
lp.re: Goal Jump: Call out a goal (e.g., 'exercise'); students jump if they agree, squat if they disagree, then switch sides for debate practice.
lp.prod: Two-Corners Debate: Label corners 'agree' and 'disagree' with 'New Year resolutions help people'; students debate with reasons like 'I think they help because...' then switch sides.
lp.rw: Read a short article on SMART goals; write a 60-word email to a friend outlining one personal resolution with steps using 'I will try...' and 'because'.
lp.st: Read a story about a teen achieving a resolution; end with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned how to talk about goals with reasons—great job, thank you!'
g: Pairs write goals and steps, pass to others to add reasons.
Act out goals for others to guess and state reasons.
Jump/squat to agree/disagree with resolutions, then debate.
Match called-out goals with reasons on bingo cards.
Add steps to a class resolution chain using 'plan to'.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second resolution with 3 steps in a paragraph.
Support: Use sentence frames like 'I want to... because... I will try to...'.
hw: Find a video about New Year goals and summarise in 3 sentences.
Write a 70-word paragraph about your biggest resolution and why.
Interview a family member about their goals and report back.
lp.tip: Encourage students to link goals to local events like Independence Day to make language relevant and culturally connected.

weeks.obj: Compare jobs with double comparatives; describe jobs and talk about work with have to
weeks.lang: job vocabulary; have to / don't have to + the more..., the more...; job collocations
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Jobs-Careers; Reading tasks/Famous people; Critical thinking
weeks.act: KET-style task carousel on jobs and dream jobs in pairs
weeks.hw: write a KET-style email (25+ words) about jobs and dream jobs

skills.L: Listen to the more..., the more... examples
skills.S: Compare jobs with double comparatives
skills.R: Read job profiles and collect collocations
skills.W: Write job comparisons with the more...

lp.wu: Job Charades: Students act out jobs (doctor, teacher, engineer) while others guess. Props: job flashcards. They shout 'You're a ___!' when correct.
wuAlt: Job Pictionary: Draw jobs on the board; classmates guess the job name.
Word Association: Start with 'job'—students say one related word each (e.g., 'hospital,' 'uniform,' 'salary').
lp.pres: Show job ads with 'have to' (e.g., 'Teachers have to work hard'). Model 'The more experience you have, the more jobs you can get.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down for true/false sentences.
presAlt: Use a story about two jobs (e.g., 'Ali is a chef; he has to stand all day. Sara is a writer; she doesn't have to travel.')
Realia: Bring in items related to jobs (stethoscope, laptop) and elicit 'have to' sentences.
lp.prac: Job Comparison Grid: Students fill in a table comparing two jobs (e.g., hours, salary) using 'have to' and 'the more..., the more...' in pairs. Support with sentence starters.
pracAlt: Find Someone Who...: Survey classmates about jobs using 'Do you have to...?' questions.
Double Comparative Race: Write sentences like 'The more you study, the more opportunities you get' on the board; students race to copy them correctly.
lp.ls: Listen to a podcast clip about dream jobs. Students note down 3 jobs mentioned and 1 'have to' requirement for each. Check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Job Relay: Teams race to write 'the more..., the more...' sentences on the board about jobs (e.g., 'The more creative you are, the better artist you are').
lp.prod: Dream Job Debate: Students work in pairs to prepare a 2-minute talk comparing their current job/studies to their dream job using 'have to' and double comparatives. Present to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short job profile of a Moroccan engineer. Underline 3 job collocations (e.g., 'work long hours,' 'solve problems'). Then write 3 sentences about your ideal job using these collocations.
lp.st: Read a short story about a teen choosing between two jobs. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we compared jobs using double comparatives—great job! Thank you, class.'
g: Students mark off jobs on a bingo card as the teacher describes them using 'have to'.
Students sit in a circle; each adds a clause to a growing sentence (e.g., 'The more I learn... the more I earn...').
Teams take turns acting out jobs; fastest to guess gets a point.
Match job words with collocations (e.g., 'doctor' + 'work night shifts').
Ask 3 classmates about their dream job and write down their answers.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 40-word paragraph comparing two jobs using 3+ double comparatives.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'The more ___ you have, the more ___ you get.'
hw: Write a KET-style email (25+ words) to a friend about your dream job, using 'have to' and one double comparative.
Create a poster for your dream job with 3 'have to' requirements and 1 double comparative sentence.
Record a 30-second voice note describing why you want your dream job, using 'the more..., the more...'.
lp.tip: Pair stronger with weaker learners during the production task to build confidence—teens often learn best from peers.

weeks.obj: Compare three things accurately; compare two cities, foods, or teams with comparative adjectives
weeks.lang: comparatives (-er, more... than) + comparatives + much/far + comparative; (not) as ... as
weeks.act: Story circle: build a story about comparatives with target tenses
weeks.hw: write a 10-12 sentence text about comparatives with 2 paragraphs

skills.L: Listen to three-way comparisons
skills.S: Compare three things accurately
skills.R: Read comparison articles and check the accuracy
skills.W: Write a three-way comparison paragraph

lp.wu: Students play 'Compare Me' in pairs. One student names two items (e.g., 'phone vs. book'), the other says which is 'more useful' and why. Teacher models: 'A phone is more useful than a book because you can call people.'
wuAlt: Students stand in a line; teacher holds up two flashcards (e.g., 'pizza vs. couscous'), students jump left/right to say 'pizza is tastier' or 'couscous is healthier'.
Teacher writes 'Oujda vs. Rabat' on the board; students brainstorm 3 comparisons (e.g., 'Rabat is bigger', 'Oujda is quieter').
lp.pres: Teacher shows 3 city photos (Oujda, Casablanca, Marrakech) and models: 'Casablanca is bigger than Oujda, but Marrakech is far bigger than Casablanca.' Students repeat chorally. Teacher checks: 'Which city is the biggest?'
presAlt: Teacher uses a Venn diagram with 3 circles (sports: football, basketball, tennis); students fill in 'more exciting', 'more popular', 'more fun'.
Teacher tells a short story: 'Last week, I visited three cafes. Cafe A was cheaper than Cafe B, but Cafe C was far cheaper than both.'
lp.prac: Students do 'Comparative Relay' in teams. Each team gets 3 flashcards (e.g., 'Camel vs. Car vs. Bike'). They race to write sentences: 'A car is faster than a bike, but a camel is far slower than a bike.' Teacher monitors for errors.
pracAlt: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid (e.g., 'Find someone who has a bigger phone than you', 'Find someone who thinks math is easier than science').
Teacher gives 3 adjectives (e.g., 'expensive, old, big'); students write 3 sentences comparing their school, a shop, and a park.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 1-minute audio comparing 3 Moroccan cities (Agadir, Fez, Tangier). They tick which is 'busier', 'cheaper', 'more modern'. Teacher plays audio twice; students compare answers in pairs.
lp.re: Students play 'Human Comparatives'. Teacher calls out 3 students (e.g., 'Ali, Sara, Omar'); class shouts: 'Ali is taller than Sara, but Omar is far taller than Ali!'
lp.prod: Students work in groups of 3. Each group chooses 3 Moroccan foods (e.g., tagine, couscous, pastilla). They create a 2-minute presentation comparing them (e.g., 'Tagine is spicier than couscous, but pastilla is far sweeter than both').
lp.rw: Students read a short text comparing 3 football teams (Raja, Wydad, ASFAR). They underline 5 comparatives (e.g., 'Wydad is more famous than ASFAR'). Then, they write 3 sentences comparing 3 local teams.
lp.st: Teacher tells a story: 'Once, three camels raced. The blue camel was faster than the red one, but the yellow camel was far faster than both!' Close with: 'Today we compared three things accurately. Thank you, class!'
g: Teacher calls out comparisons (e.g., 'bigger than a book'); students mark if they have a picture matching.
Students stand in 3 lines; teacher holds up 3 items (e.g., 'pen, ruler, pencil'); each line says a comparison (e.g., 'ruler is longer than pen').
Teams race to write 3 comparatives for 3 words (e.g., 'hot: hotter, hotter than ice, far hotter than snow').
Students get 3 pictures (e.g., 3 rooms); they write 5 comparisons (e.g., 'Room A is tidier than Room B').
Students survey 3 classmates: 'What do you prefer: tea or coffee? Why?' and report back with comparatives.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 5-sentence comparison of 3 Moroccan cities (e.g., 'Agadir is warmer than Oujda, but Marrakech is far warmer than Agadir').
Support learners: use a sentence frame: '_____ is _____ than _____, but _____ is far _____ than _____'.
hw: Write a 10-sentence text comparing 3 Moroccan festivals (Green March, Eid, Independence Day) with 2 paragraphs.
Record a 1-minute video comparing 3 local restaurants (e.g., 'Restaurant A is cheaper than B, but C is far cheaper than A').
Create a poster comparing 3 apps (e.g., TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat) using 5 comparatives.
lp.tip: Use local examples (Moroccan cities, foods, teams) to boost engagement. Teens relate better when comparisons reflect their world.

weeks.obj: Give class awards with superlatives and ever; use superlatives to nominate classmates for fun awards
weeks.lang: superlatives (the -est, the most...) + superlatives + present perfect ever: the best book I've ever read
weeks.act:
Group presentation: 3-minute talk about superlatives and class awards with visuals
Project: a guide to Ramadan in Oujda, written for foreign visitors.
weeks.hw:
record a 90-second opinion clip about superlatives and class awards
Write 6 tips for visitors during Ramadan.

skills.L: Listen to award speeches with superlatives + ever
skills.S: Give class awards with superlatives and ever
skills.R: Read award texts and find ever / superlatives
skills.W: Write ever-based award nominations

lp.wu: Superlative Speed Dating: Students stand in two lines, facing each other. They have 30 seconds to ask and answer a superlative question (e.g., 'What's the best movie you've ever seen?'). Then one line moves, and they repeat with a new partner. The teacher calls out topics like 'books', 'food', or 'Ramadan memories'.
wuAlt: Superlative Bingo: Students write 9 superlative questions in a grid. They walk around asking classmates the questions; if a classmate answers 'yes', they can mark the square. The first to get 3 in a row wins.
Find Someone Who...: Students get a handout with prompts like 'Find someone who has read the longest book'. They must ask 'Have you ever read a book longer than 300 pages?' and write down the name.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a 'Class Awards' poster with superlatives like 'The Kindest Heart' and 'The Most Creative Mind'. Models sentences: 'You are the most creative person I've ever met.' and 'This is the best project I've ever seen.' Students repeat. Teacher checks understanding by asking, 'What superlative describes someone who helps everyone?'
presAlt: Award Nomination Box: Students write anonymous nominations on paper slips using superlatives (e.g., 'The funniest joke I've ever heard'). Teacher reads them aloud, and students guess who it is.
Superlative Charades: Teacher acts out a superlative (e.g., 'the tallest') and students guess the word. Then students take turns acting out superlatives like 'the fastest' or 'the most helpful'.
lp.prac: Awards Committee: Students work in groups of 3. Each group gets a set of award cards (e.g., 'Best Dressed', 'Best Storyteller'). They take turns nominating classmates using superlatives: 'I think Sarah is the best storyteller because she tells the funniest stories.' Teacher circulates to correct grammar.
pracAlt: Superlative Chain Game: Students sit in a circle. The first student says a superlative about themselves (e.g., 'I'm the tallest'). The next student must say a superlative about the first student (e.g., 'She's the tallest') and add one about themselves (e.g., 'I'm the fastest').

Nomination Relay: Two teams race to write superlative nominations on the board. The teacher calls out a category (e.g., 'Ramadan kindness'), and the first team to write a correct sentence (e.g., 'You are the most generous person I know') gets a point.
lp.ls: Awards Speech Listening: Students listen to a 2-minute audio of a teacher giving mock awards. They fill in a worksheet with missing superlatives (e.g., 'You are the ___ student I've ever taught'). After, they discuss which award they would give and why.
lp.re: Superlative Freeze: Play music. Students walk around the room. When the music stops, the teacher calls out a superlative (e.g., 'Freeze if you've ever visited a mosque during Ramadan!'). Students who can say 'I've ever visited...' stay in the game. Others sit down.
lp.prod: Class Awards Ceremony: Students work in groups to prepare a 3-minute presentation. They create a poster with 3-4 fun awards (e.g., 'The Best Ramadan Cookie Baker'). Each group presents, explaining why they chose each winner using superlatives: 'We chose Ali because he made the most delicious cookies I've ever tasted!'
lp.rw: Ramadan Guide Writing: Students write a short guide for foreign visitors during Ramadan. They include 6 tips using superlatives (e.g., 'The most important rule is to respect fasting hours'). They also write a paragraph about their favorite Ramadan memory using 'ever' (e.g., 'The best iftar I've ever had was with my family last year').
lp.st: Teacher reads a short story about a boy who wins a 'Most Helpful' award during Ramadan. After, students share one kind thing they've done this week. Close with: 'Today we gave awards using superlatives. Great work! Thank you, class.'
g: Students draw a superlive (e.g., 'the tallest') and their team guesses.
Students write clues about a classmate using superlatives; others guess who it is.
Teams race to write superlative sentences on the board.
Students act out a superlative award and others guess.
Students mark squares when they hear a superlative about Ramadan.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a 'Superlative Trophy' for the class winner, including a reason why they deserve it using 'ever'.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'You are the ___. I've ever seen because ___.'
hw: Record a 90-second video giving a mock award to a classmate, using at least 3 superlatives.
Write 5 more tips for Ramadan visitors, using superlatives like 'the most respectful' or 'the best time'.
Interview a family member about their favorite Ramadan memory and write it down using 'ever'.
lp.tip: Use real examples from the classroom (e.g., 'You are the most creative artist I've seen') to make the language personal and memorable. Connect superlatives to Ramadan values like generosity and community.

weeks.obj: Present detailed plans with reasons; describe weekend and holiday plans with going to
weeks.lang: going to (plans); time expressions + be going to + when/after/before clauses
weeks.act: Roleplay with a complication around future plans
weeks.hw: do the future plans reading task and answer in full sentences

skills.L: Listen to plans with reasons and conditions
skills.S: Present my detailed plans with reasons
skills.R: Read plan texts and note the before / after clauses
skills.W: Write my plan with when / after / before

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Plan Relay' - students stand in teams, take turns running to the board to write one weekend plan using 'going to' (e.g., 'I'm going to visit my grandmother'), then high-five the next teammate. Fastest team with 5 correct sentences wins.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Plan Pictionary' - draw a future action (e.g., 'studying') for teammates to guess and say with 'going to'
Alternative 2: 'Quick Poll' - raise hands for 'going to the beach' vs 'going to the mountains', then say why
lp.pres: Presentation: Show a flashcard of a boy with a backpack and plane. Model: 'He's going to travel to Spain because he wants to see his cousin. He's going to leave on Friday after school.' Elicit similar plans with 'because' and time clauses. Check by asking 'Why is he going?' and 'When is he leaving?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a short story about a girl's Eid plans with 'after' and 'before' clauses
Alternative 2: Roleplay a teacher-student dialogue about Green March plans with 'going to' + reasons
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Plan Sort' - students get cards with time clauses (e.g., 'After lunch') and actions (e.g., 'I'm going to call my friend'). They match and make full sentences. Monitor for correct use of 'going to' and connectors.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Race' - teams race to unscramble sentences like 'I / going to / study / before the exam'
Alternative 2: 'Plan Chains' - each student adds one 'going to' sentence to a partner's plan
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a dialogue about two friends comparing Eid holiday plans. Students listen and fill in a chart with 'What' and 'Why' for each person. Play twice, then check in pairs.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Freeze Plans' - students walk around saying their plans (e.g., 'I'm going to bake a cake'). When teacher shouts 'Freeze!', they stop and say what they'll do 'after' (e.g., 'After baking, I'm going to share it').
lp.prod: Production task: 'Plan Complication Roleplay' - pairs receive cards with a plan (e.g., 'going to a concert') and a problem (e.g., 'your ticket is lost'). They roleplay discussing solutions using 'going to' + 'if' (e.g., 'If I can't find it, I'm going to buy a new one').
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Read a short email about a Labour Day trip to the Rif Mountains. Students underline 'before/after' clauses. Then write a 60-word reply using 3 'going to' sentences with time clauses.
lp.st: Story + goodbye: Read a short story about a teen's Independence Day plans with 'going to' and connectors. End with: 'Today we learned to talk about plans with reasons and time clauses. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams race to write 'going to' sentences on the board
Match time clauses with actions to make full sentences
Stop and say what you'll do 'after' your plan
Solve problems in future plans using 'going to'
Draw future actions for teammates to guess
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 3-step plan for their next holiday with 'before/after' clauses
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'I'm going to ___ because ___ after ___'
hw: Homework 1: Read a text about a Green March celebration and answer 3 questions in full sentences using 'going to'
Homework 2: Write a 60-word email to a friend about your weekend plans with 2 'because' and 1 'after' clause
Homework 3: Record a 1-minute voice note describing your next holiday plan using 'going to'
lp.tip: Use local holidays (Eid, Green March) to make plans relatable. Teens engage more when future plans connect to their cultural experiences.

weeks.obj: Make and justify predictions; make simple predictions about the future
weeks.lang: will/won't (predictions); maybe, probably + will / won't; probably, likely to
weeks.act: Write-swap: peer-edit a paragraph about will for predictions
weeks.hw: prepare a 1-minute presentation about will for predictions for next class

skills.L: Listen to justified predictions
skills.S: Make and justify predictions
skills.R: Read a futures article and identify likely to
skills.W: Write justified predictions for 2035

lp.wu: Predict the Weather: Students stand in a circle. Teacher shows a flashcard (sun, rain, snow) and asks 'What will the weather be like tomorrow?' Students reply 'It will be sunny/rainy/snowy.'
wuAlt: Future Timeline: Draw a line on the board from 2024 to 2035. Students write one prediction for each year.
Prediction Pictionary: Teacher draws a simple future event (e.g., flying car), students guess 'You will fly to school.'
lp.pres: Show a news clip about AI in Morocco. Model sentences: 'AI will probably help doctors.' 'Robots won't replace teachers.' 'Self-driving cars are likely to arrive by 2030.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down for true/false predictions.
presAlt: Future Jobs Poster: Display jobs (doctor, farmer, influencer). Ask 'Will this job exist in 2040?' Students use 'probably/likely to'.
Morocco 2050 Video: Play a silent clip of futuristic Oujda. Students predict using 'will/won't'.
lp.prac: Prediction Relay: Teams race to write sentences on the board about Moroccan festivals (e.g., 'Next Green March, drones will fly over the city.'). Correct spelling/grammar earns points.
pracAlt: Probability Dice: Roll a die (1=won't, 2-3=maybe, 4-5=probably, 6=will). Students make predictions about school life (e.g., 'We will have more exams.').
Find Someone Who...: Walk around asking 'Will you...?' questions (e.g., 'Will you travel abroad next year?').
lp.ls: Listen to a podcast about future tech in Africa. Students tick predictions heard: 'Solar panels will power homes.' 'People won't use cash.'
lp.re: Future Charades: Act out a future action (e.g., 'flying to Casablanca'). Class guesses 'You will travel by plane!'
lp.prod: 2035 Morocco Project: Groups create a poster with 5 predictions about life in Morocco (e.g., 'Electric cars will be common.'). Justify each with 'because...'. Present to class.
lp.rw: Read a short article about AI in Moroccan schools. Underline all uses of 'likely to'. Then write 3 predictions about your own school using 'will/won't'.
lp.st: Read 'The Boy Who Predicted the Future' story (about a boy predicting Morocco's first satellite launch). End with: 'Today we learned to make predictions. Thank you, class!'
g: Pass a ball and say a prediction about the next student (e.g., 'You will answer a question well.')
Write 9 predictions in a grid. Cross off when a classmate admits it's true.
Start with 'Maybe I will...' and each student adds one prediction to the chain.
Students brainstorm 3 things that definitely won't happen by 2030 (e.g., 'Camels won't drive cars.')
Show scenarios (e.g., 'Morocco wins the World Cup'). Students hold up 'likely' or 'not likely' cards.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 50-word story about a future day in Oujda using 5 'will' predictions.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'I think... will...' and 'It will probably... because...'.
hw: Record a 1-minute video predicting your life in 2035 (e.g., 'I will be a doctor.').
Write 5 predictions about a famous Moroccan person (e.g., 'Ronaldo will visit Morocco.').
Interview a family member about their future predictions and write 3 sentences.
lp.tip: Use local context (e.g., 'Will the new high-speed train change travel?') to make predictions relevant. Teens engage more when discussing their own future in Morocco.

weeks.obj: Give health and lifestyle advice; give simple health advice with should
weeks.lang: should/shouldn't; body and illness vocabulary + should / ought to / had better
weeks.act: Podcast-style panel discussion about health and advice
weeks.hw: find a real article or video about health and advice and summarise it in 3 sentences

skills.L: Listen to advice with ought to / had better
skills.S: Give health and lifestyle advice
skills.R: Read a health article and compare the modals
skills.W: Write an advice-column entry

lp.wu: Health Charades: Students take turns acting out illnesses (e.g., coughing, holding a stomach) while others guess the illness in English. Props: None. They say 'You have a cold!' or 'You should see a doctor!'
wuAlt: Alternative warm-up 1: Illness Bingo with flashcards of body parts and symptoms. They mark off the words on their bingo cards as you call them out.
Alternative warm-up 2: Quick survey in pairs: 'What should you do if you have a headache?' They write one tip each.
lp.pres: Show a cartoon of a teen with a stomachache. Model sentences: 'You shouldn't eat so much fast food.' 'You should drink water.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down: 'If you have a fever, should you go to school?'
presAlt: Alternative presentation 1: Use a role-play script where a doctor gives advice to a patient. Highlight 'should/shouldn't' in the dialogue.
Alternative presentation 2: Display a poster with 'good/bad' health habits. Elicit advice sentences from students using 'should/shouldn't'.
lp.prac: Modal Match: Students match health problems (headache, sunburn) to advice (rest, use sunscreen) on cut-out cards. Then practice in pairs: 'If you have a headache, you should...'
pracAlt: Alternative practice 1: Advice Relay Race. Teams race to write correct advice sentences on the board for given problems.
Alternative practice 2: 'Should or Shouldn't?' card sort. Students sort sentences into two columns and justify their choices.
lp.ls: Listen to a 2-minute podcast where teens discuss staying healthy. Students complete a table: 'Problem - Advice' (e.g., 'Problem: tired - Advice: sleep more'). Check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Simon Says Health Edition: 'Simon says you should stretch!' or 'Simon says you shouldn't run with scissors!' Students move only when the command is correct.
lp.prod: Health Panel Discussion: Groups of 3 play 'teen experts' (doctor, nutritionist, fitness coach) giving advice on a real teen issue (e.g., exam stress). Each student speaks for 2 minutes using 'should/ought to/had better'.
lp.rw: Read a short health article about Ramadan fasting. Compare the advice using 'should/ought to/had better' in a table. Then write a 60-word email to a friend giving one piece of advice from the article.
lp.st: Read a short story about a teen who follows bad advice and feels worse. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to give health advice. Thank you, class!'
g: Students draw health problems/advice while others guess in English.
Each student adds one piece of advice to a growing chain: 'You should drink water, and you shouldn't drink soda...'
Students replace 'should' with 'ought to' or 'had better' in sentences and check if meaning changes.
Teams answer questions like 'What should you do for a sore throat?' to win points.
Students pick a card (e.g., 'You have a cough') and give advice to a partner.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 'Top 5 Health Tips' list for teens using at least 3 modals.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'You should ____' or 'You shouldn't ____' for the production task.
hw: Homework option 1: Find a short health article online and write 3 advice sentences using 'should/shouldn't'.
Homework option 2: Record a 30-second video giving health advice to a friend.
Homework option 3: Write a 70-word paragraph about one health habit you should change.
lp.tip: Encourage students to connect advice to local contexts, like staying hydrated during summer in Oujda or adjusting meals for Ramadan, to make the language relevant.

weeks.obj: Narrate travel experiences; tell a simple travel story and ask travel questions
weeks.lang: past simple review; travel vocabulary + present perfect vs past simple; been/gone
weeks.res: Reading tasks (travel-themed); Listening (travel dialogues); Critical thinking
weeks.act:
Escape-room style grammar puzzle on travel and holidays
How we celebrate: compare Eid here and holidays abroad (paragraph + venn).
weeks.hw:
write a KET-style email (25+ words) about travel and holidays
Write 8 sentences comparing Eid with another holiday.

skills.L: Listening folder: travel dialogues - experiences
skills.S: Narrate travel experiences with been / gone
skills.R: Read travel articles and find the perfect forms
skills.W: Write a travel-blog entry

lp.wu: Travel Bingo: Students get a bingo grid with travel experiences (e.g., 'I have been to Paris', 'I have tried sushi'). They mingle, ask classmates 'Have you ever...?', and mark off squares. First to get a line shouts 'Bingo!'
wuAlt: Travel Charades: Teacher writes travel verbs on cards (e.g., 'pack a suitcase', 'miss a flight'). Students act them out for classmates to guess using 'Have you ever...?'
Travel Pictionary: Students draw travel-related words (e.g., 'beach', 'passport') while others guess in full sentences.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a photo of a crowded Eid celebration and asks 'Where have you been for Eid?'. Models 'I have been to my grandparents' house' and 'I have gone to the souk'. Uses flashcards of travel destinations to drill 'been/gone'. Checks understanding with 'Ask me: Where have you been?'
presAlt: Travel Story: Teacher reads a short story about a holiday using present perfect and past simple (e.g., 'I have been to Spain. I saw the Sagrada Familia'). Students underline the target forms.
Travel Video: Plays a 1-minute vlog clip where the narrator uses 'been/gone'. Students note down all examples.
lp.prac: Escape Room Puzzle: Groups receive a locked box with 4 grammar clues (e.g., 'Find a sentence with been to Egypt'). They solve travel-themed grammar questions to get the code. Teacher provides a 'been/gone' reference sheet for support.
pracAlt: Grammar Relay: Teams race to write correct 'been/gone' sentences on the board based on prompts (e.g., 'You are not here now' → 'He has gone to the market').
Travel Timeline: Students create a personal timeline of travel experiences using 'I have been to...' and 'I went to...'.
lp.ls: Listening to Travel Dialogues: Students listen to two friends talking about Eid and a summer holiday. They complete a table comparing 'What they did' (past simple) and 'Where they have been' (present perfect). Checks comprehension of time expressions.
lp.re: Travel Freeze: Teacher shouts a travel destination (e.g., 'London!'). Students freeze and say 'I have been to London!' or 'I have gone to London!'. If they hesitate, they sit down.
lp.prod: Eid vs. Holiday Venn Diagram: In pairs, students compare Eid al-Fitr with a holiday abroad (e.g., Christmas) using a Venn diagram. They write 8 sentences comparing traditions, food, and activities. Then, they share their findings with the class.
lp.rw: Travel Blog Writing: Students read a short travel blog entry (60 words) about a holiday. They identify examples of present perfect and past simple. Then, they write their own 60-word blog entry about a travel experience using both tenses.
lp.st: Travel Song: Play 'I've Been Everywhere' by Johnny Cash (edited version). Students sing along and list places mentioned. End with: 'Today we practiced talking about travel experiences using present perfect. Thank you, class!'
g: Students match travel photos with present perfect sentences ('I have seen the pyramids').
Teams race to categorize sentences into 'been' or 'gone' columns.
Students survey classmates about travel experiences using 'Have you ever...?' and report back.
Students add one sentence to a story using present perfect or past simple.
Teams take turns drawing travel words for others to guess in sentences.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 5 more sentences comparing Eid with another holiday.
Support learners: Use sentence starters ('I have been to...', 'I have gone to...') for the Venn diagram.
hw: Write a KET-style email (25+ words) to a friend about your best Eid holiday.
Write 8 sentences comparing Eid with Christmas or another holiday.
Create a travel poster using 5 present perfect sentences about places you want to visit.
lp.tip: Use the American Space Oujda context to connect travel themes—e.g., 'Have you been to the American Space for an event?'—to make language practice relevant and engaging for learners.

weeks.obj: Review a song using music vocabulary; express and justify opinions about music
weeks.lang: I think... because; opinion adjectives + opinion + review genre language
weeks.act: Two-corners debate, then switch sides on music and opinions
weeks.hw: write a 10-12 sentence text about music and opinions with 2 paragraphs

skills.L: Listen to song excerpts for review language
skills.S: Review a song using music vocabulary
skills.R: Read music reviews and collect genre words
skills.W: Write a song review with a rating (Creative writing)

lp.wu: Music Opinions Relay: Students line up in two teams. Teacher shows a flashcard with a song title (e.g., 'Shape of You'). First student runs to the board, writes one opinion adjective (e.g., 'catchy'), runs back, tags next student who writes another (e.g., 'boring'), and so on. First team with 5 correct adjectives wins.
wuAlt: Opinion Charades: Teacher acts out a song genre (e.g., 'rock'), students guess and say 'I think it's rock because...'
Song Title Association: Teacher says a song, students shout an opinion word (e.g., 'Happy' → 'funny')
lp.pres: Teacher projects a music review of 'Blinding Lights' by The Weeknd. Models sentences: 'I think it's amazing because the beat is cool' and 'The genre is synth-pop'. Underlines opinion adjectives (amazing, cool) and review phrases (genre, beat). Checks understanding: 'What's the genre? Why does he like it?'
presAlt: Genre Flashcard Sort: Students match flashcards (jazz, hip-hop) to definitions, then say 'I think jazz is... because...'
YouTube Review Analysis: Teacher plays a 30-second song review, students list 3 opinion words
lp.prac: Two-Corners Debate: Label corners 'Love' and 'Hate'. Teacher plays 30 seconds of a controversial song (e.g., 'Baby Shark'). Students go to a corner, pair up, and say 'I love/hate it because...'. After 2 minutes, switch corners and repeat with a new song.
pracAlt: Opinion Dice Game: Students roll a dice (1=Love, 2=Hate, 3=Boring, etc.), say the opinion, and justify
Music Bingo: Teacher calls out opinion adjectives, students mark them on bingo cards and make sentences
lp.ls: Song Excerpt Review: Students listen to 3 short song clips (1 min each). For each, they write: 1) Genre, 2) One opinion adjective, 3) One reason. Teacher plays clips twice, checks answers on the board.
lp.re: Musical Opinions Freeze: Teacher plays upbeat music, students dance. When music stops, they freeze and say an opinion about the last song (e.g., 'I think it's loud!').
lp.prod: Song Review Swap: Students write a 4-sentence review of their favorite song on a slip (genre, opinion, reason, rating). They swap with a partner, who reads it and says 'I agree/disagree because...'.
lp.rw: Review Reading + Rating: Students read a short music review (60 words) about a Moroccan artist (e.g., Saad Lamjarred). They underline 5 genre words (e.g., ' Rai', 'pop') and write a 1-5 star rating with a reason.
lp.st: Teacher plays 'Lah ya sahbi' by Cheb Khaled. Discuss: 'What genre is it? Is it traditional or modern?' End with: 'Today we learned to share music opinions. Thank you, class!'
g: Teacher hums a song, students guess the genre and say 'I think it's... because...'
Teams race to write opinion sentences on the board with correct 'because' clauses
Student draws a genre, others guess and say 'Is it hip-hop? I think so because...'
Roll dice to pick a song/opinion, students debate for 1 minute
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second review comparing two songs
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'I think ____ is ____ because ____'
hw: Write a 10-sentence review of a Moroccan song (genre, opinion, reason, rating)
Record a 30-second video review of a song
Find 3 music reviews online, copy 2 opinion sentences each
lp.tip: Use local music (e.g., Gnawa, Rai) to build cultural relevance. Teens engage more when opinions connect to their world.

weeks.obj: Debate a technology question in teams; talk about devices and habits; use like/love/hate + -ing with verbs
weeks.lang: tech vocabulary; verb patterns (like doing / want to do) + first conditional; arguing politely
weeks.act: KET-style task carousel on technology in pairs
weeks.hw: record a 90-second opinion clip about technology

skills.L: Listen to debate arguments with the first conditional
skills.S: Debate a technology question in teams
skills.R: Read a debate text and map the if-clauses
skills.W: Write a debate speech (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Tech Charades: Students draw tech words (e.g., 'smartphone', 'social media') from a hat and act them out while others guess. Winner gets a point.
wuAlt: Tech Pictionary: Students sketch tech devices and classmates name them.
Tech Word Association: Teacher says 'phone', students shout related words like 'call', 'app', 'screen'.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of teens using tech (e.g., 'studying with a laptop', 'scrolling on TikTok'). Model sentences: 'I like studying with my laptop', 'She hates scrolling on TikTok'. Check understanding with thumbs up/down for 'Do you like using your phone?'
presAlt: Realia Tech Talk: Bring in old phones/keyboards. Students describe their habits using 'I love/hate + -ing'.
Tech Survey: Students ask 3 classmates 'Do you like/hate using ___?' and report back.
lp.prac: Verb Pattern Match: Students match 'like/love/hate' cards to '-ing' verb cards (e.g., 'like' → 'playing games'). Play in pairs, then swap cards for a new round.
pracAlt: Tech Habit Survey: Students walk around asking 'Do you like/hate + -ing?' and tally responses.
Sentence Race: Teams race to write 5 correct sentences using 'like/love/hate + -ing'.
lp.ls: Listen to a 1-minute debate: 'Is social media good for teens?'. Students tick arguments for/against and underline 2 'if-clauses' (e.g., 'If you use it too much, you can lose sleep').
lp.re: Tech Freeze: Teacher shouts tech words (e.g., 'laptop!', 'phone!'). Students freeze and say a full sentence like 'I love using my laptop!' to unfreeze.
lp.prod: Debate Carousel: Teams debate 'Should phones be allowed in school?' using 'I think...', 'If we allow phones,...', 'I agree because...' with 2-min turns. Rotate opponents.
lp.rw: Read a short debate text about 'Are robots helpful?'. Circle all 'if-clauses' and write 2 sentences: 'If robots do our jobs, humans might be lazy' and 'If we use robots, we can save time'.
lp.st: Watch a 2-minute animated story about a teen balancing screen time and homework. Close with: 'Today we debated tech opinions using like/love/hate + -ing and conditionals. Thanks for your great ideas, class!'
g: Students describe tech words without saying 'phone', 'screen', or 'app'
Start with 'If I use my phone too much...', next student adds 'I might get bad grades'
Bingo cards with tech habits; mark off when someone says 'I love/hate + -ing'
Roll dice to get debate topics (e.g., 'Social media', 'Video games')
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 5-sentence paragraph about their ideal tech device.
Support: Use sentence frames: 'I like/hate + ___. If I ___, I might ___.'
hw: Record a 90-second video saying your opinion: 'Do you like/hate using AI? Why? Use 2 'if-clauses'.
Write 5 sentences about your family's tech habits using like/love/hate + -ing.
Interview 3 people: 'Do you think robots will replace jobs? Why?' and write their answers.
lp.tip: Encourage polite arguing with phrases like 'I understand your point, but...' to mirror real debates. Link to local tech habits (e.g., 'In Morocco, many families use WhatsApp for calls').

weeks.obj: Write a short story with a twist; tell what was happening with past continuous support
weeks.lang: past continuous (was/were + -ing) + past perfect: had + participle for flashbacks
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Stories; Reading tasks/Fables; Creative writing
weeks.act: Story circle: build a story about stories with target tenses
weeks.hw: do the stories reading task and answer in full sentences

skills.L: Listen to a story with a twist ending
skills.S: Pitch a story with a twist
skills.R: Read a fable with a flashback and find the past perfect
skills.W: Write a short story with a twist (Creative writing)

lp.wu: Story Chain: Teacher starts a story with 'While I was walking to class, I found a magic lamp.' Students take turns adding one sentence using past continuous, e.g., 'While I was rubbing the lamp, a genie appeared.' Props: None. Students speak in turn.
wuAlt: Picture Prompt: Show a photo of a chaotic scene (e.g., a messy room). Students say what was happening, e.g., 'While the mom was cooking, the cat was knocking over the vase.'
Action Charades: Teacher mimes an action (e.g., running). Students guess 'While you were running, what were you doing?'
lp.pres: Teacher tells a short story about a Moroccan teen who finds a old book while visiting the Hassan II Mosque. Model sentences: 'While I was exploring, I found a book.' 'When I opened it, I had seen my name inside.' Check understanding: 'What tense shows an action in progress?' 'What tense shows a past event before another?'
presAlt: Flashcard Sequence: Show flashcards of a story (e.g., boy walking, rain starting, umbrella blowing away). Narrate with past continuous and past perfect. Students repeat sentences.
Dialogue Drill: Present a short dialogue between two friends discussing a past event. Highlight target tenses and ask students to identify them.
lp.prac: Grammar Relay: Divide class into teams. Each team gets a sentence strip with past continuous/past perfect. They race to write the correct form on the board. Support: Provide verb charts and sentence frames.
pracAlt: Sentence Auction: Write 10 sentences (5 correct, 5 incorrect). Teams 'bid' on correct sentences using past continuous/past perfect. Support: Allow dictionaries for verb forms.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'While you were [activity], were you [something]?' and 'Had you ever [experience] before?'
lp.ls: Listen to a 2-minute audio story about a teen in Marrakech who discovers a hidden treasure. Task: Students fill in gaps in a handout with past continuous/past perfect verbs. Check: Peer review answers in pairs.
lp.re: Action Race: Teacher calls out an action (e.g., 'eating'). Students race to mime it and say 'While I was eating, I dropped my spoon!' Fast-paced and physical.
lp.prod: Twist Story Circle: Groups of 4 build a story. Each student adds one sentence using past continuous/past perfect, aiming for a surprise ending. Example: 'While we were hiking, we found a cave. When we entered, we had discovered ancient paintings.' Present to class.
lp.rw: Read a fable about a fox and a turtle with a flashback. Task: Underline all past perfect verbs ('had', 'had seen') and write one sentence explaining the flashback. Then write a 60-word continuation of the story using past continuous.
lp.st: Read a short story about a Moroccan girl who helps a lost tourist at the Festival of Roses. Close with: 'Today we wrote stories with twists using past continuous and past perfect. Thank you, class!'
g: Toss a ball and ask a question (e.g., 'What were you doing at 8 AM?'). Catcher answers in past continuous.
Students freeze in an action. Teacher says 'While you were [action], you had [past event].'
Student mimes a story with a twist. Others guess using past continuous.
Teams race to write a sentence with both tenses. Fastest wins.
Roll dice for story prompts. Build a sentence with past continuous/past perfect.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second paragraph for their twist story with more details.
Support: Provide sentence starters like 'While I was ___, I had ___.'
hw: Read the story 'The Lost Key' and answer: What was happening when the key was found? Had anyone seen it before?
Write a 70-word story about a festival in Morocco with a twist ending.
Complete the grammar exercise: Fill in blanks with past continuous or past perfect.
lp.tip: Use local context (e.g., Hassan II Mosque, Festival of Roses) to make stories relatable and boost engagement. Teens connect better when themes reflect their culture.

weeks.obj: Do KET reading under time pressure; complete sample A2 Key reading tasks and understand the format
weeks.lang: KET reading part formats; skimming and scanning + KET parts 4-5 strategies; skimming/scanning
weeks.act: Group presentation: 3-minute talk about KET reading with visuals
weeks.hw: prepare a 1-minute presentation about KET reading for next class

skills.L: KET listening - timed practice
skills.S: Swap KET speaking cards with follow-ups
skills.R: KET reading parts 4-5 under time pressure (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style writing tasks (timed)

lp.wu: KET Reading Relay: Students race to match 5 KET part descriptions (e.g., 'Part 4: Read and choose the right picture') with 5 sample tasks on the board. They shout 'Match!' when done.
wuAlt: KET Pictionary: Teacher draws KET reading parts (e.g., a multiple-choice bubble), students guess the part number.
KET Quiz: 3 quick questions about KET format (e.g., 'How many parts in KET reading?') with hand signals.
lp.pres: Teacher projects a full KET reading paper, labeling parts 4-5 with colored markers. Models skimming a text for gist (30 sec) and scanning for details (1 min). Checks understanding with 'Show me Part 4!' gestures.
presAlt: KET Parts Poster: Students draw posters for each part with examples in groups.
KET Video Clip: Play a 2-min Cambridge video explaining parts 4-5, then discuss.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs to complete 3 KET Part 4 (matching) and 2 Part 5 (multiple-choice) tasks from the KET folder under 10 minutes. Teacher circulates, whispering hints like 'Scan for names/dates'.
pracAlt: KET Task Race: Two teams race to finish one Part 4 and one Part 5 task first.
KET Error Correction: Students find mistakes in 3 sample Part 4 answers.
lp.ls: Teacher plays a 1-min audio of a student explaining their KET reading strategy. Students listen and note 2 tips they hear, then compare in pairs.
lp.re: KET Freeze Tag: Teacher calls out a KET part (e.g., 'Part 4!'), students freeze and say one strategy (e.g., 'Look for pictures!').
lp.prod: Group Presentation: Students prepare 3-minute talks with visuals (posters/drawings) about KET reading parts 4-5. Each group presents to the class, who vote for 'Most Clear Explanation'.
lp.rw: Students write 3 tips for KET reading parts 4-5 in their notebooks, then swap with a partner to add one more tip each.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a student who aced KET reading, emphasizing strategy use. Close with 'Today we mastered KET reading parts 4-5—great job! Thank you, class.'
g: Students match KET part names to tasks in 60 seconds.
Students share one strategy and get one new one from a partner.
Teams race to complete a Part 4 task first.
Teacher asks 5 KET format questions, fastest wins.
Students find 3 mistakes in a fake Part 5 answer.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a KET Part 4 task for their classmates.
Support learners: Use highlighters to mark key words in Part 5 questions.
hw: Create a KET Part 4 matching task about Moroccan festivals (e.g., Green March).
Record a 1-minute video explaining KET Part 5 tips.
Write 5 questions about KET reading for a class quiz next week.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan teen interests (e.g., football, music) in KET tasks to boost engagement—e.g., 'Read about a Moroccan footballer's day' for Part 4.

weeks.obj: Swap KET-style speaking cards; complete a KET-style paired speaking task confidently
weeks.lang: KET speaking part 1-2 frames + KET speaking part 2: agreement/disagreement
weeks.res: KET folder; Speaking tests folder; Creative writing
weeks.act: Roleplay with a complication around KET speaking
weeks.hw: find a real article or video about KET speaking and summarise it in 3 sentences

skills.L: KET listening - review the strategies
skills.S: KET speaking part 2: agree and disagree
skills.R: KET reading - full-paper strategy (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style messages and stories

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find the Match' — Students receive half of KET speaking cards (e.g., 'What's your favorite hobby?') and mingle to find the matching response ('I like playing football'). They must say the full sentence to complete the match.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Two Stars and a Wish' — Students write two positive things about their partner's last weekend and one wish for the next.
Alternative 2: 'Quick Quiz' — Teacher asks KET-style questions (e.g., 'Where do you live?'), students answer in pairs.
lp.pres: Presentation: Show KET speaking part 1-2 frames on the board (e.g., 'Could you tell me about...?' / 'I think... because...'). Model a dialogue with a complication (e.g., 'I love music, but I can't play any instruments'). Check understanding by asking students to repeat the frames and add their own example.
presAlt: Alternative 1: 'Roleplay Demo' — Teacher and a student act out a KET speaking task with a disagreement, highlighting 'I agree, but...' phrases.
Alternative 2: 'Flashcard Sort' — Students sort phrases into 'Agree' / 'Disagree' columns, then use them in a simple dialogue.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Complication Cards' — Students draw a card with a topic (e.g., 'school') and a complication (e.g., 'you don't like homework'). They practice using KET frames to discuss, with the teacher monitoring and prompting for agreement/disagreement language.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Agreement Race' — Teams race to complete sentences with 'I agree' or 'I disagree' + a reason.
Alternative 2: 'Pair Drill' — Students take turns asking KET questions and responding with a complication, swapping roles after 2 minutes.
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a KET speaking part 2 audio where two students discuss a topic with a disagreement. Students listen and tick the phrases they hear (e.g., 'I see your point, but...'). Then, they compare in pairs and report back to the class.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand Up, Sit Down' — Teacher reads a statement (e.g., 'I agree with homework'). Students stand if they agree, sit if they disagree, and must say a reason why.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Roleplay with a Twist' — Students work in pairs. One is a KET examiner, the other a candidate. The candidate must answer questions using KET frames, but the examiner adds a complication (e.g., 'What if you had no money?'). They swap roles after 3 minutes.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read a short KET-style email (60 words) about a problem (e.g., 'I can't go to the party'). They write a reply (60 words) agreeing or disagreeing with the problem and suggesting a solution, using KET frames.
lp.st: Story + goodbye: Read a short story about a student preparing for KET speaking. Close with: 'Today we practiced KET speaking with complications — well done! Thank you, class.'
g: Students match questions to responses in pairs, then swap cards with another pair.
Students stand in a circle and pass a ball, saying 'I agree' or 'I disagree' about a topic.
Teams race to write a KET dialogue with a complication on the board.
Students race to write KET speaking frames from memory on the board.
Students ask a KET question and the next student must answer with a complication.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 3-sentence dialogue with two complications using KET frames.
Support: Use a sentence starter frame (e.g., 'I think... because...') to help with responses.
hw: Homework 1: Find a video about KET speaking on YouTube and summarize it in 3 sentences.
Homework 2: Write a KET-style email to a friend agreeing or disagreeing with their plan.
Homework 3: Practice KET speaking part 2 with a family member and note one phrase they used.
lp.tip: Encourage students to use Moroccan cultural examples (e.g., 'I agree with celebrating Eid, but...') to make the language more personal and relevant.

weeks.obj: Run a review carousel with teams; review the year across stations with accuracy and speed
weeks.lang: all year outcomes + semester 2 review
weeks.act:
Mixed-skills revision circuit in teams
Project: eco-poster campaign for the Space; must/should for green rules.
weeks.hw:
revise your notes for the assessment week
