Design a 5-rule green poster with must/should.

skills.L: Listening carousel with note-taking
skills.S: Team speaking carousel, leading the rounds
skills.R: Reading carousel - mixed tasks
skills.W: Writing carousel - transformations and story

lp.wu: Earth Day Quiz Relay: Teams race to answer 10 quick review questions (e.g., 'Present perfect for experience?', 'Past continuous signal word?') by writing answers on the board. Fastest team gets a point.
wuAlt: Grammar Ball Toss: Students toss a ball and answer a review question when they catch it.
Word Chain Challenge: Teams take turns adding one word to a chain of grammar terms (e.g., 'present → perfect → continuous').
lp.pres: Show 5 eco-rules flashcards (e.g., 'Turn off lights', 'Use reusable bags'). Model: 'We must turn off lights to save energy.' Elicit more rules, then drill sentences with 'must/should'. Check understanding with thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Video Clip: Play a 1-minute Earth Day video, pause to extract rules as class sentences.
Realia: Show a plastic bottle and a reusable bag, elicit 'We should use reusable bags instead of plastic ones.'
lp.prac: Green Rules Matching: Students match rule halves (e.g., 'We must...' → '...recycle paper') in pairs. Then, play 'Rule Relay'—teams race to write correct full sentences on the board.
pracAlt: Sentence Transformation: Change 'You can litter' to 'You shouldn't litter' in pairs.
Rule Charades: Students act out eco-rules for teammates to guess in sentences.
lp.ls: Earth Day Podcast Listening: Students listen to a 2-minute teen podcast about green habits and tick 3 rules mentioned. Then, in pairs, compare answers and add one more rule they heard.
lp.re: Eco-Simon Says: Teacher calls out commands like 'Simon says turn off the lights!' Students mime the action. Fast-paced to re-energize after break.
lp.prod: Eco-Poster Design: Teams create a 5-rule green poster for the American Space using 'must/should'. They present their poster with 2-minute explanations (e.g., 'We must plant trees because...').
lp.rw: Reading Carousel: Teams rotate through 3 stations—(1) Read a short text about Earth Day history, (2) Match headings to paragraphs, (3) Find 5 'must/should' sentences. Then, write their own 2-sentence rule for the Space.
lp.st: Read 'The Lorax' excerpt, discuss its message. Close with: 'Today we reviewed grammar and made eco-rules—well done! Thank you, class.'
g: Students shoot paper balls into a bin after answering a review question correctly.
Teams race to write correct grammar sentences on the board.
Teams draw eco-rules for others to guess in sentences.
Teams bid on correct sentences, using fake money.
Students stand up and answer quick review questions in turns.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a 'Green Pledge' badge with 3 personal rules using 'must/should'.
Support: Use sentence frames ('We must...') to complete the poster rules.
hw: Design a 5-rule green poster for your home using 'must/should'.
Write 60 words: 'Why Earth Day matters to Morocco'.
Record a 30-second video explaining one eco-rule in English.
lp.tip: Use local context (e.g., 'We should preserve Morocco's beaches') to make grammar relevant and boost engagement.

weeks.obj: Show my progress in the final assessment; complete final written and speaking assessments; celebrate
weeks.lang: all year outcomes + full-year review; PET orientation
weeks.res: Tests; program certificates pack; Creative writing
weeks.act:
Mixed-skills revision circuit in teams
Dream job interviews: question forms + reporting answers.
weeks.hw:
revise your notes for the assessment week
Write your dream-job interview Q&A (6 exchanges).

skills.L: Final listening paper
skills.S: Final paired speaking and PET preview
skills.R: Final reading paper
skills.W: Final writing task and portfolio pick

lp.wu: Students play 'Speed Review' in teams of 4. Each team gets a set of 10 flashcards with key year phrases (e.g., 'I've been to...'). They race to make sentences using the prompts, scoring points for accuracy and speed.
wuAlt: Students do 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid of 8 skills (e.g., 'can write an email') and interview peers to find matches.
Students play 'Vocabulary Pictionary' with 6 target words from the year (e.g., 'interview', 'labour').
lp.pres: Teacher introduces the 'Dream Job Interview' task using a model dialogue on the board. Highlights question forms ('What do you like about...?') and reporting answers ('She said she wanted to...'). Checks understanding with thumbs-up/down for sample questions.
presAlt: Teacher uses a short video of a teen mock interview to elicit target language.
Teacher distributes a 2-sentence handout with question stems and reporting phrases for students to complete.
lp.prac: Students practice in pairs with a 'Job Interview Role Card' (e.g., 'You want to be a video game designer'). They ask 3 questions and report answers using 'He/She told me...'. Teacher monitors and corrects errors.
pracAlt: Students play 'Interview Relay' in teams: one student interviews another, then reports to the group.
Students use a 'Question Bank' handout to match questions to job topics (e.g., 'travel' for pilot).
lp.ls: Students listen to a 2-minute audio of a PET-style interview between two teens discussing their dream jobs. They tick 5 correct statements from a list (e.g., 'Maria wants to be a doctor').
lp.re: After break, students play 'Stand Up, Sit Down' with 5 job-related adjectives (e.g., 'creative'). Teacher calls an adjective, students stand if it describes their dream job.
lp.prod: Students conduct a full 'Dream Job Interview' in pairs (2 minutes each). They prepare 3 questions, interview, then report 2 key answers to the class using 'He/She said...'. Teacher provides a feedback rubric.
lp.rw: Students complete a PET-style reading task: a 150-word text about 'Labour Day in Morocco' with 6 multiple-choice questions. Then, they write a 60-word email to a friend about their Labour Day plans.
lp.st: Teacher shares a short story about a teen's first job experience. Students discuss 1 question: 'What job would you like to try?' Close with: 'You showed your English progress today. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams race to write 5 job-related words from memory.
Students ask a question, next student answers and asks a new one.
Students act out jobs while others guess.
Students bid on correct sentences about jobs.
Teams answer 10 mixed-skill questions for points.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a 50-word paragraph about their ideal job interview.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence starter frame for their interview report (e.g., 'He told me he likes...').
hw: Write your dream-job interview Q&A (6 exchanges).
Review 5 key grammar points from the year (e.g., present perfect).
Complete the PET reading practice handout.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan Labour Day (May 1st) to connect the theme locally—ask students how their families celebrate or what jobs they admire in Oujda.
checklist: I can ask and answer questions about jobs.
I can report what someone said using 'He/She told me...'.
I can understand a 2-minute interview audio.
I can read a short text about Labour Day.
I can write a 60-word email about my plans.
I can use present perfect for experience.
I can use past continuous for descriptions.

levels.desc: For teens aged 14–18 working at A2–B1. The year covers present perfect, past continuous, used to, conditionals 0/1, relative clauses, and reported speech basics, with extended speaking (2-minute turns), multi-paragraph reading, and 60–80 word emails and stories — bridging KET to PET with real-world teen themes and critical-thinking prompts.

levels.label: Adults · Beginners

weeks.obj: introduce themselves, state learning goals, and use key classroom language
weeks.lang: be (am/is/are); Wh- questions; classroom language
weeks.act: Speed introductions; goals discussion in pairs; course overview walk-through
weeks.hw: write a 4-sentence self-introduction

skills.L: Listen to introductions and catch names and goals
skills.S: Introduce myself and state my learning goals
skills.R: Read classroom-language phrases and match them to moments
skills.W: Complete a personal-details form (Worksheets)

lp.wu: Human Bingo: Students mingle with bingo cards listing traits like 'likes tea' or 'has a car', asking 'Do you like tea?' and marking names. First to get BINGO wins.
wuAlt: Name Chain: Students stand in a circle, each saying 'I'm [Name] and I like [hobby]', repeating all previous names and hobbies.
Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three statements about themselves, two true and one false; others guess the lie.
lp.pres: Teacher introduces a self-introduction model: 'I'm [Name]. I'm [Age]. I'm from [City]. I want to learn English for [Job/Travel].' Uses flashcards with flags and job icons. Checks understanding with 'What's my name? Where am I from?'
presAlt: Guest Speaker: A volunteer student (prepped) introduces themselves first, then the teacher breaks down their sentences.
Video Model: Show a short clip of two people introducing themselves, then pause to elicit key phrases.
lp.prac: Speed Introductions: Students form two lines, facing each other. They introduce themselves with the model, then one line moves. Teacher monitors and corrects 'be' errors. After 5 rounds, students report their partner's name and goal.
pracAlt: Introduction Circle: Students sit in a circle, passing a ball. The holder introduces themselves and asks 'What's your name?' to the next person.
Fill-in-the-Blank: Students complete a worksheet with 'I ___ [Name]. I ___ from [City]. I ___ to learn English for ___.'
lp.ls: Listen and Match: Teacher reads 5 short introductions (e.g., 'I'm Ali. I'm 25. I'm from Casablanca. I want to learn English for work.'). Students match each to a photo on their worksheet.
lp.re: Stand Up If...: Teacher calls out 'Stand up if you want to learn English for travel!', 'Stand up if you're from Oujda!', etc. Students stand and say 'I want to learn English for [reason]!'
lp.prod: Pair Goal Discussion: Students interview their partner using 'Why do you want to learn English?' and note their answers. Then, each student introduces their partner to the class: 'This is [Name]. He/She wants to learn English for [reason].'
lp.rw: Classroom Language Matching: Students read 10 phrases ('Can I borrow a pen?', 'Open your book, please.') and match them to classroom situations (e.g., 'Someone needs a pen'). Then, they complete a personal-details form with name, age, phone, email.
lp.st: Goodbye Song: Teacher leads 'See You Later, Alligator' with gestures. Recap: 'Today we learned to introduce ourselves and say our goals. Thank you, class! Goodbye!'
g: Students ask 'Do you like...?' to fill their bingo cards.
Students repeat names and hobbies in a circle.
Students guess false statements about peers.
Students stand and state goals for prompts.
Partners ask 'Why learn English?' and report back.
Students pass a ball and introduce themselves.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 5-sentence introduction including a hobby.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'My name is ___. I am ___. I want to learn English for ___.'
hw: Write a 4-sentence self-introduction on paper.
Record a 30-second video introducing yourself to a friend.
Find 3 classroom language phrases online and practice them.
lp.tip: Use local examples (e.g., 'I want to learn English for a job at the American Space') to make goals relevant. Avoid correcting every error—focus on communication.

weeks.obj: give and spell personal details; complete a simple form
weeks.lang: the alphabet; numbers 0-100; name/age/address fields
weeks.act: Form-filling pairs; spelling bee (names and cities); number dictation race
weeks.hw: complete the sample registration form

skills.L: Listening folder: spelling dialogues - catch the letters
skills.S: Spell my name and details aloud
skills.R: Read form fields and match them to answers
skills.W: Complete a simple registration form

lp.wu: Human Bingo: Students mingle asking 'What's your name? How old are you? Where do you live?' to fill bingo cards with classmates' details.
wuAlt: Alphabet Chain: Students stand in a circle and say 'A is for apple, B is for banana...' taking turns.
Number Race: Teacher calls out numbers 0-20, students write them on mini-boards.
lp.pres: Show a sample registration form on the board; model filling it with your details ('My name is... I am... years old. I live at...'); drill pronunciation of 'name', 'age', 'address'.
presAlt: Realia props: Hold up an ID card, ask 'What's this? It's my ID. My name is...'; students repeat.
Dialogue: Roleplay a registration scene with a student ('Hello, what's your name? My name is...').
lp.prac: Form-filling pairs: Students get blank forms, take turns asking and writing partner's details; teacher circulates to correct spelling and pronunciation.
pracAlt: Spelling Bee: Teacher says a name/city (e.g., 'Oujda'), students spell it aloud; fastest wins a point.
Number Dictation Race: Dictate ages (e.g., 'twenty-five'), students write numbers on paper; first pair correct wins.
lp.ls: Listen and fill: Play a dialogue where two people exchange personal details; students listen and complete a half-filled form with missing letters/numbers.
lp.re: Alphabet Jump: Teacher calls out a letter (e.g., 'G'), students jump and say a word starting with it; repeat with numbers (e.g., '15' = 'Fifteen!').
lp.prod: Registration Roleplay: Students pretend to register at the American Space Oujda; one asks 'What's your name? How old are you? Where do you live?', the other answers and fills a form.
lp.rw: Read and Match: Students read short form fields ('Name: __', 'Age: __') and match them to answers ('Fatima', '25') from a list; then copy the completed form.
lp.st: Close with a song: 'Hello, Hello, What's Your Name?' (to the tune of 'Twinkle Twinkle') + recap: 'Today we learned to give and spell personal information. Thank you, class!'
g: Teams race to write the alphabet on the board, one letter per student.
Teacher calls numbers, students cross them off cards; first to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Students spell names in a line; one mistake and they sit down.
Students guess teacher's age by asking 'Are you 20? 25? 30?' until correct.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph introducing themselves (e.g., 'My name is... I am... I live at...').
Support: Use a word bank with alphabet letters and numbers 0-20 for spelling practice.
hw: Complete the sample registration form from class (write name, age, address).
Interview a family member: Ask their name, age, address and write it down.
Write 5 names and 5 ages in English (e.g., 'Layla: 22', 'Omar: 30').
lp.tip: Use Moroccan names and addresses (e.g., 'Oujda, Morocco') to make the task relevant; praise effort over accuracy to build confidence.

weeks.obj: say where people are from and ask follow-up questions
weeks.lang: countries/nationalities; from / live in; he/she + is
weeks.act: World map mingle; guess the country quiz; where-are-you-from chain
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to where-people-are-from dialogues
skills.S: Say where people are from and ask follow-ups
skills.R: Read short profiles and complete the country table
skills.W: Write 3 sentences about countries (he/she is from)

lp.wu: Teacher greets students and shows a world map. Students point to their home country and say: 'I am from Morocco.' Teacher models and drills pronunciation.
wuAlt: Teacher holds up flag flashcards; students say the country name and nationality in chorus.
Teacher says a country; students jump and say the nationality.
lp.pres: Teacher presents 5 country flashcards (Morocco, USA, UK, France, Spain) with flags and nationalities. Models 'He is from Morocco. She is from Spain.' Checks understanding with thumbs up/down for true/false sentences.
presAlt: Teacher draws simple country outlines on the board; students guess and repeat the country name.
Teacher uses a short video clip of people saying 'I am from...' with subtitles.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs with a country table worksheet. They take turns asking 'Where are you from?' and answering 'I am from [country].' Teacher monitors and corrects errors.
pracAlt: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid of countries; they ask classmates and write names.
Teacher gives each student a country card; they mingle and ask 'Where are you from?' to the group.
lp.ls: Students listen to a KET-style audio of 3 people introducing themselves. They complete a table with names and countries. Teacher plays audio twice.
lp.re: Teacher calls out a country; students race to point to it on the world map. Fastest student gets to call the next country.
lp.prod: Students stand in a circle. The first student says 'I am from Morocco.' The next student says 'He is from Morocco. I am from France.' The chain continues around the circle.
lp.rw: Students read 3 short profiles (e.g., 'My name is Amina. I am from Morocco.') and fill in a table with countries. Then they write 3 sentences: 'He is from Spain. She is from France. I am from Morocco.'
lp.st: Teacher sings a simple 'Where Are You From?' song with clapping. Class says goodbye with 'Thank you, teacher. See you next time!'
g: Students mingle, ask 'Where are you from?', and mark countries on their map.
Teacher describes a country (language, flag); students guess the name.
Students write nationalities on a grid; teacher calls them out.
Students sit in a circle; each adds a country to the growing list.
Students match country flags to their names on flashcards.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 5 sentences about famous people's countries.
Support: Use word bank with countries/nationalities for writing task.
hw: Complete the 'Where Are You From?' survey with 5 family members.
Draw 3 flags and write the country names.
Write 3 sentences about your classmates from today's class.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'I am from Morocco, like Hassan II.') to build connection and pride in the learners' identity while practicing the target language.

weeks.obj: describe jobs with a/an and say where people work
weeks.lang: jobs vocabulary; a/an; work in/at/on
weeks.act:
Job charades; workplace matching; what-does-she-do guessing game
Discussion: Halloween between commerce and culture; compare with local celebrations.
weeks.hw:
describe 3 family members' jobs
Write a short opinion paragraph: should Oujda celebrate Halloween?

skills.L: Listen to job descriptions with a / an
skills.S: Describe jobs and workplaces with in / at / on
skills.R: Read job ads and check the a / an usage (Lesson Plans/Jobs)
skills.W: Write about my job (3 sentences)

lp.wu: Job Charades: Teacher writes 5 job words (e.g., doctor, teacher, chef, driver, nurse) on slips. Students take turns drawing a slip, miming the job silently, and classmates guess by shouting 'Is he a...?' or 'Is she a...?'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who: Hand out a grid with jobs (e.g., 'Find someone whose father is a doctor'). Students mingle and ask 'Is your father a doctor?' and write names.
Flashcard Quick Review: Show 10 job flashcards one by one. Students shout the job name and use 'a/an' (e.g., 'A doctor!').
lp.pres: Teacher shows 10 job flashcards (doctor, teacher, chef, driver, nurse, engineer, artist, farmer, pilot, waiter) and says 'He is a doctor. She is a teacher.' Elicits 'a/an' rule. Then shows workplace flashcards (hospital, school, restaurant, taxi, office, farm, plane, kitchen) and models 'He works in a hospital. She works at a school. He works on a farm.' Checks understanding with 'Where does a doctor work?'
presAlt: Realia Presentation: Bring props (stethoscope, book, chef's hat). Students guess the job and teacher models sentences.
Storytime: Read a simple story 'Sam the Chef' with pictures, highlighting 'a chef' and 'works in a kitchen'.
lp.prac: Workplace Matching: Students get 10 job cards and 10 workplace cards. They match pairs (e.g., nurse + hospital) and say 'A nurse works in a hospital.' in pairs. Teacher monitors and corrects 'a/an' and 'in/at/on'.
pracAlt: Fill-in-the-Blanks Worksheet: Students complete sentences like 'He is _____ engineer. She works _____ office.' with a/an or in/at/on.
Job Bingo: Teacher calls out 'a doctor' or 'works in a hospital', students cross off the matching picture.
lp.ls: Listen and Draw: Teacher describes 3 jobs (e.g., 'He is a pilot. He works on a plane. She is a teacher. She works at a school. He is a farmer. He works in a field.') Students draw and label the jobs and workplaces.
lp.re: Stand Up If...: Teacher calls out 'Stand up if you work in a hospital!' or 'Stand up if you know a teacher!' Students stand up and say 'I know a teacher!' or 'My friend is a doctor!'
lp.prod: Guess the Job: Student A thinks of a job and says 'He works in a hospital. He helps people.' Student B guesses 'Is he a doctor?' Continue in pairs. Teacher models first.
lp.rw: Read and Correct: Students read 5 job ads (e.g., 'We need a nurse. Work in a hospital. We need a teacher. Work at a school.') and circle mistakes in 'a/an' or 'in/at/on'. Then write 3 correct sentences about their own dream job.
lp.st: Halloween Song: Sing 'Five Little Pumpkins' with gestures. End with 'Today we learned about jobs and Halloween. Thank you, class! Goodbye!'
g: Student mimes a job, others guess 'Is he a...?'
Teacher calls out 'works in a hospital', students cross off the picture.
Ask 'Is your mother a teacher?' and write names.
Describe a job with 'He works in a hospital. He helps people.'
Complete sentences with a/an or in/at/on.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 more sentences about jobs using 'a/an' and 'in/at/on'.
Support: Use word bank with jobs and workplaces for matching activity.
hw: Describe 3 family members' jobs (e.g., 'My father is a teacher. He works at a school.')
Write a short opinion paragraph: 'Should Oujda celebrate Halloween? Why or why not?'
Draw a picture of your dream job and write 2 sentences about it.
lp.tip: Connect Halloween to local culture by comparing it to Moroccan celebrations like Mawlid al-Nabi or Aid al-Fitr. Ask students to share their opinions on imported festivals vs. traditional ones.

weeks.obj: describe their day with present simple and time expressions
weeks.lang: present simple I/you/we; at + time; adverbs of frequency
weeks.act:
Routine survey mingle; my-day timeline; adverb line-up (always-never)
Discussion with for/since: "Morocco HAS HAD the southern provinces SINCE 1975..."
weeks.hw:
Participation quiz
Write 6 for/since sentences about national milestones.

skills.L: Listen to a daily routine and note the times
skills.S: Describe my day with present simple + at + time
skills.R: Read a routine text and find the time expressions
skills.W: Write my daily routine (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Routine Relay: Students stand in two lines. Teacher shows a flashcard of a morning routine (e.g., 'brush teeth'). First student in line mimes it and says 'I brush my teeth at 7 AM'. Next student mimes another routine and says their time. Fastest line wins.
wuAlt: Time Bingo: Teacher calls out times (e.g., '8:15 AM'). Students mark them on a bingo grid with pictures of routines.
Find Someone Who: Students walk around asking 'Do you...?' (e.g., 'Do you exercise at 6 PM?') and find classmates who say 'Yes, I do.'
lp.pres: Teacher draws a timeline on the board from 6 AM to 10 PM. Uses flashcards of common routines (eat breakfast, go to work, sleep) and places them on the timeline with times. Models 'I eat breakfast at 7 AM'. Checks understanding by asking 'What time do I eat breakfast?' and 'What do I do at 9 AM?'
presAlt: Routine Story: Teacher tells a simple story about their day using present simple and times. Students repeat sentences chorally.
Adverb Line-Up: Teacher writes 'always' to 'never' on the board. Students place flashcards of routines (e.g., 'pray', 'eat pizza') on the line to show frequency.
lp.prac: Routine Survey Mingle: Students get a worksheet with names and routines. They walk around asking classmates 'What time do you...?' (e.g., 'What time do you pray?') and fill in the times. Teacher monitors and helps with pronunciation.
pracAlt: My-Day Timeline: Students draw a timeline of their own day and label 3-5 activities with times. They practice saying their timeline to a partner.
Adverb Practice: Teacher gives each student a routine flashcard. Students line up from 'always' to 'never' and say a sentence like 'I always pray.'
lp.ls: Listen to a short audio of someone describing their daily routine. Students listen and fill in the missing times on a worksheet. Teacher plays audio twice. Checks answers by having students compare with a partner.
lp.re: Stand Up Sit Down: Teacher says a routine with an adverb (e.g., 'I always pray'). If it's true for them, students stand up. If false, they sit down. Fast-paced and energetic.
lp.prod: My-Day Presentation: Students use their timeline from practice to prepare a short 3-sentence talk about their daily routine. They present to a small group, using 'I... at...'. Teacher provides feedback on pronunciation.
lp.rw: Read a short text about a Moroccan's daily routine. Students circle all the time expressions (e.g., 'at 6:30 AM'). Then, they write 3 sentences about their own day using present simple and 'at + time'.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about the Green March, using simple past tense (e.g., 'In 1975, Morocco went to the Sahara'). Students repeat key sentences. Close with 'Today we learned to describe our daily routine. Thank you, class!'
g: Students race to mime and say a routine with time.
Students mark times called by the teacher on their bingo cards.
Students ask 'Do you...?' to find classmates who match routines.
Students place routine flashcards on a frequency line.
Students draw and label their daily routine with times.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 6 sentences about national milestones using 'for' and 'since' (e.g., 'Morocco has had the Sahara since 1975').
Support learners: Use a sentence frame 'I ____ at ____.' to write their routine.
hw: Write 6 sentences about national milestones using 'for' and 'since' (e.g., 'Morocco has had the Sahara since 1975').
Draw a timeline of your family's day and label 5 activities with times.
Record yourself saying 3 sentences about your daily routine and send it to the teacher.
lp.tip: Connect daily routines to local customs, like prayer times, to make the language relevant. Use the Green March story to introduce 'since' naturally, linking to national identity.

weeks.obj: talk about free-time activities and preferences
weeks.lang: like/love/enjoy + -ing; free-time activities
weeks.act: Find someone who...; preference corners; weekend plan discussion pairs
weeks.hw: 5 sentences about your free time

skills.L: Listen to like / enjoy + -ing mini-talks
skills.S: Talk about my free-time preferences
skills.R: Read free-time profiles and underline the -ing forms
skills.W: Write my free-time paragraph (4 sentences)

lp.wu: Students stand up. Teacher shows flashcards of free-time activities (playing football, reading books, cooking). Students walk around and ask each other: 'Do you like...?' and respond with 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'.
wuAlt: Teacher writes 'free time' on the board. Students brainstorm activities in pairs, writing 3 each on sticky notes and sticking them up.
Teacher mimes an activity (e.g., swimming). Students guess: 'Do you like swimming?' Teacher responds with 'Yes, I love it' or 'No, I enjoy reading'.
lp.pres: Teacher presents 3 model sentences: 'I like playing football', 'I love reading books', 'I enjoy cooking'. Uses flashcards to show each activity. Checks understanding by asking: 'What do I love?' and 'Do I like cooking?'
presAlt: Teacher tells a short story: 'On weekends, I like walking in the park. I love drinking mint tea. I enjoy listening to music.' Underlines the -ing forms.
Teacher uses realia: a football, a book, a cooking pot. Holds each up and says the sentence, then gestures for students to repeat chorally.
lp.prac: Students do 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid of activities. They walk around and ask: 'Do you like...?' and write names. Teacher monitors and models questions.
pracAlt: Students work in pairs. Teacher gives each pair a set of activity cards. They take turns saying: 'I like/love/enjoy...' and the partner responds with 'Me too' or 'I don't, I prefer...'.
Teacher plays 'Guess the Activity'. Mimes an activity; students guess using: 'Do you like...?' Teacher responds with 'Yes, I love it' or 'No, I enjoy...'
lp.ls: Students listen to 3 short audio clips of people talking about their free time. They tick the activities mentioned on their worksheet. Teacher plays each clip twice.
lp.re: Students stand in a circle. Teacher says an activity (e.g., 'swimming'), and students jump if they like it, squat if they don't. Quick and energetic.
lp.prod: Students work in pairs. They plan their ideal weekend using 'I like/love/enjoy...'. They then present their plan to the class: 'On Saturday, I like... On Sunday, I love...'
lp.rw: Students read 3 short profiles of people's free-time activities. They underline all the -ing forms. Then they write 4 sentences about their own free time using 'like/love/enjoy + -ing'.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a character's weekend using target language. Ends with the goodbye routine: 'Today we talked about free time. Thank you, class!'
g: Students match flashcards to sentences like 'I love swimming'.
Teacher labels corners of the room: 'love', 'like', 'enjoy'. Students go to the corner for an activity when called out.
Student mimes an activity; others guess using 'Do you like...?'
Students have bingo cards with activities. They ask classmates: 'Do you like...?' to mark off squares.
Student 1 says: 'I like playing football'. Student 2 repeats and adds: 'I love reading books'.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 6 sentences about their friends' free time.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'I like ___. I love ___. I enjoy ___.'
hw: Write 5 sentences about your free time using like/love/enjoy + -ing.
Interview a family member about their free time and write 3 sentences.
Draw a picture of your ideal weekend and label 3 activities with -ing words.
lp.tip: Connect activities to local context: ask about free time during Ramadan or holidays like Green March. Use real-life examples like 'liking mint tea with friends' to build rapport.

weeks.theme: Culture corner: festivals and small talk
weeks.obj: compare celebrations; use small-talk openers comfortably
weeks.lang: festival vocabulary; small talk questions and safe topics
weeks.act:
Festival photo discussion; small talk elevator game; reading with questions
Discussion: independence and identity; past perfect practice ("by 1956, Morocco had...").
weeks.hw:
Participation quiz
Write 5 sentences in the past perfect about Moroccan history.

skills.L: Listen to festival small talk (Seasonal/culture)
skills.S: Use small-talk openers in festival chat
skills.R: Read a short festival text
skills.W: Write 3 small-talk questions with answers

lp.wu: Festival Bingo: Students receive bingo cards with pictures of different festivals (Eid, Independence Day, Christmas, etc.). Teacher calls out names, students mark the pictures. First to get a line shouts 'Bingo!' and names the festivals they marked.
wuAlt: Guess the Festival: Teacher describes a festival (e.g., 'It's in November, people celebrate independence, there are parades'), students guess the name. Then students take turns describing Moroccan festivals for others to guess.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Have you ever celebrated [festival]?' and find classmates who have, writing their names.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a photo of a Moroccan Independence Day celebration and a US Independence Day celebration. Elicits vocabulary like 'parade', 'flag', 'speech', 'family gathering'. Models sentences: 'In Morocco, we celebrate on November 11th. In the US, they celebrate on July 4th.' Asks checking questions: 'When do we celebrate?' 'What do we see?'
presAlt: Festival Comparison Chart: On the board, draw two columns. Students call out words to fill it for Eid and Independence Day (food, clothes, activities).
Realia Display: Teacher brings in items for a celebration (Moroccan flag, US flag, a small plate of mint tea, a small piece of baklava) and elicits vocabulary and uses for each.
lp.prac: Festival Photo Pairs: Students work in pairs. Each pair gets two photos (one Moroccan festival, one American festival). They use the model sentences to compare them: 'This is Eid. We eat couscous. This is Thanksgiving. They eat turkey.' Teacher monitors and helps with pronunciation.
pracAlt: Match the Words: Students get a worksheet with festival vocabulary (parade, flag, speech, music) and pictures. They draw lines to match the words.
Sentence Builders: Students get sentence strips with the structure '[Country] celebrates [festival] on [date]. They eat [food].' They arrange the strips to make correct sentences.
lp.ls: Listen and Order: Students listen to a short audio recording of two people making small talk at a festival. They have a jumbled list of sentences (e.g., 'Great food, isn't it?', 'Have you been to the parade before?'). They listen and put the sentences in the correct order to make a conversation.
lp.re: Stand Up, Sit Down: Teacher says a statement about festivals (e.g., 'You like parades.'). Students who agree stand up, students who disagree sit down. Teacher says statements using 'By 1956, Morocco had...' to reactivate the past perfect.
lp.prod: Small Talk Elevator Game: Students are in pairs. They pretend to be in an elevator at a festival. They have 30 seconds to make small talk using the openers: 'Nice day for a festival, isn't it?', 'Have you been to this before?', 'What's your favorite part?'. They swap partners and repeat with a new topic.
lp.rw: Reading and Writing: Students read a short text (5-6 sentences) about the history of Moroccan Independence Day. Then, they write 3 small-talk questions they could ask someone at a celebration, e.g., 'Do you like the music?', 'Is this your first time here?', 'What do you usually do on this day?'
lp.st: Teacher tells a short, personal story about a memorable celebration, using simple past tense. Then, the class says goodbye together: 'Today we learned to compare celebrations and make small talk. Thank you, everyone. Have a good day.'
g: Students act out a festival (e.g., waving a flag, eating) and others guess.
In pairs, students have two similar festival pictures and take turns asking questions to find five differences.
Students sit in two lines. They have 1 minute to ask small talk questions, then one line moves.
Teacher asks questions like 'When is Independence Day?' 'What color is the Moroccan flag?' Students answer in teams.
Teacher says a prompt like '1956', students race to say a sentence like 'By 1956, Morocco had become independent.'
diff: Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame to write their small talk questions: 'Do you like ___?' 'What is ___?'
hw: Write 5 sentences in the past perfect about Moroccan history (e.g., 'By 1956, Morocco had gained its independence.')
Interview a family member about their favorite celebration and write down 3 things they said.
Write down 3 small talk questions you could ask a tourist at a festival in Morocco.
lp.tip: Connect the lesson to students' lives by explicitly linking the language of comparison and small talk to their goals of interacting with tourists or international visitors at the American Space.

weeks.obj: describe family members and relationships
weeks.lang: possessive 's; family vocabulary; have got
weeks.act:
Family photo description circle; possessive relay; family riddles
Discussion: gratitude rituals across cultures; polite dinner-language practice.
weeks.hw:
describe 3 people in your family
Write a thank-you message (email or card) in English.

skills.L: Listen to family descriptions with possessive s
skills.S: Describe family members and relationships
skills.R: Read a family text and find the possessives
skills.W: Write about my family (4 sentences)

lp.wu: Family Chain: Students stand in a circle. The first student says 'This is my mother.' The next student says 'This is his mother. This is my father.' and so on, adding one family member each time. They use possessive 's to link the previous person to their own family.
wuAlt: Find the Pair: Students receive half a family photo (e.g., 'My father') and must find the other half ('is a teacher') to make a complete sentence.
Speed Greetings: Students mingle and ask 'Have you got a brother/sister?' and respond with 'Yes, I have' or 'No, I haven't.'
lp.pres: Show a large family tree flashcard. Point to each member and model sentences: 'This is my uncle. He's my mother's brother.' Drill the sentences chorally. Ask students to repeat and point to their own family members on the card. Check with thumbs up/down if they understand 'mother's brother'.
presAlt: Bring in a real photo of your family. Describe each person: 'This is my husband. He's a doctor. This is our daughter. She's five.' Students ask questions.
Use a simple story about a family. Draw stick figures on the board and label them with possessives as you read the story aloud.
lp.prac: Possessive Relay: Divide the class into two teams. Give each team a set of family member cards (mother, father, sister, etc.). The first student runs to the board, writes a sentence like 'This is my mother', runs back, and tags the next student who writes a possessive sentence about another family member. The team with the most correct sentences wins.
pracAlt: Family Riddles: I write a riddle on the board: 'I am my father's mother. Who am I?' Students guess 'You are your grandmother.' In pairs, students write and solve riddles.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Have you got a [family member]?' and write names on a bingo grid.
lp.ls: Listen to a short audio recording of a person describing their family. Students listen and tick the family members they hear (a worksheet with pictures of mother, father, sister, brother, grandmother, grandfather). Play the audio twice. Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Family Charades: One student acts out a family member (e.g., cooking for 'mother', reading for 'grandfather'). The class guesses 'Is he your father?' or 'Is she your sister?' using target language.
lp.prod: Thanksgiving Dinner Roleplay: In pairs, students are at a Thanksgiving dinner. One person is the host, the other is a guest. The guest asks 'Is this your aunt?' and the host responds. They practice polite dinner language: 'Can I have some more turkey, please?' 'Thank you for the meal.'
lp.rw: Read a short text about a family. Students circle all the possessive 's (e.g., 'My father's name is...'). Then, they write 4 simple sentences about their own family using 'This is my...' and 'He/She has got...'
lp.st: Read a short story about gratitude, like 'Thankful for My Family'. End with a one-minute gratitude share: each student says one thing they are thankful for about their family. Close with 'Today we learned to describe our family. Thank you for your hard work and have a great day!'
g: Students draw a 3x3 grid and write family member words. The teacher calls out clues like 'This person is your mother's mother.' Students mark the square.
A student thinks of a family member. The class asks yes/no questions: 'Is it a man?' 'Has he got a beard?' to guess who it is.
Wrap a box with layers of paper. In each layer is a family member card. When the music stops, the student opens a layer and makes a sentence with the card.
Students draw their family tree on a paper plate and label each member with a possessive 's sentence.
Each student adds one sentence to a story about a family, using 'and' or 'but' to connect ideas.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph (5 sentences) about their ideal family dinner.
Support: Use a sentence frame worksheet with pictures to complete sentences like 'This is my ____.' and 'He/She has got ____ ____.'
hw: Draw your family and write 4 sentences: 'This is my... He/She has got... He/She is...'.
Write a thank-you email to a family member. Include: 'Thank you for... I love your...'.
Interview a family member in Arabic and write 3 sentences in English about them using 'He/She has got...'
lp.tip: For adults, connect the family theme to their real lives by asking about their roles as parents, children, or siblings. This respects their life experience and makes the language relevant.

weeks.obj: ask and answer about prices; handle a simple purchase
weeks.lang: How much...?; numbers/prices; this/that
weeks.act: Market roleplay with real price lists; bargaining dialogues; listening gap-fill
weeks.hw: Roleplay performance check

skills.L: Listening folder: shopping mp3 - prices and totals
skills.S: Ask and answer about prices; buy an item
skills.R: Read price tags and a receipt
skills.W: Write a shopping dialogue (6 lines)

lp.wu: Students play 'Price Guess' with realia: teacher holds up items (apple, pen, notebook), students guess 'How much is it?' in Moroccan Dirhams, then reveal the price tag.
wuAlt: Students match picture cards to price tags (e.g., 'book' to '20 DH')
Students count out play money for simple amounts (e.g., 'Show me 50 DH')
lp.pres: Teacher introduces 'How much is this/that?' using fruit flashcards, models asking and answering, then mimes shopping gestures; students repeat chorally and individually.
presAlt: Teacher uses a simple dialogue script on the board: 'How much is this?' 'It's 10 DH'
Teacher draws a market scene on the board, labeling items with prices
lp.prac: Students do 'Find the Price' in pairs: each has a flyer with items, they ask 'How much is this?' and mark the prices; teacher monitors for pronunciation.
pracAlt: Students play 'Bargaining Bingo': listen to teacher say prices, cross off matching numbers on their grid
Students do 'Price Dictation': teacher says items/prices, students write them down
lp.ls: Students listen to a market dialogue (MP3) and fill in gaps in a receipt worksheet (e.g., '1 apple = ___ DH, total = ___ DH')
lp.re: Students play 'Quick Shop': teacher calls out an item, students race to grab the correct price tag from the board.
lp.prod: Students roleplay a market stall in pairs: one is the seller (with price list), one is the buyer; they bargain using 'How much is this?' and 'Can I have this, please?'
lp.rw: Students read a simple receipt (e.g., 'Milk: 5 DH, Bread: 3 DH, Total: 8 DH') and write 3 sentences about what they bought.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about 'Ahmed's Market Day' using flashcards, then closes with: 'Today you learned to ask about prices—well done! Thank you, class.'
g: Students race to match picture cards to price tags on the board
Students repeat a dialogue chain: 'How much is this?' 'It's 10 DH.' 'How much is that?'
Students mime bargaining and others guess the price
Students race to circle matching items and prices on a worksheet
Students roleplay a quick bargain with a discount (e.g., 'It's 20 DH.' 'Okay, 15 DH.')
diff: Fast finishers: write a 6-line shopping dialogue with bargaining
Support learners: use sentence starters like 'How much is ___?' and 'It's ___ DH.'
hw: Write a 6-line shopping dialogue for buying fruit
Draw a market scene with 5 items and prices
Ask a family member about the price of 3 items in the souk
lp.tip: Use Moroccan Dirhams in all activities to build real-world relevance; praise bargaining attempts as culturally authentic.

weeks.obj: order a meal and ask about dishes politely
weeks.lang: would like; menu vocabulary; Can we have...?
weeks.act: Restaurant roleplay with menus; dish-of-the-day presentations; ordering dialogues
weeks.hw: write a 6-line restaurant dialogue

skills.L: Listening folder: restaurant mp3 - orders
skills.S: Order a meal and ask about the dishes
skills.R: Read a menu and match dishes to courses
skills.W: Write my order in full sentences

lp.wu: Students play 'Menu Pictionary' in pairs. Teacher shows a food flashcard, student draws it, partner guesses 'Is it...?' and names the dish.
wuAlt: Students play 'Food Bingo' with 9 images on a grid; teacher calls out dishes and students mark them.
Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their favorite foods using 'I like...' and 'I don't like...'.
lp.pres: Teacher presents a laminated menu with images and prices. Models 'I would like...' and 'Can we have...?' for ordering. Asks comprehension questions 'What would you like?' to check understanding.
presAlt: Teacher uses a story about a person ordering food, highlighting key phrases.
Teacher acts out a dialogue with a student waiter using real plates and cutlery as props.
lp.prac: Students complete a 'Fill the Gap' worksheet with sentences like 'I ___ like the soup.' They then practice in pairs using a dialogue prompt card with 'Would you like...?' and 'Can we have...?'
pracAlt: Students play 'Restaurant Role Cards' where one is a waiter and the other a customer using a provided menu.
Students play 'Memory Match' matching food images to their names while saying 'I would like...'.
lp.ls: Students listen to a KET-style audio of a restaurant order and tick the correct dishes on a worksheet. They then listen again and write down the drinks ordered.
lp.re: Students play 'Pass the Plate' while saying a food word when the music stops; the student holding the plate must say a full sentence 'I would like...'.
lp.prod: Students work in pairs to roleplay a restaurant scenario using laminated menus. One is the waiter, the other is a customer. They must use 'Can we have...?' and 'What is the dish of the day?'
lp.rw: Students read a short menu text and match dishes to courses (starter, main, dessert). They then write 3 simple sentences about what they would order, e.g., 'I would like the soup.'
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a customer who orders food politely and gets a free dessert. Close with 'Today we learned to order food politely. Thank you, class.'
g: Students match food flashcards to menu words in a race.
Students race to write correct sentences from spoken prompts.
Students act out a food word for others to guess using 'Is it...?'
Students present a dish using flashcards and say 'The dish of the day is...'
Teams take turns running to a menu to find and write a dish name.
diff: Fast finishers write a 4-line dialogue with a waiter asking about allergies.
Support / weaker learners use a sentence frame: 'I would like the ______, please.'
hw: Write a 6-line restaurant dialogue between a customer and waiter.
Draw your ideal meal and write 3 sentences about it.
Find 5 food words in English and write a sentence for each.
lp.tip: Model polite intonation for 'Would you like...?' as Moroccan learners may use direct translations. Connect to local dining customs like offering tea to guests.

weeks.obj: ask for and give simple directions around town
weeks.lang: imperatives; prepositions of place/movement; transport words
weeks.act: Map of Oujda task; listen-and-trace routes; transport survey mingle
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to directions audio and trace the route
skills.S: Ask for and give simple directions
skills.R: Read direction phrases and order them on a map
skills.W: Write directions to a nearby place

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Simon Says' with directions. Teacher says 'Simon says turn left', students turn left; 'Simon says go straight', students march in place. Focus on movement verbs: turn, go, stop.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Draw the Route' - teacher draws a simple path on the board, students call out directions to describe it.
Alternative 2: 'Quick Survey' - students ask each other 'How do you get to class? Bus or walk?' and tally answers.
lp.pres: Presentation: Show a large map of Oujda with key landmarks (Poste, Med V, City Center). Model giving directions: 'Go straight, turn left at the mosque.' Use finger to trace route on map. Check by asking 'Where do I turn?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use realia - toy car and street signs to demonstrate movements.
Alternative 2: Draw a simple town map on the board with students naming the places.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Map Pairs'. Students get a blank map of Oujda with streets. Student A traces a route with a pencil, Student B writes directions. Teacher circulates to correct prepositions (next to, opposite).
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Flashcard Directions' - students arrange transport flashcards (bus, taxi) to match a spoken route.
Alternative 2: 'Error Correction' - students fix preposition mistakes in a worksheet (e.g., 'turn in the bank' -> 'turn at the bank').
lp.ls: Listening slot: 'Trace the Route'. Students listen to an audio of someone giving directions from the American Space to the train station. They trace the route on their map with a different color crayon. Play twice.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Four Corners'. Label corners 'North', 'South', 'East', 'West'. Teacher calls out directions like 'Go to the corner opposite North!', students race there.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Mingle Survey'. Students ask 5 classmates 'How do you get to the souk?' and note answers (walk, taxi, bus). Then, in pairs, they give directions to one of the places mentioned using 'Go straight...'.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: 'Order the Directions'. Students read 5 jumbled sentences (e.g., 'Turn right at the pharmacy.', 'Go straight.') and glue them in order on a mini-map worksheet. Then they write 3 directions from their home to the American Space.
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Sing 'The Wheels on the Bus' with added verses ('The doors on the bus go open and close'). Close with: 'Today we learned to ask for and give directions. Thank you, class.'
g: Teacher says a landmark, students point to it on the map.
Student mimes a direction (turn left), others guess.
Two teams race to trace a correct route on the board.
Students hop to 'next to' the chair, 'opposite' the door.
Students mark transport words called out.
diff: Fast finishers: Draw a map of their neighborhood and write directions to a friend's house.
Support: Use a pre-highlighted map with key words to trace routes.
hw: Homework 1: Write 5 directions from your home to the souk.
Homework 2: Record yourself giving directions to the train station.
Homework 3: Ask a family member for directions to a local place and write them down.
lp.tip: Use landmarks familiar to students (Poste, Med V) to make directions meaningful. Pair strong/weak learners to build confidence.

weeks.obj: describe their home with there is/there are
weeks.lang: there is/there are; rooms and furniture
weeks.act:
Dream house presentations; furniture battle (describe-and-draw); listing races
Discussion: Christmas as a global pop-culture event; polite refusal/acceptance language for invitations.
weeks.hw:
6 sentences describing your home
Write an invitation and a polite reply to it.

skills.L: Listen to home descriptions (there is / there are)
skills.S: Describe my home room by room
skills.R: Read home ads and count the rooms
skills.W: Write about my home (4 sentences)

lp.wu: Quick Review: 'Find Someone Who'. Hand out a sheet with prompts like 'Find someone who has a big living room'. Students mingle and ask 'Do you have a big living room?', responding 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Room Pictionary'. Teacher draws a room on the board, students guess 'Is it a kitchen?'
Alternative 2: 'Memory Game'. Show 6 flashcards of rooms/furniture for 10 seconds, students list what they saw.
lp.pres: Show a large picture of a house. Point to different rooms and model: 'There is a living room. There are two chairs.' Use flashcards for 'bedroom', 'kitchen', 'sofa', 'table'. Check by asking 'What room is this?' and 'What is there?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a simple floor plan drawing on the board, adding furniture as you teach.
Alternative 2: Bring a small model house and point to the rooms inside.
lp.prac: Controlled Practice: 'Furniture Battle'. Pairs get a paper with a blank room outline. Student A says 'There is a bed', draws it. Student B says 'There are two windows', draws them. They take turns describing and drawing items in the room.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Race'. Write scrambled sentences like 'a / there / is / table' on the board, teams race to write the correct order.
Alternative 2: 'Matching Game'. Match picture cards of furniture to sentence cards with 'There is/are'.
lp.ls: Listening Slot: Play a short audio of someone describing their home. Students listen and tick the rooms/furniture they hear on a worksheet. Check answers by asking 'What did you hear?'.
lp.re: Reactivation Game: 'Simon Says'. Teacher says 'Simon says there is a window'. Students point to the window. 'Simon says there are three chairs'. Students point to three chairs. Fast-paced and physical.
lp.prod: Production Task: 'Dream House Presentation'. In pairs, students design their dream house on a large paper. They present it to the class using 'There is/are', e.g., 'There is a big garden. There are five bedrooms.'
lp.rw: Reading and Writing Slot: Read a simple classified ad for a flat. Students count the rooms and write 4 sentences about it using 'There is/are', e.g., 'There is one kitchen. There are two bedrooms.'
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Read a short, illustrated story about a family preparing for Christmas in their home. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to describe our homes. Thank you, class.'
g: Teams race to name as many rooms as possible in 60 seconds.
Teacher calls out items like 'There is a sofa', students cover the picture on their bingo card.
Student A draws a room, Student B guesses what is in it using 'Is there a...?'
Students compare two similar pictures of a home and spot differences using 'There is/are'.
Teacher describes a decorated Christmas home, students draw it.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write 6 sentences about their dream home.
Support / weaker learners: Use a word bank with 'living room', 'bedroom', 'sofa', 'table' to write sentences.
hw: Homework option 1: Write 6 sentences describing your real home using 'There is/are'.
Homework option 2: Write a Christmas invitation to a friend using 'Would you like to come?'. Write a polite reply.
Homework option 3: Draw a picture of your home and label 5 rooms/furniture items.
lp.tip: Connect the lesson to local context by comparing Moroccan home layouts (e.g., 'dar') with Western homes, highlighting shared values like family spaces.

weeks.obj: talk about the past with was/were and last-time expressions
weeks.lang: was/were; last night/week/year
weeks.act:
Last weekend board; where-were-you quiz; pair interviews about the past
Discussion: resolutions that stick; will vs going-to for plans and promises.
weeks.hw:
Participation quiz
Write your own 3 resolutions + how you will keep them.

skills.L: Listen to last-weekend stories with was / were
skills.S: Talk about the past with was / were
skills.R: Read a diary text and underline was / were
skills.W: Write about last weekend (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Last Weekend Board: Teacher draws a 3x3 grid on the board with squares for 'Saturday morning', 'Saturday afternoon', 'Saturday night', 'Sunday morning', etc. Students ask 'Where were you last Saturday morning?' and teacher answers 'I was at home' or 'I was at the market', drawing a simple icon in the square. Students then ask each other in pairs.
wuAlt: Find Someone Who...: Hand out a sheet with prompts like 'Find someone who was at the cinema last weekend'. Students walk around asking 'Were you at the cinema last weekend?' and writing names.
Memory Chain: Teacher says 'Last weekend I was at home'. Student 1 says 'Last weekend [teacher] was at home and I was at the market'. Student 2 repeats the chain and adds their own.
lp.pres: Teacher shows two flashcards: one of a person sleeping at home, one of a person at a cafe. Teacher says 'Last night, I was at home' and 'Last night, Ali was at the cafe'. Elicits 'was' and 'were' from students. Teacher then presents last-time expressions: 'last night', 'last weekend', 'last year', pointing to a calendar. Checks understanding by asking 'Where were you last night?' to a few students.
presAlt: Timeline Drawing: Teacher draws a simple timeline from 'Friday' to 'Sunday' on the board. Asks students to draw a picture of where they were on Saturday and say the sentence 'I was at [place]'.

Photo Story: Teacher shows 3-4 photos of themselves from last weekend (e.g., at a restaurant, at home, at a park). Tells a short story using 'was' and 'were' and asks students to guess the location for each photo.
lp.prac: Where Were You? Quiz: Teacher writes 5 sentences on the board, some true, some false, about herself last weekend (e.g., 'I was at the cinema', 'I was at work'). Students in teams get points for guessing correctly. Then, in pairs, students write 3 true and 1 false sentence about their own last weekend. They read their sentences to their partner, who guesses the false one.
pracAlt: Grammar Auction: Teacher writes 10 sentences with was/were errors (e.g., 'I was happy'). Students in teams have 100 points. They 'bid' on sentences they think are correct. Correct sentences earn them points, incorrect ones lose points.

Sentence Race: In pairs, students race to write 5 correct sentences using 'was/were' and a last-time expression from a list of prompts (e.g., 'last year', 'last night'). The first pair to write all 5 correctly wins.
lp.ls: Listening for Details: Teacher plays a short audio recording (30-45 seconds) of two people talking about their New Year's Eve. The script is: 'A: Hi Leila! How was your New Year's Eve? B: It was great! I was at my cousin's house. We were very happy. A: Nice! And you, Sarah? A: I was at home. I was tired, so I was in bed at 11 pm.' Students listen and answer two questions: 'Where was Leila?' and 'Where was Sarah?' on a handout.
lp.re: Past Tense Charades: Teacher writes 'was/were' actions on small slips of paper (e.g., 'was happy', 'was at the market', 'was sleeping'). A student picks a slip, acts it out without speaking, and the class guesses, asking 'Were you...?' The student answers 'Yes, I was' or 'No, I wasn't'.
lp.prod: Pair Interviews: Students work in pairs. Student A asks Student B three questions: 'Where were you last night?', 'Where were you last weekend?', 'Were you happy last year?'. Student B answers. Then they swap roles. After, each student stands up and introduces their partner to the class: 'Last weekend, [partner's name] was at [place]'.
lp.rw: Diary Entry Reading: Students receive a short, simple diary entry about a person's last weekend. Example: 'Friday: I was tired. I was at home. Saturday: I was happy. I was at my friend's house. Sunday: I was busy. I was at the market.' Students read the text and underline all examples of 'was' and 'were'. Then, they write 5 simple sentences about their own last weekend using the same structure.
lp.st: Teacher reads a very short, simple story about New Year's resolutions using 'will' and 'going to'. Example: 'For the New Year, I will eat more vegetables. I am going to walk every day.' After the story, the class discusses resolutions. Teacher leads the goodbye routine: 'Today we talked about the past with was/were. Thank you, class. Have a good day.'
g: Students write 9 places in a bingo grid (e.g., 'park', 'home', 'cinema'). Teacher calls out sentences like 'I was at the park last weekend'. Students mark the square if they have it.
Students work in pairs with two similar pictures of a 'last weekend' scene. They take turns asking 'Was he at the market?' to find the differences.
Teacher starts a story: 'Last weekend, I was at home...'. Each student adds one sentence using 'was/were' to continue the story.
Students play in teams. To place an X or O, a team member must correctly make a sentence with 'was/were' from a prompt.
Teacher shows a picture of a scene for 20 seconds. Hides it. Students write 5 sentences using 'was/were' to describe what was in the picture.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a short paragraph (6-7 sentences) about their last weekend using 'was/were'.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'Last weekend, I was at ___. I was ___. I was ___.' to write their sentences.
hw: Participation Quiz: Interview 3 family members or friends about their last weekend. Ask 'Where were you last night?' and write down their answers in a simple sentence.
Resolutions: Write 3 New Year's resolutions. For each, write one sentence using 'will' and one using 'going to'. Example: 'I will learn English. I am going to study every day.'
Write About Your Weekend: Write 5 sentences about your last weekend. Use 'was/were' and a last-time expression in each sentence.
lp.tip: Connect the language to students' personal experiences by asking about local holidays like Independence Day or the Green March to make 'last weekend' and 'last year' more relevant and meaningful.

weeks.obj: narrate simple past events with regular verbs; read a seasonal text
weeks.lang: past simple regular -ed; past time expressions
weeks.act: Yesterday story chain; -ed pronunciation sorting; Christmas culture reading
weeks.hw: 6 sentences about a good day

skills.L: Listen to a Christmas culture text
skills.S: Narrate simple past events with -ed verbs
skills.R: Read the seasonal text and find the -ed verbs (Seasonal pack)
skills.W: Write 5 past sentences about last year

lp.wu: Yesterday Timeline: Students draw a simple timeline on paper. Teacher asks 'What did you do yesterday?' and students write 2-3 activities with pictures. Volunteers share their timeline with a partner using 'Yesterday I...'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who... Past: Students walk around asking 'Did you...?' questions (e.g., 'Did you watch TV?') and write names. Teacher reviews answers as a class.
Flashcard Recall: Teacher shows 5 flashcards of daily activities (e.g., cook, walk, clean). Students say the past form and make a sentence: 'Yesterday I...'.
lp.pres: Christmas Culture Story: Teacher shows a photo of a Christmas tree. Reads a short story: 'Last week, I decorated my home. I bought a tree. I hung lights. I baked cookies.' Underlines all -ed verbs. Checks understanding: 'What did I do?' and 'When did I do it?'
presAlt: Realia Demonstration: Teacher brings a small decorated box. 'Yesterday, I opened the box. I found a gift. I smiled.' Students repeat and ask questions.
Video Clip: Plays a 1-minute clip of someone preparing for a local holiday (e.g., Eid). Pauses to ask 'What did he/she do?' and elicit past tense sentences.
lp.prac: -ed Pronunciation Sort: Students receive 15 verb cards (e.g., walked, played, watched). In pairs, they sort them into three columns: /t/ (liked), /d/ (opened), /ɪd/ (wanted). Teacher models and monitors pronunciation.
pracAlt: Past Simple Bingo: Teacher calls out base verbs (e.g., 'walk'). Students cross off the past form (walked) on their bingo card. First to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Chain Drill: Teacher starts a story: 'Yesterday, I woke up.' Student 1 adds: 'I brushed my teeth.' Student 2 adds: 'I ate breakfast.' Continue around the class.
lp.ls: Christmas Culture Listening: Students listen to a 1-minute audio about how Christmas is celebrated in Morocco. They listen and tick activities mentioned (e.g., 'exchange gifts', 'eat special food'). Teacher plays audio twice and reviews answers.
lp.re: Past Tense Relay: Two lines of students. Teacher shows a flashcard (e.g., 'clean'). First student runs to the board, writes 'cleaned', runs back. Next student does the same with a new verb. Team with most correct wins.
lp.prod: Holiday Memory Roleplay: In pairs, Student A is a tourist asking 'What did you do last Eid?'. Student B answers using 3-4 past verbs. Swap roles. Teacher provides sentence frames: 'Last Eid, I...', 'I... with my family.'
lp.rw: Seasonal Text Reading: Students read a short text about 'A Good Day in Oujda'. Underline all -ed verbs. Then write 3 sentences about their own good day using those verbs (e.g., 'I walked in the park. I talked to my friend. I smiled a lot.')
lp.st: Song + Goodbye: Play 'Jingle Bells' with lyrics adapted to past tense ('Yesterday I decorated a tree...'). End with recap: 'Today we talked about past events. Thank you, class. Have a good day!'
g: Student draws a past verb (e.g., 'cooked') and others guess 'Did you cook?'
Teacher says a base verb; teams race to write the past form on the board.
Students scan the seasonal text and circle all -ed verbs within 2 minutes.
Students sit in a circle. Each adds a past verb to a growing story (e.g., 'I walked... and I talked...').
Students match base verbs to their past forms in a speed-matching activity.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 5-sentence story about a bad day using past verbs.
Support: Use a word bank with 10 past verbs to complete sentences.
hw: Write 6 sentences about a good day you had last week.
Interview a family member about their day yesterday and write 3 sentences.
Draw 4 pictures of things you did yesterday and label them in past tense.
lp.tip: For adults, connect past tense to personal stories (e.g., 'Last week, I visited the American Space'). This builds confidence and respects their life experience.

weeks.obj: complete the written paper and a short speaking interview
weeks.lang: all S1 outcomes
weeks.act: Written paper (35 min); individual speaking slots while others review
weeks.hw: Semester marks recorded; feedback sheets

skills.L: Listening paper (teacher-selected items)
skills.S: Short speaking interview
skills.R: Reading paper across S1 topics
skills.W: Guided writing task

lp.wu: Greetings and Name Chain: Students stand in a circle, one student says 'Hello, my name is [name]', the next repeats the name and adds their own, continuing around the circle to review personal introductions.
wuAlt: Interview Bingo: Students mingle asking 'What's your name?' and 'Where are you from?' to fill a bingo grid with classmates' names.
Flashcard Quick Review: Teacher holds up flashcards of S1 topics (food, shopping, directions) and students shout the English word.
lp.pres: Teacher distributes the S1 written paper (35 min) with clear instructions, modeling the first question on the board to ensure understanding before students begin individually.
presAlt: Oral Exam Demo: Teacher conducts a short mock speaking interview with a volunteer student, showing the format and questions to the class.
S1 Topic Review: Teacher uses a mind map on the board to recap all S1 vocabulary and functions (greetings, shopping, etc.).
lp.prac: While waiting for their speaking slot, students complete a 'Find Someone Who...' worksheet with S1 topics (e.g., 'Find someone who likes coffee'), practicing question forms in pairs.
pracAlt: Vocabulary Matching: Students match S1 words (e.g., 'apple', 'bread') to pictures on a worksheet, working in pairs to check answers.
Error Correction: Teacher writes 5 S1 sentences with errors on the board; students work in pairs to find and correct them.
lp.ls: Teacher plays a short KET-style listening track (3-4 questions) about daily routines, where students listen and tick correct pictures on their paper, checking comprehension of simple present tense.
lp.re: Stand Up Sit Down: Teacher calls out S1 verbs (e.g., 'eat', 'drink', 'walk') and students stand up if they do the action daily, sitting down if not, reactivating vocabulary physically.
lp.prod: Individual speaking interviews: Students take turns with the teacher for 2-3 minutes, answering KET-style questions (e.g., 'What's your job?', 'Where do you live?') while others quietly review S1 flashcards.
lp.rw: Writing Task: Students write 3-5 sentences about their weekend using past simple (e.g., 'I went to the market. I bought bread. I ate with my family.'), with a model sentence on the board for support.
lp.st: Teacher closes with a quick 'Good Job!' clap routine, then says: 'Today you completed your S1 assessment. Well done! Thank you, class.'
g: Teacher calls out S1 words; students mark them on their bingo cards and shout 'Bingo!' when they have a line.
Students act out S1 verbs (e.g., 'shop', 'eat') for others to guess, saying the word when correct.
Two teams race to match S1 word cards to picture cards on the board.
Students use word cards to make correct sentences about S1 topics.
Students quiz each other with S1 questions, then trade cards and find a new partner.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write 5 extra sentences about their favorite S1 topic (e.g., food, shopping).
Support / weaker learners: Use a word bank with S1 verbs to complete the writing task.
hw: Review S1 vocabulary list and write 3 sentences using 3 new words.
Listen to a short English song (e.g., 'Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes') and write down 5 words they know.
Practice introducing themselves and asking 2 questions (e.g., 'What's your name?', 'Where are you from?') with a family member.
lp.tip: For adults, frame the assessment as a 'progress check' to reduce anxiety; emphasize their growth since S1 began to build confidence.
checklist: Can introduce themselves and ask for personal information
Can ask and answer about daily routines
Can understand simple shopping dialogues
Can write 3-5 sentences about past events
Can give simple directions
Can order food in a restaurant
Can make a simple phone call

weeks.obj: review S1 language and agree on listening practice habits
weeks.lang: review; self-study strategies
weeks.act: Listening strategies clinic; S1 team quiz; personal study plan writing
weeks.hw: choose 3 listening files for the month

skills.L: Listening folder: mp3 library tour - self-study guide
skills.S: Agree listening-practice habits with a partner
skills.R: Read the strategy tips and choose my plan
skills.W: Write my study plan (3 targets)

lp.wu: Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their 2024: write three sentences (two true, one false) about their year, then guess which is false. Teacher models first with her own year.
wuAlt: Students interview a partner about their best and worst moment of 2024 using 'How was your...?' and 'What did you do?'
Teacher shows 5 photos of local Oujda events (Green March, Independence Day) and students describe what they see using 'This is...' and 'People are...'.
lp.pres: Teacher introduces 'self-study strategies' with flashcards: 'Listen every day', 'Use a dictionary', 'Write sentences'. Models each sentence and asks 'What does this mean?' with thumbs up/down. Checks understanding with 'What strategy is this?' holding up a flashcard.
presAlt: Teacher draws a mind map on the board: 'How to practice listening?' Students brainstorm ideas in Arabic/English, then teacher adds English labels like 'Podcasts', 'Songs', 'Movies'.
Teacher shares her personal study plan (photo) and explains 'I listen to 10 minutes of news every day. Why? Because I want to understand more.'
lp.prac: Students do 'Strategy Match-Up': 6 strategy cards (e.g., 'Listen to songs') and 6 benefit cards (e.g., 'Learn new words'). In pairs, they match them and say 'This is good for...'. Teacher monitors and helps with pronunciation.
pracAlt: Students play 'Strategy Bingo': Teacher calls out strategies (e.g., 'Watch a YouTube video'), students mark them if they do them. First to get a line says 'Bingo! I do these!'
In groups, students rank 3 strategies from 'easiest' to 'hardest' using 'First, I can... Second, I can... Third, I can...'.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 1-minute KET-style audio about a student's study plan. They tick the strategies he mentions (e.g., 'Listen to podcasts') and write one new idea for themselves.
lp.re: After break, students play 'Quick Review': Teacher says a strategy (e.g., 'Read a book'), students stand up if they agree, sit down if they don't. Fast-paced to re-engage.
lp.prod: Students interview a partner about their listening habits using 'Do you...?' (e.g., 'Do you listen to music in English?'). They note answers and report back to the class: 'Maria listens to music. Karim doesn't.'
lp.rw: Students read a short text (5 sentences) about 'Ahmed's Study Plan' and circle the strategies he uses. Then they write 3 sentences about their own plan using 'I can...' and 'I want to...'.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about 'Lina's New Year Goal' using simple past verbs (e.g., 'She started listening to English podcasts'). Ends with the goodbye routine: 'Today we made study plans. Thank you, class! Goodbye.'
g: Two lines race to match strategy cards to benefit cards on the board.
Student mimes an activity (e.g., reading a book), others guess 'Do you...?'
Teacher reads study plans, students tick if it matches their own.
Pairs flip over strategy/benefit cards and find matches.
Students write 3 study goals in 60 seconds, then share.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a 5-sentence paragraph about why listening is important for them.
Support / weaker learners: Use sentence frames: 'I can ___. I want to ___. I will ___.'
hw: Choose 3 listening files from the class folder (e.g., songs, dialogues) and listen to them this week.
Write 3 questions you have about listening practice (e.g., 'How can I understand fast speakers?').
Ask a family member about their study habits in English or Arabic and report back.
lp.tip: Connect strategies to local context: suggest Moroccan podcasts or YouTube channels in English to make self-study relatable and accessible.

weeks.obj: make an appointment and describe simple symptoms
weeks.lang: should/shouldn't; illness vocabulary; appointment language
weeks.act: Doctor roleplay; pharmacy dialogues; advice-giving pairs
weeks.hw: Roleplay performance check

skills.L: Listen to a doctor-appointment dialogue
skills.S: Make an appointment and describe symptoms
skills.R: Read an appointment card and complete it
skills.W: Write 3 symptom sentences with should

lp.wu: Symptom Charades: Teacher writes 5 illness words (headache, fever, cough, stomach ache, cold) on slips. Students take turns acting them out while others guess, saying 'You have a ___.'
wuAlt: Illness Pictionary: Teacher draws illness flashcards; students say the word and a full sentence like 'I have a headache.'
Quick Survey: Students ask 3 classmates 'Do you have a headache?' and tally answers on the board.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of symptoms and model sentences like 'I have a headache.' Introduce 'should/shouldn't' with advice cards: 'You should rest' / 'You shouldn't go out.' Elicit examples from students using their own experiences.
presAlt: Dialogue Modeling: Read a short doctor-patient dialogue; highlight should/shouldn't phrases; students repeat in pairs.
Realia Demo: Teacher pretends to be sick; students give advice using should/shouldn't from cue cards.
lp.prac: Matching Game: Students match symptom cards (e.g., 'sore throat') to advice cards (e.g., 'You should drink tea') in pairs. Teacher monitors for correct sentences.
pracAlt: Sentence Building: Students arrange word cards into correct 'should/shouldn't' sentences (e.g., 'You / should / see / a doctor').
Advice Relay: Teams race to write advice on the board for symptoms like 'sunburn' using should/shouldn't.
lp.ls: Listen to a KET-style dialogue between a doctor and patient. Students complete an appointment form with the patient's symptoms and the doctor's advice.
lp.re: Simon Says: Teacher calls out 'Simon says touch your head if you have a headache' or 'Simon says don't move if you have a fever'. Students react physically.
lp.prod: Roleplay: In pairs, one is a patient, one is a doctor. Patient describes symptoms (e.g., 'I have a stomach ache'); doctor gives advice using should/shouldn't. Swap roles.
lp.rw: Read a short pharmacy dialogue. Students write 3 sentences about what they should/shouldn't do for a cold using the dialogue as a model.
lp.st: Sing 'Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes' with new lyrics like 'Headache, fever, cough, stomach ache'. Close with: 'Today we learned to make appointments and give advice. Thank you, class.'
g: Students mark off illness words called out by the teacher; first to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Students roleplay booking an appointment over the phone using phrases like 'I want to see a doctor.'
Teams list as many 'should' sentences as possible for a symptom in 2 minutes.
Students match symptom pictures to advice sentences in a timed game.
Each student adds one sentence to a story about a visit to the doctor using should/shouldn't.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a dialogue for a pharmacy visit asking for medicine.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'I have ___' and 'You should ___' during roleplays.
hw: Write 3 sentences about what you should/shouldn't do for the flu.
Record yourself roleplaying a doctor-patient conversation on your phone.
Draw 4 symptom pictures and write advice for each using should/shouldn't.
lp.tip: Connect advice to local customs, e.g., 'You should drink mint tea for a headache' to build rapport with Moroccan learners.

weeks.obj: handle service calls: asking for information politely
weeks.lang: Could I...? / I would like to...; polite requests
weeks.act: Phone roleplay with backs to each other; service request cards; politeness ranking
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listening folder: phone dialogues - polite requests
skills.S: Handle service calls: Could I...? politely
skills.R: Read phone scripts and match the responses
skills.W: Write a short phone-request script

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Service Match' — students stand in two lines; teacher holds flashcards of city services (e.g., police, hospital, taxi); each student says a service and the partner responds with the number; teacher models first: 'Police?' '190!'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Service Charades' — students mime a service (e.g., fixing a pipe) and partners guess the word
Alternative 2: 'Service Bingo' — teacher calls out services, students cross them off their bingo cards
lp.pres: Presentation: Show flashcards of a phone and a service (e.g., hospital); model 'Could I speak to a doctor, please?'; drill the phrase with rising intonation; check understanding by asking 'What do we say to be polite?' and 'What number do we call for the hospital?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a real phone prop; dial a fake number and model the request
Alternative 2: Show a short video clip of someone making a polite service call
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Service Request Cards' — students pick cards with service scenarios (e.g., 'My taxi is late'); in pairs, they practice 'Could I...?' requests; teacher circulates and corrects pronunciation
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Polite Request Drill' — students repeat after teacher with different services
Alternative 2: 'Matching Game' — match requests to responses (e.g., 'Could I get a taxi?' to 'Yes, of course')
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a KET-style phone dialogue between a caller and a service; students listen and circle the correct service (police/hospital/taxi) on their worksheet; check answers as a class
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Number Relay' — students line up; teacher calls out a service (e.g., 'fire'); first student shouts the number (e.g., '150') and runs to the back of the line
lp.prod: Production task: 'Back-to-Back Roleplay' — students sit back-to-back with a partner; one is a caller, the other a service worker; they use 'Could I...?' to make requests and respond; swap roles after 3 minutes
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read short phone scripts and match requests to responses; then write their own polite request for a service (e.g., 'Could I book a table for two, please?')
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Sing 'The Wheels on the Bus' with service-themed verses (e.g., 'The phone on the bus goes ring, ring, ring'); Close with 'Today we learned to make polite phone calls. Thank you, class!'
g: Students mime a service (e.g., plumber) and partners guess
Teacher calls out service numbers, students cross them off
