Students repeat 'Could I...?' with rising intonation
Teams race to match services to numbers
Students roleplay phone calls with backs to each other
diff: Fast finishers: Write a dialogue for a tricky call (e.g., 'My electricity is out')
Support: Use sentence starters like 'Could I...?' on a worksheet
hw: Option 1: Write 3 polite requests for different services
Option 2: Record a phone call with a family member
Option 3: Draw a picture of a service and write the number
lp.tip: Emphasize rising intonation in 'Could I...?' to sound polite; connect to local services in Oujda (e.g., police number) for relevance.

weeks.obj: describe a problem with a purchase and ask for help
weeks.lang: complaint language; item + problem frames
weeks.act:
Customer service roleplay; problem-solution matching; dialogue repair task
Discussion: daily rhythm in Ramadan; present simple for routines + frequency adverbs.
weeks.hw:
write a short complaint message
Write your Ramadan daily routine in 8 sentences.

skills.L: Listen to a shop-problem dialogue
skills.S: Describe a problem with a purchase
skills.R: Read complaint phrases and order the dialogue
skills.W: Write a 6-line problem-and-return dialogue

lp.wu: Students play 'Find the Pair' with shopping flashcards. Teacher places 10 item cards on the board. Students take turns finding two matching cards and saying 'I have a [shirt].'
wuAlt: Students play 'Shopping Bingo' with 3x3 grids of food items. Teacher calls out items, students mark them and shout 'Bingo!' when full.
Students do a quick 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their favorite shops using 'I like...' and 'I don't like...'.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a broken toy and says 'This toy is broken. I need help.' Elicits complaint frames using flashcards: 'This [item] is [problem].' Models 'This T-shirt is too small.' Checks understanding with 'Show me a problem with a bag.'
presAlt: Teacher uses a dialogue video of a customer returning a phone. Pauses to elicit problem phrases.
Teacher writes a complaint on the board with gaps, students guess the missing words like 'This laptop is not working.'
lp.prac: Students do 'Problem-Solution Matching' in pairs. They match 6 problem cards ('This phone doesn't charge') to solution cards ('Can I have a refund?'). Teacher monitors and models pronunciation.
pracAlt: Students play 'Dialogue Repair' in groups. They get a jumbled dialogue and reorder it to make a logical complaint conversation.
Students do 'Chain Complaints' in a circle. Each student adds one problem to the previous one: 'This phone is broken. This charger is lost.'
lp.ls: Students listen to a shop dialogue and tick the problems they hear (e.g., 'too expensive', 'wrong color'). Teacher plays the audio twice, then checks answers as a class.
lp.re: Students play 'Charades' with action words from the lesson (e.g., 'return', 'complain', 'refund'). One student mimes the word, others guess 'Are you returning?'
lp.prod: Students roleplay a customer service scenario in pairs. One is a customer with a problem (e.g., 'This dress is torn'), the other is a shop assistant. They must use at least 2 complaint phrases and 1 solution phrase.
lp.rw: Students read a short complaint message and circle the problem words. Then, they write their own 6-line complaint dialogue using frames like 'I bought this [item] yesterday. It is [problem]. Can I...?'
lp.st: Teacher reads a short story about a man who returns a gift during Ramadan. Students discuss 'What would you do?' and close with 'Today we learned to complain about problems. Thank you, class.'
g: Teams race to write 3 problems on the board using 'This [item] is [problem].'
Students flip cards to find matching item and problem pairs.
Each student adds a problem to the previous one: 'This bag is old. This shirt is red.'
Pairs swap roles after each complaint practice.
Students find the mistake in a written complaint dialogue.
diff: Fast finishers write a second complaint with a different problem.
Support learners use a sentence frame handout with 'This [item] is [problem].' pre-filled.
hw: Write a short complaint message to a shop about a broken item.
Write your Ramadan daily routine in 8 sentences using 'I' and frequency adverbs like 'always'.
Draw 3 shopping problems and write the complaint for each.
lp.tip: Link the language to Ramadan by discussing shopping routines during the holy month. Use realia like dates or lanterns to make complaints culturally relevant.

weeks.obj: explain plans with going to and give reasons
weeks.lang: going to; because / so
weeks.act: Plan a trip group task; intentions board; listening: what are their plans?
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to plans with because / so
skills.S: Explain plans with going to + reasons
skills.R: Read a plan text and find because / so
skills.W: Write my plans with reasons

lp.wu: Students play 'Find Someone Who' with future intentions prompts like 'Find someone who is going to travel next month'. They mingle, ask 'Are you going to...?', and write names. They report back: 'Ali is going to travel because he wants to see his family.'
wuAlt: Students draw a simple future plan on a sticky note and guess classmates' plans: 'Is she going to study?' 'Yes, she is because she wants to pass the exam.'
Students play 'Memory Race' with picture cards showing future actions (e.g., plane, book, diploma). They flip cards and make sentences: 'He is going to fly because he has a job.'
lp.pres: Show flashcards of a man packing a bag and a woman buying a book. Model: 'He is going to travel because he has a holiday. She is going to study because she has an exam.' Check understanding by asking 'Why is he going to travel?' and eliciting 'because he has a holiday.'
presAlt: Use a simple story about a boy who wants to be a doctor. Draw a picture of him with a stethoscope: 'He is going to study medicine because he wants to help people.'
Bring realia: a map, a textbook, a calendar. Point and say: 'I am going to use the map because I want to go to Casablanca. I am going to read the book because I want to learn English.'
lp.prac: Students do 'Going to Dominoes' matching cards with pictures and reasons (e.g., picture of cooking + 'because I want to eat'). In pairs, they place cards and say the full sentence. Monitor and correct errors like 'He go to' instead of 'He is going to'.
pracAlt: Play 'Sentence Auction' with correct/incorrect sentences about future plans. Students bid on true sentences like 'She is going to swim because it's hot.'
Do 'Chain Drill': Student A says 'I am going to cook tonight.' Student B repeats and adds 'because I am hungry.' Student C repeats and adds, 'so I am going to buy food.'
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio of three people talking about their weekend plans. They tick the correct reason from a list (e.g., 'Why is Fatima going to the market? a) She needs food b) She wants to meet friends'). Check answers by replaying and pausing at 'because'.
lp.re: After break, play 'Simon Says' with future actions: 'Simon says: Pretend you are going to travel.' Students mime and say 'I am going to travel because I have a ticket.'
lp.prod: In groups of 3, students plan a one-day trip to Oujda using a worksheet with prompts: 'Where are you going? What are you going to do? Why?' They present their plan: 'We are going to the old medina because we want to buy spices. We are going to eat tagine because we are hungry.'
lp.rw: Students read a short paragraph about 'Amina's Plans' and underline all 'because' and 'so' sentences. Then, they write 3 simple sentences about their own plans using 'going to' and 'because', e.g., 'I am going to call my mother because I miss her.'
lp.st: Sing a simple chant: 'What are you going to do? I'm going to learn, because it's new! What are you going to see? I'm going to travel, because I want to be free!' Close with: 'Today we learned to explain plans with going to and because. Thank you, class.'
g: Students write 6 future plans on a grid (e.g., 'go to the cinema'). Teacher reads sentences like 'He is going to watch a movie', and students cross off matching plans.
Teams race to match picture cards (e.g., umbrella) with reason cards (e.g., 'because it might rain') and make a full sentence.
One student draws a future plan (e.g., a plane), others guess 'Are you going to travel?' and ask 'Why?'
Students act out future actions (e.g., studying) while others say 'He is going to study because he has a test.'
Groups unscramble word cards to make correct 'going to' sentences with 'because', e.g., 'She / going to / buy / because / she needs / food / is'.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph about their ideal future using 3 'going to' sentences with 'because' and 'so'.
Support / weaker learners: Use sentence frames: 'I am going to ______ because ______.' with picture prompts.
hw: Option 1: Interview a family member about their weekend plans and write 2 sentences using 'going to' and 'because'.
Option 2: Draw 3 pictures of your future plans and label them with 'going to' and 'because' sentences.
Option 3: Complete a worksheet with 5 gaps to fill in 'going to' or 'because' in sentences about plans.
lp.tip: For adults, connect language to real-life goals like work or family. Use Moroccan examples (e.g., 'I am going to learn English because I want a better job') to increase relevance and motivation.

weeks.obj: invite, accept, and decline politely; fix a time and place
weeks.lang: Shall we...? / Would you like to...?; arrangements
weeks.act: Invitation roleplay cards; diary schedule negotiation; accept-decline race
weeks.hw: write an invitation message

skills.L: Listen to invitation dialogues (accept / decline)
skills.S: Invite, accept and decline politely; fix a time
skills.R: Read invitation messages and match the replies
skills.W: Write an invitation message with a reply

lp.wu: Last week we learned about daily routines. Today we start with a 'Find Someone Who' game. Students mingle with a grid of activities like 'goes to the cinema' and ask 'Do you go to the cinema?' to find classmates who do, writing their names.
wuAlt: Alternative warm-up 1: Students write 3 sentences about their last weekend using 'I went to...' or 'I ate...'. Volunteers share.
Alternative warm-up 2: Teacher shows flashcards of leisure activities (cinema, park, restaurant) and elicits 'What is this?' in chorus.
lp.pres: Introduce the theme with a model dialogue: Teacher asks 'Shall we go to the cinema on Friday?' and student replies 'Yes, that sounds good. What time?' Use flashcards of cinema, café, park to elicit places. Drill the model sentences chorally and individually. Check understanding by asking 'What do I say to invite?' and 'How do you accept?'
presAlt: Alternative presentation 1: Show a short video clip of two friends making plans. Pause after each line to ask 'What did he say?' and write on the board.
Alternative presentation 2: Use a roleplay with a realia prop like a diary. Teacher says 'I'm free on Saturday. Would you like to have lunch?' and student responds with 'Yes, let's meet at 1 PM.'
lp.prac: Distribute 'Invitation Roleplay Cards' with prompts like 'Invite a friend to the café'. Students practice in pairs, using the target phrases. Teacher monitors and provides sentence starters on the board: 'Shall we...?' / 'Would you like to...?' / 'How about...?'
pracAlt: Alternative practice 1: 'Accept-Decline Race'. Teacher calls out 'Would you like to...?' and students race to respond 'Yes, please' or 'No, thank you' with a reason.
Alternative practice 2: 'Fix the Time' drill. One student says 'Let's meet tomorrow' and the other suggests a specific time and place, e.g., 'OK, at 3 PM at the library.'
lp.ls: Students listen to a dialogue between two friends arranging to meet. They fill in a simple schedule with the day, time, and place (e.g., 'Saturday, 2 PM, café'). Play the audio twice; check answers as a class.
lp.re: After the break, play 'Stand Up If You...' to reactivate language. Teacher says 'Stand up if you would like to go to the cinema' and students respond with 'Yes, I would' or 'No, thanks'.
lp.prod: Students work in pairs to negotiate a diary schedule. Each has a weekly planner with some free/busy slots. They must invite their partner to an activity, agree on a time, and write it in both planners, using phrases like 'Are you free on...?' / 'Let's meet at...'
lp.rw: Students read 3 short invitation messages (e.g., 'Would you like to come to my house for tea?'). They match each to a correct reply (e.g., 'Yes, that would be lovely. What time?'). Then, they write one simple invitation message to a friend, including a day and time.
lp.st: Close with a chant: 'Shall we go? Yes, let's go! What time? At two!' End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to invite and make plans. Thank you, class.'
g: Students match invitation phrases to replies on cards.
Students negotiate time slots on a shared planner to find a free meeting time.
Teams race to respond correctly to teacher's invitation prompts.
Pairs plan a real outing (e.g., coffee) and present it to the class.
Students draw cards with roles (e.g., 'You are busy') and practice declining politely.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a longer invitation message with two activity options, e.g., 'Would you like to go to the park or the cinema on Sunday?'
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame to write: 'Would you like to...? Let's meet at... on...'
hw: Homework option 1: Write a text message inviting a classmate to an activity of your choice, including a day and time.
Homework option 2: Create a dialogue between two friends making plans, using the phrases from class.
Homework option 3: Draw a picture of you and a friend doing an activity together, and write a caption like 'We meet at the park on Saturday.'
lp.tip: For Moroccan learners, connect invitations to local contexts like tea invites or Green March celebrations to make it culturally relevant. Use real-life examples like 'Would you like to come for mint tea?'

weeks.obj: handle booking and travel conversations simply
weeks.lang: travel vocabulary; I have a reservation...
weeks.act: Hotel check-in roleplay; travel buddy interviews; reading jigsaw
weeks.hw: Roleplay performance check

skills.L: Listening folder: travel mp3 - reservations
skills.S: Handle booking and travel conversations
skills.R: Read a hotel confirmation and check the details
skills.W: Write a short booking email

lp.wu: Travel Bingo: Students draw 4 travel words on a grid. Teacher calls out words (e.g., 'hotel', 'reservation', 'passport'). Students cross off matches and shout 'Bingo!' when complete.
wuAlt: Travel Pictionary: Teacher writes words on slips (e.g., 'suitcase', 'check-in'). Students draw while others guess.
Travel Charades: Students act out travel actions (e.g., 'boarding a plane') for others to name.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of hotel items (key, room number, reception). Model: 'I have a reservation.' 'My name is...' 'I need a room.' Check understanding by asking: 'What do you say at a hotel?'
presAlt: Roleplay demo: Teacher acts as receptionist, student as guest. Use a toy phone and a fake registration form.
Realia: Display a hotel key and brochure. Point to items while modeling sentences.
lp.prac: Pair drill: Student A is receptionist, Student B is guest. They practice 'I have a reservation' and 'My name is...' with cue cards (e.g., 'Smith', 'double room'). Teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation.
pracAlt: Chain game: Students pass a toy phone, saying 'I have a reservation for...' and adding a new word each time.
Gap-fill worksheet: Complete sentences like 'I have a ______ for two nights.' with options (reservation, ticket, passport).
lp.ls: Listen to a hotel check-in dialogue. Students tick details heard (name, room type, nights). Play twice. Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Stand up, Sit down: Teacher calls out travel words. Students stand if they match 'hotel' or 'reservation', sit for others. Quick review after break.
lp.prod: Travel buddy interviews: Students ask partners about their dream holiday. Use prompts: 'Where do you want to go?' 'What kind of room do you need?' Share 2 findings with the class.
lp.rw: Read a short hotel confirmation email. Circle the correct details (name: Ali/Amal, nights: 1/2). Then write 1 sentence: 'My name is...' using the email info.
lp.st: Sing 'The Travel Song' (tune of 'Twinkle Twinkle') with actions. Close with: 'Today we learned hotel phrases. Thank you, class.'
g: Students mark off hotel words called by the teacher.
Teams race to write 'I have a reservation' on the board.
Match cards with room numbers to guest names.
Act out travel words for others to guess.
Pass a box while music plays; say a travel word when it stops.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 more sentences about their ideal hotel.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'My name is...' for the roleplay.
hw: Practice the hotel roleplay with a family member.
Write 3 questions you would ask at a hotel check-in.
Draw a picture of your dream hotel and label 2 items (bed, pool).
lp.tip: Use Moroccan travel examples (e.g., booking a hotel for Agadir or Marrakech) to make it relevant. Pair adults with similar life experiences for roleplays.

weeks.obj: write a short clear email for work or daily life
weeks.lang: email openings/closings; formal vs informal
weeks.act:
Email transformation (text to email); pair editing; subject-line game
Discussion: Eid traditions and family; narrative past tense storytelling.
weeks.hw:
write a real-life email draft
Write a short story: my best Eid memory.

skills.L: Listen to model emails read aloud
skills.S: Say openings and closings formally and informally
skills.R: Read model emails and compare the registers
skills.W: Write a short clear email (greeting, body, sign-off)

lp.wu: Eid Memory Chain: Teacher starts with 'Eid al-Fitr is a happy time.' Each student adds one true sentence about Eid, e.g., 'We visit family,' 'We eat special food.'
wuAlt: Eid Pictionary: Teacher draws 'family gathering' or 'new clothes' for students to guess the English word.
Eid Word Association: Teacher says 'Eid', students shout related words like 'family', 'gifts', 'prayer'.
lp.pres: Show two emails on the board: a formal one to a boss (Subject: Eid Holiday Request) and an informal one to a friend (Subject: Eid Plans!). Highlight openings (Dear Mr. Smith / Hi Fatima) and closings (Best regards / See you soon!). Ask students to spot the differences.
presAlt: Email Sorting Game: Print/email examples. Students sort them into Formal/Informal piles.
Realia Display: Show a physical Eid card vs. a printed email. Discuss which is for whom.
lp.prac: Email Transformation: Students receive a text message like 'Can we meet for coffee after Eid?' and transform it into a formal email to a teacher. They write the greeting, body, and sign-off. Circulate to help with 'Dear' vs. 'Hi'.
pracAlt: Pair Editing: Student A writes a short informal email, Student B adds a formal closing. Swap roles.
Subject Line Game: Give students a topic (e.g., 'Eid Party Invite'). They write 3 subject lines: formal, informal, and neutral.
lp.ls: Listen to two model emails being read aloud. Students raise a red card for formal and a blue card for informal. Check answers by asking, 'Why was the first one formal?'
lp.re: Stand Up, Sit Down: Teacher says a phrase. Students stand if it's for a friend (e.g., 'See you later!'), sit if it's for a boss (e.g., 'Thank you for your consideration.').
lp.prod: Pair Work: Roleplay two scenarios. 1) Student A is a boss, Student B requests Eid leave. 2) Student A is a friend, Student B invites them to an Eid dinner. Use email language from the lesson.
lp.rw: Write a short email draft: Students choose one real-life purpose (e.g., request a day off, invite a cousin). Write 3 sentences: opening, one body sentence, closing. Teacher checks individually.
lp.st: Read a short story, 'My Best Eid Memory,' using simple past tense (e.g., 'Last year, we visited my grandparents. They gave me gifts. We ate a big meal.'). End with 'Goodbye, and thank you for your emails today!'
g: In teams, write the best subject line for a given topic (e.g., 'Eid Gift').
Match greetings (Dear Sir) with closings (Yours faithfully).
One student writes a greeting, the next adds a body sentence, the last a closing.
Ask 3 classmates 'What is your favorite Eid food?' and write the answers.
Write a formal email to a shop about a broken gift.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second email with two body sentences.
Support: Use a template with sentence starters like 'I would like to request...'.
hw: Write a real email draft to a teacher about a holiday.
Write a short story: My best Eid memory (3-5 sentences).
Find an example of a formal email online and bring it to class.
lp.tip: Always connect functional language to students' real goals; in Oujda, emailing for work or study is highly relevant, so use authentic examples like leave requests.

weeks.obj: hold 3 minutes of small talk including weather
weeks.lang: weather words; conversation openers/closers
weeks.act: Small talk speed-dating rounds; weather reporter roulette; exit-line practice
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to weather small talk and note the openers
skills.S: Hold 3 minutes of small talk including weather
skills.R: Read small-talk tips and try 3 openers
skills.W: Write 3 small-talk exchanges

lp.wu: Weather Charades: Teacher mimes weather actions (e.g., shivering for cold, fanning for hot), students guess the word in English. Students then take turns miming for partners.
wuAlt: Flashcard Race: Show weather flashcards quickly, students shout the word. Fastest wins a point.
Weather Bingo: Teacher calls out weather words, students cross them off their bingo sheets.
lp.pres: Teacher presents weather flashcards (sunny, rainy, windy, cold, hot) with gestures. Model sentences: 'It's sunny today.' 'It's raining.' Ask students 'How's the weather?' to elicit responses, checking understanding with thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Weather Song: Play 'How's the Weather?' song, students repeat and do actions. Then review key words.
Realia: Bring a fan (hot), umbrella (rainy), sunglasses (sunny) to demonstrate vocabulary and model sentences.
lp.prac: Weather Reporter Roulette: Students sit in a circle. Teacher spins a pointer; when it stops, the student it points to pretends to be a weather reporter and says 'Good morning! The weather is...' using a flashcard. Teacher helps with pronunciation.
pracAlt: Matching Pairs: Students match weather words to pictures, then practice saying the sentences in pairs.
Weather Dice: Roll a die with weather symbols, students say the corresponding sentence.
lp.ls: Listen to a 1-minute dialogue between two people talking about the weather. Students circle the weather words they hear on a worksheet. Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Weather Action Relay: Students line up. Teacher calls a weather word, the first student in line mimes it, then the next student says the word and mimes the next one. Fast team wins.
lp.prod: Small Talk Speed Dating: Students pair up. Each pair has 2 minutes to have a small talk conversation starting with 'Hello! How are you?' and including the weather (e.g., 'It's sunny today, isn't it?'). They switch partners after 2 minutes.
lp.rw: Read 3 small-talk tips on a worksheet (e.g., 'Ask about the weather,' 'Smile'). Students then write 3 small-talk exchanges using the tips, e.g., 'A: Hello! B: Hi! A: It's hot today, right? B: Yes, very hot!'.
lp.st: Read a short story about two friends meeting and talking about the weather. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we practiced small talk about the weather. Thank you, class! Goodbye!'
g: Students mark off weather words on a bingo card as the teacher calls them.
Students mime weather actions for others to guess the word.
Students match weather words to pictures on flashcards.
Students roll a die and say a sentence about the weather shown.
Students practice small talk with different partners about the weather.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph about their ideal weather day.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'It's...' and 'I like...' for their exchanges.
hw: Homework 1: Write 3 small-talk conversations with a family member about the weather.
Homework 2: Watch a weather forecast in English and write down 3 weather words they hear.
Homework 3: Draw 4 weather pictures and write a sentence for each.
lp.tip: Connect weather to local context: ask about the weather in Oujda or during holidays like Green March to make it relevant.

weeks.obj: talk about life stages with past and present contrast
weeks.lang: past vs present review; life-stage vocabulary
weeks.act: Timeline creation and narrating; guess whose life; pair interviews
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to life-stage stories (past vs present)
skills.S: Contrast my past and present life
skills.R: Read a timeline text and match the stages
skills.W: Write my life timeline (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Timeline Race: Students form two teams. Teacher writes 'birth', 'school', 'now' on the board. Teams race to write one word each for a past stage (e.g. 'played football') and one for present (e.g. 'work') under the correct column. First team with correct wins.
wuAlt: Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Did you...?' questions (e.g. 'Did you live in Oujda?') and tally answers on a grid.
Picture Prompt: Show a baby photo and current photo of a teacher. Students guess 'past' vs 'present' activities.
lp.pres: Teacher draws a personal timeline on the board, labeling 'When I was 5' (past) and 'Now' (present). Uses flashcards of life stages (baby, child, teenager, adult) to model sentences: 'I lived in Casablanca. I work in Oujda.' Checks understanding by asking 'Past or present?' for each sentence.
presAlt: Guest Speaker: Invite a volunteer to share their timeline using simple prompts. Teacher models questions like 'Where did you live?' and 'Where do you work now?'
Video Clip: Show a short clip of someone talking about their past and present (e.g., a Peace Corps volunteer in Morocco). Students list past/present verbs.
lp.prac: Life Stage Dominoes: Students match past/present sentence halves (e.g. 'I was born...' + '...in 1995'). Teacher monitors and corrects errors. In pairs, they then quiz each other: 'Where did you live?' 'Where do you live now?'
pracAlt: Timeline Gap Fill: Students complete a worksheet with sentences like 'I _____ (live) in a small village. Now I _____ (study) in Oujda.'
Verb Sort: Cut up past/present verb cards. Students sort them into two columns and make sentences.
lp.ls: Listen to three short audio clips of people talking about their past and present (e.g., a teacher, a shopkeeper, a student). Students match each speaker to a timeline on their worksheet by circling past or present activities.
lp.re: Stand Up, Sit Down: Teacher calls out a past activity (e.g., 'rode a camel') and students stand; present activity (e.g., 'use WhatsApp') and students sit. Fast-paced review after break.
lp.prod: Guess Whose Life: Students write 3 past and 3 present sentences about their own lives on a paper timeline. In groups, they take turns reading sentences while others guess who the timeline belongs to. Teacher models first: 'I lived in a village. Now I live in the city. Who is it?'
lp.rw: Read a short text about Fatima's timeline (e.g., 'Fatima was a student. Now she is a teacher. She lived in Rabat. Now she lives in Oujda.'). Students match each sentence to a picture of her past/present life on a worksheet.
lp.st: Sing 'This Is the Life' (simplified lyrics) with actions. End with: 'Today we talked about past and present. Thank you for sharing your stories. Goodbye!'
g: Teams race to write past/present words under correct columns on the board.
Students ask 'Did you...?' questions and tally answers.
Match past/present sentence halves and quiz each other.
Read timeline sentences; group guesses the person.
Stand for past verbs, sit for present verbs.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 6-sentence timeline about a family member.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'I was... Now I...'. Trace words from the board.
hw: Option 1: Write 5 sentences about your parent's past and present life (e.g., 'My father was a farmer. Now he is a teacher').
Option 2: Draw a timeline of your day (past: 'I woke up at 7', present: 'I am studying now').
Option 3: Record a 30-second audio describing your past and present life using simple sentences.
lp.tip: Respect learners' life experience—some may have moved from rural to urban areas or changed careers. Frame comparisons as positive growth, not 'better/worse'.

weeks.obj: describe how celebrations happen; write an invitation
weeks.lang: customs vocabulary; invitation writing
weeks.act: Plan a celebration in teams; invitation texts; culture exchange presentations
weeks.hw: invitation text (5 sentences)

skills.L: Listen to celebration descriptions
skills.S: Describe how a celebration happens
skills.R: Read a customs text (Reading tasks)
skills.W: Write an invitation to my celebration

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Celebration Charades'. Teacher writes 'wedding', 'birthday', 'Eid', 'Green March' on slips. Students take turns acting out a celebration while others guess, saying 'Is it a birthday?'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Celebration Bingo' - Students have cards with words like 'cake', 'gifts', 'music', 'family'. Teacher calls out words, students mark and shout 'Bingo!' when complete
Alternative 2: 'Quick Share' - Students turn to a partner and say 'My favorite celebration is... because...'
lp.pres: Presentation: Show flashcards of celebration customs (cutting cake, dancing, gifts, praying). Model sentences: 'At a wedding, people dance.' 'On Eid, families visit each other.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down: 'Do people eat cake at Eid?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a short story about a Moroccan wedding, highlighting customs like 'henna' and 'music'
Alternative 2: Bring in realia (a gift box, a small cake model) and describe each item's role in celebrations
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Match the Custom' worksheet. Students match pictures of celebrations to sentences (e.g., 'At a birthday party, people sing Happy Birthday'). In pairs, they practice saying the sentences with correct stress.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Auction' - Write correct and incorrect sentences on the board. Students 'buy' the correct ones with play money
Alternative 2: 'Chain Drill' - Teacher starts 'At a wedding...', next student adds 'and people dance', next adds 'and eat cake'
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a short audio of someone describing a Moroccan Independence Day celebration. Students listen and tick three customs they hear from a list (e.g., 'flags', 'parades', 'family meals')
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand Up, Sit Down'. Teacher says celebration words (e.g., 'gifts' - stand, 'prayer' - sit). Students move quickly to check recall of vocabulary.
lp.prod: Production task: In teams of 3, students plan a 'Green March Celebration' for the American Space. They must decide: 1) What food? 2) What music? 3) What activity? Each team presents their plan using 'We will...' and 'People can...'
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read a short text about a typical Moroccan wedding custom (e.g., 'henna night'). Then, they write 5 sentences for an invitation: 'You are invited to my wedding. It is on... We will... Please bring... Wear...'
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Sing 'Happy Birthday' with actions. Close with: 'Today we learned to describe celebrations and write invitations. Thank you, class!'
g: Students draw a celebration custom (e.g., 'gifts') while others guess
Walk around asking 'Find someone who has been to a wedding. When?'
Teacher asks 'What do people eat at Eid?' Students race to answer 'couscous'
Match invitation phrases ('You are invited...') to celebration pictures
Students race to write 5 celebration words from memory on the board
diff: Fast finishers: Design a poster for their celebration with 3 customs and a date
Support learners: Use a sentence frame for writing: 'My celebration is on... We will... Please come...'
hw: Homework 1: Write 5 sentences about your favorite Moroccan celebration
Homework 2: Create an invitation to a family event using the phrases from class
Homework 3: Draw a picture of a celebration and label 3 customs
lp.tip: Connect lessons to local culture by always including Moroccan celebrations (Eid, weddings, Green March) alongside Western ones. This builds relevance and respect for learners' backgrounds.

weeks.obj: understand A2 Key formats and complete sample tasks
weeks.lang: KET reading/writing part formats
weeks.act: Guided KET practice; strategy notes; team answer hunt
weeks.hw: KET-style homework set

skills.L: KET listening part 1 tour
skills.S: KET-style personal questions
skills.R: KET reading part 1 samples (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style form filling

lp.wu: KET Bingo: Students write 5 words from last week's KET practice (e.g., 'form', 'tick', 'name', 'address', 'date') on a grid. Teacher calls out clues like 'You write this with a pen', and students cross off matches. First to 3 in a row wins.
wuAlt: KET Flashcard Race: Two teams race to match KET reading/writing part 1 flashcards (e.g., 'form' card with 'fill in a form' card).
KET Word Association: Teacher says 'KET', students shout related words like 'exam', 'reading', 'writing', 'parts'.
lp.pres: Teacher projects a KET reading part 1 sample (3 short texts with A, B, C options). Models reading aloud and thinking aloud: 'Text A says 'Open 9am-5pm', but question asks 'When does it close?', so answer is C.' Checks understanding by asking students to explain why B is wrong.
presAlt: Teacher uses a KET form filling sample on the board, filling it in step by step with student input (e.g., 'What's my surname?').
Teacher shows a KET writing part 1 email sample, highlighting key phrases like 'Dear Sir/Madam' and 'Yours faithfully'.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs on a KET reading part 1 worksheet (3 tasks). Teacher circulates, prompting with 'Read the question first' or 'Check the text again'. Fast finishers write their own KET-style question for a classmate.
pracAlt: Team Answer Hunt: Teams race to find correct answers to KET reading part 1 questions hidden around the room, then match them to the questions on the board.
KET Jigsaw: Each team gets one KET reading part 1 task, teaches it to another team, then swaps.
lp.ls: Students listen to a KET listening part 1 audio (3 short conversations). They tick the correct option (A, B, or C) on their worksheet. Teacher plays audio twice, then reviews answers, pausing to replay key phrases.
lp.re: KET Relay: Two lines of students race to the board to write a KET word (e.g., 'form', 'address', 'date') from memory. First team to write all 5 correctly wins.
lp.prod: Students roleplay a KET-style form filling scenario: one is a receptionist at a clinic, the other is a patient filling in a form. They use phrases like 'What's your first name?' and 'Can I have your address, please?'
lp.rw: Students complete a KET-style writing part 1 task: writing a short email to a friend about a weekend plan (5-6 sentences). They use 'I'm going to...' and 'I want to...'. Teacher checks for correct punctuation and basic spelling.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a student taking the KET exam, using simple past tense verbs (e.g., 'He walked to the exam. He felt nervous. He answered the questions. He passed!'). Close with: 'Today we practiced KET reading and writing formats. Thank you, class.'
g: Students match KET reading part 1 questions with correct answers from a list.
Teams take turns answering KET questions to place X or O.
Students race to read 3 short texts and find the answer to a question.
Teams race to fill in a KET-style form correctly on the board.
Teams answer KET reading/writing questions for points.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a KET-style question for a reading part 1 text.
Support / weaker learners: Use a word bank with KET keywords to complete the reading tasks.
hw: Complete a KET reading part 1 worksheet (5 tasks).
Write a short email to a friend using KET writing part 1 format (5-6 sentences).
Review KET vocabulary words (e.g., 'form', 'address', 'date') and make flashcards.
lp.tip: For Moroccan adults, connect KET to real-life goals like applying for a visa or a job, as this increases motivation. Use local examples like 'Green March' in practice tasks to make it relevant.

weeks.obj: complete a mini practice test under time
weeks.lang: all A1-A2 core language
weeks.act: Mini-test administration; self-marking with key; error discussion
weeks.hw: Practice test score recorded

skills.L: KET listening mini-set
skills.S: KET-style interview practice
skills.R: KET reading mini-paper (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style short message

lp.wu: Quick Quiz: Teacher shows flashcards of daily routines (brush teeth, eat breakfast, go to work). Students stand up and say the action when they see it, then sit down. Teacher asks, 'What do you do in the morning?'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who: Students walk around asking, 'Do you like tea?' and writing names. Share results.
Word Race: Write 'daily routines' on the board. Students race to write 5 verbs in 1 minute.
lp.pres: Show a KET-style reading paper (Part 1: matching questions). Model answering Q1 with a think-aloud: 'I see a picture of a man buying bread. The text says 'He is at the bakery.' So, I match them.' Check with thumbs up/down: 'Is the man at the bakery?'
presAlt: Realia Demo: Bring a shopping list and coins. Say, 'I need milk and bread.' Ask, 'What do I need?'
Storyboard: Draw 3 pictures (buying fruit, paying, leaving). Narrate: 'First, she buys apples. Then, she pays. Finally, she leaves.'
lp.prac: Pair work: Students get a KET reading Part 1 worksheet with 5 pictures and 5 short texts. They take turns matching and saying, 'Picture 1 matches text C because it shows a market.' Teacher monitors and helps with pronunciation.
pracAlt: Flashcard Match: Students match picture cards to sentence cards (e.g., 'He is buying a newspaper' + picture of a newsstand).
Board Game: Roll dice, land on a square, match a picture to a sentence to move.
lp.ls: KET listening mini-set (Part 1): Play a short audio of 5 people describing what they bought (e.g., 'I bought some apples'). Students listen and write the items next to the speakers' names. Play twice, then check answers as a class.
lp.re: Simon Says with KET vocabulary: 'Simon says point to the bakery.' 'Simon says say, 'I need milk.' Students who make a mistake sit down. Last student standing wins.
lp.prod: Roleplay: In pairs, one student is a customer (with a shopping list), the other is a shopkeeper. They use target language: 'Can I have some bread, please?' 'Yes, that's 5 dirhams.' 'Thank you.' Switch roles.
lp.rw: Writing task: Students write a short message (3-4 sentences) to a friend about their shopping. Example: 'Hi Fatima. I went to the market. I bought apples and milk. See you soon.' Use the board for sentence starters.
lp.st: Play a simple song like 'What Do You Like to Do?' with actions. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we practiced KET reading and writing. Thank you, class. Goodbye!'
g: Teacher calls out shopping words (e.g., 'bread'), students cross them off if on their card.
Students flip over picture/sentence cards and find matching pairs.
Start with 'I went to the market,' each student adds one item.
Students race to circle 5 food items in a supermarket flyer.
Teacher writes wrong sentences on board (e.g., 'I buyed bread'), students fix them.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 more sentences about their favorite shop.
Support: Use sentence frames like 'I need ______.' and 'I bought ______.'
hw: Complete a KET reading Part 2 worksheet (multiple choice).
Write 5 sentences about what you bought yesterday.
Record yourself saying a short shopping dialogue and send to teacher.
lp.tip: For KET practice, focus on task strategy (e.g., 'Read the question first') over perfection. Moroccan learners may need extra time with British English terms like 'chemist' (pharmacy).

weeks.obj: review the year through stations and games
weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.act:
Station carousel; error auction; team challenge
Discussion: what one person can actually change; cause and effect language.
weeks.hw:
Pre-assessment checklist completed
Write a paragraph: one green habit I will start.

skills.L: Listening station - mixed audio
skills.S: Speaking stations with games
skills.R: Reading station - mixed texts
skills.W: Writing station - forms and messages

lp.wu: Students play 'Memory Chain' with Earth Day vocabulary: I say 'recycle', student 1 says 'recycle, reuse', student 2 says 'recycle, reuse, reduce', and so on. Use flashcards for prompts.
wuAlt: Students brainstorm Earth Day words on the board in pairs, then share with the class.
Students match picture flashcards (e.g., bottle, tree, bin) to word cards on the table.
lp.pres: Show a short video clip about Earth Day actions. Elicit sentences like 'I can recycle bottles' and 'We should save water'. Use a poster with key phrases: 'I can...', 'We should...', 'I will...'. Check understanding by asking 'What can you do?'
presAlt: Use a story about a Moroccan family planting trees on Green March Day to elicit past simple and future forms.
Model a roleplay between a shopkeeper and customer using 'paper or plastic?' to introduce environmental choices.
lp.prac: Students play 'Error Auction': listen to sentences like 'I can to recycle' and bid on correct/incorrect ones. In pairs, they then correct the sentences on a worksheet.
pracAlt: Students complete a 'Find Someone Who...' grid with questions like 'Find someone who turns off lights'.
Play 'Green Bingo' with prompts like 'has a reusable bag'.
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio clip of a radio interview about Earth Day and tick the actions mentioned (e.g., 'plant trees', 'use less water').
lp.re: After the break, play 'Green Charades': students act out actions like 'recycling' or 'watering plants' for their team to guess.
lp.prod: In teams, students complete a 'Team Challenge' poster: draw a local problem (e.g., plastic in streets) and write three solutions using 'We can...'. Present to the class.
lp.rw: Students read a short email from a friend asking about green habits and reply using 'I will...' sentences. Focus on correct punctuation and simple past forms for habits.
lp.st: Read a short story about a Moroccan student who starts a recycling club at their school. End with: 'Today we reviewed how to talk about actions for Earth Day. Thank you, class.'
g: Listen to sentences, bid if correct/incorrect, then fix errors.
Add an Earth word each turn: recycle, reuse, reduce...
Ask classmates about green habits using 'Do you...?'
Act out eco-actions for teams to guess.
Draw a local problem and write three solutions on a poster.
diff: Fast finishers write a short paragraph: 'My family and Earth Day'.
Support learners use sentence starters: 'I can...', 'We should...' on a worksheet.
hw: Complete the pre-assessment checklist for the course.
Write one paragraph: 'One green habit I will start' using 'I will...'.
Watch a 2-minute video about Earth Day and list three new words.
lp.tip: Connect local context by discussing Morocco's Green Generation Initiative and how small actions align with Islamic values of stewardship (khalifa).

weeks.obj: complete final assessments and a feedback interview
weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.act:
Final paper; speaking interviews; course feedback forms; celebration
Discussion: work and value; presenting an opinion with reasons (IELTS-style).
weeks.hw:
Final report cards; certificates at ceremony
Write a for/against paragraph on unpaid internships.

skills.L: Final listening paper
skills.S: Final feedback interview, then celebrate
skills.R: Final reading paper
skills.W: Final writing task

lp.wu: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a Labour Day twist: ask 3 classmates 'Do you have a job?' or 'Do you want a job?' and write names. Teacher models first with a volunteer.
wuAlt: Teacher shows 5 job flashcards (teacher, doctor, engineer, chef, driver); students stand up and say 'I am a...' for their dream job.
Teacher writes 'Work is...' on board; students brainstorm 1 word each (e.g., 'important', 'hard').
lp.pres: Teacher presents a short dialogue about unpaid internships using flashcards (student, boss, money bag, clock). Model: 'Internships help you learn, but not getting paid is bad.' Check understanding by asking 'Is this fair?' and having students thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Teacher reads a short paragraph for/against unpaid internships; students repeat key phrases like 'It is good experience' and 'It is not fair.'
Teacher draws a simple T-chart on board; students copy and write 1 'pro' and 1 'con' with teacher guidance.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs to complete a gap-fill worksheet with sentences like 'Internships are ______ because you learn skills.' Teacher monitors and helps with spelling. Then pairs swap papers and check answers together.
pracAlt: Teacher gives each pair a set of 6 sentence strips (3 for, 3 against); students sort them into two columns on their desk and read them aloud.
Students play 'Sentence Relay': teams race to write 1 for/against reason on the board, e.g., 'You can get a job later.'
lp.ls: Students listen to a 2-minute audio clip of two people discussing unpaid internships (KET-style). They tick 'for' or 'against' on a simple worksheet. Teacher plays audio twice; check answers as a class.
lp.re: After break, students play 'Stand Up If...' with work-related prompts: 'Stand up if you think work is important!' 'Stand up if you want a good job!'
lp.prod: Students write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) with reasons for or against unpaid internships. Teacher provides sentence starters: 'I think internships are good because...' or 'I think they are bad because...'. Students share their paragraph with a partner.
lp.rw: Students complete the final reading paper (KET-style multiple-choice questions about a short text on Labour Day) and final writing task (writing a paragraph about their ideal job). Teacher collects papers for assessment.
lp.st: Teacher tells a simple story about a young person who gets their first job, emphasizing hard work and celebration. End with: 'Today we finished our course! Great job, everyone. Thank you for your hard work this year.'
g: Students mark off job words on a bingo card as teacher calls them out.
Students practice asking/answering 'What can you do?' and 'Why do you want this job?'
Teams stand on opposite sides of the room for/against unpaid internships and give 1 reason each.
Students say a work-related word (e.g., 'job') and the next student says a word that starts with the last letter (e.g., 'work').
Teacher acts out a job (e.g., teaching); students guess 'Are you a teacher?'
diff: Fast finishers: write 3 more sentences about why work is important.
Support: use a word bank with 5 key words (experience, skills, money, fair, learn) to write their paragraph.
hw: Review your final report card and write 1 goal for next year.
Bring a photo of your dream job to class next week.
Practice the 'job interview' roleplay with a family member.
lp.tip: For the feedback interview, sit in a circle and use Moroccan Arabic for complex questions to ensure clarity—this respects learners' life experience while building English confidence.
checklist: I can introduce myself and give basic personal information.
I can ask and answer simple questions about daily routines.
I can understand short, simple texts on familiar topics.
I can write short, simple sentences about my life.
I can make simple transactions (e.g., buying something).
I can give reasons for my opinions (e.g., 'I like... because...').
I can participate in a short conversation about work and jobs.

levels.desc: Survival English for adults aged 18+ with little or no previous English. Thirty weeks cover the language of daily life — greetings, personal information, shopping, food, directions, health, appointments, phone calls — through functional, needs-based learning and roleplays, with KET-style tasks appearing from mid-S2.

levels.label: Adults · Intermediate

weeks.obj: express opinions fluently on familiar topics; agree personal goals
weeks.lang: review diagnostic; opinion language (I think / In my opinion...)
weeks.act: Opinion circles; diagnostic discussion groups; goal-setting interviews
weeks.hw: 8-sentence opinion paragraph

skills.L: Listen to opinions and spot the support phrases
skills.S: Express opinions fluently and agree personal goals
skills.R: Read the PET orientation and map the exam (PET folder)
skills.W: Write my goals paragraph

lp.wu: Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three statements about their summer—one false. They mingle, share, and guess the lie. They say, 'I learned French,' 'I visited the Sahara,' 'I ate couscous every day.'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who: Students interview peers to find who 'watched an English movie,' 'traveled to another city,' or 'started a new hobby.' They ask, 'Did you...?' and tally responses.

Speed Introductions: In pairs, students introduce themselves with name, job, and one English goal. They rotate every 30 seconds, saying, 'My name is ___, I'm a ___, and I want to learn English for ___.'
lp.pres: Display flashcards with opinion phrases ('I think,' 'In my opinion,' 'From my perspective'). Model sentences: 'I think learning English is important for work.' 'In my opinion, practice is key.' Check understanding by asking, 'What phrase means you have a personal view?'
presAlt: Realia with local context: Show a photo of the American Space Oujda. Ask, 'What do you think about this space?' Elicit opinions, then model phrases.
Short dialogue: Read a dialogue between two learners discussing their goals. Highlight opinion phrases and ask students to underline them.
lp.prac: Opinion Circles: Students sit in groups of 3. Each group gets a topic (e.g., 'Learning English online vs. in class'). They take turns sharing opinions using target phrases. I monitor and prompt, 'Say what you think.'
pracAlt: Matching game: Match opinion phrases to sentence starters ('I believe...', 'It seems to me...'). Students practice in pairs, completing sentences.
Role-play cards: Students draw cards with topics (e.g., 'Best way to learn vocabulary') and role-play a conversation using opinion language.
lp.ls: PET-style listening: Play a short audio of two people discussing their learning goals. Students listen and write down two opinion phrases they hear. They compare in pairs, saying, 'I heard 'In my opinion, speaking is hard.''
lp.re: Quick Poll: After the break, I ask, 'Who thinks English is useful for travel?' Students stand up if yes, sit if no. They shout 'I agree!' or 'I disagree!'
lp.prod: Diagnostic Discussion Groups: Students form groups of 4. Each group discusses, 'What are your personal goals for English this year?' They use opinion phrases and note one goal per person. They report back, 'Fatima thinks she wants to improve her writing.'
lp.rw: PET Orientation: Students read a short text about the PET exam (from the PET folder). They map the sections (Reading, Writing, Listening, Speaking) and discuss, 'Which part do you think is hardest?' They write one sentence about their goal, e.g., 'I want to pass the PET speaking test.'
lp.st: Closing song: Play a short, upbeat English song (e.g., 'Happy' by Pharrell Williams). Students wave and sing along. End with: 'Today we practiced opinions and set goals. Thank you, class!'
g: Students write 9 opinion phrases in a grid. I call out phrases; they cross them off. First to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
I read a statement (e.g., 'English is easy'). Students stand if they agree, sit if not. They must say why using 'I think...'
One student starts a sentence (e.g., 'I think coffee is delicious'). The next adds, 'In my opinion, it's better than tea.'
Students write goals on cards. Mix and redistribute. They read a card and say, 'I think [name] wants to...'
Label corners with 'Strongly Agree,' 'Agree,' 'Disagree,' 'Strongly Disagree.' I read statements; students move to corners and justify.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 5-sentence paragraph about their best learning experience using opinion phrases.
Support weaker learners: Use sentence starters (e.g., 'I think... because...') to scaffold their goal-setting.
hw: Write an 8-sentence paragraph about your English goals. Use 'I think' and 'In my opinion.'
Record a 1-minute voice note explaining why you want to learn English. Send it to the teacher.
Read a short article about learning English (provided) and write 3 opinions using today's phrases.
lp.tip: Leverage the American Space Oujda context by connecting goals to real-world opportunities, like accessing English resources or participating in U.S.-Morocco exchange programs. This increases motivation.

weeks.obj: compare habits and lifestyles accurately
weeks.lang: present simple vs present continuous; adverbs of frequency
weeks.act: Habit comparison pairs; lifestyle interview; difference-detection listening
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to habit descriptions and catch the -s endings
skills.S: Compare habits and lifestyles accurately
skills.R: Read a lifestyle article and find both tenses
skills.W: Write habits with present simple vs continuous

lp.wu: Habit Race: Students stand in two lines. Teacher calls a habit (e.g., 'wake up early'). The first student in each line races to the board and writes it in present simple. Winners stay, new students come.
wuAlt: Frequency Charades: Teacher acts out an adverb of frequency (e.g., 'always' = exaggerated nod). Students guess and say the sentence (e.g., 'You always wake up early').
Habit Bingo: Students draw a 3x3 grid and write habits. Teacher calls sentences (e.g., 'I sometimes drink coffee'). Students cross off matches.
lp.pres: Teacher shows two flashcards: 'My brother (picture of sleeping)' vs 'My brother (picture of studying)' and says: 'He sleeps 8 hours. He is studying now.' Elicits the difference (habit vs now). Highlights -s endings and adverbs (always/never). Checks with thumbs up/down for sentences like 'He works here?'
presAlt: Lifestyle Venn Diagram: Teacher draws two circles for 'Me' and 'My Partner'. Students write habits in each circle and the middle. Teacher models: 'I eat couscous. He eats pizza. We both walk.'
Habit Survey Demo: Teacher asks a student: 'Do you usually exercise?' Student answers. Teacher writes the question/answer on the board, highlighting 'usually'.
lp.prac: Find Someone Who...: Students walk around with a grid. They ask: 'Do you ever...?' (e.g., 'Do you ever eat fast food?'). They write names and check 'always/usually/sometimes/never'. Teacher monitors for -s errors.
pracAlt: Habit Pairs: Students get cards with habits (e.g., 'I drink tea'). They find a partner with a contrasting habit (e.g., 'I drink coffee'). They make a dialogue: 'I drink tea.' 'I drink coffee.' 'We have different habits.'
Adverb Race: Teacher writes adverbs on the board. Students race to put them in order (never → always). Then they make sentences with teacher prompts (e.g., 'coffee' → 'I never drink coffee').
lp.ls: Habit Comparison Audio: Students listen to two people (A/B) talking about their daily routines. They tick habits in A's column or B's column. Teacher plays again to check -s endings (e.g., 'A wakes up at 6' vs 'B wake up at 7').
lp.re: Habit Switch: Students form two lines. Teacher calls a habit (e.g., 'brush teeth'). Students in line 1 do the action, line 2 does nothing. Teacher switches quickly. Last one standing wins.
lp.prod: Lifestyle Interview: Students interview a partner using: 'What do you usually do on weekends?' 'What are you doing this weekend?' They take notes. Then they introduce their partner to the class: 'Maria usually cooks. She is visiting her family this weekend.'
lp.rw: Reading: Students read a short article about 'A Day in the Life of a Moroccan Student'. They underline present simple habits (e.g., 'He prays five times') and continuous actions (e.g., 'He is learning English'). Writing: They write 80 words about their own day, using both tenses.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about 'Hassan's Habits' using target language (e.g., 'Hassan always eats breakfast. He is running now to catch the bus.'). Ends with: 'Today we compared habits. Thank you, class.'
g: Students match habit cards with adverb cards (e.g., 'exercise' + 'sometimes').
Teams race to write sentences on the board (e.g., 'She reads a book' vs 'She is reading a book').
Students put adverb cards in order and make sentences.
Students act out habits; others guess using present simple.
Students compare two lifestyle pictures and write 3 differences (e.g., 'He is eating vs He eats').
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 100-word paragraph comparing their habits to a celebrity's.
Support: Use sentence starters (e.g., 'I usually...') and a word bank for adverbs.
hw: Interview a family member about their habits. Write 5 sentences in present simple.
Watch a short video about a Moroccan festival (e.g., Green March). Write 3 sentences about what people do (present simple) and what they are doing now (continuous).
Do the 'Find Someone Who...' grid with 5 new habits. Bring it next class.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'praying', 'family meals') to make habits relatable. Encourage students to share real-life examples to boost engagement.

weeks.obj: narrate past events with past simple and continuous
weeks.lang: past simple vs past continuous; when/while
weeks.act: Photo storytelling; interrupted-action chains; while-clause game
weeks.hw: a memory paragraph using while

skills.L: Listen to a story and note the when / while moments
skills.S: Narrate past events with narrative tenses
skills.R: Read a story extract and map the tenses
skills.W: Write a memory narrative with when / while

lp.wu: Memory Chain: Teacher starts with 'Last week, I visited a market.' Student 1 repeats and adds 'While I was visiting, I bought fruit.' Student 2 repeats and adds 'While they were buying, they met a friend.' Continue around the class.
wuAlt: Photo Prompt: Show a photo of a local Moroccan festival (like Green March). Ask 'What was happening?' Students use past continuous to describe.
Timeline Toss: Write 3 past events on the board. Students toss a ball and make sentences with 'when' or 'while'.
lp.pres: Use 3 flashcards: a wedding, a rainstorm, a power cut. Model: 'I was sleeping when the storm started.' 'We were eating when the lights went out.' Elicit rules for past simple (interrupted actions) and 'when/while'. Check with thumbs-up/down for true/false sentences.
presAlt: Story Chain: Write a 2-sentence story on the board. Students add one sentence with past continuous, then one with past simple to interrupt it.
Realia Show: Bring in a traditional Moroccan tea set. Narrate: 'I was pouring tea when the cup broke.' Students describe their own experiences with objects.
lp.prac: Interrupted Action Chains: In pairs, Student A mimes an action (e.g., cooking). Student B mimes an interruption (e.g., phone rings) and says 'You were cooking when the phone rang.' Swap roles. Teacher circulates to correct tense errors.
pracAlt: While-Clause Game: Give each pair a card with a 'while' clause (e.g., 'While I was walking...'). They must complete it with a past simple action. First pair to shout 'Finished!' gets a point.
Sentence Race: Write 'when' and 'while' on the board. Teams race to write correct sentences using past simple/continuous about local events.
lp.ls: Listen to a 1-minute story about a power cut during Ramadan. Students listen and note 2 'when' moments and 2 'while' moments on a worksheet. Play twice for comprehension.
lp.re: Action Freeze: Teacher calls out an action (e.g., 'praying'). Students mime it. Teacher shouts 'BANG!' and says 'You were praying when the lights went out.' Students freeze and repeat the sentence.
lp.prod: Memory Circle: Each student shares a true memory about a Moroccan holiday (e.g., Eid, Independence Day). They must use one 'when' and one 'while' sentence. Listeners ask follow-up questions.
lp.rw: Read a short story extract about a wedding in Fez. Underline all past continuous verbs with a green pen and past simple with red. Then write 3 sentences about a personal memory using both tenses.
lp.st: Read a short folktale about a clever djinn who interrupts a farmer's work. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we practiced telling stories about the past using when and while. Thank you for sharing your memories.'
g: Match past simple and continuous cards to make logical sentences (e.g., 'was walking / saw a friend').
Teams race to write sentences on the board using prompts like 'shopping / rain started'.
Student A mimes; Student B interrupts and says a sentence with past simple.
Groups use 3 photos to create a 2-sentence story with past continuous + past simple.
Students toss a ball and make sentences about events on a class timeline.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 50-word story about a Moroccan festival using 3 'while' and 2 'when' sentences.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'I was ______ when ______.' on a worksheet.
hw: Write a paragraph (80 words) about a childhood memory using at least two 'while' sentences.
Record a 1-minute voice message telling a family memory with past simple/continuous.
Find a photo online and write 3 sentences about what was happening when the photo was taken.
lp.tip: Use local context (Moroccan holidays, family gatherings) to make the grammar memorable. Adults connect better to personal stories.

weeks.obj: talk about experiences with present perfect (basics)
weeks.lang: present perfect (have/has + participle); ever/never
weeks.act:
Find someone who has... mingle; experience bingo; interview grids
Discussion: Halloween between commerce and culture; compare with local celebrations.
weeks.hw:
Participation quiz
Write a short opinion paragraph: should Oujda celebrate Halloween?

skills.L: Listen to an ever/never experiences interview
skills.S: Talk about experiences with present perfect
skills.R: Read experience profiles and find the forms
skills.W: Write 5 experience sentences (ever / never)

lp.wu: Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their life experiences. Each student writes three sentences about things they have/never have done, one false. They mingle, share, and guess the lie. Teacher models first: 'I have eaten camel meat. I have never been to Paris. I have climbed Mount Toubkal.'
wuAlt: Students complete the sentence frame 'I have never ____, but I have ____' with personal truths. They share with a partner.
Teacher shows 5 photos of activities (e.g., hiking, cooking, traveling). Students guess which one the teacher has never done using 'Have you ever ____?'
lp.pres: Teacher presents 6 flashcards showing Halloween activities (carving pumpkins, wearing costumes, trick-or-treating). Models present perfect sentences: 'I have carved a pumpkin. I have never gone trick-or-treating.' Elicits forms from students: 'Have you ever...?' 'Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.' Checks understanding with thumbs-up/down for true/false statements.
presAlt: Teacher tells a short personal story about a Halloween experience using present perfect, then asks students to underline the target language. They identify the pattern.
Students read 3 short experience profiles (e.g., 'Fatima has celebrated Halloween twice.') and circle the 'have/has + past participle' structures.
lp.prac: Students play 'Find Someone Who Has...' with a bingo grid. They mingle, ask 'Have you ever...?' questions (e.g., 'eaten Halloween candy?', 'worn a scary costume?'), and write names in boxes. First to get a line shouts 'Bingo!'. Teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation of 'ever/never'.
pracAlt: Students complete a gap-fill worksheet with present perfect sentences about Halloween, choosing between 'have/has' and the correct past participle (e.g., 'I have ____ (see) a ghost movie').
In pairs, students interview each other using a grid with 5 'Have you ever...?' questions about life experiences. They write down answers and report back to the class.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 2-minute audio of two people discussing their Halloween experiences. They tick the activities mentioned (e.g., 'watched a horror movie', 'attended a party') on a worksheet. Teacher plays audio twice. Feedback: students compare answers in pairs, then class check.
lp.re: After the break, students play 'Stand Up If...'. Teacher calls out experiences (e.g., 'Stand up if you have ever eaten Halloween candy!', 'Stand up if you have never worn a costume!'). Students stand up if true, stay seated if false. Quick energy boost.
lp.prod: In groups of 3, students discuss 'Halloween: Commerce or Culture?'. They compare Halloween with local Moroccan celebrations like Eid or Aid Al Adha. Teacher prompts: 'Is Halloween just for shops? Is it like our holidays?'. Each group prepares a 2-minute summary to present to the class, using present perfect to share personal experiences (e.g., 'In our group, none of us has celebrated Halloween, but we have...').
lp.rw: Students read a short article (100 words) about Halloween traditions in the US and Morocco. They underline all present perfect forms. Then, they write 5 sentences about their own experiences using 'ever/never' (e.g., 'I have never carved a pumpkin, but I have eaten Halloween candy.'). Teacher checks for accuracy.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short, culturally respectful story about a Halloween misunderstanding in Morocco, focusing on experiences. Ends with the goodbye routine: 'Today we talked about our experiences using present perfect. Thank you for sharing, and have a great week!'
g: Students mingle, ask 'Have you ever...?' questions, and mark off squares on a bingo grid when someone says 'yes'.
Students walk around the class asking questions to find classmates who match specific experiences.
Students write three sentences about their experiences, one false, and others guess the lie.
Teacher calls out experiences; students stand if true, sit if false.
Groups debate if Halloween is commercial or cultural, comparing it to local holidays.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph (3-4 sentences) comparing Halloween with a Moroccan holiday.
Support weaker learners: Use a sentence frame worksheet to write their 5 experience sentences (e.g., 'I have never ____ before.')
hw: Write a short opinion paragraph (80-100 words): 'Should Oujda celebrate Halloween? Give two reasons.'
Interview a family member about their experiences with celebrations (e.g., 'Have you ever celebrated Halloween?') and write 3 sentences in present perfect.
Complete a 'My Life Experiences' chart with 10 things you have/never have done, using 'ever/never'.
lp.tip: Connect the grammar to their lives by using local examples (e.g., 'Have you ever eaten msemen on a holiday?'). This makes the target language more relevant and memorable for Moroccan learners.

weeks.obj: describe how long with for and since
weeks.lang: present perfect + for/since; time expressions
weeks.act:
Timeline interviews; how-long chains; for-since sorting relay
Discussion with for/since: "Morocco HAS HAD the southern provinces SINCE 1975..."
weeks.hw:
6 sentences about your life experiences
Write 6 for/since sentences about national milestones.

skills.L: Listen to How-long Q and A with for / since
skills.S: Describe how long with for and since
skills.R: Read duration texts and complete the table
skills.W: Write for / since sentences about my life

lp.wu: Timeline Interviews: Students draw a personal timeline from birth to now with 5 key life events. In pairs, they ask 'How long have you lived in Oujda?' and 'How long have you studied English?' using for/since.
wuAlt: For/Since Chain: Students stand in a circle. One student says 'I have lived in Morocco for 10 years.' The next says 'I have studied English since 2020,' and so on, building a chain.
National Milestones Quiz: Show flashcards of Moroccan events (Green March, Independence). Students guess the year and make a sentence with 'for' or 'since'.
lp.pres: Present perfect + for/since is introduced using a Green March timeline (1975-present). Model sentences: 'Morocco has had the Sahara since 1975.' 'We have celebrated the Green March for 48 years.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down for true/false sentences about the timeline.
presAlt: Realia Display: Bring in Moroccan currency or a map. Point to the Sahara and say 'Morocco has controlled this area since 1975.' Students repeat and make their own sentences about national symbols.
Video Clip: Show a 1-min clip of the Green March. Pause to ask 'How long have Moroccans remembered this event?' and elicit 'since 1975'.
lp.prac: For-Since Sorting Relay: Divide into 2 teams. Give each team a set of cards (time expressions: '5 years', '2018', 'last month', 'ages') and sentence starters ('I have worked here...', 'He has lived here...'). Teams race to sort cards into 'for' or 'since' columns on the board.
pracAlt: How-Long Chains: In groups of 3, students take turns making present perfect sentences with for/since about national achievements (e.g., 'Morocco has hosted CANAFCON since 2023'). The chain continues until someone hesitates.
Sentence Builder: Distribute word cards (I/have/lived/in/Oujda/for/10 years). Students arrange them to make correct sentences, then swap cards with another group.
lp.ls: Listen to short dialogues where people discuss their experiences with for/since (e.g., 'How long have you been a teacher? 'For 5 years.'). Students complete a table with names, jobs, and durations. Check answers by replaying key phrases.
lp.re: Stand Up Sit Down: Call out time expressions (e.g., 'since 2020', 'for a month'). Students stand if it's 'since', sit if it's 'for'. Speed up to make it challenging and fun.
lp.prod: National Milestone Interviews: Students choose a Moroccan milestone (Green March, Independence, etc.). In pairs, they interview each other: 'How long has Morocco celebrated this?' and 'What does it mean for you?' They prepare a 2-minute presentation to share findings.
lp.rw: Read a short article about the Green March. Complete a table with events (e.g., 'Green March', 'Reunification') and durations (e.g., 'since 1975', 'for decades'). Then write 3 sentences about their own experiences using for/since.
lp.st: Play a short clip of a Moroccan song about national unity. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to describe duration with for and since. Thank you for your participation!'
g: Teams race to place event cards on a timeline, saying sentences like 'Morocco has had the Sahara since 1975'.
Students write 9 time expressions on a grid. Teacher calls out sentences; students mark the matching expression.
Students stand in a circle. Each adds a for/since sentence to the chain, e.g., 'I have lived in Morocco for 20 years. My father has worked here since 1995.'
Students mingle asking 'Find someone who has studied English for more than 2 years' and write names.
Teams bid on correct for/since sentences. Incorrect sentences are 'bought' but don't earn points.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 6 for/since sentences about national milestones.
Support: Use sentence frames like 'Morocco has ______ since ______' and a word bank.
hw: Write 6 sentences about your life experiences using for/since (e.g., 'I have lived in Oujda for 5 years').
Write 6 for/since sentences about national milestones (e.g., 'Morocco has been independent since 1956').
Interview a family member about their experiences with for/since and share 3 sentences in class.
lp.tip: Connect grammar to local history to boost engagement. For example, using the Green March makes 'for/since' meaningful and culturally relevant.

weeks.obj: describe trips using present perfect and superlatives
weeks.lang: superlatives; the best place I have (ever)...
weeks.act: Travel talk triads; best-of city presentations; listening: travel experiences
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to travel talks with superlatives
skills.S: Describe trips with present perfect + superlatives
skills.R: Read destination reviews and check the claims
skills.W: Write the best / worst trip paragraph

lp.wu: Travel Pictionary: Students draw a travel-related word (e.g., 'beach', 'hotel', 'passport') on the board while others guess. The drawer says 'It's a place you go to...' or 'It's something you use for...' to elicit vocabulary.
wuAlt: Travel Charades: Students act out travel verbs (e.g., 'check-in', 'board a plane') while others guess the action.
Word Association: Teacher says 'travel', students take turns saying related words (e.g., 'suitcase', 'flight', 'destination').
lp.pres: Show flashcards of famous Moroccan cities (Marrakech, Casablanca, Chefchaouen). Model sentences: 'Marrakech is the most exciting city I have ever visited.' 'Chefchaouen has the bluest streets.' Check understanding by asking 'Which city is the most...?' and having students complete sentences.
presAlt: Travel Story: Read a short story about a trip to Morocco using superlatives (e.g., 'The best meal I had was in Fez.').', 'Realia: Bring in photos of travel souvenirs (e.g., a tagine, a carpet) and have students compare them using superlatives.
lp.prac: Superlative Sort: Students work in pairs to match superlative adjectives (e.g., 'biggest', 'most beautiful') to pictures of landmarks (e.g., Hassan II Mosque, Atlas Mountains). Teacher monitors and corrects errors.
pracAlt: Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Have you ever been to the most... place in Morocco?' and fill in a grid.
Superlative Race: In teams, students race to write superlative sentences about famous places in Morocco.
lp.ls: Listen to a short podcast about travel experiences. Students fill in gaps in sentences like 'The best thing about the trip was ________.' and 'The most difficult part was ________.'
lp.re: Travel Relay: Students line up and take turns running to the board to write a superlative sentence about a travel topic (e.g., 'The best food in Morocco is ________.').
lp.prod: Best-of City Presentations: In triads, students prepare a 2-minute presentation about the best place they have ever visited. They must use present perfect and superlatives (e.g., 'I have been to Agadir, and it has the most beautiful beaches.').
lp.rw: Read a short review of a Moroccan hotel. Students underline all superlatives and then write their own 50-word review of a hotel or restaurant using at least three superlatives.
lp.st: Watch a 2-minute video clip of a travel vlogger in Morocco. Close with the goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to describe trips using superlatives. Thank you for your participation.'
g: Students create bingo cards with superlative adjectives and mark them off when the teacher calls them out.
Students describe a travel word using superlatives without saying the word itself.
Students describe a place using superlatives (e.g., 'It's the oldest medina in Morocco.') for others to guess.
Students sit in a circle and take turns adding a superlative to a sentence (e.g., 'I have visited the most... place, which is...').
Teams race to draw and guess travel words using superlatives.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 100-word paragraph about the best trip they have ever taken.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'The best ________ I have ever seen is ________ because ________.'
hw: Write a 80-word email to a friend describing the best place you have ever visited using superlatives.
Record a 1-minute voice message about your best travel experience using superlatives.
Read a travel review online and write down 5 superlatives used.
lp.tip: Encourage students to share personal travel experiences from Morocco or abroad to make the language practice more meaningful and relevant to their lives.

weeks.obj: debate comparisons with accuracy (comparatives review + nuance)
weeks.lang: comparatives (much/far + -er); as...as
weeks.act:
City comparison debate; as...as role cards; comparative auctions
Discussion: independence and identity; past perfect practice ("by 1956, Morocco had...").
weeks.hw:
5 nuanced comparisons
Write 5 sentences in the past perfect about Moroccan history.

skills.L: Listen to nuanced comparisons (as...as)
skills.S: Debate comparisons with accuracy
skills.R: Read a comparison article and find the modifiers
skills.W: Write balanced comparisons (much / far / as...as)

lp.wu: Students stand in a circle. Teacher holds up two flashcards: a picture of Casablanca and a picture of Rabat. Teacher says: 'Casablanca is bigger than Rabat.' Students pass the cards to the left and each student must say a true comparative sentence using the two cities.
wuAlt: Teacher writes 'Oujda' and 'Tangier' on the board. Students brainstorm comparative sentences in pairs and share them with the class.
Teacher reads a sentence: 'Marrakech is more exciting than Fes.' Students change the sentence to use 'as...as' if possible.
lp.pres: Teacher projects a short infographic comparing two Moroccan cities, e.g., 'Casablanca vs. Fez'. Teacher highlights model sentences: 'Casablanca is much larger than Fez.' 'Fez is as historic as Meknes.' Teacher uses gestures to show 'much' and 'as...as' and checks understanding by asking: 'Which city is bigger? How do we say they are equally historic?'
presAlt: Teacher uses two realia items: a small apple and a large orange. Students make comparisons, then teacher introduces 'much bigger' and 'as heavy as'.
Teacher distributes a short text with missing comparative words. Students fill in the gaps, then teacher explains the rules.
lp.prac: Students receive 'City Comparison Role Cards' (e.g., 'You are a tourist. You prefer the coast. Compare Agadir to Chefchaouen.'). They work in pairs to prepare a dialogue using 'much/far + -er' and 'as...as'. Teacher monitors and corrects errors.
pracAlt: 'Comparative Auction': Teacher writes 10 sentences on the board with errors. Students 'bid' to correct them, with the highest bidder explaining the change.
Students play 'Find Someone Who...': 'Find someone who thinks Casablanca is more modern than Rabat.' They ask questions and write down the answers.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 1-minute audio clip from a travel podcast comparing two Moroccan cities. They must complete a chart with the comparisons made (e.g., 'Fez: older, quieter; Rabat: more modern, cleaner').
lp.re: Students stand. Teacher calls out a city name (e.g., 'Marrakech'). Students must quickly say one comparative fact about it (e.g., 'Marrakech is hotter than Rabat!').
lp.prod: Students are divided into two groups: 'Team Casablanca' and 'Team Rabat'. They have 10 minutes to prepare a 3-minute debate arguing why their city is 'better' using nuanced comparatives. After, they vote for the most convincing team.
lp.rw: Students read a short article (100 words) comparing life in a city and a village in Morocco. They underline all the comparative adjectives and modifiers (e.g., 'much', 'far', 'slightly'). Then, they write 5 sentences comparing their own city to another Moroccan city.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short, personal story: 'When I was young, I thought Casablanca was the best city. Now, I think Rabat is as beautiful.' Students share one sentence comparing their past and present opinions. Close with: 'Today you debated with nuance. Thank you, class.'
g: Teacher says a sentence. If it's true, students snap. If false, they stomp.
Students compare city cards (population, size) and the highest value wins.
Students look at two pictures of Moroccan cities and write 5 comparisons.
Students start a sentence: 'Rabat is as...as...' and the next student must complete it.
