Teams race to write comparative sentences on the board for a given prompt.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 50-word email comparing two Moroccan cities for a friend.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: '______ is much ______ than ______ because ______.'
hw: Write 5 nuanced comparisons between two Moroccan cities using 'much/far' and 'as...as'.
Write 5 sentences in the past perfect about Moroccan history (e.g., 'By 1956, Morocco had gained its independence.').
Record a 1-minute video comparing two cities in Morocco and post it on the class forum.
lp.tip: Encourage learners to connect comparisons to personal experiences, e.g., 'Casablanca is more expensive than my hometown,' to increase engagement and authenticity.

weeks.obj: choose correctly between will, going to, and might
weeks.lang: will vs going to vs might; prediction vs plan
weeks.act:
Decision roleplays; prediction panel; plan-change listening
Discussion: gratitude rituals across cultures; polite dinner-language practice.
weeks.hw:
Participation quiz
Write a thank-you message (email or card) in English.

skills.L: Listen to future-form dialogues and label will / going to / might
skills.S: Negotiate plans with three future forms
skills.R: Read plan texts and classify the forms
skills.W: Write my decisions with will / going to / might

lp.wu: Future Tense Charades: Write will, going to, might on cards. Students mime actions (e.g., 'I will travel to Paris') while others guess the form and meaning.
wuAlt: Plan Prediction Relay: Teams race to write sentences about future plans using correct forms (e.g., 'We are going to eat turkey').
Gratitude Brainstorm: Students share 3 things they 'will', 'are going to', or 'might do' to show gratitude this week.
lp.pres: Show a picture of a Thanksgiving dinner. Model: 'I will cook the turkey (decision), I am going to invite my family (plan), I might try pumpkin pie (possibility).'. Use flashcards with icons (lightbulb for will, calendar for going to, question mark for might). Check understanding with thumbs up/down: 'Is this a plan or a prediction?'
presAlt: Real-life Stories: Teacher shares personal Thanksgiving plans, highlighting forms. Students repeat sentences.
Form Sorting Game: Display sentences on board; students group them into will/going to/might columns.
lp.prac: Decision Roleplay: Pairs receive scenarios (e.g., 'Plan a Thanksgiving meal with $50 budget'). They negotiate using 'I will...', 'I am going to...', 'I might...'. Teacher monitors and corrects errors.
pracAlt: Form Match-Up: Cards with prompts (e.g., 'It's cloudy') and responses (e.g., 'It might rain'). Students match pairs.
Might Maze: Worksheet with paths; students write sentences using 'might' to describe possible outcomes.
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue about Thanksgiving plans. Students label sentences as will (W), going to (G), or might (M). Play twice; check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Stand Up Sit Down: Teacher says sentences (e.g., 'I will eat turkey'). Students stand if it's a decision, sit if it's a plan, jump if it's a possibility.
lp.prod: Gratitude Panel: Small groups discuss 'What will you do to show gratitude this year?'. Each member shares 1 plan (going to), 1 decision (will), and 1 possibility (might). Present to class.
lp.rw: Read a short text about Thanksgiving traditions. Underline all future forms (will/going to/might). Then write 3 sentences about your own future plans using these forms.
lp.st: Read a story about gratitude in different cultures (e.g., Moroccan 'Aïd' vs. Thanksgiving). End with: 'Today we practiced future forms for decisions, plans, and possibilities. Thank you for your participation!'
g: Students act out prompts (e.g., 'win the lottery') while others guess the form (will/going to/might).
Listen to a dialogue; draw arrows to show how plans change (e.g., 'We are going to... but we might...').
Ask 3 classmates: 'What will you do for gratitude?' and note responses.
Navigate a worksheet maze by writing 'might' sentences to describe possible paths.
Roleplay hosting a dinner; negotiate plans using all three future forms.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 50-word email inviting someone to Thanksgiving, using all three forms.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'I will _____. I am going to _____. I might ____.'
hw: Write a thank-you email (80-100 words) to someone, using will/going to/might for future promises or plans.
Create a gratitude list with 5 items, using 'I will...' for actions and 'I might...' for hopes.
Record a 1-minute video explaining your Thanksgiving plans, using correct future forms.
lp.tip: Link future forms to local contexts: e.g., 'I might visit my family during the Green March' or 'I will prepare for Eid by...'. This makes grammar relevant to learners' lives.

weeks.obj: discuss real possibilities with if-clauses
weeks.lang: zero and first conditional; result clauses
weeks.act: Problem-scenario problem-solving pairs; if-chains; real-conditions debate
weeks.hw: 5 first-conditional sentences about your goals

skills.L: Listen to if-sentences and choose the conditional
skills.S: Discuss real possibilities with if-clauses
skills.R: Read a problem-solutions text and find the conditionals
skills.W: Write 4 first-conditional sentences

lp.wu: Conditional Chain Game: Teacher starts a zero conditional (e.g., 'If it rains, the ground gets wet'), students add first conditionals in a chain (e.g., 'If the ground gets wet, people use umbrellas'), each student adds one sentence, chain continues until it breaks.
wuAlt: Real-Life Scenario Cards: Students draw cards with simple situations (e.g., 'You have a headache') and respond with zero/first conditionals ('If you have a headache, you take medicine').
If-Then Charades: One student acts out a conditional action (e.g., pretending to study), others guess the clause ('If you study, you pass exams').
lp.pres: Show a weather forecast video clip with rain; present zero conditional model: 'If it rains, the ground gets wet.' Then show a job interview scenario; present first conditional: 'If you study hard, you get the job.' Check understanding by asking students to create their own examples for each type.
presAlt: Picture Stories: Use flashcards showing cause-effect (e.g., sun/ice cream melting) to elicit zero conditionals, then flashcards showing future plans (e.g., saving money/buying a car) for first conditionals.
Dialogue Roleplay: Teacher models a dialogue using conditionals, students identify and label the types (0/1).
lp.prac: Match the Conditionals: Students receive a worksheet with mixed clauses (if-clauses and result clauses) to pair correctly; teacher monitors and provides sentence starters for struggling learners. Then play 'Conditional Relay'—teams race to write correct sentences on the board for prompts like 'If you miss the bus...'.
pracAlt: Sentence Building Blocks: Students use colored cards (blue for if-clause, green for result) to physically build sentences, then swap with partners for correction.
Error Correction Race: Teams find and fix errors in 10 conditional sentences, first team to correct all wins.
lp.ls: Listen to three short dialogues (e.g., weather forecast, doctor's advice, travel plans) and tick whether each uses zero or first conditional. Then listen again and write down one correct conditional sentence from each dialogue.
lp.re: Stand If True: Teacher reads conditional statements (e.g., 'If you live in Morocco, you speak Arabic'); students stand if the statement is true for them, sit if false. Quick movement to refocus post-break.
lp.prod: Problem-Solution Debate: In pairs, students receive a Moroccan-themed problem (e.g., 'If there is a power cut, how do you study?'). They discuss and present their first conditional solutions to the class, defending their choices.
lp.rw: Read a short article about how Moroccans prepare for Ramadan (e.g., 'If the month starts, families buy special foods'). Underline all conditional sentences, then write 4 first-conditional sentences about your own holiday plans.
lp.st: Watch a 2-minute animated story about conditional decisions (e.g., 'If you help others, you make friends'). Close with a one-line recap: 'Today we discussed real possibilities with if-clauses.' Thank the class.
g: Students take turns adding to a conditional sentence chain, each adding one clause.
Students act out conditional actions for others to guess the clauses.
Pair if-clause and result clause cards to make correct sentences.
Students stand/sit based on truth of conditional statements about them.
Teams race to write first-conditional solutions to given problems.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 second-conditional sentences about imaginary changes in Morocco.
Support learners: Use sentence frames ('If ___, I ___') to build first conditionals.
hw: Write 5 first-conditional sentences about your personal goals for this year (e.g., 'If I exercise daily, I will be healthier').
Find a news article and highlight all conditional sentences, then write 2 new ones about Moroccan current events.
Record a 1-minute voice note explaining what you will do if you travel to America next year.
lp.tip: Use local examples (e.g., 'If you visit the Hassan II Mosque, you see beautiful architecture') to make conditionals culturally relevant and memorable for Moroccan learners.

weeks.obj: imagine and discuss hypothetical situations
weeks.lang: second conditional; I would... / If I were...
weeks.act: If I could... discussion circles; dream scenario role cards; hypothetical auctions
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to dream-scenario interviews
skills.S: Imagine and discuss hypotheticals (second conditional)
skills.R: Read a wishes text and find I wish
skills.W: Write my dream-life paragraph

lp.wu: Dream Catcher: Students write one dream on a slip of paper and put it in a 'dream jar'. Teacher draws one and asks 'If you could make this dream come true, what would you do?'
wuAlt: Alternative warm-up 1: Two Stars and a Wish - students share two real-life achievements and one wish using 'I wish I could...'
Alternative warm-up 2: Dream Lottery - students pick a dream card from a hat and discuss it in pairs
lp.pres: Teacher shows a picture of a Moroccan desert camp and says 'If I were in the Sahara now, I would ride a camel'. Model 3-4 sentences with 'If I were... I would...'. Check understanding with thumbs up/down: 'If I were a bird, I would fly to the Atlas Mountains' - true or false for me?
presAlt: Alternative presentation 1: Dream Scenario Cards - teacher holds up a card 'Win 1 million dirhams' and models 'If I won 1 million dirhams, I would build a school in my village'
Alternative presentation 2: Realia - teacher shows a plane ticket and says 'If I had this ticket, I would visit New York to see the Statue of Liberty'
lp.prac: Hypothetical Auction: Students get dream scenario cards (e.g., 'Speak English fluently', 'Meet a celebrity'). In groups, they 'bid' using 'If I could [dream], I would [action]'. Highest bidder explains their plan. Teacher monitors and corrects 'If I were' vs 'If I was'.
pracAlt: Alternative practice 1: Conditional Chain - students sit in a circle and each adds to the story: 'If I had a magic lamp, I would wish for... and if that happened, I would...'
Alternative practice 2: Dream Role Cards - students draw roles (e.g., 'You are a famous chef') and interview each other with 'If you were me, what would you cook?'
lp.ls: Dream Interviews: Students listen to 3 short audio clips of people talking about their dreams (e.g., 'If I could travel anywhere, I would go to Japan'). They fill in a table: 'Dream', 'Action', 'Reason'. Teacher plays twice, then checks answers in pairs.
lp.re: Dream Relay: After break, students stand in two lines. Teacher whispers a conditional sentence (e.g., 'If I were rich, I would buy a car') to the first student. They whisper it down the line. Last student says it aloud. First correct team wins.
lp.prod: Dream Scenario Role Cards: Students pick a card (e.g., 'You are a tour guide in Oujda', 'You are a student studying abroad'). In pairs, they roleplay a conversation using 'If I were you, I would...'. They must give advice about achieving a dream. Teacher observes and takes notes.
lp.rw: Wishes Paragraph: Students read a short text about a Moroccan's dream to open a business. They underline all 'I wish' sentences. Then, they write their own 80-word paragraph about their dream life, using at least 3 second conditionals and 2 'I wish' sentences.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a Moroccan who achieved their dream (e.g., starting a cooperative). End with: 'Today we imagined dreams using second conditionals. Thank you for sharing your ideas. Goodbye!'
g: Students bid for dream cards using 'If I could [dream], I would [bid]' - highest bidder wins the card
Students sit in a circle and each adds to a story using 'If I were... I would...'
Students roleplay giving advice about dreams using 'If I were you, I would...'
Students interview each other about dreams and fill in a table
Whisper a conditional sentence down a line - last student says it aloud
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a conditional dream poem (4 lines using 'If I were... I would...')
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame 'If I were ___, I would ___' to complete 5 sentences
hw: Homework option 1: Write a 100-word email to a friend about your dream vacation using 3 second conditionals
Homework option 2: Record a 1-minute voice note describing your dream job using 'If I were a..., I would...'
Homework option 3: Draw a picture of your dream life and write 3 sentences about it using conditionals
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'If I were in charge of the Sahara Festival, I would...') to make conditionals more relevant and engaging for learners.

weeks.obj: discuss rules and give advice with must, have to, should
weeks.lang: must/mustn't/have to/don't have to/should
weeks.act: Signs and meanings matching; rules debate (home/school/work); advice clinic
weeks.hw: 5 rules for your ideal school

skills.L: Listen to rules and advice dialogues
skills.S: Discuss rules and give advice with modals
skills.R: Read rules notices and match the modals
skills.W: Write advice for 3 situations

lp.wu: Play 'Rules Pictionary': write 'must', 'mustn't', 'should', 'have to', 'don't have to' on slips, students draw the rule (e.g., 'must wear uniform'), others guess the modal and the rule.
wuAlt: Play 'Modal Hot Seat': students describe rules/advice using modals, teammates guess the situation
Play 'Find Someone Who...': mingle to find people who 'must wake up early' or 'should study more', using target language
lp.pres: Show flashcards of signs (no smoking, fasten seatbelt, quiet please) and elicit the rule, model sentences like 'You mustn't smoke here', 'You have to wear a seatbelt', 'You should be quiet', check understanding with 'What does this sign mean?' and 'Which modal is for rules? Advice?'
presAlt: Use a story about a new employee at a Moroccan café, highlight rules with modals
Bring in real objects (helmet, phone, book) and give rules/advice using modals
lp.prac: Do 'Modal Match-Up': worksheet with signs and modal sentences, students match them, then drill in pairs saying the rule, play 'Modal Relay' in teams: one student says a rule, next adds another, no repeats.
pracAlt: Play 'Modal Charades': students act out rules/advice, others guess using modals
Do 'Sentence Scramble': unjumble sentences like 'You / must / homework / do' into correct order
lp.ls: Listen to a dialogue between a teacher and student about school rules, students tick the rules mentioned (e.g., 'You must be on time', 'You should bring your books'), check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Play 'Simon Says' with modals: 'Simon says you must jump!', 'Simon says you should touch your nose' – those who follow the wrong modal are out.
lp.prod: Run a 'Rules Debate': split into groups (home/school/work), discuss and write 3 rules using must/mustn't/should/have to, then present to class with reasons (e.g., 'Students must wear uniforms because...')
lp.rw: Read short notices from American Space Oujda (e.g., 'You must register for events', 'You should keep the library quiet'), underline all modal verbs, then write 2 sentences giving advice for using the space.
lp.st: Read a short story about a visitor to Oujda who breaks rules (e.g., 'He didn't have to remove shoes, but he should have'), end with 'Today we learned to give rules and advice using must/mustn't/should/have to. Thank you, class!'
g: Students write 9 rules with modals, teacher calls out situations, they cross off matching rules
Teams race to write modal rules on the board for given situations
Student acts out a rule, others guess using modals
Roll dice, land on square, make a sentence with the modal and topic
Groups 'bid' on giving the best advice for problems using modals
diff: Fast finishers: write a 100-word email to the American Space Oujda manager suggesting 3 new rules using modals
Support: use a sentence frame 'You ______ (modal) ______ (rule)' to write sentences
hw: Write 5 rules for your ideal school using must/mustn't/should/have to
Record a 1-minute video giving advice for tourists visiting Morocco using modals
Find 5 examples of modals in English signs around Oujda and write them down
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural context (e.g., 'You must remove shoes in mosques') to make rules relatable, and encourage students to compare with American Space rules to bridge cultures.

weeks.obj: talk about work, skills, and interviews with confidence
weeks.lang: work vocabulary; skills language; interview Q&A
weeks.act:
Mock interview pairs; skills inventory; job ad analysis
Discussion: Christmas as a global pop-culture event; polite refusal/acceptance language for invitations.
weeks.hw:
Mock interview performance check
Write an invitation and a polite reply to it.

skills.L: Listen to job-interview Q and A
skills.S: Talk about work, skills and interviews with confidence
skills.R: Read a job ad and profile; note collocations
skills.W: Write my skills profile (interview prep)

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Two Truths and a Lie' about work. Students write three statements about their jobs/skills (two true, one false). In pairs, they guess which is the lie. Teacher models first: 'I've worked in three countries (true), I can speak Japanese (false), I love Mondays (true)'.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Find Someone Who...' worksheet with prompts like 'Find someone who has worked in a team', 'Find someone who can use Excel'.
Alternative 2: 'Mime the Job' - students mime a job (teacher, chef, engineer) and others guess.
lp.pres: Presentation: Show a job ad for a 'Christmas Event Coordinator' on the board. Highlight key skills: 'organize events', 'work under pressure', 'communicate with clients'. Model interview Q&A: 'Why do you want this job?' 'I want to use my organizational skills to create memorable events.' Check understanding with 'thumbs up/down' for 'What skills are needed?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a short video clip of a job interview, pausing to highlight phrases like 'My strength is...' and 'I'm looking for a challenge'.
Alternative 2: Bring in props (a phone, calendar, notepad) to demonstrate 'organize events' physically.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Interview Match-Up' game. Students receive cards with interview questions (e.g., 'Tell me about your experience') and answers (e.g., 'I've organized three parties'). In pairs, they match them, then practice asking/answering. Teacher circulates to correct pronunciation.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Role Card Swap' - students get role cards (interviewer/interviewee) with sentence starters, then swap roles.
Alternative 2: 'Drill the Phrase' - choral repetition of key phrases like 'I'm good at...' and 'I've never...' with gestures.
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a PET-style audio of a job interview. Students listen and tick the skills mentioned (e.g., 'teamwork', 'problem-solving'). Replay to check answers, focusing on linking words like 'because' and 'for example'.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand Up If...' - Teacher calls out skills (e.g., 'Stand up if you can cook!', 'Stand up if you've worked with a team!'). Students stand and share a brief example. Quick energy boost after the break.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Mock Interview Pairs'. One student is the interviewer, the other is the interviewee for a 'Christmas Party Planner' role. They use the job ad and skills inventory to ask/answer questions for 5 minutes. Teacher notes language use for feedback.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read a short profile of 'Amina, Event Coordinator' and underline collocations like 'organize events' and 'meet deadlines'. Then, they write their own 80-word skills profile for a job application, using the model text.
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Play a short video of 'The Story of Christmas as a Global Celebration' (2 mins). End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we practiced job interviews and Christmas vocabulary. Thank you, class! Have a great week!'
g: Cut job ads into sections; groups reassemble and match skills to requirements.
Students act out skills (e.g., 'typing', 'negotiating') for others to guess.
Bingo cards with phrases like 'I'm a team player'; students mark when they hear them.
Match invitation phrases ('Would you like to...?') with polite replies ('I'd love to, but...').
Students interview 3 different partners in 3 minutes about their dream job.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a full email accepting a Christmas party invitation with details.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame for their skills profile: 'I can... I have... I want...'
hw: Homework option 1: Record yourself doing a 2-minute mock interview and self-check using the class rubric.
Homework option 2: Write a polite email accepting or declining a Christmas party invitation (80 words).
Homework option 3: Find a job ad online and list 3 required skills and 2 qualities.
lp.tip: Tip: For Moroccan learners, connect 'work' to local contexts like tourism or tech startups. Use 'Green March' or 'Labour Day' as examples of career-related celebrations to build cultural relevance.

weeks.obj: write a clear formal request email
weeks.lang: email register; request and reply frames
weeks.act:
Register transformation task; guided formal email writing; peer editing
Discussion: resolutions that stick; will vs going-to for plans and promises.
weeks.hw:
send-ready formal email draft
Write your own 3 resolutions + how you will keep them.

skills.L: Listen to model request emails
skills.S: Roleplay the request and phone follow-up
skills.R: Read formal vs informal emails and compare
skills.W: Write a clear formal request email

lp.wu: Students play 'Two Truths and a Resolution': each shares two past resolutions and one new one for the class to guess which is the new one using 'Will you...?' questions.
wuAlt: Students write three resolutions on slips of paper; teacher collects and reads aloud for class to guess the writer
Students interview a partner about their resolutions using 'How will you...?' and report back to the class
lp.pres: Teacher displays a formal email template on the board with blanks for subject, greeting, request, closing; models filling it for a 'requesting a holiday extension' scenario; checks understanding with 'What do we say in a formal email?' questions.
presAlt: Teacher uses a real email from a local company (with sensitive info removed) to highlight formal phrases
Teacher roleplays a phone call followed by an email to show the connection between spoken and written requests
lp.prac: Students complete a gap-fill exercise with formal email phrases (e.g., 'I am writing to...', 'Could you please...', 'Thank you for your consideration'); then rewrite an informal email into a formal one in pairs.
pracAlt: Students match request phrases to email parts (greeting, body, closing) in a cut-and-paste activity
Students play 'Email Bingo' with formal phrases they mark off when heard in a teacher dictation
lp.ls: Students listen to two model emails (one formal request, one informal) and tick differences in a T-chart; then listen again to note specific request phrases.
lp.re: Students play 'Simon Says' with action verbs related to email tasks (e.g., 'Simon says attach the document', 'Simon says send the email') to refocus after the break.
lp.prod: Students write a formal email to a manager requesting time off for the New Year, using a checklist for structure and polite language; then swap drafts for peer feedback.
lp.rw: Students read two short emails (one formal, one informal) about New Year plans and answer true/false questions about the register; then write a 50-word reply to one email using the formal frame.
lp.st: Teacher shares a short story about 'A Resolution That Worked' and ends with the class saying 'Thank you for a great lesson!' as the goodbye routine.
g: Teams race to write a formal email line by line, passing the paper
Students roleplay a phone call and email exchange for a request
Students match phrases to email functions (e.g., 'Dear...' = greeting)
Students unscramble a formal email into correct order
Students act out a request for others to guess and write the email
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: write a follow-up email with a new request using 'Furthermore...'
Support / weaker learners: use a sentence frame template with options (e.g., 'I would like to request...')
hw: Draft a formal email to a teacher requesting a meeting about your progress
Write three resolutions and one strategy for each using 'I will...' and 'I am going to...'
Find a formal email online (e.g., a company) and list three formal phrases
lp.tip: Model the email structure on the board step-by-step; Moroccan learners benefit from clear visual scaffolding for formal writing tasks.

weeks.obj: complete PET-style written and speaking components
weeks.lang: all S1 outcomes at A2+ level
weeks.act: Written paper; paired speaking with rubric; feedback slots
weeks.hw: Semester marks recorded

skills.L: PET-style listening paper
skills.S: PET-style speaking parts 1-2
skills.R: PET-style reading paper
skills.W: PET-style writing (part 1 email)

lp.wu: Speed Review: Students stand in a circle. Teacher shows PET exam flashcards (e.g., 'email', 'interview', 'travel'), students race to say the task type in 10 seconds. Incorrect answers sit down. Last student standing wins.
wuAlt: Word Association: Teacher says 'PET exam', students shout related words (e.g., 'writing', 'speaking', 'timer').
Quick Quiz: 3 rapid-fire questions: 'How long is the PET speaking test?', 'How many parts?', 'What's the word limit for emails?'
lp.pres: Teacher displays a sample PET Part 1 email question (e.g., 'Write an email to your friend about a trip'). Model the structure: greeting, purpose, details, closing. Highlight 'I'm writing to...' and 'I look forward to...'. Check understanding: 'What's the first sentence?'
presAlt: Realia Analysis: Show a real email. Students label parts (greeting, body, closing).
Gap Fill: Project an email with blanks. Students complete it as a class.
lp.prac: Guided Email Draft: Students use a template (greeting, 3 bullet points, closing) to write a 60-word email about their favorite Moroccan festival (e.g., Green March). Teacher circulates, correcting grammar/vocabulary.
pracAlt: Pair Correction: Students swap emails and use a checklist (greeting, 3 details, closing) to peer-review.
Sentence Scramble: Unscramble email sentences into logical order.
lp.ls: PET Listening Part 1: Play a short audio (2 people planning a trip). Students answer 5 multiple-choice questions (A/B/C) on a worksheet. Replay difficult parts for clarification.
lp.re: Stand Up/Sit Down: Teacher calls out PET task names ('Reading!', 'Writing!'). Students stand if they like it, sit if they dislike it. Fast-paced to refocus after break.
lp.prod: Speaking Simulation: Students pair up. One is the examiner (asks Part 1 questions: 'Where do you live?', 'What do you like about Oujda?'). The other is the candidate (answers for 1 minute). Swap roles. Use a timer.
lp.rw: PET Reading Part 2: Students read a short text about 'Digital Life in Morocco' (150 words). Match headings to paragraphs (5 options). Then write 1 sentence about their own digital habits.
lp.st: Close with: 'Today we practiced all PET exam sections. Thank you for your hard work!'
g: Students create 3x3 grids with PET words (e.g., 'email', 'interview', 'travel'). Teacher calls out definitions; students mark matches.
Teacher writes 3 PET emails with errors. Students race to find and correct them.
Timer runs for 1 minute. Students take turns saying sentences about exams (e.g., 'I need to practice writing emails').
Teacher says a PET word (e.g., 'speaking'), students volley back a related word (e.g., 'questions').
Teams race to match PET task types to descriptions (e.g., 'Part 1: Q&A about yourself').
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 100-word review of a Moroccan cafe (PET Part 1).
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'I live in _______. I like ______ because ______.'
hw: Option 1: Complete PET Listening Part 3 (audio + questions).
Option 2: Write a 70-word email to a teacher about a problem (e.g., 'I missed class').
Option 3: Practice speaking Part 1 with a family member (record 1 minute).
lp.tip: For adults, focus on exam strategies (e.g., 'Read questions first in listening') to reduce anxiety. Relate tasks to their goals (work, travel).
checklist: I can write a 70-word email with a clear purpose and closing.
I can answer 5 multiple-choice listening questions.
I can speak for 1 minute about my life in Morocco.
I can match headings to reading paragraphs.
I can identify PET exam parts and their tasks.
I can use present perfect for experience (e.g., 'I have visited Casablanca').
I can use comparatives (e.g., 'Oujda is more beautiful than...').

weeks.obj: understand the PET exam map and set spring targets
weeks.lang: PET format overview; strategy language
weeks.act: PET overview walk-through; mini diagnostic stations; target setting sheet
weeks.hw: choose 2 PET practice areas

skills.L: Listen to the PET exam-map audio tour
skills.S: Set spring targets with a partner
skills.R: Read the PET handbook overview
skills.W: Write my PET target plan

lp.wu: Students play 'PET Bingo' with mixed grammar and vocabulary prompts (e.g., 'Find someone who has visited another country'). They walk around asking questions, mark squares, and shout 'Bingo!' when complete.
wuAlt: Students complete a 'Mid-Year Reflection' worksheet with 5 questions about their progress so far.
Students share one goal they achieved this semester in pairs.
lp.pres: Show the official PET exam map poster on the projector. Explain each section (Reading & Writing, Listening, Speaking) with timing and task types. Use model sentences for strategy language (e.g., 'For Part 1, I need to scan for keywords'). Check understanding with quick thumbs-up/thumbs-down.
presAlt: Distribute PET handbook excerpts and have students highlight key exam details in groups.
Play a 'PET Quiz' with Kahoot! to test their knowledge of the exam format.
lp.prac: Students rotate through 'mini diagnostic stations' (Reading gap-fill, Listening multiple choice, Speaking picture prompt). At each station, they complete 1 PET-style task while the teacher provides feedback on strategies.
pracAlt: Students work in pairs to create their own 3-question PET quiz for their peers.
Complete a 'Strategy Match-Up' activity linking PET tasks to strategies (e.g., 'Part 2 → Read the instructions first').
lp.ls: Students listen to a 5-minute audio tour of the PET exam from the Cambridge website. They fill in a worksheet with section timings and task types, then compare answers in pairs.
lp.re: Play 'PET Relay Race'—teams race to write PET section names on the board after hearing descriptions (e.g., 'This part has 6 questions and a recording').
lp.prod: Students interview a partner about their strengths/weaknesses in English using PET strategy prompts (e.g., 'How do you feel about the speaking test?'). They note 2 goals for each skill.
lp.rw: Students read a short PET-style email (80 words) about a complaint and write a reply using the 'plan, write, check' method. They then swap and mark for content and accuracy.
lp.st: Close with a 'PET Pledge'—students stand and share one spring target. End with: 'Today we mapped the PET exam and set our goals. Thank you for your hard work!'
g: Students rotate every 2 minutes to practice speaking prompts with different partners.
Teams race to write present perfect sentences on the board.
Students toss a ball and name PET-related vocabulary when caught.
Teams race to match headings to PET reading texts.
Students act out PET strategies for others to guess.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a 100-word review of a movie using PET writing Part 1 format.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame to describe their PET goal (e.g., 'I need to practice ______ to improve my ______.')
hw: Complete 2 PET practice exercises from the workbook (Reading Part 2 & Listening Part 1).
Watch a 3-minute PET speaking video on YouTube and take notes.
Write a 50-word email to a teacher asking for advice on PET preparation.
lp.tip: Emphasize that PET is about real-life communication, not just passing the test. Relate tasks to Moroccan learners' goals (e.g., work, travel, digital skills) to boost motivation.
checklist: I can identify the 4 parts of the PET exam.
I can explain the timing for each section.
I can name 2 strategies for the reading test.
I can set a specific spring target for my speaking.
I can write a 80-word email using PET format.
I can understand a 3-minute PET listening audio.
I can describe my PET preparation plan to a partner.

weeks.obj: describe cultural traditions and present a custom clearly
weeks.lang: present simple for customs; sequencing language (first, then...)
weeks.act: Custom description presentations; sequencing jigsaw reading; culture Q&A
weeks.hw: Presentation check

skills.L: Listen to a custom described step by step
skills.S: Present a custom clearly with sequencers
skills.R: Read a traditions text (History) and make notes
skills.W: Write a custom description (first, then...)

lp.wu: Start with 'Tradition Bingo': Students write 5 traditions (e.g., 'eat couscous on Fridays', 'celebrate Eid') in a grid. Teacher calls out customs, students cross off matches. First to get 3 in a row says 'Bingo!' and shares one tradition.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Two Truths and a Lie'—students state 3 traditions, one false, others guess.
Alternative 2: 'Quick Share'—each student names one tradition from their family in 10 seconds.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of Moroccan traditions (Eid, Ramadan, Green March). Model present simple: 'People visit family during Eid.' Elicit sequencers: 'First, they pray. Then, they eat.' Check understanding with 'What do people do first during Ramadan?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a short video of a Moroccan wedding, pause to describe steps.
Alternative 2: Bring a mint tea set, demonstrate the ritual while narrating with sequencers.
lp.prac: Sequencing Relay: Groups get 4 cards (e.g., 'Light candles', 'Pray', 'Eat sweets', 'Exchange gifts'). Race to put in order, then present using 'First... Then...'. Support with sentence frames on board.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Order the Steps' worksheet—students match sentences to pictures of a wedding.
Alternative 2: 'Chain Story'—each student adds one step to a tradition story using a sequencer.
lp.ls: Listen to a 1-minute audio about a Moroccan wedding. Students fill in blanks in a step-by-step worksheet (e.g., 'First, the bride... Then, the guests...'). Check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Stand Up, Sit Down: Teacher calls out traditions (e.g., 'If you break fast with family, stand up!'). Students stand/sit to respond, repeating the sentence with sequencers ('First, I pray...').
lp.prod: Pair Presentations: Each student prepares a 2-minute talk about a custom (e.g., 'How we celebrate Eid'). Use sequencers: 'First, we... Then, we...'. Partners give feedback using 'I liked when you said...'
lp.rw: Read a short text on 'History of Moroccan Tea' (100 words). Students take notes on key steps. Then write 3 sentences using sequencers: 'First, the tea is boiled. Then, mint is added...'
lp.st: End with a 2-minute video of a Moroccan folk song about traditions. Close with: 'Today we learned to describe customs with sequencers. Thank you for sharing your traditions!'
g: Groups race to reorder tradition steps on cards.
Students act out a tradition; others guess using 'First, do you...?'
Mingle to find peers who share traditions (e.g., 'Find someone who fasts Ramadan').
Draw a tradition; team guesses using sequencers.
Memory Chain (Each student repeats all previous steps + one new one)
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 50-word paragraph comparing two traditions.
Support: Use a sentence frame template for presentations (e.g., 'In my family, we... First, we... Then...').
hw: Option 1: Record a 1-minute video describing a custom at home.
Option 2: Write 80 words about a wedding tradition using sequencers.
Option 3: Interview a family member about a tradition and share notes.
lp.tip: Leverage learners' lived experiences—encourage comparisons between Moroccan and American traditions to build cross-cultural awareness.

weeks.obj: build richer descriptions with relative clauses
weeks.lang: who / which / where (basic relative clauses)
weeks.act: Describe-and-draw with relatives; place riddles; guess who writing game
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to people and place descriptions and identify them
skills.S: Build richer descriptions with relative clauses
skills.R: Read a description text and find who / which / where
skills.W: Write a description with 2 relative clauses

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find Someone Who...' with relative clauses. Students mingle with a handout with prompts like 'Find someone who has a friend who lives in Casablanca' and 'Find someone who has a job which requires English'. They write names and share findings.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Describe a Photo' - show a picture of a busy market, students take turns describing one person/place using a relative clause.
Alternative 2: 'Two Truths and a Lie' - students write three sentences about themselves using relatives, others guess the lie.
lp.pres: Presentation: Use a photo of Oujda's medina. Model sentences like 'This is the souk where you can buy spices' and 'The man who sells tea is my friend'. Elicit more examples, then check understanding with 'Is the man selling tea or bread?' questions.
presAlt: Alternative 1: 'My Perfect City' - draw a dream city on the board, using 'which' for places and 'who' for people.
Alternative 2: 'Describe the Teacher' - students ask questions to guess a secret person I describe using relatives.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Describe-and-Draw' in pairs. Student A describes a person/place with a relative clause (e.g., 'Draw a woman who wears a hijab'), Student B draws and vice-versa. Monitor for accuracy.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Relative Clause Dominoes' - match sentence halves to form correct relatives.
Alternative 2: 'Fix the Sentence' - incorrect sentences on cards, students correct them in teams.
lp.ls: Listening slot: PET-style audio of a tour guide describing a Moroccan landmark. Students listen and circle the correct place from three options, then complete sentences with missing relatives.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Human Sentences'. After break, students line up and form sentences physically (e.g., one student holds 'who', another 'lives in', etc.) to make a relative clause about a classmate.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Place Riddles'. In groups, students write 3 riddles about famous Moroccan places using relatives (e.g., 'I'm a city which has a blue gate. I'm where the King lives. What am I?'). Groups take turns guessing.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Read a short text about the Green March, then write 80-word email to a friend describing a festival they attended, using two relative clauses. Peer-check for correct use of 'who/which/where'.
lp.st: Story + goodbye: Read a short story about a traveler who visits Oujda. Close with: 'Today we learned to describe people and places with relative clauses. Thank you for your hard work!'
g: Students write 3 clues about a classmate using relatives (e.g., 'She is someone who likes mint tea'). Others guess.
Draw a Moroccan place, others guess using relatives (e.g., 'Is it a place where people pray?').
Teams race to write the longest correct relative clause about Oujda on the board.
First group to solve 3 place riddles wins.
Read sentences, stand up if it contains a relative clause.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 100-word description of their ideal workplace using 3 relatives.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'This is a place where...' and 'The person who...'.
hw: Homework 1: Write 5 sentences about your family using relatives (who/which).
Homework 2: Record a 30-second voice note describing a local landmark with relatives.
Homework 3: Complete a 'Describe Your Hometown' worksheet with relatives.
lp.tip: Tip: Encourage students to share real-life examples (e.g., describing a coworker or a favorite café) to make the language more relevant. Avoid over-correction during fluency activities to build confidence.

weeks.obj: tell a complete short story with narrative tenses
weeks.lang: narrative tenses; linking (suddenly, after that...)
weeks.act: Story from 6 pictures; fable retelling; story train (add a sentence)
weeks.hw: write a 10-sentence story

skills.L: Listen to a model story and note the linkers
skills.S: Tell a complete short story with narrative tenses
skills.R: Read a fable and collect the linking words
skills.W: Write a linked short story (suddenly, after that)

lp.wu: Story Chain: Students sit in a circle. Teacher starts a story with 'Once upon a time in Oujda...' and each student adds one sentence using a past tense or linker. They pass a small Moroccan teacup as they speak.
wuAlt: Picture Prompt: Show a photo of a busy souk. Students write 2 sentences about what happened yesterday using past simple or continuous.
Linker Race: Write 'suddenly', 'after that', 'finally' on the board. Students race to say a sentence starting with each.
lp.pres: Teacher shows 6 flashcards of a man losing his wallet in a souk. Models the full story using past simple/continuous and linkers. Checks understanding by asking 'What happened first? What happened suddenly?'
presAlt: Real Story: Teacher shares a personal story about getting lost in Fes, using linkers. Students note the tenses.
Fable Intro: Read 'The Tortoise and the Hare' aloud, pausing to highlight linkers like 'while' and 'finally'.
lp.prac: Picture Story: Students get 6 cards in random order. In pairs, they arrange the cards and write 3 sentences using linkers. Teacher monitors and corrects tense errors.
pracAlt: Linker Bingo: Create bingo cards with linkers. Teacher reads a story; students mark linkers they hear. First to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Sentence Relay: Teams race to write a 5-sentence story on the board using given linkers.
lp.ls: Listen to a 2-minute audio of a tourist's story about a taxi ride in Casablanca. Students list all linkers they hear and answer 'What happened suddenly?'
lp.re: Stand and Link: Teacher calls a linker (e.g., 'after that'). Students stand up, say a sentence using it, and sit down. Fast-paced to re-energize.
lp.prod: Story Train: Groups of 4. Each student adds one sentence to a story, starting with a linker. The story must have a beginning, middle, and end. They perform their story for the class.
lp.rw: Read a short fable (e.g., 'The Lion and the Mouse') and underline all linking words. Then write a 10-sentence story about a time they helped someone, using 3 linkers.
lp.st: Read a modern Moroccan folktale about kindness. End with: 'Today we practiced telling stories with linkers. Thank you for your great stories! Goodbye!'
g: Groups sort 6 story cards into logical order and retell the story.
Match linkers to their meanings (e.g., 'suddenly' = unexpectedly).
Roll dice with pictures; create a story using the tenses shown.
One student starts a story; next student continues with a linker.
Read a text; circle all linkers and categorize them.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second story using 5 different linkers.
Support weaker learners: Use a sentence frame (e.g., 'Suddenly, ___ + past simple').
hw: Write a 10-sentence story about a festival in Morocco (e.g., Green March).
Record yourself telling a short story using 3 linkers.
Write a 50-word email to a friend about a recent trip using past tenses and linkers.
lp.tip: Encourage students to use personal stories from Moroccan culture (e.g., Ramadan, Eid) to make language practice meaningful and relatable.

weeks.obj: report what someone said accurately
weeks.lang: reported statements (said/told + backshift)
weeks.act:
Gossip chain game; headlines to reported speech; news reporter roleplay
Discussion: daily rhythm in Ramadan; present simple for routines + frequency adverbs.
weeks.hw:
Participation quiz
Write your Ramadan daily routine in 8 sentences.

skills.L: Listen to conversations and report them
skills.S: Report what someone said accurately
skills.R: Read dialogue-to-report examples and check the backshift
skills.W: Rewrite a dialogue as reported speech

lp.wu: Students sit in a circle. Teacher whispers a Ramadan-related sentence in Arabic to the first student, e.g., 'I eat suhoor at 4 AM.' They whisper it in English to the next student, who reports it to the next, and so on. The last student says what they heard. Teacher writes the original and final sentence on the board to compare.
wuAlt: Teacher shows 3 flashcards: 'eat suhoor,' 'pray taraweeh,' 'visit family.' Students ask each other 'What did you do yesterday?' and report back to the class.
Teacher writes 5 Ramadan routine verbs on the board. Students stand up and say a sentence about their routine, e.g., 'I always break my fast with dates.' when the teacher claps.
lp.pres: Teacher presents a dialogue on the board: 'Youssef: "I will visit my aunt tonight." Fatima: "He said he would visit his aunt tonight."' Teacher explains 'said' and 'told' + object, and backshift (will → would). Students turn to a partner and practice similar sentences with 'said' and 'told'.
presAlt: Teacher uses a Ramadan story with two characters. Students read short exchanges and rewrite them as reported speech in pairs, with teacher monitoring.
Teacher gives each student a card with a direct speech sentence about Ramadan. They walk around and report what others said, using 'said' or 'told me'.
lp.prac: Students play 'Gossip Chain.' Teacher gives each row a Ramadan sentence to whisper down the line. The last student reports it to the class. Teacher checks for accuracy in reported speech and backshift.
pracAlt: Students work in pairs. One is a 'reporter,' the other a 'source.' The source says a sentence about their Ramadan, and the reporter writes it down correctly.
Teacher writes 5 headlines on the board, e.g., 'Local Mosque Opens Iftar Early.' Students rewrite them as reported speech in their notebooks.
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio of two people discussing their Ramadan plans. They listen twice and write down 3 sentences in reported speech. Teacher plays the audio again if needed.
lp.re: Teacher says a direct speech sentence about Ramadan, e.g., 'I love eating harira.' Students stand up and shout the reported version, e.g., 'He said he loved eating harira.' The fastest pair gets a point.
lp.prod: Students roleplay 'News Reporters.' One student interviews another about their Ramadan routine using direct speech. The other student reports the interview back to the class in reported speech.
lp.rw: Students read a short dialogue about two friends' Ramadan plans. They then rewrite the dialogue as a paragraph in reported speech, using 'said' and 'told'. Teacher checks for backshift.
lp.st: Teacher tells a short story about a family's Ramadan evening in Morocco. Students reflect on one sentence they would report from the story. Close with: 'Today we learned to report what someone said accurately. Thank you for your participation.'
g: Students whisper a Ramadan sentence down a row, and the last student reports it.
Students find headlines in a text and rewrite them as reported speech.
One student interviews another about Ramadan, and the other reports it back.
Teacher says a sentence, students shout the reported version.
Students rewrite a short dialogue as reported speech.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 3-sentence report about a classmate's Ramadan plans.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'He said he ________ (verb) ________ (object).'
hw: Write your Ramadan daily routine in 8 sentences using reported speech.
Interview a family member about their Ramadan and report 3 things they said.
Find a news article about Ramadan and rewrite 2 sentences as reported speech.
lp.tip: Use real-life examples from Moroccan Ramadan culture to make reported speech relatable, like reporting what a family member said about suhoor or iftar.

weeks.obj: discuss news sources and give supported opinions
weeks.lang: media vocabulary; opinion + reason + example frames
weeks.act: News panel discussion; headline matching; listening with viewpoints
weeks.hw: opinion paragraph on a news topic

skills.L: Listen to a news bulletin and note the key facts
skills.S: Discuss news sources and give supported opinions
skills.R: Read a news article and check the facts
skills.W: Write an opinion paragraph on a news item

lp.wu: Headline Race: Students form teams. Each team gets 5 news headline flashcards. They race to match them to the correct news category (politics, sports, entertainment, technology, local) on the board. The first team to match all correctly wins points.
wuAlt: News Source Sort: Students sort a pile of news source cards (TV, radio, newspaper, blog, social media) into 'trustworthy' and 'less trustworthy' piles and explain why.
Opinion Line: Students stand in a line. The teacher reads a news topic (e.g., 'Social media is good for news'). Students move to the left (agree) or right (disagree) and say one reason.
lp.pres: Show a short video clip of a news bulletin. Introduce media vocabulary (e.g., 'headline', 'source', 'bias', 'fact', 'opinion') using flashcards with images. Model sentences: 'I think... because...' and 'For example...'. Check understanding by asking students to categorize words as fact or opinion.
presAlt: Realia Display: Bring in a newspaper, a phone showing a news app, and a radio. Elicit the names and ask students to compare them. Use a Venn diagram on the board to show similarities and differences.
Role Model: Teacher plays a news anchor, then a biased commentator. Students identify the difference in language and label the examples on the board.
lp.prac: Headline Matching: Students work in pairs. They receive a worksheet with 5 headlines and 5 short news summaries. They match them, then practice saying: 'This headline is about... because...'. Teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation.
pracAlt: Opinion Frames Drill: In groups, students get a list of news topics. They take turns completing the frame: 'In my opinion, [topic] is [adjective]. For example, [example]. This is because [reason]'.
Media Bingo: Each student gets a bingo card with media vocabulary (e.g., 'breaking news', 'editorial'). The teacher reads definitions, and students mark the words.
lp.ls: Listening to a news podcast: Students listen to a 2-minute bulletin about a local Moroccan issue (e.g., tourism). They complete a table with 'Who', 'What', 'Where', 'Why'. They then compare in pairs before class feedback.
lp.re: Quick Debate: Students stand. The teacher says a news topic (e.g., 'AI in news'). Students quickly turn to a partner and state their opinion with one reason using 'I believe... because...'. After 30 seconds, switch partners.
lp.prod: News Panel Discussion: Students form groups of 4. Each group is a panel discussing 'Are social media news sources reliable?'. They assign roles (moderator, two panelists, audience). They prepare for 5 mins, then discuss for 8 mins using frames: 'I agree with [name] because...' and 'On the other hand...'.
lp.rw: Reading and Writing: Students read a short, simplified news article about a Moroccan festival (e.g., Rose Festival). They underline 3 facts. Then, they write a 80-word opinion paragraph using the frame: 'I think this festival is important because... For example...'.
lp.st: Story + Goodbye: Read a short news story about a positive event in Morocco (e.g., a community project). End with: 'Today, you practiced giving opinions about news. Thank you for your thoughtful contributions. Have a great day!'
g: Teams match headlines to categories on the board.
Students move left/right for agree/disagree and state a reason.
Students mark vocabulary words as the teacher defines them.
Partners state opinions on news topics with reasons.
Groups discuss reliability of social media news in assigned roles.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second opinion paragraph arguing the opposite view of their first one.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame worksheet to write their opinion paragraph.
hw: Watch a 5-minute news segment. Write 3 facts and 1 opinion in your notebook.
Choose a news topic from class. Write a 100-word paragraph using 'I think... because... For example...'.
Interview a family member about their favorite news source. Write 3 sentences about their choice.
lp.tip: Encourage students to connect news topics to their lives in Morocco, e.g., discussing how global news affects local issues. This builds relevance and confidence.

weeks.obj: apply reading strategies to timed PET tasks
weeks.lang: skimming, scanning, detail reading
weeks.act: Timed PET reading parts; strategy debrief; answer justification pairs
weeks.hw: Timed task score recorded

skills.L: PET listening paper - timed
skills.S: Speaking warm-up circles
skills.R: PET reading paper - timed strategies (PET folder)
skills.W: PET writing part 1 email

lp.wu: Students stand in a circle and play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their recent reading habits, e.g., 'I read a news article yesterday,' 'I love scanning for numbers,' 'I never skim headings.'
wuAlt: Students share one reading strategy they used this week with a partner.
Students quickly list 3 things they remember about PET reading parts from last class.
lp.pres: Display a PET reading part 1 text on the board. Model skimming (reading headings in 30 sec), scanning (finding dates in 20 sec), and detail reading (answering Q3 in 45 sec). Check understanding by asking: 'Which strategy finds specific info?'
presAlt: Hand out a short article with questions; model marking the text for each strategy.
Use a think-aloud: 'I see the title, so I'll skim first...'
lp.prac: Students work in pairs to time each other on a PET reading part 1 text (3 min). They swap papers and use a checklist to mark which strategy their partner used. Teacher circulates to monitor timing.
pracAlt: Students race to scan for answers in different texts, then compare with the answer key.
Groups complete a 'strategy match' worksheet linking questions to skimming/scanning/detail.
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio recording of someone discussing their reading strategies (2 min). They tick the strategies mentioned (skimming, scanning, etc.) and discuss in pairs if they agree.
lp.re: Students play 'Strategy Charades'—one student acts out skimming (fast hand movements over text) or scanning (pointing quickly), others guess the term.
lp.prod: In trios, students take turns explaining how they would solve a PET reading part 2 text (matching headings to paragraphs). They justify their choices using 'I skimmed the headings first...' or 'I scanned for keywords...'
lp.rw: Students complete a timed PET reading part 3 text (multiple-choice) individually (7 min). They then swap papers and discuss answers in pairs, explaining their reasoning using 'I chose B because...'
lp.st: Read a short story about a student who improved their PET score using better strategies. End with: 'Today we practiced timed PET reading strategies. Thank you for your hard work!'
g: Students race to find the main idea of a text in 30 sec.
Students scan for numbers/words and call them out.
Students find and underline answers to detail questions.
Groups sort questions into skimming/scanning/detail piles.
Teams answer questions about PET reading parts.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 2 tips for timed reading success.
Support learners: Use a highlighter to mark key words before answering.
hw: Complete a timed PET reading part 1 at home and record your score.
Write 3 sentences about which strategy you found easiest/hardest.
Review the PET reading strategies in your folder.
lp.tip: Encourage students to reflect on their timing—many spend too long on one part. A stopwatch is your best tool for building exam pace.

weeks.obj: use prediction and note-taking for PET listening
weeks.lang: listening strategies; note-taking
weeks.act: Prediction before listening; two-stage tasks; transcript analysis
weeks.hw: Listening task score recorded

skills.L: PET listening - prediction and note-taking
skills.S: Report my notes to a partner
skills.R: PET reading - inference practice
skills.W: PET writing - article (part 2)

lp.wu: Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their week, writing three sentences on paper (two true, one false) and guessing which is false. They say 'I went to the market' or 'I watched a movie' to practice past simple.
wuAlt: Students draw a quick picture of their week and label it in English, sharing with a partner
Students ask 'Did you...?' questions about weekend activities (e.g., 'Did you cook?')
lp.pres: Show a PET listening task on the board (Part 1: short conversations). Model predicting answers by looking at the question options and circling keywords. Play a sample audio and demonstrate note-taking with symbols (✔/✗, arrows). Check understanding by asking 'What do we listen for first?'
presAlt: Use a transcript with blanks to show how keywords help fill gaps
Play a short audio without questions and ask students to jot down key words
lp.prac: Students work in pairs to predict answers for a PET Part 1 task, then listen and check. They use a table to mark 'Predicted' vs 'Heard'. Support with keyword flashcards (e.g., 'appointment', 'library').
pracAlt: Students match question types to listening strategies (e.g., 'When?' = time words)
Play 'Bingo' with predicted answers
lp.ls: Students complete a PET Part 2 multiple-choice monologue task. They first predict answers, listen once to check, then listen again to take notes. They compare notes in pairs before final answers.
lp.re: Students stand and play 'Simon Says' with listening commands (e.g., 'Simon says touch your ear if you heard 'library'').
lp.prod: Students roleplay a job interview, using note-taking to remember questions. One student asks 'Why should we hire you?' and the other answers with past experiences, then reports notes to a partner.
lp.rw: Students read a short article about 'Finding a Job in Oujda' and answer inference questions (e.g., 'Why is it hard to find work?'). They then write a 80-word email applying for a job using past experiences.
lp.st: Play a short video about 'Workplace Skills' and discuss. Close with 'Today we practiced PET listening strategies—good job! Thank you, class.'
g: Students match question types to listening keywords (e.g., 'Where?' to 'place')
Students listen to a short audio and race to write 3 key words
Students mark predicted answers on a grid and cross off when heard
Teams take turns doing job interview roleplays with notes
Students find mistakes in a transcript and explain why
diff: Fast finishers: Write a new PET listening task for the class
Support: Use a partially filled note-taking template
hw: Complete a PET listening Part 3 task online and record your score
Listen to a podcast and write 5 notes about main points
Write a 100-word review of a movie using past tenses
lp.tip: Encourage students to use Arabic to clarify predictions, then switch to English for note-taking—this builds confidence while targeting exam skills.

weeks.obj: sustain turn-taking and manage interaction (PET part 3 style)
weeks.lang: interaction language (agreeing, turn-taking, suggesting)
weeks.act:
Discussion cards with roles; interaction rubric peer check; retry rounds
Discussion: Eid traditions and family; narrative past tense storytelling.
weeks.hw:
Speaking rubric recorded
Write a short story: my best Eid memory.

skills.L: Listen to interaction models (turn-taking)
skills.S: Sustain turn-taking and manage interaction
skills.R: Read interaction phrase lists and rehearse them
skills.W: Write discussion prompts for part 3

lp.wu: Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about Eid traditions. They write three statements on a card, two true and one false, then read them aloud. The class guesses which is the lie.
wuAlt: Students complete a 'Find Someone Who...' grid with Eid activities like 'Find someone who wore new clothes for Eid'.
Students draw a quick picture of their favorite Eid memory and share it with a partner.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of Eid scenes (family dinner, giving gifts, visiting relatives). Model interaction phrases like 'I agree because...' and 'Can I add something?'. Check understanding by asking students to repeat the phrases in context.
presAlt: Read a short dialogue between two friends planning Eid celebrations. Highlight the interaction language on the board.
Play a recording of a PET-style Part 3 discussion about holidays. Students note down phrases used to agree and take turns.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs with 'Eid Discussion Cards' with roles like 'You love the food' and 'You miss the gifts'. They practice using the interaction language while discussing the prompts. I circulate to offer support.
pracAlt: Students play 'Role Card Relay' where they draw a role card and must use the target phrase before passing the card to their partner.
Students complete a gap-fill worksheet with interaction phrases from the model dialogue.
lp.ls: Students listen to a PET Part 3 recording of two people discussing Eid traditions. They complete a chart noting phrases used to agree, disagree, and take turns. We check answers as a class.
lp.re: Students play 'Pass the Phrase' in a circle. I say an interaction phrase like 'That's a good point', and students pass it around the circle, adding a new word each time to make a longer sentence.
lp.prod: Students form groups of three for a 'Family Eid Council' discussion. They use a rubric to evaluate each other's turn-taking and use of interaction language. Groups discuss 'How to make Eid more special for the family' and then retry the discussion with improved strategies.
lp.rw: Students read a short article about Eid traditions around the world. They then write five discussion prompts for a PET Part 3 task, using phrases like 'What about you?' and 'How do you feel about that?'
lp.st: I tell a personal story about my best Eid memory using the past simple and continuous. We end with the goodbye routine: 'Today we practiced taking turns in discussions. Thank you for your participation.'
g: Students stand in a line. I read a statement like 'Eid gifts are the best part'. They move to the left if they agree, right if they disagree, and say why.
Students sit in a circle. They toss a soft ball and must speak until they catch it again, practicing equal turn length.
Teams race to write interaction phrases on the board from memory after seeing them for 30 seconds.
Students swap role cards mid-discussion to practice adapting to new perspectives.
Students write their ideas on a shared paper, using symbols like '?' to ask for turn, drawing out the interaction silently.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a dialogue between two friends planning a surprise Eid party, using at least five interaction phrases.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence starter frame with phrases like 'I agree because...' and 'In my opinion...' on their desk.
hw: Record yourself having a 2-minute discussion with a friend about Eid traditions using the interaction phrases.
Write a short story (80-100 words) titled 'My Best Eid Memory', using the past simple and continuous.
Create a list of 10 discussion questions about cultural celebrations to use in next week's class.
lp.tip: For Moroccan learners, explicitly connect the target interaction language to their cultural context of respectful family discussions during Eid, as this makes the task more meaningful and memorable.

weeks.obj: produce a PET-format email or article
weeks.lang: PET writing conventions; paragraphing
weeks.act: Guided PET writing task; checklist peer review; model comparison
weeks.hw: complete the writing task

skills.L: Listen to model articles and emails
skills.S: Pitch my article idea in 30 seconds
skills.R: Read PET writing samples and grade them
skills.W: Produce a PET-format email or article

lp.wu: Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three sentences about their recent experiences using present perfect or past simple. They read them aloud, and classmates guess which is the lie. Teacher models first: 'I have visited the American Space Oujda twice. I went to Marrakech last month. I have never eaten couscous.'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who...: Students mingle to find classmates who have done specific actions (e.g., 'Find someone who has watched a movie in English this week'). They write names and ask 'When did you...?' for past simple follow-ups.
Speed Dating Opinions: Students pair up and discuss 'What is the best place to visit in Morocco?' for 60 seconds, then switch partners. Teacher monitors for comparatives/superlatives.
lp.pres: Show two PET writing models (email and article) on the projector. Highlight paragraphing, opening/closing phrases, and word count. Elicit differences between formal/informal tones. Ask: 'Which is for a friend? Which is for a magazine?' Distribute a handout with PET writing conventions checklist. Check understanding with quick 'True/False' questions (e.g., 'Articles need a title - T/F').
presAlt: Realia Analysis: Bring in printed emails/articles from local magazines (e.g., 'TelQuel' in English). Students in groups circle paragraph breaks and salutations. Teacher elicits why structure matters for PET.
Mentimeter Word Cloud: Students submit words they associate with 'email writing' and 'article writing'. Teacher groups into formal/informal categories and discusses differences.
lp.prac: Guided PET Writing Task: Students choose one prompt (email: 'Write to your friend about a bad experience at a restaurant' or article: 'Write a review of a Moroccan festival'). They draft 80-100 words using a paragraphing template (Introduction, Body, Conclusion). Teacher circulates to check for PET conventions (e.g., 'Did you start with a greeting?').
pracAlt: Sentence Scramble: Students reorder jumbled sentences to form logical paragraphs (e.g., 'Dear Sarah, / I went to the souk yesterday. / It was very busy. / Love, Ali'). They then write their own scrambled paragraph for a partner to solve.

Role-Play Drafting: Students role-play as customer/restaurant manager to email a complaint, then swap roles. They write the email based on their conversation, focusing on politeness phrases (e.g., 'I would like to complain about...').
lp.ls: PET Listening Comprehension: Play a recording of a model PET article being read aloud. Students listen and answer multiple-choice questions (e.g., 'What is the main topic?'). Replay to check answers and discuss how tone affects meaning (e.g., 'Is the writer positive or negative?').
lp.re: Stand Up if True: Teacher reads statements (e.g., 'You have written an email today', 'You like Moroccan festivals'). Students stand if true, sit if false. Fast-paced review of present perfect/past simple.
lp.prod: Peer Review Checklist: Students swap drafts and use a PET writing checklist (e.g., 'Is the word count 80-100?', 'Are there paragraphs?'). They score each other and give one positive comment and one suggestion. Teacher models first: 'Your article has a clear title. You could add more details about the festival.'
lp.rw: Reading for Structure: Students read two short PET articles (e.g., 'Best Places to Study in Oujda', 'How to Prepare for PET'). They underline topic sentences and circle linking words (e.g., 'First', 'However'). Then, they write a 50-word summary of one article using the same structure.
lp.st: Closing Reflection: Teacher says, 'Today we practiced PET writing conventions and paragraphing. Thank you for your hard work. See you next week!'
g: Teams race to write a 3-paragraph email from prompts, first correct team wins points.
Students spot PET writing errors (e.g., missing greeting, no paragraphs) in a sample text.
Students write a 100-word article in 10 minutes, closest to 100 wins.
Students sort phrases (e.g., 'Dear Sir' vs. 'Hey') into email/article categories.
Students pitch their article idea to the class in 30 seconds, best pitch gets a sticker.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a second email/article on a different prompt and add extra details.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence starter template (e.g., 'I am writing to... because...') for their draft.
hw: Complete the PET writing task at home (email or article) and bring it next class.
Read a short English article online (e.g., BBC News) and identify 3 linking words and 2 topic sentences.
Write a 50-word review of a Moroccan restaurant or cafe using comparatives (e.g., 'The food is better than...').
lp.tip: Encourage students to share real-life contexts (e.g., writing about local festivals like the Green March) to make PET tasks more meaningful and culturally relevant.

weeks.obj: debate technology topics with controlled fluency
weeks.lang: verb patterns (stop/remember/forget + -ing or to...); tech vocabulary
weeks.act: Tech debate (for/against panels); verb pattern auction; usage survey + report
weeks.hw: Participation quiz

skills.L: Listen to verb-pattern debate clips
skills.S: Debate technology topics with controlled fluency
skills.R: Read a tech article and find the patterns
skills.W: Write a for-and-against paragraph

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Tech Charades'—students draw tech-related words (e.g., 'smartphone', 'social media', 'download') from a hat and act them out while others guess. The actor says, 'I'm miming a tech word!' and the guessers respond, 'Is it a laptop?'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Tech Word Association'—students shout out tech words starting with the last letter of the previous word (e.g., 'email → laptop → password').
Alternative 2: 'Quick Poll'—stand if you use social media daily, raise hands if you prefer online shopping, etc.
lp.pres: Present verb patterns using a short story about 'Laila's tech habits': 'Laila stopped using TikTok to study.' 'She remembers to check her email.' 'She forgets to back up her files.' Model sentences on the board, then ask students to complete sentences like 'I remember to __' and 'I stopped __' to check understanding.
presAlt: Alternative 1: 'Realia Demo'—show a smartphone and say, 'I stopped using this app because it's distracting.' Then ask students to share their own examples.
Alternative 2: 'Picture Prompt'—show images of people using tech; elicit sentences like 'He remembers to charge his phone.'
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Verb Pattern Auction'—write sentences with errors (e.g., 'I stopped to play games') on slips. Teams bid to 'buy' correct sentences. The teacher says, 'The auction starts for this sentence!' and teams respond, 'We bid 2 dirhams for the correct one!'
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Race'—teams race to write correct sentences on the board using prompts like 'forget + to'.
Alternative 2: 'Matching Cards'—match verb phrases (e.g., 'stop scrolling') to the correct pattern (-ing or to + verb).
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a 2-minute clip of a debate about 'Are smartphones making us less social?' Students listen and circle all instances of 'stop/remember/forget + -ing/to'. Then they share one example with a partner, saying, 'I heard someone say, 'I stopped talking to people.''
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Tech Simon Says'—the teacher calls out commands like 'Simon says remember to charge your phone!' or 'Stop using your phones!' Students must obey only when 'Simon says' is included. Fast errors get a penalty (e.g., 10 jumping jacks).
lp.prod: Production task: Split into 'For' and 'Against' panels to debate 'Should schools ban phones?' Each panel has 3 minutes to prepare arguments using verb patterns (e.g., 'We remember to use phones for research'). Then, each speaker presents their point for 1 minute, followed by a 2-minute Q&A where the audience asks, 'Do you agree that phones distract students?'
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Read a short article about 'Digital Detox in Morocco' and underline all verb patterns. Then, write an 80-word paragraph for or against digital detoxes using at least 3 verb patterns. Example: 'I stopped scrolling social media to read more books. I remember to turn off my phone at 9 PM.'
lp.st: Story + goodbye: Share a short story about 'Ali's weekend without Wi-Fi' highlighting verb patterns. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we debated tech and practiced verb patterns—great work! Thank you, class.'
g: Teams bid on sentences with correct verb patterns (-ing or to)
Students act out tech words for others to guess
Obey commands only with 'Simon says' + verb patterns
Debate tech topics using target language
Teams race to write correct sentences on the board
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 100-word email to a friend explaining their tech habits using 5+ verb patterns.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'I stopped ___. I remember to ___. I forget to ___.'
hw: Homework 1: Interview a family member about their tech habits and write 5 sentences using verb patterns.
Homework 2: Watch a 5-minute tech video and list 3 examples of 'stop/remember/forget + -ing/to'.
Homework 3: Write a 100-word paragraph: 'My relationship with technology' using at least 4 verb patterns.
lp.tip: Tip: Encourage students to share Moroccan tech habits (e.g., using apps for haggling in souks) to make debates relatable and culturally relevant.

weeks.obj: discuss environmental problems and propose solutions
weeks.lang: cause/effect language (because of, so that); environment vocabulary
weeks.act: Solutions poster in teams; problem-solution presentations; recycling discussion
weeks.hw: Poster presentation check

skills.L: Listen to cause-and-effect explanations
skills.S: Propose solutions to an environment problem
skills.R: Read a science text and map causes and effects
skills.W: Write a solutions paragraph (because of, so that)

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Problem-Solution Chain'. Teacher writes a problem (e.g., 'plastic waste') on the board. Students take turns adding a solution (e.g., 'recycle it') and a new problem (e.g., 'not enough bins') using 'because of' and 'so that'.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Environmental Pictionary' – students draw environmental problems and guess using 'because of'
Alternative 2: 'Quick Poll' – teacher asks 'What's the biggest environmental problem in Oujda?' and students respond with 'I think... because of...'
lp.pres: Presentation: Show flashcards of environmental problems (pollution, deforestation) and solutions (recycling, planting trees). Model sentences: 'There's a lot of plastic pollution because of too much packaging.' 'We recycle plastic so that we don't waste resources.' Check understanding by asking 'Why?' and 'What can we do?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: 'Problem-Solution Matching' – match problems to solutions on the board with target language
Alternative 2: 'Realia Show' – bring a plastic bottle and a reusable one to demonstrate 'because of' and 'so that'
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Sentence Scramble'. Students work in pairs to unscramble cause/effect sentences (e.g., 'waste / because of / too much / there is / plastic'). Teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation of 'because of' and 'so that'.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Fill-in-the-Blanks' – worksheet with 'because of' and 'so that' gaps about local issues
Alternative 2: 'Chain Drill' – students take turns completing sentences: 'There's litter because of...' 'We clean up so that...'
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a short audio (1 min) about a Moroccan beach cleanup. Students listen and fill in a table: 'Problem', 'Cause', 'Solution'. Check answers as a class.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Environmental Charades'. After break, students act out environmental problems or solutions (e.g., 'planting trees', 'throwing trash') while others guess using 'Is it... because of...?'
lp.prod: Production task: 'Solutions Poster'. Teams create a poster for a Moroccan environmental issue (e.g., water waste in Oujda). They must write 3 problem-solution sentences using 'because of' and 'so that'. Present posters to the class.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Read a short text (80 words) about solar energy in Morocco. Students underline all 'because of' and 'so that' phrases. Then write 3 sentences about their own energy use using the target language.
lp.st: Story / song + goodbye: Play 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' song (lyrics on board). Close with: 'Today we discussed environmental problems and solutions using because of/so that. Thank you for your hard work.'
g: Students take turns adding problems and solutions using target language
Students draw problems and guess with 'because of'
Act out problems/solutions while others guess
Teams create and present a poster for a local issue
diff: Fast finishers: Add a 'future solution' sentence using 'will' to their poster
Support: Provide sentence starters like 'There is... because of...' and 'We can... so that...'
hw: Homework 1: Write 5 sentences about your family's habits using 'because of' and 'so that'
Homework 2: Research one environmental solution in Morocco and write a paragraph
Homework 3: Record a 1-minute video explaining a problem and solution using the target language
lp.tip: Use local examples (e.g., plastic waste in Oujda, solar energy projects) to make the lesson relevant and boost engagement.

weeks.obj: complete a timed PET-style mini test
weeks.lang: all A2+/B1-entry skills
weeks.act: Mini test administration; self-marking; strategy reflection sheet
weeks.hw: Mini test score recorded

skills.L: PET mini-test listening
skills.S: PET mini-test speaking
skills.R: PET mini-test reading
skills.W: PET mini-test writing

lp.wu: Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their recent experiences using present perfect (e.g., 'I've visited Chefchaouen,' 'I've learned to make tagine,' 'I've met a tourist from America'). They guess which statement is false.
wuAlt: Students share one 'first time' using past simple (e.g., 'The first time I tried American food was...')
Students play 'Find Someone Who' using present perfect (e.g., 'Find someone who has visited the American Space')
lp.pres: Display a PET reading part 1 text on the board. Model skimming for gist and scanning for specific information. Elicit strategies like 'read questions first' and 'underline keywords'. Check understanding with quick thumbs up/down for 'Do we read every word?'
presAlt: Show a sample PET writing task (email) and highlight structure: opening, purpose, details, closing
Play a short PET listening part 1 audio and model predicting answers before listening
lp.prac: Students complete a timed PET reading part 2 (multiple-choice cloze) in pairs, discussing answers. Monitor and provide support with vocabulary hints. Then, they swap papers and mark using the answer key.
