pracAlt: Students practice PET speaking part 1 (interview) with a partner, using prompt cards about travel and hobbies
Complete a guided PET listening part 2 gap-fill with word bank support
lp.ls: Students listen to a PET listening part 3 (multiple matching) audio about a local festival (e.g., Green March). They match speakers to statements and then compare answers in pairs. Play audio twice.
lp.re: Students stand in a circle. Teacher says a PET task type (e.g., 'Reading Part 1!'), and students quickly mime the action (e.g., 'skimming' with hands). Fast-paced to re-energize.
lp.prod: Students work in groups to create a 3-minute PET speaking part 2 (long turn) prompt about 'a place you recommend in Morocco'. They take turns describing the photo and answering partner questions.
lp.rw: Students write a timed PET writing part 1 (email) to a friend about a recent trip to Casablanca (80-100 words). Include past simple and descriptive adjectives. Peer-check for structure and word count.
lp.st: Teacher shares a short video clip of an American tourist in Morocco, then closes with: 'Today we practiced PET test strategies. Thank you for your hard work. See you next week!'
g: Teams race to answer PET-style questions (reading, grammar, vocab) on the board
Students draw PET-related words (e.g., 'examination', 'certificate') for teammates to guess
Teams correct mistakes in PET sample sentences, then run to write the correct version
Students draw cards with PET speaking topics and respond for 1 minute
Groups read different PET reading texts and summarize key points for the class
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second PET email draft with more complex adjectives
Support learners: Use a sentence frame for the writing task (e.g., 'I went to... It was... because...')
hw: Complete a full PET reading part 4 at home and score yourself
Record yourself answering a PET speaking part 2 prompt and self-reflect
Review PET writing samples and write down 3 tips for improvement
lp.tip: For Moroccan learners, connect PET tasks to local contexts (e.g., describing a souk, writing about Islamic holidays) to boost engagement and confidence.

weeks.obj: identify and correct their own most common errors
weeks.lang: personal error patterns; self-correction strategies
weeks.act: Error auction from real class work; correction stations; personal error lists
weeks.hw: rewrite 5 corrected sentences

skills.L: Listen and spot my common error patterns
skills.S: Self-correct in fluency practice
skills.R: Read error-clinic examples and fix them (Tests/Error Correction)
skills.W: Correct my own writing samples

lp.wu: Error Auction: Teams bid on sentences from their recent writing, deciding which are correct or incorrect. The teacher reads a sentence, teams hold up 'Correct' or 'Error' cards, and bid points to 'buy' the sentence. The highest bidder wins if they're right.
wuAlt: Grammar Relay: Teams race to correct errors on the board, rewriting sentences with markers. First team to fix all wins.
Find the Mistake: Students swap notebooks and hunt for each other's most common errors, marking them with sticky notes.
lp.pres: Teacher presents a 'Personal Error Clinic' poster with common mistakes (e.g., 'I have been in Marrakech since 2020' vs 'I have been to Marrakech since 2020'). Model sentences are written on the board, and students discuss which are correct. Teacher checks understanding by asking, 'Which sentence means you visited Marrakech and still live there?'
presAlt: Realia Show: Teacher holds up a photo of a trip and says, 'I went to Chefchaouen last year' vs 'I have gone to Chefchaouen'. Students vote for the correct one.
Error Stories: Teacher writes a short story with deliberate errors (e.g., 'I am living in Oujda since 2018'), and students fix it in pairs.
lp.prac: Correction Stations: Four stations around the room with different error types (present perfect, past simple, comparatives, modals). Students rotate in pairs, fixing sentences at each station with colored pens. Teacher circulates to guide.
pracAlt: Error Auction Practice: Teams bid on sentences from a worksheet, explaining why each is correct or incorrect. Teacher clarifies misunderstandings.
Grammar Maze: Students navigate a maze where each path has a sentence; they must choose the correct one to advance.
lp.ls: Listen and Spot: Teacher plays a recording of a Moroccan student describing their weekend (with deliberate errors). Students listen and write down the errors they hear. Afterwards, they compare in pairs and correct the sentences.
lp.re: Error Charades: Students act out a sentence with an error (e.g., 'I eat couscous yesterday'), and others guess the correct version. Fast-paced and physical.
lp.prod: Error Clinic Roleplay: In pairs, one student is a 'patient' with a writing problem (e.g., 'I always confuse for and since'), and the other is a 'doctor' who diagnoses and prescribes correction strategies. They then swap roles.
lp.rw: Personal Error List: Students create a list of their top 5 common errors from recent work. They write each incorrect sentence, the correction, and a rule (e.g., 'Use present perfect for experiences: I have visited Paris.').
lp.st: Teacher shares a short story about a Moroccan traveler who fixed their English errors before a trip. Close with: 'Today we learned to spot and fix our own mistakes. Thank you for your hard work!'
g: Teams bid on sentences, deciding if they're correct or incorrect.
Rotate around the room fixing different error types with colored pens.
Teams race to correct sentences on the board with markers.
Swap notebooks and hunt for each other's errors with sticky notes.
Act out a sentence with an error; others guess the correct version.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 50-word email about a Moroccan festival, applying their error corrections.
Support: Use a 'Correction Cheat Sheet' with rules and examples for each error type.
hw: Rewrite 5 corrected sentences from your personal error list, explaining the rule for each.
Write a 100-word review of a Moroccan restaurant, focusing on past simple and comparatives.
Record yourself speaking for 1 minute about your job, then listen and note any errors.
lp.tip: Encourage students to keep an 'Error Journal'—this builds metacognition and autonomy, key for adult learners in Oujda who may need English for work or travel.

weeks.obj: review the year with fluency under time pressure
weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.act:
Speaking circles rotating topics; grammar station carousel; team quiz
Discussion: what one person can actually change; cause and effect language.
weeks.hw:
Pre-assessment checklist completed
Write a paragraph: one green habit I will start.

skills.L: Listening carousel - mixed
skills.S: Speaking circles with time pressure
skills.R: Reading carousel - mixed tasks
skills.W: Writing carousel - emails and articles

lp.wu: Students play 'Memory Match' with flashcards showing key year vocabulary (e.g., 'recycle', 'volunteer', 'Earth Day', 'climate change'). They turn over two cards, say the words, and keep a pair if they match. The student with the most pairs wins.
wuAlt: Students do a 'Word Association Circle' starting with 'Earth' and adding one related word each turn.
Students complete a 'Quick Quiz' on the board with 5 true/false questions about environmental facts.
lp.pres: Teacher presents a cause-and-effect chain using flashcards: 'Littering (cause) → Pollution (effect) → Animals suffer (effect)'. Model sentences: 'If people litter, the environment gets dirty.' and 'Pollution happens because people throw trash.' Check understanding by asking students to create their own simple cause-effect sentences.
presAlt: Teacher uses a short video clip showing pollution and pauses to elicit cause-effect language from students.
Teacher draws a simple flowchart on the board and has students fill in the blanks with 'because' or 'so'.
lp.prac: Students do a 'Grammar Station Carousel' with 4 stations: 1) Match causes to effects, 2) Complete sentences with 'if/so/because', 3) Sort words into 'problem/solution', 4) Write 2 cause-effect sentences. Teacher monitors and provides sentence starters.
pracAlt: Students play 'Cause and Effect Dominoes' matching cards to form logical chains.
Students work in pairs to correct 5 wrong cause-effect sentences on a worksheet.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 2-minute podcast about 'Small Changes for Earth Day' and complete a 'True/Not Mentioned/False' worksheet. They then listen again to check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Students play 'Green Charades' acting out verbs like 'recycle', 'plant', 'save water' for teammates to guess. The team with the most correct guesses in 1 minute wins.
lp.prod: Students form speaking circles of 4 and take 3-minute turns discussing 'One green habit I can start'. They use prompts like 'If I start..., then...' and 'I will... because...'. Teacher rotates to monitor and provide feedback.
lp.rw: Students read a short article '5 Easy Green Habits' and write an 80-word email to a friend suggesting one habit to adopt. They must include one cause-effect sentence (e.g., 'If you use a reusable bag, you will reduce plastic waste').
lp.st: Teacher shares a short story 'The Day the Earth Smiled' about a child's small actions making a difference. Close with the goodbye routine: 'Today we reviewed how our actions affect the environment. Thank you for your hard work and ideas.'
g: Students match pairs of environmental vocabulary flashcards.
Students match cause cards to effect cards to form logical chains.
Students act out environmental verbs for teammates to guess.
Students rotate through 4 grammar practice stations.
Students discuss green habits in timed 3-minute turns.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second email suggesting another green habit with two cause-effect sentences.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'If I start ___, then ___ because ___.'
hw: Complete the pre-assessment checklist by marking 3 can-do statements you can now do.
Write one paragraph: 'One green habit I will start is... because... If I do this, then...'
Watch a 3-minute YouTube video about Earth Day and list 2 new ideas.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan examples like reducing plastic at souks or saving water during droughts to make the theme relatable. Encourage students to share local customs like using reusable bags for market visits.

weeks.obj: complete final PET-style assessment; celebrate the year
weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.act:
Final written paper; individual speaking; course feedback; celebration
Discussion: work and value; presenting an opinion with reasons (IELTS-style).
weeks.hw:
Final report cards; certificates at ceremony
Write a for/against paragraph on unpaid internships.

skills.L: Final listening paper
skills.S: Final speaking assessment
skills.R: Final reading paper
skills.W: Final writing task and certificates

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Work Values' word association. Students stand in a circle, say one job-related value (e.g., 'hard work'), and pass a ball to the next student who adds another (e.g., 'teamwork'). Continue for 2 minutes.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Job Charades'—students act out a profession (e.g., 'doctor') while others guess.
Alternative 2: 'My Dream Job'—quick share: 'I want to be a ___ because ___.'
lp.pres: Presentation: Show 2 PET-style speaking task cards (e.g., 'Should unpaid internships be banned?'). Model a 1-minute opinion with reasons: 'I think yes because...'. Elicit feedback on structure (opinion + 2 reasons).
presAlt: Alternative 1: 'For/Against' T-chart on board—fill with student ideas.
Alternative 2: 'Internship Dilemma' short story—discuss the moral dilemma.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Opinion Relay'—pairs take turns saying a sentence for/against unpaid internships using target phrases (e.g., 'On one hand... / On the other hand...'). Monitor and correct errors.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Builder'—use cut-up phrases to form full opinions.
Alternative 2: 'Thumbs Up/Down'—vote on statements, then justify.
lp.ls: Listening slot: PET-style listening—short debate clip (2 mins) about internships. Students tick 'for' or 'against' reasons on a worksheet. Check answers in pairs.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand for Values'—teacher reads statements (e.g., 'Unpaid internships exploit workers'). Students stand if they agree, sit if they disagree. Discuss briefly.
lp.prod: Production task: Individual PET speaking assessment—students present a 2-minute opinion on 'Should unpaid internships be banned?' with 2 reasons. Teacher scores using a rubric.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Final PET reading (multiple-choice questions on a short text about Labour Day). Then write an 80-word email: 'Apply for an unpaid internship—include your opinion on it.'
lp.st: Story/Song + Goodbye: Play 'The Intern' short video clip (3 mins) showing a success story. Close with: 'Today we assessed your English skills and discussed work values. Thank you for your hard work this year!'
g: Teams guess jobs from clues (e.g., 'saves lives').
First to write 3 for/against reasons wins.
Call out job-related words—students mark them.
Students interview each other for a dream job.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 100-word paragraph on 'The best job for Morocco's future.'
Support: Use sentence starters (e.g., 'I believe... because...') for the speaking task.
hw: Option 1: Review your PET writing—highlight 3 improvements.
Option 2: Interview a family member about their first job.
Option 3: Write 5 sentences about Labour Day in Morocco.
lp.tip: Use the assessment as a confidence booster—highlight progress made. In Morocco, connect Labour Day to local workers' contributions.
checklist: I can give my opinion with 2 reasons in a short talk.
I can understand a short debate about work.
I can write an 80-word email applying for a job.
I can read a short text and answer multiple-choice questions.
I can use phrases like 'On one hand...' to present arguments.
I can talk about my dream job using future tense.
I can identify key values in the workplace (e.g., respect, fairness).

levels.desc: For adults aged 18+ at A2 moving into B1. The year covers present perfect, past continuous, comparatives, conditionals 0/1/2, modals, and reported speech basics through workplace, travel, citizenship, and digital-life themes, with extended speaking, short-article reading, and 80–100 word emails and reviews — PET task types rehearsed throughout S2.

levels.label: Adults · Advanced

weeks.obj: Set learning goals and analyse my own needs; express opinions fluently on familiar topics; agree personal goals
weeks.lang: review diagnostic; opinion language (I think / In my opinion...) + needs-analysis language; ambitious, realistic goals
weeks.act: PET/IELTS-style task carousel on your learning goals
weeks.hw: record a 2-minute monologue about your learning goals

skills.L: Listen to a needs-analysis interview and note the priorities
skills.S: Set learning goals and analyse my own needs
skills.R: Read a needs-analysis guide and self-rate can-dos (IELTS folder)
skills.W: Write my goals and needs summary

lp.wu: Two Stars and a Wish: Students stand in pairs, say their name and two positive things about learning English (e.g., 'I think speaking is fun, and I love watching movies in English'), then one wish for improvement (e.g., 'I wish I could write faster').
wuAlt: Find Someone Who...: Students mingle with a grid asking 'Find someone who wants to improve their writing skills' and get signatures.
Word Association Chain: Teacher says 'English', students say one related word in turn around the class.
lp.pres: Show a PET-style self-assessment chart with can-do statements (e.g., 'I can write a detailed email about my future plans'). Ask students to self-rate their current level and discuss gaps. Model opinion phrases: 'In my opinion, I need to work on...' and goal-setting: 'My ambitious goal is to... but my realistic goal is...'.
presAlt: Use a short video of a learner setting goals, pausing to discuss language. Show realia like a notebook with past goals and achievements.
lp.prac: Goal-setting worksheet: Students categorize their needs (speaking, writing, etc.) and write two goals using 'ambitious' and 'realistic'. In pairs, they check each other's grammar and clarity using a checklist.
pracAlt: Carousel activity: Posters around the room with skill areas (Listening, Speaking, etc.), students write goals on sticky notes and discuss in groups.
lp.ls: Listen to a 3-minute interview where a learner discusses their English needs. Students take notes on three priorities (e.g., 'grammar', 'confidence') and compare in pairs.
lp.re: Stand Up Sit Down: Teacher reads a need (e.g., 'I want to improve my vocabulary'), students stand if it applies to them, sit if not. Quick discussion with neighbors.
lp.prod: PET-style task carousel: Three stations—1) Roleplay an interview with a teacher about goals, 2) Write a 120-word email to a study partner outlining goals, 3) Discuss in groups: 'Is it better to set ambitious or realistic goals first?'
lp.rw: Read a short IELTS-style guide on setting SMART goals. Students highlight key phrases (e.g., 'specific, measurable, achievable') and write a 150-word summary of their own needs using the framework.
lp.st: Share one 'aha!' moment from today's discussion. Close with: 'Today we set learning goals—thank you for your hard work and see you next week!'
g: Students write 9 goals on a grid, mark off when peers share similar ones.
Teams race to match needs (e.g., 'grammar') to solutions (e.g., 'do exercises').
Students stand on a line from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree' for statements like 'Goals help learning'.
Sort cards into 'ambitious' vs 'realistic' goals and justify.
Teams write 3 goals using target language in 2 minutes.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 200-word reflection on how cultural context (e.g., Green March) affects English goals.
Support: Use sentence starters: 'I think... because...' and 'My goal is... to...'.
hw: Record a 2-minute monologue about your goals using your phone.
Write a 150-word email to a classmate comparing your goals.
Find one article about learning goals and summarize it in 100 words.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan cultural references (e.g., 'Like preparing for Eid, small steps in English lead to big results') to make goals relatable.

weeks.obj: Describe habits with precise quantifiers; compare habits and lifestyles accurately
weeks.lang: present simple vs present continuous; adverbs of frequency + quantifiers review: plenty of, hardly any; tend to
weeks.act: Roleplay with complications: lifestyles and habits in a professional setting
weeks.hw: do the lifestyles and habits practice task from the library folder

skills.L: Listen for precise quantifiers in habit talk
skills.S: Describe habits with precise quantifiers
skills.R: Read a lifestyle report and check the data
skills.W: Write a quantifier-accurate habits paragraph

lp.wu: Play 'Find Someone Who...' with quantifiers: students mingle asking 'Do you have plenty of energy?' and 'Do you hardly ever skip breakfast?', tallying responses on a worksheet.
wuAlt: Play 'Frequency Auction': students bid on statements like 'I tend to drink coffee every morning' using play money.
Play 'Lifestyle Bingo': students find peers who match habits like 'plenty of free time' and mark their cards.
lp.pres: Show a photo of a busy professional and a relaxed freelancer, contrasting their routines with model sentences like 'He tends to work 12 hours a day' and 'She hardly ever checks emails after 6 PM'. Use flashcards for 'plenty of' and 'hardly any' to visualize quantity.
presAlt: Present a short video clip of two people discussing their daily habits, pausing to highlight target language.
Distribute a lifestyle survey with gaps for quantifiers, demonstrating how to complete it with 'tend to' and adverbs.
lp.prac: Complete a 'Habit Comparison' worksheet with fill-in-the-blank sentences using present simple vs continuous and quantifiers, then peer-check answers. Play 'Sentence Auction' where students correct sentences with incorrect quantifiers.
pracAlt: Play 'Quantifier Swap': students rewrite sentences replacing 'plenty of' with 'hardly any' and vice versa.
Do 'Role-Drill Pairs': one student describes a habit, the other asks follow-up questions using target language.
lp.ls: Listen to a podcast segment about work-life balance, noting down how often two professionals use quantifiers like 'plenty of' and 'hardly any' to describe their habits.
lp.re: Play 'Quick Draw': students race to draw a habit (e.g., 'plenty of exercise') while others guess using target language.
lp.prod: Roleplay a job interview where candidates discuss their work habits using precise quantifiers, and interviewers compare them to company expectations. Include a complication like a sudden deadline change.
lp.rw: Read a short article on 'Digital Detox Habits', highlighting sentences with quantifiers. Then write a 120-word paragraph comparing your own habits to those in the article.
lp.st: Read a short story about a Moroccan professional balancing work and family, using target language. Close with: 'Today we compared lifestyles with precise quantifiers—great work!'
g: Students bid on true/false habit statements using play money.
Pairs trade habits using 'I tend to...' and 'I hardly ever...'.
Students race to write sentences with 'plenty of' and 'hardly any' on the board.
Match professions to habit descriptions using quantifiers.
Act out a habit with a twist (e.g., 'hardly ever sleeping well' before a big event).
diff: Fast finishers: write a 150-word email to a friend comparing their lifestyles using target language.
Support learners: use a sentence frame worksheet to describe habits with quantifiers.
hw: Complete the 'Lifestyles and Habits' practice task from the library folder.
Interview a family member about their habits and write a 100-word summary.
Write a 120-word paragraph comparing your lifestyle to a friend's using quantifiers.
lp.tip: Encourage students to relate habits to local contexts like Ramadan or family gatherings to make language relevant.

weeks.obj: Tell a personal story with narrative tenses; narrate past events with past simple and continuous
weeks.lang: past simple vs past continuous; when/while + narrative tenses: past simple/continuous/perfect
weeks.act: Mini-presentation: 3-minute talk about memories and storytelling + Q&A
weeks.hw: prepare and rehearse a short presentation about memories and storytelling

skills.L: Listen to a personal story and map the tenses
skills.S: Tell a personal story with narrative tenses
skills.R: Read a narrative extract and analyse the structure
skills.W: Write a personal story (2 paragraphs)

lp.wu: Memory Chain: Students sit in a circle. The first student says 'I remember when I was a child, I loved to play football.' The next student repeats this and adds their own memory: 'He remembers when he was a child, he loved to play football. I remember when I was a child, I loved to eat mint tea.' The chain continues around the circle.
wuAlt: Photo Memory: Show a personal photo and ask 'What do you think was happening here?' Students guess using past continuous. Then reveal the story.
Word Association: Write 'memory' on the board. Students say one word associated with it, then explain why using a past tense.
lp.pres: Write a short story on the board: 'While I was walking home yesterday, I saw my old friend. We stopped and talked for an hour.' Underline 'was walking' and 'saw'. Explain that past continuous describes the background action, past simple describes the interrupting action. Ask: 'What was happening first? What happened then?'
presAlt: Picture Story: Show a comic strip with two panels. Panel 1: 'While the man was cooking, the phone rang.' Panel 2: 'He answered it.' Elicit the tenses from the students.
Timeline Draw: Draw a timeline on the board. Mark two points: 'Background' and 'Interrupting Action'. Ask students to create a sentence for each.
lp.prac: Worksheet 'Find the Mistake': Students correct sentences like 'While I was eating, the phone was ringing.' They should change one verb to past simple. In pairs, they compare answers. Then, they write two correct sentences of their own.
pracAlt: Tense Race: Write 'While...' and '...' on the board. In teams, students race to write correct sentences using the board. The first team to write a valid sentence gets a point.
Sentence Building: Give students cards with verbs (walk, see, call) and time expressions (yesterday, last week). They build sentences in pairs, then swap with another pair to check.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 1-minute audio of someone telling a story about getting lost. They have a worksheet with two columns: 'Past Continuous' and 'Past Simple'. They write down the phrases they hear in the correct column.
lp.re: Action Replay: The teacher mimes an action (e.g., walking). A student says 'While you were walking, the phone rang.' The teacher then mimes a new action. The next student continues the story. This continues around the class.
lp.prod: Mini-Presentation: Students prepare a 3-minute talk about a memorable event. They must use at least three past continuous and three past simple sentences. They work in groups of three to present and ask each other questions. The teacher provides feedback on accuracy.
lp.rw: Reading Task: Students read a short story extract about a festival. They underline all examples of past continuous and past simple. Then, in pairs, they discuss why the writer used each tense in the context of the story.
lp.st: Story: The teacher tells a short, personal story about a memorable event, using target tenses. Goodbye routine: 'Today we learned to tell stories about the past using past simple and continuous. Thank you for your stories and participation.'
g: Students match sentence halves (e.g., 'While I was studying...' with '...the lights went out.')
Teams race to write correct sentences on the board using prompts like 'While I was... / I...'. The first to finish wins.
Students pick a photo and tell a story using the target tenses to their partner.
One student starts a story with a past continuous sentence. Each student adds one sentence, alternating tenses.
Students bet play money on whether sentences are grammatically correct.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second paragraph to their story, using wish/should have to express regret.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'While I __________ (verb-ing), __________ (past simple verb).'
hw: Write a 120-word story about a memorable event using past simple and continuous.
Record yourself telling a 2-minute story about your childhood and send it to the teacher.
Find a short article online about a famous person's memory and write a 50-word summary.
lp.tip: For Moroccan learners, connect the theme to local cultural memories like the Green March or family gatherings to increase engagement and personal relevance.

weeks.obj: Compare experiences with both perfect tenses; talk about experiences with present perfect (basics)
weeks.lang: present perfect (have/has + participle); ever/never + present perfect vs past simple; contrast drills
weeks.act:
Debate in two teams with rebuttal time on life experiences
Discussion: Halloween between commerce and culture; compare with local celebrations.
weeks.hw:
summarise a real article about life experiences in 4 sentences
Write a short opinion paragraph: should Oujda celebrate Halloween?

skills.L: Listen to perfect vs past-simple contrasts
skills.S: Compare experiences with both perfect tenses
skills.R: Read an interview and find the tense contrasts
skills.W: Write experience comparisons using both tenses

lp.wu: Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three life experiences (e.g., 'I have visited Paris,' 'I have never eaten sushi,' 'I have met a celebrity'). In pairs, they guess which is the lie. Teacher models first: 'I have climbed Mount Toubkal, I have never been to America, I have won a poetry prize.'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who: Students mingle asking 'Have you ever...?' questions (e.g., 'Have you ever tried Moroccan mint tea?', 'Have you ever traveled abroad?'). They write names next to true statements.
Experience Bingo: Teacher calls out experiences (e.g., 'Have you ever broken a bone?', 'Have you ever missed a flight'). Students mark their bingo cards if true.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a photo of a haunted house and asks: 'Have you ever been to a haunted house?' Elicits model sentences: 'Yes, I have. I went last year.' vs 'No, I haven't. I've never been to one.' Highlights 'have/has + past participle' and 'ever/never'. Checks understanding with thumbs up/down for true/false sentences (e.g., 'She has never tried pumpkin pie').
presAlt: Timeline Story: Teacher draws a timeline on the board (childhood, teens, now). Adds events with both tenses: 'When I was 10, I broke my arm (past simple). I have never broken a bone since (present perfect).' Students ask questions.

Picture Comparison: Two photos (one of a child, one of an adult). Teacher says: 'As a child, I loved Halloween. Now, I have never celebrated it.' Students compare their own past and present experiences.
lp.prac: Tense Toss: Students stand in a circle. Teacher tosses a soft ball and says a sentence (e.g., 'I have eaten couscous'). Student catches it and changes it to past simple (e.g., 'I ate couscous last week') or asks a question (e.g., 'Have you ever eaten tagine?').
pracAlt: Sentence Race: Two teams race to write correct sentences on the board. Teacher says a prompt (e.g., 'never/see/snow'). Teams write: 'I have never seen snow.'
Interview Relay: In pairs, Student A asks 'Have you ever...?' questions. Student B answers with present perfect, then asks a follow-up past simple question (e.g., 'When did you go?'). Swap roles.
lp.ls: Listen to a short interview about Halloween traditions. Students tick experiences mentioned (e.g., 'carved a pumpkin', 'dressed up', 'trick-or-treated'). Then, in pairs, they discuss: 'Which have you done? Which haven't you?'
lp.re: Experience Charades: One student mimes an experience (e.g., riding a camel). Others guess: 'Have you ever ridden a camel?' The mimer responds: 'Yes, I have. I did it last summer.'
lp.prod: Halloween Debate: Two teams (Team Commerce: 'Halloween is just a business opportunity.' Team Culture: 'Halloween enriches traditions'). Each team has 2 minutes to present, then 1 minute for rebuttals. Teacher monitors for present perfect/past simple use (e.g., 'We have seen shops sell more decorations' vs 'Last year, we didn't celebrate it').
lp.rw: Read a short article about Halloween in Morocco. Underline all present perfect sentences. Then, write 4 sentences comparing Halloween to a Moroccan celebration (e.g., 'Many Moroccans have never celebrated Halloween, but they have always enjoyed Eid al-Fitr').
lp.st: Read a short ghost story from Morocco (e.g., 'The Jinn of the Old Medina'). Discuss: 'Have you ever heard a story like this?' End with: 'Today, we compared experiences using present perfect and past simple. Thank you, class.'
g: Students toss a ball and change present perfect to past simple or ask a question.
Students mingle asking 'Have you ever...?' questions and write names.
Students mime experiences; others guess using present perfect questions.
Teams race to write correct present perfect/past simple sentences.
Pairs ask/answer questions using both tenses.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a paragraph comparing Halloween to Green March or Independence Day.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'I have never ___. Last year, I ___ instead.'
hw: Summarise a real article about life experiences in 4 sentences (e.g., from a Moroccan news website).
Write a short opinion paragraph: 'Should Oujda celebrate Halloween? Use present perfect and past simple.'
Interview a family member about their past experiences and write 3 questions/answers using both tenses.
lp.tip: Emphasize the cultural context: Compare Halloween to local festivals like Green March to make grammar relevant. Use students' real experiences to boost engagement.

weeks.obj: Discuss durations and milestones; describe how long with for and since
weeks.lang: present perfect + for/since; time expressions + for/since + How long; time expressions
weeks.act:
Write-swap: peer-review an email or paragraph about experiences with for / since
Discussion with for/since: "Morocco HAS HAD the southern provinces SINCE 1975..."
weeks.hw:
write a PET-style email (about 100 words) about experiences with for / since
Write 6 for/since sentences about national milestones.

skills.L: Listen to milestone descriptions with for / since
skills.S: Discuss durations and milestones
skills.R: Read a biography timeline and complete it
skills.W: Write my milestones with for / since

lp.wu: Milestone Timeline: Students draw a personal timeline on the board with 3 key events (e.g., 'Started learning English', 'First trip abroad'). Classmates ask 'How long have you...?' using for/since.
wuAlt: Experience Bingo: Students find classmates who have done things for/since a certain time (e.g., 'Lived in Oujda for 5+ years') and mark their cards.
Two Truths and a Lie: Students state three experiences with for/since; others guess the lie.
lp.pres: Green March Timeline: Project a timeline of Moroccan milestones (1975 Green March, 1999 Constitution, etc.). Model sentences: 'Morocco HAS HAD the Sahara SINCE 1975.' 'The king HAS RULED for 25 years.' Check comprehension with 'True/False' questions.
presAlt: Photo Timeline: Show historical photos of Morocco with dates; students describe durations using for/since.
National Anthem Context: Play the anthem and discuss how long Morocco HAS BEEN independent (since 1956).
lp.prac: Find Someone Who...: Students mingle with a grid of prompts (e.g., 'Has studied English for 2+ years', 'Has lived in Oujda since childhood'). They ask 'How long have you...?' and write names.
pracAlt: Sentence Race: Teams race to write correct for/since sentences about Moroccan history (e.g., 'Morocco HAS HAD relations with the US since 1957').
Grammar Auction: Teams bid on correct/incorrect sentences; errors involve for/since usage.
lp.ls: Milestone Interviews: Students listen to a short audio of a Moroccan elder describing their life (e.g., 'I HAVE LIVED in this city SINCE 1960'). They complete a timeline with dates and durations.
lp.re: Duration Dash: Teacher calls out a time (e.g., 'since 2010'); students dash to the side of the room saying 'since 2010' or 'for 10 years'.
lp.prod: Email Exchange: Students write a 100-word email to a partner describing their experiences with for/since (e.g., 'I HAVE WORKED here SINCE 2018'). They swap, peer-review for accuracy, and reply.
lp.rw: Biography Timeline: Students read a short biography of a Moroccan figure (e.g., Malika Oufkir) and fill in missing dates using for/since clues in the text.
lp.st: Closing Reflection: Teacher says, 'Today we discussed durations and milestones using for/since. Thank you for sharing your experiences. See you next week!'
g: Students match event cards with duration cards (e.g., 'Green March' + 'since 1975').
Teams race to write correct sentences on the board about national milestones.
Students create a chain story: 'I HAVE LIVED in Morocco SINCE... and I HAVE STUDIED English FOR...'.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 additional for/since sentences about global milestones.
Support: Use sentence frames (e.g., 'I HAVE [verb] Morocco SINCE...') to guide writing.
hw: Write a PET-style email (100 words) to a friend describing your experiences with for/since.
Write 6 for/since sentences about Moroccan national milestones.
Interview a family member about their experiences using for/since; write 3 sentences.
lp.tip: Use local context (Green March, Independence Day) to make grammar relevant. Adults engage more when connecting language to their national identity.

weeks.obj: Compare destinations and argue a choice; describe trips using present perfect and superlatives
weeks.lang: superlatives; the best place I have (ever)... + articles in descriptions; as ... as / not nearly as
weeks.act: Listening + response: authentic travel experiences audio, then discussion
weeks.hw: write a 120-150 word text about travel experiences using this week's structures

skills.L: Listen to destination pitches
skills.S: Compare destinations and argue a choice
skills.R: Read travel articles and weigh the claims
skills.W: Write an argued destination choice

lp.wu: Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their travel experiences. Each student writes three sentences: two true, one false about places they have visited. They share in pairs, and partners guess the lie. Teacher monitors for superlatives and present perfect.
wuAlt: Students complete the sentence 'The most amazing place I have ever been is...' and explain why. Teacher writes answers on the board.
Students interview a partner about their best and worst travel experiences using 'Have you ever...?' questions.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a photo of Marrakech and a photo of Chefchaouen. Models: 'Marrakech has the most vibrant souks. Chefchaouen is not nearly as colorful as Marrakech.' Elicits superlative forms. Checks understanding with 'Which city is more crowded? Which is quieter?'
presAlt: Teacher uses a world map with pins. Students compare pinned destinations using 'as...as' and superlatives. Teacher corrects errors.
Teacher reads a short travel blog entry about Morocco and highlights superlatives. Students identify the structures.
lp.prac: Students play 'Destination Duel' in pairs. Each pair gets two destination cards (e.g., Rabat vs. Casablanca). They must write five comparative sentences using superlatives and 'as...as'. Teacher provides a sentence frame: 'The best thing about... is... because...'.
pracAlt: Students complete a gap-fill worksheet with missing superlatives and articles. They then peer-check answers.
Teacher plays a 'Find Someone Who...' game where students ask 'Have you ever visited the most famous place in Morocco?' and tally responses.
lp.ls: Students listen to a 2-minute audio of a traveler comparing two Moroccan cities (Fes vs. Essaouira). They fill in a table with 'best food', 'best weather', and 'best activities'. Teacher plays audio twice. Discusses answers to check comprehension of comparative language.
lp.re: After break, students play 'Stand Up, Sit Down'. Teacher says a comparative sentence (e.g., 'If you think the Atlas Mountains are more beautiful than the Sahara, stand up'). Students stand or sit. Teacher checks for correct responses.
lp.prod: Students choose two Moroccan destinations (e.g., Agadir vs. Tangier) and prepare a 3-minute pitch arguing which is the best. They must use at least three superlatives and two 'as...as' phrases. Pairs present, and class votes on the most convincing argument.
lp.rw: Students read a short travel article about 'Top 5 Places to Visit in Morocco'. They highlight all superlatives and then write a 120-word email recommending one place to a friend, using the target language. Teacher circulates to check for accuracy.
lp.st: Teacher shares a short personal anecdote about their favorite travel memory in Morocco, using present perfect and superlatives. Students share one travel story in groups. Close with: 'Today we compared destinations using superlatives. Thank you for sharing your experiences.'
g: Students race to write superlatives for categories (e.g., 'the most interesting city') on the board.
Students draw cards with adjectives and use them to compare two destinations in a minute.
Students look at two similar photos of Moroccan cities and write five comparative sentences.
Students create bingo cards with superlative phrases (e.g., 'the best food') and mark them off when classmates say them.
Students start a story with 'The most amazing thing I have ever seen in Morocco is...' and each adds a sentence.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 50-word review of a Moroccan restaurant using superlatives.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'The best thing about... is... because...' for their pitch.
hw: Write a 120-150 word blog post about your best trip to Morocco using superlatives and present perfect.
Record a 2-minute audio comparing two cities you have visited, using the target language.
Find a travel article about Morocco and rewrite it using five new superlatives.
lp.tip: Encourage students to use local examples (e.g., 'The Hassan II Mosque is the most impressive building I have ever seen') to make language practice culturally relevant and meaningful.

weeks.obj: Weigh options with balanced comparisons; debate comparisons with accuracy (comparatives review + nuance)
weeks.lang: comparatives (much/far + -er); as...as + comparisons + whereas, however, on the other hand
weeks.act:
Case study: solve a realistic problem about making comparisons in groups
Discussion: independence and identity; past perfect practice ("by 1956, Morocco had...").
weeks.hw:
record a 2-minute monologue about making comparisons
Write 5 sentences in the past perfect about Moroccan history.

skills.L: Listen to balanced arguments (whereas, however)
skills.S: Weigh options with balanced comparisons
skills.R: Read an op-ed and find the linkers
skills.W: Write a balanced comparison paragraph

lp.wu: Pair students. Each pair receives two cards: one with 'Morocco' and one with 'USA'. They must list 3 similarities and 3 differences between the two countries using comparatives (e.g., 'Morocco is older than the USA' or 'The USA is as large as Morocco').
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Find someone who...' with prompts like 'Find someone who thinks Morocco is more beautiful than the USA.'
Alternative 2: Show two images (a Moroccan medina vs. a US city skyline) and have students write one comparative sentence each.
lp.pres: Display a short op-ed comparing Moroccan and American Independence Days. Highlight model sentences: 'Morocco gained independence much earlier than the USA,' 'The celebrations are as vibrant as each other,' 'In Morocco, we focus on family, whereas in the USA, they focus on fireworks.' Elicit meaning of 'whereas' and 'as...as'.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a Venn diagram on the board with two circles (Morocco/USA) and fill in comparatives with student input.
Alternative 2: Present a short video clip of both celebrations and pause to elicit comparative sentences.
lp.prac: Group task: 'Independence Day Dilemma'. Groups receive a scenario: 'Your town has a small budget for Independence Day. Should you spend it on a traditional music show (like Morocco) or a big fireworks display (like the USA)?' Groups must list 3 reasons for each option using comparatives and 'whereas'.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Auction' – write 10 comparative sentences (some correct, some incorrect). Students bid on sentences they think are correct.
Alternative 2: 'Compare and Contrast' pairs – give each pair two objects (e.g., mint tea vs. coffee) and have them write 5 comparative sentences.
lp.ls: Play a 2-minute audio clip of a radio debate comparing Moroccan and American independence struggles. Students listen and fill in a table with 'Similarities' and 'Differences', using linkers like 'however' and 'on the other hand'.
lp.re: Stand up, sit down game. Teacher says a sentence (e.g., 'Morocco is older'). Students stand if true, sit if false. Include trick sentences (e.g., 'The USA is as small as Morocco') to test nuance.
lp.prod: Debate: 'Was Moroccan independence more significant than American independence?' Students split into two groups. Each group prepares a 3-minute argument using comparatives and linkers. After, they vote on the most convincing argument.
lp.rw: Read a short op-ed about the Green March. Underline all comparative structures and linkers. Then write a 120-word paragraph comparing the Green March to another historical event (e.g., Independence Day) using at least 3 comparatives and 2 linkers.
lp.st: Play a short clip of a Moroccan Independence Day song. Close with: 'Today we learned to make balanced comparisons about independence. Thank you, class.'
g: Write 9 comparatives on a grid. Teacher calls out sentences; students mark the correct comparative.
Show two similar images (e.g., two Independence Day parades). Students spot 5 differences using comparatives.
Groups race to write sentences with 'whereas', 'however', or 'on the other hand' about Morocco vs. USA.
Students stand in a line. Teacher asks: 'Is Morocco more traditional than the USA?' Students move to show agreement/disagreement and explain.
Students draw a scene (e.g., a busy medina vs. a quiet US suburb) and others guess the comparative.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 150-word email comparing a Moroccan festival to an American one.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'Morocco is _______ than the USA because _______ whereas the USA is _______ because _______.'
hw: Record a 2-minute monologue comparing life in Morocco to life in the USA using comparatives.
Write 5 sentences in the past perfect about Moroccan history (e.g., 'By 1956, Morocco had been under French rule for 44 years').
Find an article comparing two countries and highlight all comparative structures.
lp.tip: Encourage students to use personal examples (e.g., 'My family celebrates Independence Day more quietly than American families') to make comparisons more meaningful and culturally relevant.
